Two of our worse nights had exactly that shape, and in both the second engineer, once they eventually arrived, spotted the wrong assumption within minutes. The requirement is deliberately cheap to satisfy — the secondary on-call always counts, and so does anyone who volunteers — because a requirement that is expensive to satisfy gets skipped in precisely the circumstances it was written for. During working hours the ordinary review process already provides this and no extra ceremony is added. The record itself is a line in the release entry naming both people, which exists less for accountability than so that the following morning's handover knows who to ask about what happened.

The ability to use the expedited path is granted to whoever is currently on the rota and to the platform team, and it is derived from the paging schedule rather than maintained as a list somebody has to remember to update. When the schedule rotates on a Wednesday, the permissions rotate with it. Previously this was a static team in the source control provider that had accumulated eleven people, several of whom had changed roles and one who had left, and the natural consequence was that the path got used for changes that were merely inconvenient to queue rather than genuinely urgent. Tying it to the rota also has a useful social property: the person with the permission is the person who will be woken up if it goes wrong, which is a more reliable brake than any policy document. Requests from people not currently holding the permission go through whoever is, which takes about a minute and adds a second opinion for free.

The number a service reports and the name a customer sees on the website describe different things, and they were deliberately unhooked from each other. A build identifier like `atlas-api 4.11.3+b2841` names one artifact: it is generated by CI, it increments whenever anything ships, and there are several hundred of them a quarter across the estate. A product name like `Atlas Autumn` names a bundle of capabilities announced on a calendar, spanning six services that each moved through dozens of their own builds during the period it covers. There is no arithmetic that maps one onto the other, and the years we spent pretending there was produced a version number that lied. The forcing event was a support engineer telling a customer to upgrade to version six because the release notes said Atlas 6, the customer pinning `6.0.0` of a component whose own numbering was at 2.14, and a day lost to a deployment that could never have worked. Since then the machine-readable surfaces carry only the build identity — the `X-Service-Version` response header, the image tag, the `/healthz` payload — and the product name appears only in prose written for people. The mapping from a product name to the set of build identifiers it covers lives in `docs/release-names.yaml`, is generated at announcement time, and is the one place where the two namespaces are allowed to touch.

The build component of an artifact identifier is the CI run identifier, not a number a service increments for itself. We tried a self-incrementing counter stored in the pipeline's state and abandoned it, because a counter has to live somewhere and everywhere it lived turned out to be mutable: restoring a runner from a snapshot rewound it, a parallel branch build stepped on it, and a migration between CI providers reset it to one, which produced two different artifacts claiming to be build fourteen. A run identifier is issued by the system that already has to be authoritative, is monotonic by construction, and links straight back to the logs, the test results and the commit that produced it. The property that matters is that any identifier in the wild can be pasted into the pipeline UI and turned into a complete account of how that binary came to exist. Nobody is expected to read these numbers as a measure of progress, which is precisely why the gaps between them do not bother anyone.

The public interface is versioned in the URL path as `/v1/` and that segment moves only when we break a contract, which has happened once. It is not tied to anything a service reports about itself and it does not move when features are added, because adding an optional field or a new endpoint does not break any client and forcing everyone to update a path for it would be gratuitous. The alternative we considered and rejected was date-based versioning negotiated by header, of the kind some payment providers use. It is more expressive and it is genuinely better for a product with a long tail of integrations that cannot be persuaded to move, but it means every handler carries branching for every version that has ever existed, and with our client population the cost was obviously not worth it. The rule we hold instead is that anything additive ships inside the current version and anything subtractive requires a new path plus an overlap period during which both are served.

When an endpoint or a field is on its way out, the response carries a `Sunset` header with an absolute date and a link to the migration note, and the documentation says the same date in the same words. We do not say a thing will be removed in the next major release, because a customer cannot plan against that: they do not know when the next major release is, we frequently do not either, and the phrase has been used to mean anything from three weeks to a year. A date is unambiguous, it goes in a calendar, and it survives being forwarded to somebody's manager. The corollary is that the date has to be honoured, which means it has to be set with enough room to be honoured; the standing minimum is six months for anything a paying integration touches. Removal is preceded by a check of which accounts still call the deprecated surface, and if a meaningful one still does, somebody has a conversation with them rather than letting the date arrive unremarked.

Shared internal packages are versioned by the date they were released, in the form `2026.04.2`, rather than by semantic version. Semantic versioning promises something about compatibility, and inside a monorepo-adjacent set of libraries with one team of consumers, that promise was never true in a useful way: almost every change was technically breaking for somebody, so honest semver meant a new major every fortnight, and dishonest semver meant a minor bump that broke a build. Calendar versions make no compatibility claim at all, which is accurate. What replaced the compatibility signal is a changelog with a required migration section and consumers who upgrade on a schedule rather than opportunistically. The one place this is not used is anything published outside the company, where consumers reasonably expect the usual contract and get it. The distinction is enforced by the publish tooling, which refuses to push a calendar-versioned package to the public index.

The integer submitted alongside the mobile app's user-visible version has to strictly increase across every submission, forever, including builds that were rejected, withdrawn or never released, because the store rejects a submission that reuses one and there is no way to recover the number afterwards. It is therefore derived from the pipeline's run identifier rather than from the version string, and the two are allowed to move independently: several builds carrying the same user-visible version have been submitted and only one of them shipped. This tripped us up during a release where a rejected binary was fixed and resubmitted with the same number, which cost the better part of a day in review turnaround. The user-visible string is set by hand in the release ticket and rarely changes, since it exists to be spoken aloud in a support conversation rather than to identify a binary. Because the two identifiers move independently, the crash reporter is configured to report both, and support asks for the build number rather than the version when reproducing anything, since only one of the two identifies a binary.

Documentation is published in quarterly snapshots, with the current quarter at the root and previous ones archived under a dated path. It is not versioned per service release, which was the original design and lasted about two months. The problem was that a page describing a workflow touches four services, each shipping on its own cadence, so a per-release documentation version had no coherent meaning: which service's release was the page a version of? Readers landed on archived pages through search and could not tell whether what they were reading was current. Quarterly snapshots at least describe a period a human can situate themselves in, and the banner on an archived page says plainly that it is historical and links to the live equivalent. Changes that are urgent — a corrected code sample, a security note — are applied to the live snapshot immediately rather than waiting for the next one, since a snapshot is a publishing rhythm and not a freeze.

Product release names come off a list of lighthouses, taken in order, maintained by product marketing in a shared document with about forty entries left on it. The list exists so that naming is not a fresh argument every quarter and so that nobody has to check whether the clever name somebody proposed is already a competitor's trademark, which happened twice before the list existed and cost a fortnight of legal review each time. The order is fixed in advance rather than chosen per release, which removes the temptation to pick a grander-sounding name for a release somebody feels strongly about. Names are checked against the trademark register in batches when they are added to the list rather than when they are used, so the check never sits on the critical path of an announcement. Nothing about the name is allowed to imply sequence, and marketing has a standing note about that, because a name that sounds like a successor invites exactly the assumption we are trying to avoid.

Incidents on the public status page name products the way a customer would recognise them, not the way the estate is decomposed internally. A customer who bought a scheduling product does not know that it is served by four services and a queue, and telling them that a component they have never heard of is degraded generates support volume rather than reducing it. The mapping from internal services to public component names is maintained alongside the service catalogue so that the incident tooling can suggest the right public component when an incident is opened, and the person opening it can override the suggestion. What the internal timeline says is a separate matter and stays in internal language, because engineers need the precision. Getting this wrong the other way is also possible: an early status page listed every internal service by name, and the effect was that customers filed tickets asking whether something they did not use being degraded affected them.

Each service gets an active-series allowance, written in `metrics/cardinality_budget.yaml` and defaulting to fifty thousand, and the ingest layer stops accepting new series for a service once it is over, incrementing `bm_dropped_series_total` with that service's name so the drop is visible rather than silent. The cap is per service rather than one pool for everybody because the metrics backend is shared infrastructure and cardinality is the resource with the worst shared-fate behaviour in it. The afternoon that settled the design, one team added an account identifier as a label on a request-duration histogram in kestrel. Within twenty minutes the series count for that one metric passed two million, three ingesters were killed on memory, and query latency for every dashboard in the company went from under a second to over thirty — including the dashboards the on-call was using to work out what was happening. A per-service allowance turns a company-wide outage into one team's metric being truncated, which they see immediately on their own dashboard and can act on. Raising an allowance is a pull request against the budget file reviewed by the platform team, and it is usually granted; the review exists so that somebody looks at whether the growth is a legitimate new dimension or an unbounded label that will keep growing forever.

Every metric name ends in the unit it is measured in — `_seconds`, `_bytes`, `_total` for a monotonic counter — and the linter in the pre-commit hook rejects a new name that does not. This is not aesthetics. A panel showing a number called `request_latency` is uninterpretable without going to read the emitting code, and we have had two separate incidents where somebody read milliseconds as seconds on a dashboard during an outage and drew the wrong conclusion about whether a change had helped. Seconds specifically, rather than milliseconds, because the collection stack's own conventions assume it and mixing the two inside one histogram family produces buckets that cannot be aggregated. Renaming an existing metric is expensive because dashboards and alerts reference it, so a rename ships as a new name emitted alongside the old one for a full retention period, and the old one is removed only once nothing queries it. The linter has an allowlist for the handful of historical names that predate the rule and are too expensive to move.

There is one bucket layout for latency histograms, defined in the shared instrumentation package, and services do not choose their own. It runs from five milliseconds to ten seconds on a roughly exponential ladder of twelve boundaries. Services with genuinely different distributions felt cheated by this and one team ran custom buckets for a while, which is how we learned why it matters: you cannot aggregate two histograms with different boundaries into a meaningful percentile, so the moment one service diverged, every cross-service view that summed them was quietly wrong rather than obviously broken. The chosen ladder is a compromise that is slightly too coarse at the fast end for the cache layer and slightly too fine at the slow end for the report generator, and both teams have said so, and both have been told no. Changing the shared layout is possible but it invalidates historical comparisons across the boundary, so it has happened once and required a note on every affected dashboard.

The collector rewrites label values to lower case and replaces separators with underscores before anything is stored, which sounds cosmetic and is actually a correctness measure. Two services emitting an environment label as `Production` and `production` produce two series that no query joins, and the failure is invisible: the graph looks fine, it is just missing half the traffic. We found this in the worst way, during a capacity review where a region appeared to be running at half the load it actually was. Normalising centrally rather than asking each service to be careful was the obvious call once we counted how many places emit labels. There is one exception carved out: anything under the `raw_` prefix is passed through untouched, because a handful of values genuinely are case-sensitive identifiers from external systems, and mangling them makes them useless for correlation. The rewrite happens before any sampling or aggregation so nothing downstream ever sees the pre-normalised form.

Any query that a dashboard runs on load and that touches more than a few days of data is turned into a recording rule that evaluates on a schedule and writes its result back as a new series. The dashboard then reads the precomputed series and renders in well under a second instead of making the query engine re-derive the same aggregation every time somebody opens the page. The motivating observation was that the overview dashboard was being opened a few hundred times a day, each load ran the same seven expensive range queries, and those queries alone accounted for a large share of the query tier's CPU. Recording rules live next to the alert definitions in version control and are reviewed the same way, because a badly written one runs forever on a timer and nobody notices. The naming convention marks them clearly so that a person reading a dashboard can tell they are looking at a derived series with a defined evaluation interval rather than at raw data.

Questions of the form which customers are affected, or how much did this account use this month, are answered from the warehouse against event data, not from the metrics stack. The two systems are built for opposite shapes: metrics are optimised for a small number of dimensions queried over long ranges at interactive speed, and the warehouse is built for wide dimensionality at the cost of taking seconds to minutes to answer. Trying to make one do the other's job produces either an unusable metrics system or a warehouse query embedded in a dashboard that times out. The practical consequence for an engineer is that during an incident you can see that error rate is up and which endpoint and which region, and to find out which accounts are behind it you run a query against the events table, which takes about a minute. That minute has been argued about, and the answer is that it is the cost of every other query being fast.

Targets are scraped every thirty seconds unless a service asks for something else and justifies it. The number is a compromise: fifteen doubles the storage and the ingest load for a resolution improvement that almost no alert or dashboard actually consumes, and sixty makes short incidents hard to see at all, since a two-minute event becomes two data points and any percentile over it is noise. Two exceptions exist and both are documented in the scrape config with a comment explaining why. The payment path is scraped at ten seconds because its alerting needs to distinguish a thirty-second blip from a sustained failure. The batch estate is scraped at two minutes because its jobs run for hours and nothing about them changes meaningfully inside a minute. Requests to lower the interval are usually a sign that somebody wants event data rather than metrics, and the right answer to those is a different tool rather than a faster scrape.

Anything that counts occurrences is emitted as a monotonically increasing counter and never as a gauge that the application resets, because a gauge loses information the moment a scrape is missed and there is no way to tell afterwards that it happened. A counter that goes backwards is detectably a restart, and the query layer handles that case correctly; a gauge that goes backwards is indistinguishable from the value legitimately decreasing. The lesson arrived through a job-completion metric implemented as a gauge that the worker set at the end of each batch, which under-reported by a variable amount whenever a scrape landed in the wrong place, and the under-reporting was mistaken for a throughput regression for the better part of a week. Gauges remain correct for things that genuinely are a level rather than a count: queue depth, connection pool occupancy, temperature-like readings. The distinction is in the shared instrumentation package's documentation and it is the single most common review comment on new instrumentation.

There is one tenant for production and one for everything else, and there is deliberately no split along team lines. Per-team tenants were proposed as a way of isolating noisy neighbours and rejected, because the queries that matter most cross team boundaries: a request travelling through the gateway, an application service and the ledger produces three teams' metrics, and an on-call reconstructing that path should not have to run three queries against three tenants and align them by hand. The environment split, by contrast, earns its keep, because the failure it prevents is somebody's load test in staging showing up on a production dashboard and being read as real traffic, which happened repeatedly when both lived together. Access control is applied with labels within the production tenant rather than by separating the data, and retention differs between the two: the non-production tenant keeps a fraction of what production does, since nobody has ever needed a month of staging metrics.

The rates were derived from two constraints rather than picked by feel. The first is the contract: the tracing vendor bills against a hundred and fifty million spans a month, and at our span-per-request fanout that works out to a ceiling of roughly one and a half percent of production requests if we want to sit at eighty percent of the allowance and keep headroom for a traffic spike. The second is statistical: an engineer looking at an endpoint wants enough exemplars to see a pattern, and we settled on wanting at least thirty traces an hour for any endpoint that matters. Working both together gave the baseline of one percent head-based sampling, with per-route overrides for anything below about one request per second, which would otherwise be effectively uninstrumented. On top of that sit tail rules evaluated in the collector: anything that ended in a 5xx is kept at a hundred percent, anything slower than two seconds is kept at a hundred percent, and health and readiness probes are dropped outright rather than sampled because they are pure volume with no diagnostic value. The initial configuration was a flat ten percent everywhere, and it exhausted the monthly allowance on the ninth day of the first month, so we spent the last three weeks of that month with no tracing at all — including during an incident. That is the mistake the current numbers are shaped to avoid.

Traces are kept for seven days and then dropped, which is markedly shorter than we keep metrics and slightly shorter than logs. The reasoning is about how they are actually used: a trace answers a question about one specific request, and questions about one specific request are asked within hours of it happening, essentially always during or just after an incident. We looked at the access pattern before setting this and found that queries reaching back past three days were under one percent of all trace queries, and most of those turned out to be somebody who had mistyped a date. Longer retention was priced and would have cost more than the ingest itself. Where a trace genuinely needs to outlive the window — attached to a postmortem, or evidence in a vendor dispute — it is exported to an object store as a permanent artifact and linked from the incident record, which is a manual step somebody has to remember and which the incident template prompts for.

Only attributes on a published allowlist are attached to spans; anything else is stripped in the collector before export. The list covers the obvious identifiers — route template, method, status, tenant, region, upstream — and a small set of per-domain additions that teams have asked for and justified. The stripping exists for two reasons that pull in the same direction. One is cost, since attributes are charged by volume and a well-meaning engineer attaching an entire request context to every span moves the bill noticeably. The other is disclosure: a span attribute is the easiest place in the whole stack to accidentally export customer data to a third party, and we found an email address in a span attribute during a review, put there by somebody debugging a problem months earlier who had entirely forgotten about it. An allowlist fails closed, which is the correct direction for a mechanism whose failure mode is sending data to somebody else's servers.

Whether a request is traced is decided once, at the first service that touches it, and every downstream hop honours the flag it receives in the `traceparent` header rather than making its own decision. Any other arrangement produces broken traces: if each service rolls its own dice, a request is sampled at the gateway and dropped at the third hop, leaving a stump that is worse than nothing because it looks like the request ended there. This is standard practice and we follow it, but it has one consequence people trip over regularly. A team cannot unilaterally raise the visibility of their own service by turning their rate up, because the decision has already been made upstream by the time the request arrives. Requests that originate internally, from a scheduled job or a queue consumer, are roots in their own right and do make their own decision, which is why the batch estate's tracing behaves differently from the request path.

Every structured log line carries the active `trace_id`, injected by the logging middleware rather than passed around by application code, and the log store indexes that field. This is what makes the two systems usable together: from a slow span you jump to the log lines emitted inside it, and from an error in the logs you jump to the full request path. Before it existed, correlating the two meant matching on timestamps and hoping, which works for a quiet service and fails completely under load when a hundred requests share a millisecond. The middleware is in the shared framework so no service opts in, and the one service that logs without it, the legacy import worker, is the one everybody complains about debugging. There is a wrinkle worth knowing: the identifier is present on log lines from requests that were not sampled, so a log line can carry an identifier that resolves to no trace at all, and that is expected rather than a fault.

Applications export spans to a collector running on their own node over the loopback interface, and that collector batches, applies the tail rules and forwards to the vendor. Exporting directly from each process was the original arrangement and it was replaced for three reasons. Every process was holding its own connection to an external endpoint, so a vendor slowdown produced backpressure inside application processes and, in one memorable case, request latency. Retry and batching logic was duplicated into every runtime we use and behaved differently in each. And changing anything about the export path meant redeploying every service. A node-local collector makes the application's export a fire-and-forget call to localhost that cannot block a request, and moves all the policy to a component the platform team can update on its own. The daemonset holds a bounded in-memory queue and drops on overflow, which is the correct tradeoff for telemetry.

Calls to the cache are recorded as attributes on the enclosing span rather than as child spans of their own, while database queries do get their own span. The line is drawn where it is because a span costs money and screen space, and a request that hits the cache forty times produces a trace waterfall that is forty rows of two-hundred-microsecond bars and one row that actually explains the latency. What matters about the cache is the count and the hit ratio, and both fit comfortably in attributes on the parent. Database calls are different: they are individually slow enough to matter, they carry a statement worth reading, and the specific one that was slow is usually the answer. This was not obvious in advance and we did instrument cache calls fully at first; the change came after a review of what people actually clicked on in the trace viewer, which was almost never a cache span. The same reasoning is applied whenever somebody proposes new instrumentation: a span has to be something a person would click on, and if the answer to what you would learn from it is a number that could have been an attribute, it should be one.

Services were instrumented with the tracing vendor's own agent until we replaced it with the vendor-neutral SDK and an exporter configured at the collector. The trigger was a renewal negotiation in which it became clear that changing vendors would have meant touching every service, and that fact was itself worth money to the other side of the table. With the standard SDK the vendor is a configuration value in one place. There were costs to the move: the vendor agent's automatic instrumentation covered a few libraries the community packages did not, and we wrote two of those instrumentations ourselves and lost a third feature entirely. There was also a fortnight where both were running and the duplicate spans made a couple of dashboards nonsense. Nobody has proposed going back. A side benefit that mattered more than expected is that local development can now point the same instrumentation at a console exporter and read spans on a laptop.

Requests generated by the synthetic monitoring suite and by load tests carry an `x-synthetic: 1` header, which the gateway turns into a label on metrics and an attribute on spans, and every default dashboard filters it out. Without that, the synthetic suite's own behaviour distorts exactly the numbers it exists to protect: it hits a fixed set of endpoints at a fixed rate against a test tenant with a tiny data set, so it is faster than real traffic and it drags percentiles down, and it does so most on the quietest services where its share of requests is largest. During one quiet weekend the checkout service's p50 was almost entirely synthetic. The tagging is applied at the edge based on the calling credential rather than trusting the header from outside, since a customer setting that header could otherwise remove themselves from our monitoring, which is not a capability we want to hand out.

The test is whether the thing being measured implies an action by the person who gets woken up. If the honest answer to a firing alert is that somebody would go and look at it, then it is not an alert, it is a dashboard panel, and it belongs on the service's overview page where a human already investigating will find it. An alert has to name something a customer is experiencing and has to come with a runbook whose first step is a verb. This is enforced as far as it can be enforced by machine: definitions in `alerts/*.yaml` require a `runbook_url` and an `owner`, and the pipeline check rejects a rule missing either, plus a new rule is created in the ticket-routed class and cannot be promoted to paging until it has run for two weeks without a false positive. Everything diagnostic — queue depth, garbage-collection pauses, connection pool occupancy, per-node resource curves — is dashboard material, linked from the runbook so it is one click from the page rather than a page of its own. The rule was written after an audit of a quarter's paging traffic found that sixty-one percent of pages were closed with no action taken, and that the median such page was a threshold set years earlier by somebody who had since left. The blunt version, which is what people actually quote at each other in review: if it fires at three in the morning and the on-call does nothing, delete it.

Dashboards live as JSON in the service's repository under `observability/dashboards/` and are applied by the pipeline; the web editor is read-only for everybody except a break-glass account. Editing in the browser was allowed for a long time and the result was predictable, if slow to become undeniable. Panels drifted, nobody could tell who had changed a query or why, an accidental drag would silently rescope a graph to one instance, and when the visualisation service was rebuilt after a storage failure we discovered we had no way to reconstruct about thirty dashboards because they had never existed anywhere but in that database. Defining them in code gives review, history and disaster recovery in one move, and it also lets a new service start with a working overview by copying a neighbour's file. The cost is real: a quick experimental panel now takes a pull request, so people keep a scratch dashboard in a personal folder for exploration and promote panels into the repository once they have earned a place.

The top of every service dashboard is identical across the estate: request rate, error ratio, latency percentiles and saturation of whichever resource that service is bounded by, in that order, in the same positions. Service-specific panels start below the fold. The uniformity is for the benefit of the person who is looking at a service they have never touched, at an hour when they are not at their best, which is the situation the dashboard exists for. Before this convention, each team laid out its own and the good ones were excellent, but an on-call moving between them spent the first minutes of every investigation orienting rather than diagnosing. The layout is generated from a template so adopting it is not manual work, and a team that wants to argue with the ordering has to make the case for changing it everywhere rather than just on their own page. The fourth panel is the only one where teams choose the metric, since what saturates first differs genuinely between a queue consumer and an API.

Which team receives a page is read from the `owner` field in the service catalogue at evaluation time, not written into the alert definition. Ownership changes — reorganisations, a service being handed over, a team being split — and every time routing was duplicated into rule files, some of those files were missed. The worst case took eleven minutes of an outage to resolve because the page went to a team that had given the service up two quarters earlier and had to find somebody who knew it. Now a handover is one field in one file and every alert for that service follows. A consequence people find surprising at first is that an alert with no catalogue entry has nowhere to go, so the pipeline refuses to deploy alerts for a service that is not registered, which has become the practical forcing function that keeps the catalogue populated. Escalation targets are resolved the same way, from the on-call schedule the catalogue points at.

Alerts that open a ticket rather than paging are worked through together in a fixed hour on Thursday morning, by the team that owns them, with the previous week's tickets in front of them. The mechanism only works because of that meeting; a ticket queue nobody has committed to reading is a way of making an alert disappear while feeling responsible about it, and that is exactly what happened for the first several months, when the queue reached four hundred items and was declared bankrupt in one go. The hour has a rule that every ticket leaves the queue in one of three states: fixed, converted into a piece of planned work with a ticket of its own, or the alert is deleted because it turned out not to be worth having. Deferring to next week is not one of the options, because a thing that is deferred twice will be deferred forever. Attendance is the on-call for the week plus whoever owns the noisiest signal.

The alert manager tracks firing frequency per rule and automatically demotes any rule that pages more than three times in a rolling seven days to the ticket route, posting a notice into the owning team's channel when it does. The rule stays demoted until somebody either fixes the underlying condition or changes the rule and clears the demotion deliberately. This is a blunt instrument and it was contentious, since it can in principle mute something genuinely important during a genuinely bad week. The argument that won was that a rule firing that often has already stopped working: people stop reading it, they stop responding to it promptly, and its signal is gone whether or not the notification is still being delivered. Automating the demotion at least makes the loss of signal explicit and puts a notice in front of the people who can do something about it, rather than leaving it to be discovered in a postmortem where somebody says they had assumed it was the usual noise.

Dashboards open on the last six hours rather than the last hour. An hour is too narrow to see whether what you are looking at is unusual; you get a wiggle with no baseline, and during an incident that is precisely the question — is this shape normal for a Tuesday afternoon. Six hours reaches back far enough to include a different traffic regime and to make a deploy annotation from earlier in the day visible on the same axis. Longer than that and the resolution drops enough that a short spike disappears into the downsampling, which defeats the purpose in the other direction. This was measured rather than argued: we sampled how far people zoomed out after landing on a dashboard and the modal answer was somewhere between four and eight hours, so the default was moved to the middle of that. Comparison against the same window a week earlier is available as a toggle rather than being on by default, since it doubles the query cost.

A runbook is a Markdown file next to the rule that references it, in the same repository as the service, and the link in the alert definition is checked at deploy time so a rule pointing at a page that does not exist fails the pipeline. Runbooks used to live in the wiki and they rotted, because the wiki is not where anyone is when they change the behaviour the runbook describes. Keeping them adjacent to the code means the person renaming a command has the document open in the same diff, and reviewers ask about it. The test we apply is that a runbook must be usable by somebody who does not own the service: named commands with their arguments, the exact dashboards to open, the conditions under which to escalate and to whom. Prose explaining the architecture belongs elsewhere and gets linked. Runbooks that have not been touched in a year are surfaced in the ownership report, because an unchanged runbook for a service that has changed is worse than none.

Every production deploy writes an annotation into the visualisation layer, and the annotation is rendered as a vertical line on every dashboard in the relevant environment rather than only on the owning service's page. Cross-service visibility is the whole point: the thing that changed is very often not the service whose graph is misbehaving, and an engineer staring at a latency curve on their own dashboard would otherwise have no reason to suspect a deploy of a dependency. The annotation carries the service, the version and the person who triggered it, and hovering gives a link to the compare view. Adding this shortened the opening phase of several incidents from tens of minutes to seconds, because the first question in almost every investigation is what changed, and the answer is now on the same screen as the symptom. Configuration flips write annotations in the same stream, with a distinct colour, for the same reason.

The host CPU pages were deleted, all fourteen of them, and the decision was made from a lookback rather than from an opinion. Somebody went through eighteen months of paging history and asked two questions of every CPU page. Did it arrive before a customer noticed anything, and did the responder do something as a result. The answers were nothing and nothing: not one customer-visible incident in that period was first detected by a CPU threshold, and every one of the pages was resolved by acknowledging it and waiting. Most of them fired between 01:00 and 04:00 during the nightly reporting run, which is exactly when the machines are supposed to be busy, so the alert was firing on the system working correctly. The second reason is that something already responds to this signal and responds faster than a human can: the autoscaler is driven by the same number, so by the time a fifteen-minute threshold had been breached long enough to page, capacity had usually already been added and the number was on its way down. What remains is one narrow rule that has nothing to do with our own load: sustained steal time above ten percent for fifteen minutes still pages, because that means the hypervisor is oversubscribed and the fix is to move, which no automation of ours will do. Utilisation did not go away; it is on the dashboard and feeds the quarterly capacity review.

Disk pages are keyed on how long until the volume fills, not on how full it currently is, using a linear projection over the previous six hours and firing when the projection crosses four hours remaining. A percentage threshold is wrong in both directions and we had both failures within the same quarter. A slowly growing archive volume sat at ninety-two percent for months and paged every time it wobbled across the line, and a log volume on a small instance went from forty percent to full in under twenty minutes during a retry storm without ever tripping a static threshold in time to matter. Time to exhaustion is the quantity an on-call actually needs, because it answers whether this can wait until morning. The projection is deliberately naive: fitting anything cleverer than a straight line produced worse results on the bursty volumes and nobody could explain the alert afterwards. Volumes that legitimately run near full, like the append-only archive, carry an annotation that raises their threshold and names who set it.

Memory is alerted on differently from other resources: nothing fires on how much is in use, and a page is sent when the kernel kills a process, which is visible as a restart with the out-of-memory reason on the pod. High memory use is normal and frequently desirable, since a runtime with a generational collector or a database with a healthy page cache will occupy whatever it is given and give it back under pressure. A threshold on utilisation therefore fires constantly on well-behaved services and says nothing. A kill, by contrast, is unambiguous: work was lost, a request failed, and there is a specific process to look at. The one addition to this is a slow-growth detector that opens a ticket rather than paging when a process's resident size trends upward across restarts over several days, which is the signature of a genuine leak and is the case the kill-based alert catches only after the damage. That detector was added after a leak in a queue consumer that was restarting every few hours and had been mistaken for ordinary deploy churn.

Capacity is planned in a scheduled review each quarter rather than being driven by anything that fires. The review takes the previous quarter's peak for each service, the growth trend, and the known commitments from product for the coming period, and produces a headroom number per service that the platform team then provisions against. The target is that every service can absorb twice its observed peak without new capacity, which sounds generous and is roughly what a regional failover plus a marketing push at the same time actually demands. Doing this on a calendar rather than reactively is the entire point: the alternative, which we lived with for a year, is discovering capacity problems during the event that causes them, when procurement lead times are measured in weeks and the only available lever is to spend money badly. The review's output is a document with numbers in it that finance sees before the quarter starts, which has also made the infrastructure line item substantially less surprising to them.

Horizontal scaling for request-serving services targets sixty percent average CPU across the deployment, with a floor of three replicas and a per-service ceiling. Sixty was arrived at empirically. Higher, around seventy-five, left too little slack to absorb the interval between load arriving and new pods becoming ready, so latency spiked on the way up. Lower, around forty, meant paying for a lot of idle capacity to buy a response improvement nobody could measure. The scale-down side is deliberately asymmetric, with a ten-minute stabilisation window against two minutes on the way up, because scaling down too eagerly during a lull in a spiky traffic pattern produces oscillation and the cost of being briefly overprovisioned is much lower than the cost of being briefly underprovisioned. Queue consumers do not use this at all and scale on queue depth instead, since their utilisation is a function of how much work exists rather than of how well they are keeping up.

Host-level collection moved from the commercial monitoring agent to the standard node exporter, scraped by the same pipeline as everything else. The agent had been in place since before the metrics platform existed and it was the last thing sending data to a separate system with a separate query language and a separate set of dashboards, which meant any investigation touching both application and host metrics involved two browser tabs and mental arithmetic to align timestamps. The migration was mostly mechanical and took a couple of weeks, with a period of running both to confirm the numbers matched, and they did not at first: the agent and the exporter compute utilisation over different windows and the discrepancy at low load was large enough to be alarming until it was understood. The licence saving was real but secondary. What actually justified the work was having one query language and one place to look, which shortened investigations more than any dashboard change we have made.

The nightly reporting run between 01:00 and 04:00 is excluded from the latency percentiles that appear on the service overview and from anything that feeds the availability calculation. During that window a small number of very long internal requests run alongside ordinary traffic, and because the interactive volume at that hour is low, those few requests dominate the tail: the p99 during the window is essentially a measurement of the reporting job, which nobody is waiting on and which has its own completion-time signal. Leaving them in produced a nightly hump on every graph that people learned to ignore, which is the dangerous kind of normal, and it made week-over-week comparisons noisy. The exclusion is by request class rather than by clock time, so a genuine interactive request at two in the morning is still counted, and that distinction took a while to get right — the first attempt filtered on the time window itself and hid a real regression that happened to start overnight.

The saturation panel on the host dashboard plots run queue length normalised by core count rather than plotting utilisation, because the two answer different questions and only one of them is about whether work is waiting. A machine can sit at ninety percent busy with nothing queued, which is a machine being used efficiently, and it can sit at sixty percent with a growing queue if the work is bursty or if threads are blocking on something other than the processor. The queue length is the number that correlates with the latency our customers experience, and putting it in the saturation position on the standard layout was a deliberate choice to nudge people to read it first. Utilisation is still on the same panel as a fainter second series, mostly so that the relationship between the two is visible and people build the intuition. Neither of them has an alert attached and both exist to be read by somebody already investigating.

When a container's throttled time exceeds a quarter of its running time over an hour, a ticket is filed against the owning team with the workload named and the current limit in it. This is an efficiency signal, not an availability one: a throttled container is usually a limit set too tightly by somebody copying a manifest from a neighbour, and the symptom is a service that is mysteriously slower than its resource graphs suggest it should be. Because the fix is always the same — look at actual use over a week and raise the limit to something defensible — it is well suited to being worked through in planned time rather than at night. We generate about six of these a month and the majority are closed by a one-line manifest change. The threshold was set after a period at ten percent produced a flood of tickets for workloads whose brief throttling at startup was harmless and self-correcting. Workloads that are deliberately capped, such as the batch importers that are allowed to run slowly overnight, are annotated as exempt so they stop generating tickets nobody intends to act on.

Each service declares an objective in `slo/<service>.yaml`, and the budget derived from it is what decides whether that team is allowed to ship anything new. There are three states and the deploy tool reads them from the budget API before every production release. Above twenty-five percent of the budget remaining, nothing changes. Between zero and twenty-five, the service is in caution: releases continue, the state is posted into the team's channel daily, and the team is expected to carry a reliability item at the top of the next sprint. At zero the service is frozen, and `deployctl` rejects any release whose pull requests are not labelled `reliability`, `revert` or `security`. The freeze lifts by itself when the rolling window recovers past twenty percent, which means waiting out the bad period is a legitimate way to exit without anybody having to sign anything. The gate exists because persuasion had already failed. One team missed its availability target for three consecutive months while shipping at its usual rate, and every quarterly review produced agreement that reliability work would be prioritised, and then it was not, because nothing mechanically stopped anything. Overriding a freeze is possible and needs a director's approval recorded against the service with an expiry date on it; it has been used twice, both times for a contractual deadline.

Objectives are written against journeys a customer would recognise — placing an order, retrieving a statement, authenticating — rather than against individual services, even though each journey crosses several of them. A per-service target sounds tidier and it is what we started with, and it produced the situation that killed it: five services each comfortably meeting a three-nines target while the journey that traverses all of them met barely two, because their failures were largely independent and multiplied. Every team could point at a green dashboard while the customer experience was plainly bad. Journey objectives are harder to attribute when they are missed, which is the honest complaint against them, and the answer is that attribution is a question the incident review answers rather than something the objective should try to encode. Each journey has a named owner who is accountable for it end to end even though they own none of the code, and that role turned out to be the hardest part of the arrangement to fill.

A report goes out on the first working day of each month listing every objective, its attainment for the previous thirty days, and the direction of travel, and it goes to everybody rather than only to the owning teams. Publishing widely was contentious and the fear was that it would become a league table used to embarrass people. What happened instead was that it became the main way teams discover they depend on something that is struggling, and the questions it generates are mostly of the form we are seeing timeouts, is that you. The report is generated from the same data the gating uses, so there is no separate spreadsheet that can drift, and it deliberately shows attainment rather than a pass or fail, because the interesting information is in the trend. Services that have no objective at all appear in the report as an empty row, which is more effective than any reminder at getting one written.

The numerator and denominator for availability come from load balancer access logs, not from counters inside the application. An application cannot count the requests it failed to receive, and the failures that matter most to a customer are exactly those: a process that is not listening, a deployment with no healthy pods, a crash loop, a connection refused. Every one of those is invisible to in-process instrumentation and every one of them is a total outage from outside. We learned this the expensive way during a rollout that left a service with no healthy endpoints for eleven minutes while its own dashboards showed a perfect success ratio over the trickle of requests still being served. The tradeoff is that the load balancer's view is coarser: it knows status codes and durations and nothing about which operation was attempted, so per-endpoint objectives still need application-side data, and those two sources disagree slightly and permanently for reasons involving connection reuse that nobody has fully chased down.

Announced maintenance windows are counted against availability exactly like any other unavailability, and the request to exclude them has been made and refused more than once. The argument for excluding is that the customer was told in advance and it was therefore not a failure. The argument that won is that the customer still could not do the thing they wanted, and a number that excludes the downtime we chose to take measures our intentions rather than their experience. There is also an incentive question: once planned downtime is free, the cheapest way to do risky work is to declare a window, and the pressure to build systems that can be maintained without going offline evaporates. Keeping it in the numbers is what funded the work on rolling schema changes and connection draining. What we do allow is that maintenance-driven budget consumption is annotated in the record, so the monthly review can distinguish a bad month caused by a deliberate migration from one caused by surprises.

A latency objective is expressed as the proportion of requests completing under a fixed threshold — ninety-nine percent under four hundred milliseconds — rather than as a target for a percentile. The two look equivalent and are not, once you have to aggregate. Percentiles cannot be averaged or summed across instances, regions or time buckets, so a target expressed as a percentile is either computed from raw data every time it is asked, which is expensive, or computed from precomputed percentiles, which is arithmetically wrong in a way that is hard to notice and always flatters the number. Counting requests on either side of a threshold gives two counters that add up correctly across every dimension, which makes the budget computation trivial and exact. The cost is that the threshold has to be chosen and defended, and moving it later breaks comparison with history. Percentiles remain on dashboards, where their inability to aggregate matters much less.

Time lost to an upstream provider is tracked as a separate dependency objective rather than being excused from ours or silently absorbed into it. The payment provider, the tax rate service and the identity provider each have a target derived from what their contract promises us, and their attainment is reported alongside our own. This keeps two things straight that used to be tangled. Our objective stays honest about the customer's experience, because a customer who cannot pay does not care whose fault it is, and it therefore keeps pressure on us to degrade gracefully rather than to propagate somebody else's outage. And the dependency numbers accumulate into evidence, which is what a renewal conversation needs; the last renewal moved on price specifically because we could show a year of attainment against what had been promised. When a dependency objective is missed badly enough, the remediation is usually a fallback path or a cache rather than a conversation.

Alerting on budget consumption uses a pair of windows evaluated together: a long one of six hours and a short one of thirty minutes, both required to be burning above the same multiple of the sustainable rate before anything fires. The short window alone is jumpy and pages on brief spikes that recover before anyone opens a laptop. The long window alone is sluggish and lets a severe burn continue for a long time before the average crosses the line. Requiring both gives fast detection with far fewer false alarms, and requiring the short window to stay lit is also what resolves the alert quickly once the burn stops, instead of leaving it firing while a long average decays. Two severities are configured from the same pattern with different multiples: a fast burn that would exhaust the whole budget within a day pages, and a slower one that would exhaust it within the window opens a ticket. The numbers came from replaying six months of history against candidate configurations.

An objective without a named owner is deleted, and every objective is revisited once a year whether or not anything about it seems wrong. Ownership is a person rather than a team, because a team-owned target is one nobody feels obliged to defend when it is inconvenient. The annual review asks three questions: is the target still what the business wants, is it being met so comfortably that it is measuring nothing, and is it being missed so consistently that it has become decoration people have learned to ignore. Both of the latter states are failures of the same kind, since a target that never binds and a target that always binds carry equally little information. The first review moved four targets and deleted two entirely, one of which had been inherited from a system that no longer existed and was being computed from a metric that had stopped updating months earlier without anybody noticing, which is its own kind of finding.

A flaky test is never deleted as a way of getting the build green. It goes into quarantine instead: the test gets `@pytest.mark.quarantined("HAL-4417")` with a required ticket id, drops out of the blocking pull request suite, and keeps running every night in the `flake-watch` job whose outcomes are written to `test_flake_history` so anyone can see whether it is drifting better or worse. The reason for the rule is that a test is the only durable record that somebody once decided a behaviour mattered, and removing one silently retires that decision without anybody reviewing it. We learned that expensively. A test asserting that duplicate settlement lines are suppressed was cut during a red-build cleanup because it failed roughly once in thirty runs, and eleven weeks later duplicate settlements reached four customers. Nobody could point at the moment the requirement was dropped, because there had never been such a moment. Deletion now takes the same argument as removing a feature: a pull request naming the behaviour that is no longer required and why, approved by the team that owns the code. Quarantine carries a thirty day deadline, and when it expires the ticket escalates rather than the test disappearing. The flake is treated as a product signal first, because about half of ours turned out to be genuine races in the application rather than in the test.

The runner is allowed exactly one automatic rerun of a failed test, and a test that fails and then passes is recorded as a flake rather than as a pass. `pytest-rerunfailures` writes each retry into the junit xml with a `rerun` outcome, and `tools/collect_flakes.py` parses that file in the post-job step, incrementing a counter keyed on the test node id and the calendar week. The pull request still goes green, which is deliberate — a single transport hiccup should not cost an engineer twenty minutes of waiting — but the event is not forgotten, which is the other half of the deal. Before this, reruns were invisible. The job summary said passed, instability accumulated quietly for months, and the first anyone knew of it was when a test started failing twice in a row. The counter is what makes the weekly conversation possible at all, because it turns a vague feeling that the suite is unreliable into a ranked list with numbers beside each entry. One rerun is the cap, on purpose. Two reruns make a test that fails half the time look green seven attempts out of eight, and at that point the signal has been engineered away rather than fixed.

Every Monday morning a scheduled job rebuilds the instability ranking and posts the top ten into the engineering channel. The rank is failures divided by executions over a trailing fourteen days, restricted to tests with at least forty runs so that a rarely executed test cannot top the chart on the strength of one bad afternoon. Alongside the rate the digest prints engineer-minutes lost, computed as failures multiplied by the median wall clock time of the job the test sits in, and that second column is what actually moves people. A test failing three percent of the time in a job nobody waits on is noise; a test failing one percent of the time in the pull request suite everyone blocks on is worth a morning of somebody's attention. The ranking is a prioritisation aid and nothing more — it does not open tickets, assign owners, or change any status anywhere. It exists because the previous arrangement, which was for whoever got annoyed enough to complain in chat, systematically fixed whatever had failed most recently rather than whatever cost the most.

Tests execute in a randomised order and the seed is printed in the first line of every run. We use `pytest-randomly`, the seed is derived from the run id rather than from the clock, and reproducing an ordering failure is `pytest -p randomly --randomly-seed=48211` with the value copied out of the failing job. This came from a fortnight of confusion over the tariff cache tests, which passed alone, passed in their own file, and failed only when a particular earlier module had populated a module-level dictionary that nothing ever cleared. Alphabetical ordering had hidden that coupling for two years and would have hidden it indefinitely. Random ordering surfaces the class of bug where one test leaves state behind for another, which is a real defect in the tests regardless of whether the product is affected. The trade is that a proportion of failures are now ordering-dependent and cannot be reproduced without the seed, so the seed being visible in the log and accepted on the command line is not a convenience, it is the thing that makes the whole arrangement workable.

The dispatch suite has its own soak job that runs the same eighty-odd tests two hundred times in a loop overnight on a dedicated runner, reporting a per-test pass ratio rather than a pass or fail verdict. It exists because that suite coordinates three worker processes through a real broker, and a race that shows up once in four hundred executions is effectively undetectable in the normal pipeline where each test runs once per pull request. The soak turned up two genuine ordering bugs in the acknowledgement path within its first month, both of which had been dismissed as infrastructure noise for the better part of a year. The output is a ratio table posted as a job artifact, and the convention is that anything short of a perfect ratio gets looked at, because in a loop of two hundred a single failure is not bad luck, it is a race with a measured frequency. The soak is deliberately scoped to dispatch. Running the whole suite this way would take most of a night and produce a table nobody reads, and the value here comes entirely from the concentration of concurrency in one place.

No test may read the wall clock directly. `datetime.now()` and `time.time()` are banned inside `tests/` by a flake8 plugin, and anything time-sensitive takes the `frozen_clock` fixture from `tests/clock.py`, which pins the clock to 2024-03-05T12:00:00Z and hands back a `tick(seconds)` method for advancing it explicitly. The rule was written the morning after the billing period tests failed for everyone for about ninety minutes, which turned out to be the last day of a month landing on a Sunday and a proration test that had quietly assumed otherwise since the day it was written. Before that we had a scattering of tests that only failed near midnight UTC, which the team in the later timezone experienced constantly and the rest of us never saw at all. Freezing also made the interval assertions honest: several tests had been asserting that something happened within a generous window, which passes on an idle laptop and fails on a loaded runner. With an explicit tick they now assert on exact elapsed values, which is what they meant in the first place.

Whoever is holding test duty that stretch reads the instability digest, picks up whatever is at the top, and either fixes it or writes down what they learned before handing it on. It is a named duty on the same rotation as on-call precisely so that it belongs to somebody, because for a long stretch it belonged to whoever was most irritated on any given afternoon, and that person was always the one least able to spare the attention. The duty is time-boxed and explicitly does not carry an obligation to finish. Handing over a note saying the failure is in the acknowledgement path and appears only when the broker reconnects is genuinely useful to the next person, and far better than the previous pattern where three people investigated the same failure from scratch over a season and none of them wrote anything down. The other thing the duty buys us is that somebody is looking at the suite as a whole rather than at the single test currently in their way, which is how patterns get noticed at all.

An unstable test belongs to the team that owns the code under test, not to whoever wrote the test and not to the platform group who maintain the runners. This was contested for a while and the argument that settled it is that instability is nearly always a property of the thing being tested rather than of the harness around it. A service whose startup ordering is nondeterministic, a handler that leaks a background task, a cache with no defined invalidation point — each of these presents as a test that fails sometimes, and each is a defect that will eventually present as an incident instead. Routing them to the platform group meant they were investigated by the people with the least context, who could usually only make the symptom go away. Ownership is resolved from the code ownership file for the module the failing assertion touches, and where that genuinely spans two teams the rule is that the caller investigates first, since the caller is the one who chose to depend on the behaviour. Nobody may reassign an unstable test on the grounds of being busy.

The standing worry about quarantine is that it becomes somewhere tests go to die, and the worry is legitimate — we watched it happen once already on the web repository, where the skip list grew steadily for most of a year and by the end nobody could say which of the entries described behaviour anybody still wanted. The agreement that came out of that is that the list has a ceiling, and adding an entry when the list sits at its ceiling means fixing or formally retiring an existing entry first. It is a crude mechanism and it is meant to be, because the failure mode is not that any single test gets parked, it is that parking is frictionless and so nobody ever chooses the harder option. Making the cost visible at the moment of adding is the only thing we found that works; reminders and periodic reviews of the list did not, because a review that can be deferred always is. The ceiling itself is not a considered figure, it is simply small enough that the whole list stays readable on one screen.

Fixtures are derived from the schema rather than maintained beside it, and a pipeline check makes the derivation mandatory. Every test row is built through a factory in `tests/factories/`, one per mapped model, and the factories read column metadata off the mapped class at import time instead of carrying their own field lists, so a renamed attribute breaks the factory loudly at collection. On top of that, `make fixtures-check` runs on every pull request: it upgrades a throwaway database to the migration head, writes the resulting column and constraint set to `tests/fixtures/schema_snapshot.json`, and fails if the committed file differs. Regenerating that file is what forces the author of a migration to notice they have added a NOT NULL column with no server default, because the same job then refuses to build the default factory instance and names the attribute that has no value. The arrangement exists because `shipments.carrier_ref` once went to production as NOT NULL while the suite stayed green for nine days — the fixtures at the time were literal INSERT statements naming their own columns, so the database simply never saw the new constraint. Factories are therefore also forbidden from writing rows through raw SQL; everything goes through the ORM so that a constraint the fixtures violate fails a test instead of being quietly stepped around.

Reference data — currency codes, tariff bands, country and carrier lookups — is loaded exactly once per test session into the template database and never rebuilt between tests. It is roughly fourteen thousand rows and inserting it per test cost around four hundred milliseconds each time, which was most of the suite's runtime for data that no test has any business modifying. The loader runs from a session-scoped fixture, and to keep the invariant honest the reference tables are revoked for the test role after the load, so a test that tries to insert a new currency gets a permission error naming the table rather than mysteriously polluting the run that follows it. Two tests genuinely needed to modify a lookup table and both were rewritten to assert against an injected mapping instead, which is what they actually meant. This split — mutable data per test, immutable data per session — is the single largest speedup we have made to the suite, and it holds only because the immutable half is enforced rather than agreed.

Each test runs inside a transaction that is rolled back at teardown, and nothing truncates tables between tests. The session fixture opens a connection, begins an outer transaction, binds the ORM session to it with a nested savepoint, and rolls the whole thing back afterwards, so the database is byte-identical at the start of every test without paying for a delete pass over forty-odd tables. Truncation was what we did before and it was costing about two hundred milliseconds per test on the larger schemas, plus the sequence resets made ids predictable in a way several tests had accidentally come to depend on. The one place it does not work is code under test that commits and then expects a separate connection to see the row — background worker tests mostly — and those are marked `@pytest.mark.real_commit` and get a schema of their own that is dropped at the end. Keeping that escape hatch narrow matters, because the rollback pattern quietly stops protecting you the moment something commits outside the session it was given.

Anything bigger than a couple of lines of payload lives in `tests/data/` as a real file with a real extension and gets loaded by a helper, rather than sitting inline in the test as a triple-quoted string. The threshold in review is roughly twenty lines. Inline blobs were making diffs unreadable, they defeated every editor's syntax highlighting, and worst of all people copied them between tests with one field changed, so a format update meant hunting through forty near-identical strings. The files are validated on load against the same parser the production code uses, which caught the fact that three of our carrier response samples had never been valid documents at all and only worked because the test asserted on a substring. Naming convention is `<carrier>_<scenario>.json`, and the helper resolves relative to the test module so moving a test file moves its data with it. Files are read-only in the suite; a test that needs a mutated variant deep-copies the parsed structure and edits the copy in memory.

The local development seeder and the test factories are deliberately separate codebases with no shared module between them, and merging them has been proposed twice and declined twice. They pull in opposite directions. The seeder wants a plausible-looking world — a few hundred accounts with realistic names, a spread of shipment states, enough volume that the console screens look like something — and it wants to be fast to run once and then forgotten. Factories want the minimum viable row, constructed explicitly, with every field the test cares about visible at the call site. When they shared code, every change to make the demo data look better added another implicit default that some test was silently relying on, and the tests grew steadily less readable because the interesting value was buried under twenty uninteresting ones somebody else had chosen. The duplication is real and it is the price. What they do share is the models, which is the only layer where agreement actually matters.

Multi-tenant behaviour is tested through `with_second_tenant()`, a helper that provisions a second account with its own users, api key and shipments, and returns both handles. Before it existed each test that cared about isolation built its own second tenant inline, in about six different ways, and half of them shared a row somewhere — usually the organisation-level tariff profile — which meant they passed while proving nothing. The helper builds the full object graph and includes an assertion at construction time that the two graphs share no primary key, so the fixture itself fails rather than the test giving a false green. The convention that goes with it is that any handler taking an account context gets at least one test using the helper, checking that the second tenant's identifier is rejected rather than merely absent from the result. The distinction matters: a filtered-out row and a rejected request look the same in a list endpoint and very different in a detail endpoint.

A factory call in a test should set only the fields the test is about, and the factory should supply everything else with values that are obviously placeholder. Anything the assertion depends on has to appear at the call site, even when the default would have done, because a test whose expected value comes from a default two files away is a test nobody can read a year later. The corollary is that defaults are chosen to be boring and unmistakable rather than realistic — a name that reads like a placeholder, an amount nobody would confuse with a meaningful figure — so that when one leaks into an assertion message it is immediately obvious what happened. We drifted the other way for a while, towards factories that produced beautifully realistic objects, and the result was tests that read as three lines and could only be understood by someone willing to go and read the factory. Review now pushes back on both sides of this: on hidden dependence on a default, and on setting eleven fields when the test is about one.

No test data originates from production, scrubbed or otherwise. The proposal comes back every so often, usually after a bug that only reproduced against real shapes of data, and the answer has stayed the same for two reasons. The first is that scrubbing is a claim you have to keep proving: every new column is a new opportunity to leak something, the reviewer of the scrubbing rules is never the person adding the column, and one missed free-text field is a customer address sitting in a repository every contractor can clone. The second is that captured data quietly becomes a specification. Once a captured row is in the suite, nobody remembers which of its properties matter, so tests come to depend on incidental facts about whichever week the capture was taken. Constructed data forces someone to state what the interesting property is. Where a real shape genuinely matters we take the shape and not the content — the field structure of a carrier response, the ordering of a settlement file — and write it down by hand.

Every nullable column has to be exercised by at least one test that leaves it null and asserts on the resulting behaviour, and reviewers ask for this by name. The rule came out of a run of bugs that all had the same shape: a column added as nullable because backfilling was inconvenient, every test constructing rows with a value present, and the null path meeting real data for the first time in production, where it produced a stack trace in a template or a comparison against nothing at all. Nullability is a claim about what the application must tolerate, and an untested claim of that kind is just an intention. In practice this is one extra test per column and it usually takes minutes, which is the argument for doing it rather than debating it. The stronger version of the advice, and the one people reach for after being bitten a few times, is to avoid the nullable column in the first place where a sensible default exists, since a column that cannot be null needs no such test at all.

We deleted the full browser suite from the web repository in February and replaced it with two smoke journeys plus coverage pushed down and out. The numbers behind the decision: the suite was forty-one minutes on a good run, it accounted for sixty-eight percent of pull request failures, and when we went back through a year of those failures only three had been genuine product defects — everything else was a timing assumption, a fixture drift, or the shared environment being mid-deploy. Average time to work out which of those it was ran to about two hours, usually spent by whoever was trying to ship something unrelated. The replacement is three-part and it is what makes deletion defensible rather than reckless. Handlers and rendering are covered by component tests, cross-service behaviour is covered by consumer contract verification against the api, and the journeys we actually care about — sign in, and creating a shipment through to the confirmation screen — moved to a synthetic monitor that drives real Chrome against production every five minutes. That is the real trade: we gave up a pre-merge signal that lied most of the time in exchange for a post-deploy signal that is checked constantly and against the environment that matters. Two browser tests remain in the pipeline, both smoke, both under ninety seconds, and adding a third needs an argument.

Component tests execute under jsdom through vitest, not in a real browser engine, and that boundary is stated explicitly so nobody wastes an afternoon on it. Anything depending on real layout — element widths, scroll position, intersection observers, the way a sticky header behaves at a breakpoint — cannot be asserted in jsdom and must not be faked into passing with a stubbed `getBoundingClientRect`, which is where two people separately ended up before the rule was written. Those behaviours belong to the visual snapshots instead. What jsdom does cover, and covers cheaply, is everything about component behaviour: props to output, event handling, conditional rendering, focus management, and the accessible name and role of what gets emitted. The whole suite runs in about ninety seconds for roughly nine hundred tests, which is the property that makes it usable in watch mode while writing a component. The rule of thumb in review is that if a test needs a real box model it is in the wrong file, and if it needs a real network it is in the wrong repository.

Screenshot comparison is limited to the design system package. Every exported component renders in the gallery at two widths against a pinned browser build, and the diff runs on pull requests touching that package only. We used to snapshot application screens too and it was unworkable: any content change, any date rendered relative to today, any change to seeded data produced a wall of red images, so the reviewers who were supposed to look at them started approving the whole batch without opening them, which is worse than not having the check. Narrowing to the design system fixed it, because a button or a table cell changes appearance only when somebody meant it to, and the baseline update then carries real information. Baselines live in the package under `visual/baselines/` and are regenerated by a labelled job so they are never quietly overwritten by a rerun.
