Application screens get no pixel coverage at all now and that is accepted; the failures that used to be caught there were nearly always in a shared component anyway.

Frontend tests intercept at the network layer with msw rather than talking to a locally started fake backend. The fake was a small express application maintained by hand, and it rotted in the way those always do — it accumulated endpoints nobody used, drifted from the real response shapes, and the person adding a field to the api had no reason to know it existed. Handlers now live in `src/mocks/handlers/` next to the client code that calls them, and the default set is generated from the api's published openapi document, so a response shape that no longer exists fails to build rather than quietly serving stale json. Per-test overrides use `server.use()` for the error and empty cases, which is most of what tests actually need and was the clumsiest thing to do with the old fake. The same handlers back the storybook stories, so a component's documented states and its tested states cannot diverge. Starting a separate process per test run also disappeared, which took a noticeable amount of flakiness with it.

Responsive checks run at exactly three widths — 375, 834 and 1440 — and those are pinned in `test/viewports.ts` rather than chosen per test. Previously each author picked whatever width demonstrated their bug, so the suite carried eleven distinct viewports, several of them a few pixels either side of a breakpoint, and the ones sitting on a boundary failed whenever a font metric shifted. Three widths were selected to sit clearly inside the phone, tablet and desktop ranges rather than at their edges, and boundary behaviour is asserted directly against the breakpoint constants instead of by rendering near them, which is both faster and actually says what it means. Analytics backs the choice: those three cover the great majority of real sessions, and the long tail of unusual widths has never produced a reported layout bug that the three did not also show. Adding a fourth width is a conversation rather than a commit, because each one multiplies straight through the responsive part of the suite.

Anything automation needs to find carries an explicit `data-testid`, and selecting by class name, tag structure or visible copy is not supported. Text selectors were the first to go — a marketing pass reworded four buttons and broke a dozen assertions that had nothing to do with the change — and structural selectors went shortly after, because `div > div:nth-child(2)` is a promise about markup that no component author knows they are keeping. Test ids are treated as an interface: they appear in the component's props table, renaming one is a breaking change to that package, and the linter rejects a test id built by string concatenation so that grepping for a value always finds both ends. They are stripped from production builds by a compiler plugin, so the attribute costs nothing at runtime. The convention is `area-thing-action`, for example `shipment-row-cancel`, and reviewers push back on ids that encode position or ordering since those quietly reintroduce exactly the fragility the rule was written to remove.

The synthetic journeys are owned by the web team, not by the platform group who run the monitoring stack, and the distinction is written down because it was fought over once. Platform owns the runner, the alert routing and the credentials the checks use. The web team owns what each journey does, what it asserts, and whether a given failure is worth waking somebody for. That split follows the only rule that has ever made ownership stick here: the people who can fix the thing being tested decide what the test says. When platform owned the journeys, every change to a screen quietly broke one, the platform on-call got paged for a product change they had no context on, and the fix was invariably to make the assertion weaker until it stopped complaining. Journeys are reviewed at the same time as the screens they exercise, by the same reviewers, and a screen change that makes one obsolete is expected to delete it in the same change rather than leaving it failing for somebody else to interpret.

Tests must not assert on class names. A class is an implementation detail of the styling approach, and we have changed styling approaches twice; each time, the tests that broke were the ones checking whether an element carried a particular modifier rather than whether the user could tell the difference. The replacement is to assert on what a person or a screen reader would perceive — that the control is disabled, that the row is marked as selected, that the error message is present and associated with its field. Those assertions survive a restyle and, more usefully, they fail when the visible behaviour is actually wrong, which the class assertions frequently did not: a component can carry every expected class and still be invisible or unreachable. There is one grudging exception for a handful of animation states that have no accessible representation at all, and those tests are commented with the reason so nobody tidies them into consistency. The general shape of the rule is that a test should break for the same reasons a user would complain.

Automated accessibility checks run against the component gallery rather than against assembled application pages. Running them page by page produced an enormous backlog of violations, most of them the same handful of component defects repeated across every screen that used the component, and the report was so long that nobody could tell whether a change had made things better or worse. Checking components in isolation gives a small, stable list where each entry maps to one owner and one fix, and fixing it once removes the violation everywhere at once. The obvious gap is composition — contrast against an unexpected background, duplicated landmarks, a heading order that only goes wrong when two components sit together — and we accept that gap deliberately rather than pretending otherwise. Composition problems are caught in the manual review that goes with any new screen, which is slower and less complete but at least gets read. The automated check is treated as a floor, never as the definition of accessible.

Coverage is measured on every pull request and no coverage number can fail a build. The report is produced by `pytest --cov` and posted as a comment listing which lines the diff added without exercising, and that comment is a prompt for the reviewer, not a verdict. We ran a hard eighty percent threshold for about eight months and stopped because of what it produced rather than because anyone disliked the idea. People wrote tests to move the number: calls with no assertions, loops over every enum member, one that imported a module and asserted nothing. Coverage went up, the suite got slower, and the settlement rounding bug still shipped from a module sitting at ninety-four percent — the offending function was called by four tests and its return value checked by none. That was the argument that ended it. Line coverage tells you a line ran; it says nothing about whether anyone looked at what it did, so gating on it optimises the wrong quantity and, worse, teaches people that the wrong quantity is what we care about. What replaced the gate is the diff-level comment plus reviewers actually asking about uncovered branches, which is slower and depends on people, and we accepted that. Two files carry per-path floors — the ledger posting module and the tariff calculator — because they are money and a mechanical backstop there outweighs the general objection.

Generated code is excluded from the coverage report through the `omit` list in `.coveragerc`, and the list is deliberately short: the protobuf output directory, the openapi client package, and the alembic revision files. Each entry has a comment giving the reason, and adding one without a comment fails review. The justification is the same in all three cases — the code is not written by us, it is verified by the generator's own test suite, and including it produced a report where a hundred and forty thousand generated lines drowned the eight thousand we actually maintain. Before the exclusion the overall figure moved several points whenever we regenerated a client, which made the number meaningless as a trend. Migration files are the interesting entry: they do execute during the schema tests, so they inflate the figure while telling you nothing, since a migration is exercised for correctness by the fixture check rather than by anything resembling a unit test. The rule for new exclusions is that the code must be generated and covered elsewhere; inconvenience to test is not a reason.

The report shows branch coverage rather than line coverage, set by `branch = True` in `.coveragerc`, and the headline number dropped about nine points on the day we switched. That drop was the point. Line coverage counted a one-line `if` as fully covered the moment the true case ran, which is exactly the case where a bug hides — the error handler that has never once executed, the early return nobody has taken, the fallback branch that turns out to reference a variable that does not exist in that scope. We found two of those within a week of switching, both in retry paths that had been sitting in the report as green. The cost is a slower run, roughly fifteen percent on the unit suite, and a report that some people found demoralising at first because the number looked worse than the one they were used to. Partial branches are what reviewers scan for now, since a half-covered branch is a much stronger signal than an uncovered file, which is usually just something nobody has got to yet.

The reporting bot posts one comment per pull request and edits it in place on every subsequent run, keyed on a hidden marker in the comment body so it can find its own previous message. This sounds trivial and it was not: the earlier version appended a new comment per push, and on a branch that took thirty pushes the discussion thread became unreadable, with the actual review conversation buried between nearly identical tables. Two people said they had stopped reading the comments entirely, which meant the whole reporting arrangement was doing nothing. The edited comment also gives a natural place for the delta against the base commit, since the bot already has to fetch its own prior state. The same pattern is now used by the bundle size reporter and the migration summary, all three writing into one comment with three sections rather than three comments, and the convention is that any bot posting on a pull request must be able to find and update its own output.

Unit and integration coverage are collected into two separate reports and never combined into a single figure. Merging them is technically easy and we did it for a while, and the result was actively misleading: the integration suite walks through nearly every module on its way to doing anything, so the combined report showed most of the codebase as covered while whole classes of behaviour had no direct test at all. Split apart, the two answer different questions. The unit report says whether a module's own logic has been exercised in isolation, which is what you want when reviewing a change to that module. The integration report says which paths a realistic request touches, which is more useful for spotting code that no request reaches any more. Each is written to its own file under `reports/` and posted in its own section of the comment, and the pair are frequently interesting precisely where they disagree — a module high in one and low in the other is usually either dead code or a missing unit test.

The unit suite runs across eight parallel shards, each writing its own `.coverage.<shard>` data file, and a final job runs `coverage combine` before anything is reported. Missing that step is how the report spent a fortnight claiming a plausible-looking but entirely wrong figure — whichever shard finished last overwrote the others, so the report described one eighth of the suite and the number moved randomly depending on how the split happened to fall. The combine job is a required part of the reporting workflow rather than a step inside each shard, and it fails loudly if it finds fewer data files than there were shards, which catches the case where a shard crashed and the report would otherwise have quietly under-counted. Paths are normalised through `[paths]` in the config because the shards run in different working directories and the same module would otherwise appear under several names. None of this is interesting when it works, and all of it is confusing when it does not.

Mutation testing is run against the settlement module and nothing else. It works by making small changes to the code — flipping a comparison, dropping a negation, replacing a return with a constant — and checking whether any test notices, which answers the question that coverage cannot: not whether the code ran, but whether anybody is looking at what it produced. Its first run on settlement survived an embarrassing number of mutants, several of them in rounding logic where a test called the function and only asserted that no exception came back. The reason it stays scoped to that one module is cost. A run takes long enough that it cannot sit anywhere near the pull request path, and the value scales with how expensive a silent wrong answer is, which for settlement is very expensive and for most of the codebase is a mild annoyance. The output is a list of surviving mutants that the owning team works through as ordinary tickets, not a threshold anyone has to clear.

Finding unused code is a job for the static analyser, not for the coverage report, and conflating the two wasted a fair amount of time before we separated them. A module showing zero coverage means only that no test touched it, which is a statement about the tests. It might be dead, or it might be the disaster recovery path, or an admin command that runs monthly, or something reached exclusively through a webhook. Deleting code on that evidence went wrong once already, when a rarely-used export routine was removed during a cleanup and reappeared as a support escalation the following quarter. The analyser reasons about references instead: nothing imports this symbol, nothing names it in an entrypoint, nothing resolves it dynamically through a registry it knows about. Its findings are still reviewed by a human, because dynamic dispatch defeats it in a handful of places, but the evidence it offers is the right kind. The two reports are read together, and agreement between them is what makes a deletion comfortable.

The benchmark job runs with instrumentation switched off entirely. Tracing every executed line changes the shape of what you are measuring — some functions slow by a little and tight loops slow by a great deal — so a run with coverage enabled will happily tell you that a hot path got worse when nothing about it changed except that it was being watched. We discovered this the tedious way, chasing an apparent regression in the tariff evaluation loop for the better part of a day before noticing the job had inherited the instrumented configuration from the suite it was copied from. The benchmark now runs from its own entrypoint with its own settings and asserts at startup that no tracer is installed, failing immediately if one is, because a silently mismeasured benchmark is worse than no benchmark. Nothing is reported about coverage from that job and nothing should be; the two jobs are asking unrelated questions and each is best served by not carrying the other's baggage.

Contracts are consumer-written and provider-verified, and the ownership split is the whole design. The consumer team writes the expectations, the file lands in the provider's repository under `contracts/<consumer-name>/`, and a `CODEOWNERS` entry makes the consuming team the required reviewer for that directory. A provider can see the contract, run it, and open a pull request against it — a provider cannot merge a change to it. That restriction exists because of the release where the gateway team loosened an expectation on the shipment payload so their build would pass, shipped, and broke the mobile client for most of a morning; every step of that was locally reasonable and the outcome was that a promise got weakened by the party it constrains. Verification runs on every provider pull request against the consumers' published contracts and again nightly, and `bin/can-i-deploy --service gateway` is a required step in the deploy pipeline so a provider cannot ship while any consumer's expectations are failing. Breaking changes go the other way round: the provider opens a pull request against the contract, the consumer approves or does not, and the two versions run side by side until the consumer's own change has shipped. Ownership of the contract text follows the party that would be hurt by it being wrong, which in every case so far has been the caller.

The mock a consumer runs locally is generated from the same contract file the provider verifies against, by `make mocks` writing into `.mocks/` at the repository root. Hand-written mocks were the previous arrangement and they drifted the moment anybody was in a hurry — the classic failure being a mock returning a field with a plausible name that the real service had never emitted, which meant the feature worked all the way through review and failed on first contact with staging. Generating them closes that gap by construction: if the response shape is not in the contract, the mock cannot produce it, and a developer noticing the mock will not give them what they need is exactly the moment the contract should be extended. The generated mock is deliberately dumb, matching on method and path and returning the canonical example, with no attempt to simulate business logic. Anyone needing conditional behaviour writes it in their own test rather than teaching the mock to be clever, because a clever mock is just the hand-written one with extra steps.

Internal service clients are not hand-written. Each service publishes an openapi document from its route definitions, and `tools/gen_clients.py` produces a typed client package per consumer at build time, checked into the consumer under `generated/` with a header saying which commit of the provider it came from. The rule that goes with it is that generated files are never edited: a needed change goes into the provider's route definition or into the generator, never into the output, and a lint step compares the checked-in files against a fresh generation to enforce it. What this buys is that a removed field becomes a compile error in every consumer rather than a runtime `None` discovered by a customer. What it does not buy is agreement about behaviour — the client knows the shape of a response and nothing about whether the semantics changed underneath, which is a real limit and the reason the generation exists alongside other checks instead of replacing them. Regeneration is a scheduled pull request, so consumers move deliberately rather than being dragged.

A field being retired from an internal contract stays in it, annotated `deprecated: true` with a `remove_after` date at least sixty days out, and the verification job warns rather than fails for the whole of that window. The date is a real commitment: a scheduled check fails the provider's build once the date passes and the field is still being emitted, which stops the graveyard of fields that everyone agreed to remove and nobody did. Sixty days came from measuring how long a consumer change actually takes to reach production once someone starts it, and rounding generously; shorter windows meant the last week became somebody's emergency. The provider is expected to say in the annotation what replaces the field, because half the delay in the old process was consumers working out what they were supposed to migrate to. Adding a field needs none of this — additive changes are always safe here since consumers ignore unknown keys by construction — and it is only removals and type changes that go through the window.

Asynchronous message payloads live in their own registry and are not modelled as contracts at all. The registry is a repository of schemas keyed by topic and version, and producers validate against it at publish time in staging, which is a different mechanism from the request-response verification the http services use. Trying to force events into the same tooling failed for a structural reason: a contract is a two-party agreement between a named caller and a named provider, while an event has one producer and an unknown, changing set of consumers, several of which are analytics jobs that nobody in the producing team has ever met. There is no single consumer whose expectations can define the promise. So events get a stricter, simpler rule instead — the schema is append-only, fields are never removed or retyped, and a genuine break means a new topic version — which is a heavier constraint on producers, accepted because the alternative is a promise to people you cannot enumerate.

A failing verification opens a ticket and never pages. The nightly job posts into the owning team's channel and files an issue tagged `contract-break` with the diff between expected and actual, and that is the extent of the escalation. This was argued about after the mobile incident, where the position was reasonably enough that a broken promise between services is serious and should wake somebody. What settled it is that verification runs against the current contract and the current provider build, so a failure means an incompatibility exists in the repository, not that anything in production is broken — the deploy gate is what stops it reaching production, and that gate is checked at deploy time regardless. Paging on it would have meant waking people for a condition that cannot cause harm before the morning. The pattern generalises and we have applied it since: page for conditions that are hurting someone now, ticket for conditions that will hurt someone if ignored, and be honest about which one you have.

A caller with no registered contract gets no compatibility promise, and that is stated plainly rather than left implicit. Several internal tools and one long-forgotten reporting script were calling service endpoints directly with no expectations recorded anywhere, and their authors were understandably upset the first time a response shape changed underneath them. The position we settled on is that the register of contracts is the definition of who is being supported; if you are not in it, your dependency is invisible to the people making changes, and no amount of goodwill fixes that because they genuinely cannot see you. Registering is not onerous, which is what makes the position defensible — write down the fields you rely on, put it where the provider's pipeline will run it, and you are covered. The corollary is that providers are expected to check the register rather than guess about callers, and to treat an unregistered caller discovered in the logs as a prompt to go and ask them to register.

The old cross-service suite that deployed every service into a shared environment and drove them together has been retired. It failed in a way that was impossible to argue with: nobody could tell whether a red run meant a real incompatibility or that somebody else's deploy was halfway through, and because it exercised every service at once, every team saw failures caused by other teams. Attribution was so poor that the standard response became rerunning it, which is the point at which a check stops being a check. The replacement covers the same ground from two directions — pairwise contract verification for the promises between services, and monitoring of the real journeys after deploy for the emergent behaviour — and the honest accounting is that a narrow band in the middle is no longer covered before merge. Things involving three services and a particular ordering. We decided that band was better served by watching production closely than by a suite whose verdict nobody believed.

Contract examples must be obviously synthetic. No real customer names, no real account identifiers, no amounts or reference numbers copied out of a production trace, and no addresses that resolve to anywhere. The rule started as a privacy concern — the files are readable by everyone with access to the repository, they get pasted into tickets and chat threads freely, and a captured example is exactly the kind of thing that ends up somewhere it should not be. It stayed for a second reason that turned out to matter more day to day: examples get read as documentation, and a realistic-looking value invites people to infer rules from it that nobody ever intended, such as an identifier that happens to be numeric in every example being treated as numeric by a consumer that then breaks. Deliberately artificial values make the shape the only thing you can learn from an example, which is the only thing the example is there to teach.

Exactly one repository runs on our own runners: `atlas`. Everything else uses hosted runners and that will not change. Two things forced it, both specific to it. Its integration suite has to reach the customs vendor's certification sandbox, and the vendor will only allowlist fixed addresses — they refused, in writing, to allowlist the hosted provider's published ranges, which is reasonable for them and a hard constraint for us, so jobs must originate from our own egress addresses. Second, the suite loads a sixty-two gigabyte reference dataset of tariff and route geometry, and pulling that from object storage on every run cost more in transfer and wall clock than the tests did; on our own hosts it sits on a local volume that survives between jobs. Note what is not on that list: speed. Self-hosting is faster, and that is explicitly not sufficient reason for another repository to follow, because the cost is real — patching, capacity, a fleet that is ours to fix at three in the morning. The runners register with the labels `self-hosted,atlas`, an organisation policy restricts that label to the one repository, jobs run with `--ephemeral` so a runner takes one job and is replaced, and fork pull requests are routed to hosted runners with the sandbox tests skipped, because a self-hosted runner inside our network running a stranger's code is the one failure mode we will not accept.

A monthly report breaks hosted runner minutes down by repository and by workflow and posts it into the engineering channel. It is a report and not a budget — nobody has ever been told to reduce their minutes — and it exists because consumption is otherwise completely invisible to the people creating it. The first edition was startling: one workflow that regenerated a documentation site on every push to any branch accounted for close to a fifth of the total, and it had been doing so unnoticed for months because each individual run was cheap and nobody sees the aggregate. Three teams changed a trigger condition within a fortnight of the first report, which is the entire mechanism by which it works. The report also tracks minutes per merged pull request, which is a better trend line than raw minutes since the raw figure mostly follows how much work is happening. What it deliberately does not do is rank teams against each other, because the moment the numbers became competitive people would start optimising the number rather than the waste.

The runner image is baked weekly from `infra/packer/runner.pkr.hcl` and rolls out on the following Monday, and workflows are expected to install nothing at job start beyond their own project dependencies. Baking the toolchain in — language runtimes, the database client, the graphics libraries the report renderer needs — took about ninety seconds off every single job, which matters more than it sounds because it applied to every job in every matrix leg. The stronger reason is reproducibility: before the image existed, jobs installed packages from upstream repositories at run time, so a run's behaviour depended on what a mirror happened to be serving that morning, and we lost most of a day to a transitively upgraded system library that broke image decoding in a way nobody could reproduce locally. Image versions are dated and the previous two are retained, so a workflow that starts failing after a rollout can be pinned back with a one line change while the cause is worked out rather than while everyone waits.

The web build moved to the hosted provider's larger runner size — four times the cores, eight times the memory — after a trial in which we measured the bundling step dropping from just over eleven minutes to three and a half. Cost per minute is roughly four times higher, so on paper it is close to a wash, and in practice it is clearly better because the thing being bought is not minutes but the interval between pushing and knowing. The trial was set up as a matrix running both sizes on the same commits for a fortnight, which was worth the trouble: the memory was what mattered, not the cores, since the previous size had been swapping during the type check and most of the improvement disappeared when we tested cores alone. That result is the reason the standing advice is to measure before upsizing rather than assuming a job is compute-bound. Everything else stays on the default size, where the difference is not worth the price.

Model training runs on the vendor's managed training service, invoked from a workflow that submits the job and polls for completion. We do not own any accelerator hardware and the proposal to buy some was declined on utilisation: training runs a few times a week, the machines would have been idle the rest of the time, and the numbers put the break-even somewhere past the point at which the hardware generation changes. Submitting from the workflow keeps the provenance intact — the commit, the dataset version, and the resulting artifact reference are all recorded in the same run — which was the failure of the previous arrangement, where somebody trained on a workstation and the resulting model had no traceable lineage at all. The workflow itself is tiny and runs on an ordinary hosted runner, since all it does is submit, wait and record. The credentials are scoped to job submission only, so a compromised workflow can queue work and cannot read the training corpus.

Scheduled and nightly workflows run in a separate runner group with a lower concurrency ceiling, currently six jobs against the twenty-four available to pull request workflows. The split exists because of a bad Tuesday morning when a nightly regeneration job and the start of the working day collided: the nightly work filled the queue, pull request feedback went from a few minutes to over forty, and by the time anybody diagnosed it the morning was gone. Nothing was broken, the capacity was simply allocated first-come to work that nobody was waiting on. Group assignment is by trigger type in the shared workflow template rather than by anything the workflow author configures, so a job cannot opt itself into the interactive pool by accident. Nightly work finishing at seven instead of five in the morning costs nothing; a queued pull request costs an engineer their attention. Where a scheduled job genuinely is urgent — the security scan is the only current example — it is granted the interactive group by name.

Moving to a different continuous integration provider was evaluated seriously and turned down. The case for it was real — a nicer configuration language, better matrix ergonomics, and a caching model that would have suited our larger builds. What sank it was everything welded to the current provider that does not appear in a feature comparison: the deploy identity that our cloud accounts trust, branch protection reading check results, the review bots, the tooling that reads workflow history, and a great deal of accumulated knowledge about how the thing behaves when it misbehaves. Migrating meant either running two systems for a long stretch or a flag-day cutover on the path everything ships through. The judgement was that the improvement was real but incremental, while the risk was concentrated and hard to bound, and that the specific pains driving the proposal were mostly addressable where they were. Revisiting this is fine, and the bar is a problem that cannot be solved without moving.

Workflows triggered by a fork get no access to any secret. The trigger that runs on a fork's changes is the restricted one, which means no repository secrets, a read-only token, and no ability to write comments or statuses directly. Everything a fork's run wants to report goes through a second workflow that runs on our side against the recorded outcome, and never against the fork's code. This is not a hypothetical concern: a workflow file is code, a fork can change it, and any secret exposed to that run is a secret handed to whoever opened the pull request. The awkward consequence is that checks needing credentials cannot report on a fork's pull request at all until a maintainer moves the change onto a branch in the repository, which is friction we accept because the alternative is trusting strangers with production credentials. Contributors are told this up front in the contributing guide, since the failure otherwise looks like a broken pipeline rather than a deliberate boundary.

Nothing that matters may live on a runner host. Anything a job needs must be fetched at the start and anything it produces must be pushed somewhere durable before it ends, and a host can be destroyed at any moment without notice or ceremony. This is stated bluntly because the drift towards treating a machine as a pet is gradual and always well-intentioned: somebody leaves a checkout in place because cloning is slow, somebody else configures a tool by hand to unblock an afternoon, and a few months later a job only passes on one particular host and nobody knows why. We had exactly that, a build that worked on three machines out of four, and the difference turned out to be a manually installed certificate nobody remembered adding. Rebuilding a host from its definition has to be a boring operation that anybody can do without hesitation, and the only way to keep it boring is to destroy them regularly enough that a host never accumulates history worth preserving.

Three tiers, and which tier something lands in is decided by what produced it rather than by what it is. Anything from a pull request run — junit xml, coverage html, the built bundle, screenshots — is uploaded with `retention-days: 7` and then deleted, because after a week the branch has either merged or been abandoned and nobody has ever asked for one older than that. Builds from `main` keep their artifacts for ninety days, which covers the window in which somebody bisects a regression back through recent commits. Anything belonging to a tagged release is copied into `s3://halyard-artifacts/releases/<tag>/` with object lock and a two year expiry, and that tier exists because of a support escalation where a customer's integration had been failing since an upgrade fourteen months earlier and we could not reproduce the exact bundle they were running — the ninety day window had eaten it, and we were reduced to rebuilding from the tag and hoping the toolchain resolved identically. Note that the release tier is a copy made by the promotion job, not an extended expiry on the original; we tried extending expiries first and it failed constantly, because it depended on somebody remembering at the right moment. Container images are not covered here at all and follow the registry's own retention rules, which trips people up about twice a year.

Verbose logs are uploaded only when the job fails. Every job writes its full output to `build/logs/` and the upload step carries `if: failure()`, so a green run produces nothing beyond the summary line. The change came after somebody worked out that the vast majority of what we were storing had never been downloaded by anybody: successful runs generate the most logs, precisely because there are far more of them, and nobody reads the debug output of a job that worked. The saving was substantial and the loss is nearly nil, with one genuine exception — investigating a change in behaviour between two green runs, where you want the passing log from before, and it is gone. That case comes up perhaps twice a year and the answer is to rerun with debug logging enabled, which is slower than having it and much cheaper than keeping everything forever on the chance. The failure branch uploads the whole directory rather than a filtered subset, because filtering at upload time invariably drops the one file that mattered.

Every uploaded artifact is named `<repo>-<job>-<matrix-leg>-<short-sha>`, built from a shared workflow helper rather than typed by hand in each workflow. The short sha is the important part: before it, matrix builds all uploaded under the same name, the provider quietly kept whichever finished last, and we spent an afternoon debugging a linux failure using an artifact that turned out to have come from the macos leg. Including the leg makes the download list self-describing, which matters when a matrix has nine entries and you are trying to find the one that failed. Including the sha means an artifact found on somebody's laptop weeks later can still be traced to the commit that produced it, which used to be guesswork based on file timestamps. The helper also rejects names containing a branch name, because branch names get reused and rewritten while a sha does not, and an artifact named after a branch tells you nothing about what is actually inside it.

The artifact bucket accepts writes from exactly one identity, the `ci-publisher` role, and that role is assumable only by workflows running on a protected branch through the provider's oidc trust. Nothing else can put an object there — not an engineer with an admin session, not a service, not a laptop. The policy also denies overwriting an existing key, so a publish to a path that already holds an object fails rather than replacing it, which is what makes the path a stable reference for anything downstream. This came out of a review question nobody could answer at the time: if a build artifact is what we ship, what stops somebody replacing one after the fact? The answer was nothing, other than nobody having tried. Read access is broad by comparison, since the contents are our own compiled output and the value of the control is entirely in the write path. The deploy tooling refuses to consume an object whose recorded writer is anything other than that role.

Every release tag gets a software bill of materials generated during the build and attached to the tag alongside the binaries. It is produced from the resolved lockfiles by `tools/sbom.py` in the same job that assembles the release, deliberately not as a separate later scan, because a scan of the repository describes what should have been installed and the build knows what actually was. The difference is not academic — the first comparison we ran turned up two transitive packages present in the image and absent from every manifest, pulled in by a build stage nobody had looked at in a year. The document is what makes a vulnerability disclosure answerable in minutes instead of days: the question is always whether a given version of a given library is in a customer's release, and without a per-release record you are reconstructing history from git and guesswork. Customers on the enterprise agreement can request it, which is the other reason it exists, though internal triage is what uses it weekly.

Release binaries ship stripped and their debug symbols go to the symbol server as a separate upload keyed by build id. Shipping symbols inside the binary made the artifact roughly three times larger and gave anybody with a copy a very comfortable reverse engineering experience, while stripping without keeping the symbols anywhere made production stack traces useless — we had a fortnight of crash reports that were nothing but addresses before the server existed. Splitting them gives both properties. The crash reporter looks symbols up by build id at symbolication time, so a trace from any version we have ever published resolves as long as its symbols are on the server, and the upload is a required step of the release job rather than a manual afterthought precisely because a missing symbol set is discovered at the worst possible moment. Access to the symbol server is internal only, which is what keeps the stripping meaningful.

The build bot posts the artifact links into the pull request as part of its status comment, so reviewing a change to the console means clicking the preview build rather than checking out the branch and running it. This sounds like a small convenience and it changed review behaviour more than anything else we have tried. Reviewers who would not have gone to the trouble of a local checkout do look at a build that is one click away, and the comments that come back are about how the thing behaves rather than only about how the code reads. The links point at the artifacts the run produced, so what a reviewer sees is exactly what the pipeline made, not an approximation rebuilt on somebody's machine with a different toolchain. Nothing about the links is privileged — they are only reachable by people who can already see the repository — and the comment says plainly which commit the build came from, because a stale link from an earlier push caused enough confusion once to justify saying so every time.

Profiling output does not go through the pipeline's artifact store. Traces from the benchmark job are sent straight to the profiling service, which understands the format, can diff two profiles against each other, and keeps its own history. When we uploaded them as build artifacts instead, the workflow for using one was to find the run, download a file, and open it in a local viewer, which meant that in practice nobody ever compared anything and the traces were write-only. The service also gives the comparison the whole exercise is for: this profile against the one from the last release, with the differences ranked. Keeping them out of the artifact store has a second benefit, which is that profiles are large and the artifact store is not the right place for something whose value is entirely in being compared with its neighbours. The build records a link to the uploaded profile in its summary so the trail from a commit to its measurements is still one hop.

An unusually large artifact gets a question in review rather than a silent upload. There is no hard limit and deliberately so, because the cases where something genuinely big needs to be kept are real and a limit would only teach people to split things up to get under it. What there is instead is a size printed in the job summary and a convention that a big jump gets explained. Nearly every instance so far has been accidental: a build that started including its own dependency directory, a test that wrote its temporary database into the upload path, a bundle carrying source maps nobody intended to publish. Each of those is a defect in the build rather than a legitimate need for space, and each was found by somebody noticing the number had grown. The rare genuine case — a full dataset snapshot for a reproducible experiment — is fine, and asking about it costs a sentence in a review. Making the size visible is doing nearly all the work here; the convention just makes looking at it normal.

Four checks are required on `main` and no others: `lint`, `unit`, `migration-guard` and `contract-verify`. Everything else the pipeline produces — coverage, bundle size, the smoke journeys, licence scanning, the spelling pass — reports and cannot stop a merge. The bar for adding a fifth is written into the platform team's charter and it is deliberately high: the candidate must have run on `main` for thirty consecutive days with no failure that was later shown to be its own fault, it must have a named owning team, it must finish inside eight minutes at the ninetieth percentile, and it must be added by a pull request against `.github/rulesets/main.json` that the platform team reviews. The governing invariant is a single sentence — a required check is one where red always means do not merge — and any check that can be red for a reason unrelated to the change fails that test by definition. We arrived here after a stretch with eleven required checks, during which the median pull request carried three red checks that had nothing to do with it, and the working culture became routine admin merges. That is strictly worse than a small gate, because at that point nobody reads any of them, including the two that were telling the truth. Removing a check from the required set needs no ceremony at all; adding one does.

Checks that are not gates report by editing a summary comment on the pull request rather than by publishing a commit status. This started as an ergonomic complaint — the status list had grown to about twenty entries, all collapsed behind a link, and finding the one that mattered meant expanding the lot — and it turned into a useful separation. A comment is read by people; a status is consumed by the branch protection machinery. Putting advisory output in comments made it obvious at a glance which entries were mechanical gates and which were somebody's opinion. The comment is assembled by one bot from several jobs' outputs so the pull request carries a single table rather than five bots competing for attention, with each section naming the job that produced it and linking to its run. The unexpected benefit was that advisory output started getting read again once it was on the page instead of behind a click, and two of the sections have since produced genuinely useful catches that would have gone unnoticed as a status entry.

Branch protection is defined in `.github/rulesets/main.json` and applied by a workflow on merge, and changing it through the web interface is not allowed — a drift check runs hourly, and any live configuration that differs from the file is reverted and reported. The file came out of an afternoon nobody enjoyed: protection had been relaxed by hand during an incident, put back incompletely, and for six weeks a repository everyone believed was protected was accepting direct pushes. Nobody noticed, because the settings page looks the same whether you have read it recently or not. Keeping the definition in a file gives a review trail, a diff, and an owner, and it makes the question of what changed answerable from git history rather than from an audit log nobody has bookmarked. The workflow that applies it uses an app installation scoped to administration on that one repository, and the drift check reports into the platform channel with the difference spelled out rather than a link to go and look.

Workflows use path filters so that a change touching only `docs/` or a markdown file does not start the backend suite, and the same applies in reverse for the web directory. The saving is real — documentation changes are a decent fraction of all pull requests and each one was pulling twelve minutes of unrelated compute — but the reason it survived a serious objection is more subtle. The objection is that a skipped job reports as skipped rather than as passed, and branch protection treats those differently, which meant that when we first added filters a docs change could not merge at all until somebody worked out why the required entry never arrived. The fix is a small always-running job that reports the required check name and either runs the real suite or passes trivially depending on the filter, so the status is present either way. Filters are listed once in the shared workflow rather than repeated in each file, because the first version drifted between workflows within a month and produced exactly the confusion it was meant to remove.

A pull request in draft runs the fast jobs and nothing else — lint, types and the unit suite, which together come in around four minutes — and the heavier work starts when it is marked ready for review. People open drafts early and push to them often, sometimes twenty times in a morning, and running the full pipeline on each of those was consuming a visible share of capacity to answer a question nobody was asking yet. The fast set was chosen so that the feedback a person actually wants while working still arrives: a typo, a broken import, a test they have obviously broken. Marking ready triggers the rest, and the convention is to do that before requesting review rather than after, so a reviewer never opens something with half its checks missing. The one recurring annoyance is a draft that sits for days and then turns out to fail something expensive the moment it is marked ready, which is the cost of the arrangement and has never been bad enough to change it.

The licence scanner runs on a nightly schedule against `main` rather than on each pull request. It takes around seven minutes because it resolves the full transitive graph for four package ecosystems, and its findings almost never relate to the change in front of you — the overwhelming majority come from a transitive dependency updated by a bot in a pull request that merged days earlier. Running it nightly puts the finding where it can be acted on: one report, one owner, a ticket if something needs replacing, rather than an alarming red entry on an unrelated change whose author has no idea what to do with it. The report writes into the compliance channel with a diff against the previous night, so a new licence appearing is visible immediately and the steady state is a quiet channel. Anyone adding a dependency can run the same scan locally with a make target, which is the moment the answer is actually useful and cheap to get.

Formatting is fixed rather than reported. A job runs the formatter and, if anything changed, commits the result back to the branch with a conventional message instead of failing and telling the author to run it themselves. The reasoning is that formatting has exactly one correct answer that a machine can compute, so a human round trip adds latency and irritation and no information whatsoever. Before this, a meaningful share of pipeline failures were formatting, each costing a push, a wait and a context switch, and reviewers were regularly leaving comments about whitespace because it was the thing most visible in the diff. There is a guard against the obvious hazard: the job refuses to push if it would be its own second consecutive commit, which stops a loop when the formatter and some other tool disagree. Authors are asked to run the formatter locally through the pre-commit hook anyway, since a bot commit landing under your name in the history is untidy even when it is correct.

Approvals and check results are separate mechanisms and conflating them causes trouble every time. A required reviewer is a statement about judgement — somebody who knows this area has looked and agrees — while a check is a statement about mechanics. The confusion usually appears as a request to make a team's approval optional when their checks are green, or the reverse, to treat a passing pipeline as standing in for review of a sensitive path. Both were argued and both were declined, because the failures they guard against are unrelated: a green pipeline says nothing about whether a change to the settlement rules is the change anyone intended, and an approval says nothing about whether the code compiles on the other platform. They are also configured in different places and reviewed by different people, which is deliberate, and the practical rule for anyone confused about why a merge is blocked is to read which of the two is complaining before doing anything else.

Merging with a gate unsatisfied is possible for a small group during an incident, and every use writes a record. The bypass exists because the alternative — no path at all — produces something worse: people find a way round under pressure, and the way they find is undocumented. What makes it acceptable is that using it is noisy rather than quiet. A message lands in the platform channel naming the person, the change and the reason they typed, and the following morning somebody reads the list. Usage is low, a handful of times a year, and the review has twice found that the underlying obstacle was a genuine defect in the pipeline that nobody had reported because working around it was easier than complaining. That is the real value of the review: not catching misuse, which has not happened, but discovering the friction that made the bypass attractive. Anyone with the permission is expected to open a follow-up describing what would have made the bypass unnecessary.

Pushing a new commit to a branch kills the run that was still going for the previous one. Every pull request workflow declares `concurrency: group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}` with `cancel-in-progress: true`, so one branch holds one running pipeline and the older attempt is abandoned the moment it is out of date. The reason is capacity, measured rather than assumed. On a sampled Wednesday afternoon the queue was thirty-eight minutes deep and just over half the jobs occupying runners belonged to commits that had already been superseded — work whose result nobody would ever look at, keeping work people were waiting on out of the queue. After the change, median time from push to first failing check on the backend repository went from about twenty-six minutes to eleven. Two exceptions, both deliberate. Runs on `main` are grouped per commit sha with cancellation off, because every commit on the trunk needs its own artifact and its own recorded provenance and a gap in that sequence is a hole in the bisect history. Nightly and scheduled jobs get their own group for the same reason. One thing to know when reading a cancelled run: the teardown step is marked `if: always()`, because cancellation used to leave orphaned preview namespaces and database containers behind, and cleaning those up by hand was a weekly chore before somebody noticed the pattern.

The deploy workflow takes a single global lock and queues behind itself rather than cancelling. Its concurrency group is a fixed string with `cancel-in-progress: false`, so two deploys triggered close together run one after the other and the second waits. Cancelling a deploy halfway is the failure we are avoiding: the workflow migrates, rolls the service, then updates the routing weights, and a run stopped between the second and third of those leaves the system in a state no code path expects and no human is watching. Waiting is cheap by comparison, and a queue two or three deep on a busy afternoon costs minutes. The lock is held for the whole workflow rather than around the risky steps only, which is more conservative than strictly necessary and much easier to reason about at three in the morning. There is a manual abort for the case where a deploy genuinely must be stopped, and it runs the same teardown path the normal failure branch uses rather than simply killing the run.

Every job declares `timeout-minutes` and the shared template refuses to run one that does not. Values are set at roughly double the observed ninetieth percentile — six for lint, twenty for the unit suite, forty-five for the integration matrix — which is loose enough not to trip on a slow morning and tight enough to matter. The default when nothing is specified is six hours, and that is how we discovered we needed the rule: a test that opened a socket to a service that had gone away sat in a blocking read on four runners for most of a Sunday, and the first anyone knew was the invoice. A hung job is worse than a failed one in every respect. It holds capacity, it tells you nothing, and it blocks whatever is waiting behind it. Timeouts are reviewed when a job legitimately grows past one rather than being raised reflexively, because a suite that has quietly doubled in runtime is itself worth knowing about and the timeout is often the only thing that ever mentions it.

The pipeline is staged: lint, type check and unit tests run first as a fast group, and the integration matrix, container build and smoke journeys only start if that group is green. The fast group finishes in about three minutes and catches a good half of all failures, so most red pull requests now cost three minutes of compute instead of twenty-five. The counter-argument was made and is fair — an author who fails on lint would have liked to know their integration tests also fail, and now they find out on the next push instead. We measured how often that actually mattered and it was rare, because a change that fails lint has usually not been run locally at all and is going to change substantially anyway. Staging is defined once in the shared workflow through job dependencies rather than being reimplemented per repository. The one job exempted from the ordering is the migration guard, which runs immediately and in parallel, because knowing a migration is unsafe is worth having early and it costs seconds.

When one leg of a matrix fails, rerun that leg rather than the whole workflow. The provider's interface offers both and the wrong one is the more prominent button, so this gets said in review often enough that it is written down. A full rerun of the nine-leg matrix costs around fifty minutes of runner time to reproduce eight results that were already green, and on a busy afternoon that is capacity taken from somebody else's first attempt. There is a correctness argument too, and it is the stronger one: rerunning everything replaces a set of results you understood with a fresh set you have to read again, and if the failure was genuinely flaky you have just lost the evidence of which leg it was. The single-leg rerun keeps the original run's results beside the new one. The exception is a failure that could plausibly be environmental across the whole run — the package registry being unreachable, for instance — where a full rerun is the honest response.

Each run writes a table into the job summary listing every step with its duration and the delta against the median for that step on `main`. It costs almost nothing to produce — the timings are already in the run metadata — and it changed how people reason about the pipeline. Before, the pipeline was slow in an undifferentiated way and proposals to speed it up were guesses; now anybody who waits too long can open the summary and see that dependency installation took four minutes because a cache key missed, or that one integration leg is consistently twice the others. Two of the larger improvements we have made started with somebody noticing a row in that table rather than with a deliberate investigation. The delta column is the part that earns its place, since an absolute number tells you nothing about whether this run was unusual. Steps slower than double their median are highlighted, which is a crude threshold and has proved to be about right in practice.

A dashboard on the wall screen shows queue depth, the number of busy runners and the oldest waiting job, and it is the first thing anybody looks at when the pipeline feels slow. Making it visible settled a recurring argument. The complaint was always that continuous integration was slow, and the response was always that the jobs themselves had not got slower, and both were true — the wait was in the queue rather than in the work, and nobody could see the queue. With the display up, the conversation moved on to what was consuming capacity, which is a question with answers. It also gives an honest signal during the morning peak: seeing a real backlog is much better than assuming your own run has hung, which is what people used to conclude. The panel is deliberately three numbers rather than a rich set of charts, because it is read from across the room and glanced at rather than studied, and every attempt to add more detail has made it less useful.

Pull requests opened by the dependency bot run a reduced workflow: build, unit tests and the security scan, skipping the integration matrix and the browser smoke checks. They arrive in a batch, they are numerous, and the full pipeline on each one was a meaningful share of weekly capacity for a class of change that is nearly always either trivially fine or obviously broken at build time. What makes the reduction safe is that these changes are merged into the trunk where the full suite runs anyway, so an incompatibility that only the integration tests would catch is caught there, before any release, with the offending bump identifiable by its own commit. That is a slightly later signal in exchange for a lot of capacity. Bumps to anything on the money path are excluded from the reduction and get the whole pipeline, identified by a path list rather than by the bot deciding for itself, since the bot has no notion of which dependencies we consider dangerous.

Pushing a branch does not start a pipeline; opening a pull request does. Workflows are triggered on pull request events and on merges to the trunk, and a branch pushed without one sits there quietly. This was contentious when it changed, because people liked pushing work in progress and seeing it checked. What it fixed was a large volume of runs on branches that were nowhere near ready, including the common pattern of pushing a checkpoint at the end of the day and getting a red pipeline nobody was going to look at. The workaround for anybody who genuinely wants the checks early is to open a draft, which costs one click and makes the intent visible to everybody else as well. There is one carve-out for branches under a reserved prefix used by the release tooling, which need their pipeline without a pull request existing. The general principle is that a pipeline run should correspond to somebody wanting an answer.

A gate that lies gets taken off the gate list automatically. `tools/check_health.py` runs every Sunday night, pulls the last two hundred runs of each required check from the api, and counts false failures — a failure followed by a pass on an identical tree hash, meaning the code did not change between the two verdicts. Any required check over two percent for two consecutive weeks is demoted: the tool opens a pull request moving it out of the required list in `.github/rulesets/main.json`, the platform team merges it, and a ticket goes to the owning team with the run links attached. The check keeps running and keeps reporting; it simply stops being able to block anybody. Getting it back is the ordinary route for adding any gate, and nobody may shortcut that because their check used to be required. The mechanism came from three weeks of `contract-verify` flapping on a broker timeout. Everyone learned to click rerun without reading, which is a rational response to a check that is usually wrong, and then a genuine incompatibility got rerun three times and merged, and the mobile client started failing on shipment creation that evening. Demotion is not a punishment and is not framed as one — the damage from a flapping gate is that it teaches an entire team to ignore red, and that habit does not stay confined to the one check that earned it.

Every check run's conclusion, duration and commit is exported to the warehouse each week into `ci_check_runs`, retained for two years. The pipeline provider keeps this data too, but only for ninety days and only through an interface that answers one question at a time, which makes anything historical unreasonably tedious — working out whether a job had got slower over a quarter meant clicking through pages of runs and writing numbers on paper. In the warehouse it is a query. That has settled a few arguments with evidence instead of impressions, notably the claim that the pipeline had got dramatically slower over a year, which turned out to be true for one repository and false for the rest. The export is a scheduled job that pages through the api and writes parquet, with a watermark so a failed week backfills on the next run rather than leaving a hole. Nobody looks at the table often, and when somebody does they generally need a year of it, which is exactly the shape of thing worth storing cheaply.

The last line of every check's output names the team that owns it and links to the runbook entry for that check, injected by the shared workflow from the `owner` field in `ci/checks.yaml` rather than written by hand. It exists because of the amount of time people spent asking in the wrong channel. A failing check whose message means nothing to you is a dead end, and the previous move was to post the log in the general engineering channel and hope somebody recognised it, which usually worked and usually cost two people an hour. Owner and runbook in the output turns that into a direct message or, more often, into reading the runbook and not asking anybody. The entry in the manifest is required — a check without an owner fails the config validation and does not run — and that requirement has quietly killed off two checks that nobody was willing to claim when the manifest was introduced, which was arguably the more valuable outcome.

Clicking rerun records who clicked, which check, and on which commit, into `ci_rerun_events`. There is no policy attached to the record and nobody is judged by it — the log exists because reruns are otherwise the least visible thing in the whole system. A rerun leaves the run looking as though it passed the first time, so the aggregate volume of them is invisible even though it is the clearest available signal about which checks people have stopped believing. The counts turned out to be much higher than anyone guessed, roughly one rerun for every nine runs across the organisation, concentrated in three checks. Two of those we already knew about and one was a surprise to everybody including its owners. The event carries the commit so a rerun on a genuinely changed tree can be told apart from a rerun on identical code, which is the distinction that makes the number mean anything. Access to the table is open, and the counts are quoted often enough in discussions about pipeline health that people know they exist.

A job that hits its timeout reports a failed conclusion, never a neutral or skipped one. The shared workflow wraps each step so that a timeout is caught and turned into an explicit failure with a message naming the step and its limit. This matters because of how branch protection reads conclusions: a neutral result satisfies a required check, so for a while a job that hung until the runner gave up was indistinguishable to the gate from a job that had passed. We found that during a review of why a bad change had merged cleanly — the integration job had timed out on a deadlock, reported neutral, and the merge went through with the required entry showing as satisfied. The wrapper also captures a stack dump of the process before it is killed, which is frequently the only evidence available about a hang, and it uploads that with the failure. The general rule taken from it: any outcome that is not a clear pass has to be reported as a failure, because the machinery only distinguishes those two.

The name of a check is an interface and is not to be edited casually. Branch protection matches required entries by exact string, so renaming `unit-tests` to `unit` does not rename the requirement — it creates a check nobody is waiting for and leaves a requirement nothing will ever satisfy, and every open pull request becomes unmergeable pending a status that no longer exists. That happened once, on a Friday, during a tidy-up that was in every other respect an improvement, and it took an hour of confusion before anybody connected the two. Names are declared in `ci/checks.yaml` and a validation step compares the declared set against the required list in the ruleset file, failing if a required entry has no producer. Renaming is therefore a two-step change: add the new name alongside the old, update the ruleset once both are reporting, then remove the old one. Tedious, and considerably less tedious than the alternative.

An advisory check that nobody reads is deleted rather than left running. This is easy to say and it took a deliberate cull to actually do, because every one of them had been added by somebody for a reason and deleting other people's work feels rude. The cull went through each non-blocking check and asked one question: when this last produced a finding, did anybody act on it? Where the answer was no, or nobody could remember, the check went. Four went in the first pass, including a complexity metric that had been reporting into a comment section for well over a year with no recorded response from anyone. The argument for removal is that a check producing output nobody reads is not neutral — it costs compute, it adds noise to every pull request, and it contributes to the general sense that most of what the pipeline says can be safely ignored, which is corrosive to the parts that matter. Anything genuinely valuable is easy enough to reinstate, and none of the four has been.

The shared workflow templates belong to the platform team, and repositories consume them by reference rather than copying them. Ownership here means responsibility for the parts every repository depends on — how jobs are structured, how runners are selected, how outputs are reported — and it also means that a change to a template is reviewed by people who can reason about the effect on forty repositories rather than one. The arrangement replaced a period in which every repository had its own copy, diverged from all the others, and any improvement had to be applied by hand in as many places as anybody had the patience for. Repositories can still override specific behaviour through documented inputs, which is what keeps the arrangement from becoming a bottleneck, and the general request is that anyone wanting something the inputs do not offer asks for it rather than forking the template quietly. The one rule that is not negotiable is that a repository may not lower a security-relevant default set by the template.

A digest lands in the engineering channel at the start of every week with the state of continuous integration: how long the median pull request pipeline took, how deep the queue got at its worst, how many runs failed and roughly how they split between real failures and everything else. It reports and recommends nothing, which is deliberate — the value is in the trend being in front of people rather than in anybody being told to act. Trends caught this way include a slow creep in pipeline duration over a couple of months, invisible day to day and obvious in a series, and a jump in failures after a runner image change that would otherwise have been attributed to whatever people happened to be working on. It is short enough to read in the time it takes to sit down. Longer versions were tried and were not read, which is the whole lesson: a digest that requires effort competes with everything else on somebody's Monday morning, and it loses.

Every advisory that reaches us lands in one queue with one named owner. Alerts from GitHub and from the nightly `trivy` image scan all file into the `dep-triage` board, and the dependency steward owns that board for their week: a one-week rotation across the platform team, published in the same calendar as the oncall shift. The job is deciding, not fixing. The steward first establishes reachability, whether the vulnerable code path can be entered from one of our entrypoints at all, then assigns one of three dispositions. Reachable without authentication is a severity two, patched inside three business days, and the steward may merge the bump into the owning service without waiting for that team. Reachable only behind an authenticated admin route gets fourteen days and goes to the owning team as an ordinary ticket. Not reachable, usually a parser we never call inside a library pulled in for one helper, is accepted with a written note naming the reason and an expiry date, and reopens when that package version next changes. Security review is consulted for the accept case only, never as a gate on the other two: the old arrangement put everything behind one part-time reviewer and the median advisory age ran over a month. The rotation exists because a severity two in an HTTP parser sat in a shared inbox for nineteen days while three teams each assumed one of the others had it.

Every language in the monorepo commits its resolved lockfile and the build refuses to proceed if the tree it resolves differs from the one checked in. That means `poetry.lock` for the Python services, `package-lock.json` for the web apps, `go.sum` for the two Go sidecars, and `Cargo.lock` even for the binary crates where the tooling would happily leave it out. `make deps-verify` runs a frozen install in the pipeline and fails on any drift, so a pull request that changes a dependency has to carry the lockfile diff with it and the reviewer can see exactly which transitive versions moved. Before this, installs resolved at build time against whatever was newest, which meant two builds of the same commit could produce different binaries. That is not a theoretical complaint: a Friday afternoon rebuild of an unchanged commit picked up a minor release of a JSON serializer that changed how it rendered large integers, and invoice totals came out of the templating layer in scientific notation for about forty minutes. Nobody had merged anything. The rule that came out of it is that the lockfile is the artifact under review and the manifest is only an expression of intent, so a manifest edit with no corresponding lockfile change is treated as an incomplete change and sent back.

Automated version bumps arrive once a week in grouped branches rather than one pull request per package. The configuration lives in `.github/dependabot.yml` with `schedule: weekly` set to Monday 07:00 UTC and grouping rules that collapse each ecosystem into a single branch, so a normal week produces four pull requests instead of the thirty or forty we used to get. Test suites run against the grouped branch, and if one package inside a group breaks the build the whole group is held back and split by hand rather than merged partially. The change was made because reviewers had visibly stopped reading them. We sampled a month of merged bump pull requests and found the median time between the review request and the approval was under ninety seconds, which is not review, it is clicking. Batching gets the volume down to something a person will actually open, and grouping by ecosystem keeps related version moves in one diff where an incompatible pair is obvious. Advisory-driven upgrades do not ride this queue at all and never wait for Monday. The residual cost is that a group failure takes longer to untangle than a single-package failure would, which we consider a fair trade against approvals nobody read.

Adding a new third-party library to a service requires a short written justification in the pull request description, and reviewers are expected to refuse the change without one. The note has to answer four things: what problem the library solves, what we would write ourselves instead and roughly how much of it, whether something already in the tree does the same job, and what the maintenance signal looks like. That last one is judgement rather than a metric, and deliberately so, because the numbers people reach for are easy to game and easy to misread. A single maintainer who has been steadily answering issues for years is a much better bet than a project with a wall of contributors who all stopped a year ago. The habit came from a cleanup week where someone counted the date handling libraries in the web apps and found three, each pulled in by a different person for a different narrow reason, each with its own view of what a timezone is. None of the three additions were unreasonable in isolation. What we lacked was the moment where somebody had to write down why the existing one was insufficient, which almost always turns out to be enough friction. The justification is not an approval process and nobody has ever been denied on grounds of taste, but a dependency that nobody could defend in a paragraph has generally not been worth carrying.

Service images build from an internal base image that is referenced by digest, never by tag. Dockerfiles start with a line pinning `registry.internal/base/python@sha256:` plus the full digest, and a pipeline rebuilds that base every night from the upstream distribution image, runs the smoke suite against a canary service, and opens a single pull request that moves the digest for every consumer at once. `make base-bump` does the mechanical part of rewriting the pinned line across the tree. Tags were the previous arrangement and they failed us in the worst possible circumstance. During an incident we redeployed a service to roll back an application change, the floating tag had moved underneath us in the meantime, and the rollback deployed a different base image with a different libc than the version it was supposed to restore. We spent the next hour debugging a symptom that had nothing to do with the outage. Pinning by digest makes the base image an explicit, reviewable, revertible input like any other dependency, and it means a redeploy of an old commit produces the same image today that it produced then. The nightly rebuild keeps the patch lag bounded so the pinning does not quietly turn into staleness.

All package installs go through our own index mirror rather than to the public registries directly. `pypi.internal.aldercross.net` is a pull-through cache in front of the upstream index, the build environment sets a single `--index-url` at it with no extra-index fallback configured, and internal libraries are published into the same namespace so there is exactly one place a resolver ever looks. The no-fallback detail is the important half. The old setup listed the internal index as an extra index alongside the public one, which means the resolver considers both and picks the highest version it finds, so anybody who registers a public package with the name of one of our internal libraries and a large version number gets their code executed in our build. That is not hypothetical; we found a squatted name matching one of our older internal helper packages sitting on the public index, uploaded three weeks after we first published the internal one under the same name. It had a couple of downloads, both from our own pipeline. The mirror also gives us a cache that survives an upstream outage and a record of every artifact any build has ever pulled, which has been useful more often for archaeology than for security.

Transitive version pins go in `constraints.txt`, never into the service's own requirements file. The distinction matters because a line in requirements declares that this service depends on that package, while a line in constraints says only that if something happens to pull this package in, it must land on this version. Putting a transitive pin in requirements creates a dependency that outlives its reason and that nobody dares remove, because the person reading it two years later cannot tell whether the service imports the package or whether someone was working around a bug in a release that has long since been fixed.
