Every line in the constraints file carries a comment with three things: who added it, the reason in one sentence, and the condition under which it can go away, usually an upstream issue number or a version to wait for. `tools/constraints_audit.py` runs monthly and reports pins whose stated condition has been met, which is how most of them eventually get removed. The file has held around a dozen entries for the last year, down from over forty when we started keeping the comments, and almost all of that reduction came from the audit rather than from anybody deliberately going looking.

We do occasionally carry a patched fork of an upstream library, and when we do it comes with two obligations that are checked at review time. The first is that the change has to exist as a standalone patch applied at build time, not as a hand-edited copy of the source tree, so that anybody can see the exact delta between what upstream ships and what we run without diffing whole directories. The second is a written exit condition: the upstream pull request we are waiting on, the release that would make the patch unnecessary, or an honest statement that upstream has rejected the change and we intend to carry it indefinitely. The last of those is allowed, but writing it down forces the conversation about whether we should be using that library at all. The rule exists because of a fork we carried in the gateway for most of two years. It began as a small fix, accumulated four more edits from four different people, and by the end nobody could say what it changed or whether the upstream version had fixed any of it. Upgrading meant reading the whole diff, so we did not upgrade, and by the time we had to we were many major versions behind. A fork you cannot describe is not a fork, it is a private library you did not mean to write.

The build refuses to complete when a newly introduced package carries a strong copyleft licence, and that check runs on every pull request rather than as a periodic sweep. The allowlist covers the permissive families we have already cleared with counsel, anything already in the tree stays in the tree under a grandfather list, and everything else stops the build with the package name and the licence it declares. Copyleft in particular is blocked because we ship a self-hosted appliance build to a handful of enterprise customers, and in that distribution the obligations are real rather than theoretical in a way they are not for a service we only ever run ourselves. The exception path is deliberately human: the requester writes down what the package does and how it is linked, and the answer comes back from legal rather than from an engineer reading a licence text and forming an opinion. We have granted exactly two exceptions, both for tooling that never leaves the build container and therefore never reaches the shipped artifact. The check was added after an audit ahead of a large customer contract turned up a network-copyleft library sitting in the appliance image, which took a fortnight to replace under time pressure that nobody enjoyed.

A service gets a distinct machine identity in every environment it runs in, and the same credential is never valid in two of them. The naming is mechanical, `svc-<service>-<env>`, so `svc-ledger-staging` and `svc-ledger-prod` are separate principals in separate cloud accounts with separate policies, and no staging workload can present a credential production will accept. This is not tidiness, it is blast radius. A shared identity collapses the environments into one trust domain: anything that can read the credential out of a staging pod, and staging is where we run half-finished code and let contractors deploy, can then act against production with the union of both environments' permissions. The night that settled it, a staging load test used a connection string copied from a production runbook months earlier, and because the account behind it was shared the writes were accepted. We spent the evening reconstructing four hours of settlement rows. The second reason is that shared identities make audit useless. When one principal is used by two environments you cannot tell from the access logs whether a call came from a test or from a customer request, so every investigation starts with guesswork. `tools/iam_lint.py` fails the plan if a role trust policy names a principal from another environment's account, which is the mechanical backstop for the rule.

People do not hold long-lived credentials for production. Console and CLI access both go through the identity provider, which mints a session against an assumed role with a one-hour lifetime, and there are no IAM users with access keys left in the production account at all beyond the two break-glass principals. `aws-vault` wraps the local flow so an engineer runs a command and gets a fresh session rather than exporting a key into their shell profile, which is where the old keys tended to end up and then get committed. Two things forced the change. A laptop was stolen at an airport and we spent a day working out which keys had been on it, and the honest answer at the end was that we were not certain. Separately, a routine scan of the repositories found a key from a departed engineer still valid nine months after their last day, because the offboarding checklist covered the identity provider but not the keys people had created for themselves. Short sessions mean the answer to both questions collapses to something bounded: the worst case exposure is an hour, and revocation is disabling one account in the identity provider rather than an archaeology exercise across every cloud account we own.

Where a static key genuinely cannot be avoided, it rotates every ninety days on a clock the owner does not control. `ops/iam/rotate_keys.py` runs on the first of each month, finds any access key older than sixty days, mints a replacement, writes it into Secrets Manager alongside the current one, and marks the old key inactive after a seven-day overlap window in which both are valid. The overlap exists because the first version of this job cut over instantly and took the payment provider callback handler offline for eleven minutes at two in the morning. Consumers that read the secret at boot rather than at point of use are the ones that break, and the overlap gives them a deploy cycle to pick up the new value. Keys that are still in use on day ninety with no successor page the owning team rather than silently extending, and the page is deliberately noisy because the failure mode we care about is a key that lives forever. The population this applies to is small and shrinking, currently four keys, all of them for third-party systems that will not accept a federated identity. Every one of them has a ticket for its removal.

A machine identity is named for the workload it belongs to, never for the person who created it. This sounds obvious and was not the practice for the first couple of years, when a robot account carrying somebody's first name was the normal way to get a nightly job running. The problem is not aesthetic. When the person leaves, nobody can tell whether the identity is a leftover of theirs or something load bearing, so it survives every cleanup on the grounds that removing it might break something. We inherited three of those and confirmed the last one was unused only by disabling it and waiting a fortnight to see what complained. There is a second failure mode: a personally named identity accumulates permissions from whatever its namesake happened to be working on, so its policy ends up describing a career rather than a job. Naming for the workload keeps the permission question answerable, because you can look at what the service does and say whether a grant belongs. The convention is enforced socially at review rather than by a check, and it has held because the alternative is now something everyone here has had to clean up at least once.

Staging runs on a scrubbed copy of the production dataset, refreshed weekly, never on a live replica. The refresh job restores the most recent nightly snapshot into the staging cluster, then runs `ops/scrub/anonymise.sql` before the cluster accepts any connections: customer names and addresses are replaced from a fixture pool, email addresses are rewritten to `user+<id>@example.invalid`, payment instrument tokens are dropped entirely, and the two free-text columns that support agents type into are truncated to empty. The scrub runs inside the same transaction as the restore, so there is no window in which real values are queryable. Fabricated data was the previous approach and it failed for a boring reason: our generator produced tidy records, and the bugs we ship are almost all caused by untidy ones, such as a shipping address with a newline in it or an account with eleven thousand child records. Restoring real shapes without real values gets us the first property without the second. The rule that came with it is that the scrub list is append-only and adding a column to the production schema that holds anything personal requires adding it to the scrub in the same change, checked by a test that compares the column list against the registry.

Pipeline jobs authenticate by exchanging their OIDC token for a role, so there is no secret in the CI configuration to leak. The trust policy on each deploy role names the repository and the branch or tag pattern that is allowed to assume it, meaning a job running from a fork or from a feature branch simply cannot get production credentials no matter what the workflow file says. That condition on the subject claim is the whole security property and it is easy to get wrong; a wildcard there restores exactly the hole you were trying to close, so `iam/trust/*.json` is in the CODEOWNERS list for the platform team. We moved off stored keys after a contributor's pull request modified the workflow to echo the environment during a debugging session, and although the secrets were masked in the log output, the exercise made it clear that a workflow file is user input and had been treated as trusted configuration. Federated tokens also expire in under an hour and cannot be replayed outside the job, so a leaked log line is worth nothing by the time anyone reads it.

Tokens that let automation push to or read from source control are issued per repository, never at the organisation level. An organisation-wide token is a convenience that costs you the ability to reason about anything: once a build for a small internal tool holds a credential that can read every repository we own, the security posture of that tool becomes the security posture of the whole codebase, and nobody is treating a small internal tool that carefully. Per-repository tokens make the question local. If the documentation site's publishing token leaks, the damage is bounded by what that token could reach, and you can say so within a minute instead of assuming the worst. The change was prompted by a vendor integration we were evaluating that asked for broad read access as its only option during setup. Somebody noticed that granting it would put our entire history in the hands of a product we had not finished evaluating, and the conversation that followed produced the standing rule. Requests for a broader grant are not refused outright, but they go to the platform team rather than being self-served, and in practice the narrower option has always existed once someone looked for it.

Every non-human identity has a row in `platform/identities.yaml` naming an owning team, the workload it belongs to, and a one-line description of what it is for. The file is the source of truth and Terraform reads from it, so an identity created outside the file has no configuration behind it and gets flagged by the weekly drift report. The reason for the registry is that unowned credentials never get cleaned up. Before it existed we had accumulated somewhere north of forty machine principals across the accounts, and when we sat down to audit them we could attribute maybe half. The rest were archaeology: a name, a creation date, and a policy that hinted at what somebody had been doing two years earlier. You cannot revoke something when nobody can tell you what breaks, so the safe move is always to leave it, and that is how the pile grows. Requiring an owner at creation time means the question is answered while the answer is still known. The registry also drives the quarterly attestation mail, which goes to the owning team with the list of what they own and asks them to confirm each entry is still needed; anything unconfirmed after two cycles is disabled rather than deleted, then deleted a month later if nobody notices.

There are two credentials in production that bypass the normal federated path, kept for the case where the identity provider itself is unavailable. They are stored offline, split so that no single person holds a complete one, and their only permitted use is an incident in which nobody can authenticate by the usual route. What makes them safe to keep is the alerting rather than the storage. Any authentication by either principal raises a page to the security oncall immediately and posts to the incident channel, unconditionally, with no suppression window and no way to mark it expected in advance. If they are used legitimately, the responder acknowledges it in the channel and the use gets written up in the incident notes anyway. We built them after an identity provider outage left us unable to reach the console during a customer-visible degradation, which was a genuinely frightening hour spent discovering that our recovery path depended on the thing that was down. The discipline that keeps them honest is a drill twice a year: someone breaks the seal on purpose, we confirm the page fires and the split halves still combine, and then both are rotated and resealed regardless of outcome.

Access to production customer data is recertified once a quarter, in the first two weeks of January, April, July and October, and the default outcome is removal. `tools/access_review.py` snapshots four things into a dated directory under `compliance/reviews/`: members of the `prod-data-reader` and `prod-data-writer` groups, the database roles that hold SELECT on any table in the `customers` or `payments` schemas, every account with a saved connection in the BI tool, and the service principals that read from the warehouse. Each owning manager gets their team's slice and has ten business days to mark each entry keep or drop with a reason. Anything not marked keep by the deadline is dropped, not escalated, which is the part that makes the exercise work: the earlier version escalated unanswered rows to the security lead and the backlog simply moved rather than shrinking. Revocations are executed by the platform team the following Monday and the signed snapshot is retained for seven years as the audit evidence. The policy exists because a contractor's read access to the payments schema survived eight months past the end of their engagement, found not by us but by an auditor sampling the group. Nothing had gone wrong, which was exactly the problem: we had no mechanism that would ever have noticed.

Nobody connects to the production database directly, not even with a read-only role. Sessions go through `pgproxy` on the bastion, which authenticates against the identity provider, rewrites the session to the caller's own role, and writes every statement it forwards to an append-only log with the caller, the timestamp and the statement text. The proxy is not a security boundary in the sense of blocking anything a role could otherwise do, and we are careful not to describe it as one. It exists so that the question of what a person actually looked at has an answer. During a customer escalation about how a support agent knew a detail they should not have, we could not reconstruct what had been queried, only what permissions existed, and permissions turned out to be a very unsatisfying thing to show a customer. The proxy also gave us something unplanned and more useful day to day, which is a picture of which tables humans read by hand. Two of the top five turned out to be things people were querying because a report was missing, and we built the report instead.

The internal support console masks personal fields until an agent asks for them. Full payment instrument details, date of birth, and the complete street address render as dots with a reveal control next to each, and using that control writes a row to `support_field_reveals` with the agent, the customer, the field and the ticket the agent has open. There is no approval step and the reveal is instant, which is deliberate: an agent on a call cannot wait for a second person, and a control that gets in the way of the job gets routed around. What changes behaviour is that the reveal is attributable and that agents know their reveal counts are visible to their team lead. The volume dropped by roughly two thirds in the first month after we turned it on, and nothing about the job got harder, which tells you most of that access had been habit rather than need. The design came out of a review that asked what a curious employee could see about a public figure who happened to be a customer. The answer at the time was everything, silently, and the fix that mattered was not restriction but attribution.

The BI tool holds a single database credential and that credential is a read-only role on the reporting replica, with no grants at all on the primary. Two separate incidents pushed us here. A dashboard with a badly written filter ran a sequential scan over the events table during a Monday morning peak and added noticeable latency to checkout, which is the ordinary argument for keeping analytical load off the writer. The second was worse and less obvious: the tool supports a feature where a dashboard can run arbitrary SQL supplied at view time, and somebody demonstrated that a saved query with a parameter could be coaxed into a statement the author had not intended. On a read-only role against a replica the ceiling on that is a slow query. On the primary it would not have been. The role also has `statement_timeout` set to thirty seconds at the role level rather than in the tool's configuration, because configuration in the tool is editable by anyone with an admin seat there, and we did not want the safety property to depend on the settings of a product we do not control.

Deprovisioning is driven by the HR system rather than by anyone remembering to do it. A nightly sync reads the employment feed and, for any record whose status has moved to terminated, disables the identity provider account, revokes active sessions, removes group memberships, and files a ticket listing the systems that need a human to finish the job because they have no API worth using. The manager's checklist still exists but it is now a reconciliation aid, not the mechanism. The change followed a routine sample where we picked five people who had left in the previous year and checked what they could still reach. Three of the five still had a working account somewhere: two in a vendor tool bought by a single team on a card, one in the source control organisation because their invitation had been to a personal address that the checklist never mentioned. None of them had done anything. The uncomfortable part was that the checklist had been completed and signed in all three cases, because the checklist only ever covered the systems whoever wrote it happened to know about, and it was two years old.

Every request for elevated access is filed on the same short form and every grant carries an expiry date chosen by the requester. The form asks four things: what you need to reach, what you are trying to accomplish, whether a report or an existing tool would do instead, and the date you expect to be finished. That last field cannot be left blank and cannot be set to never, and the grant is written with that date attached so it lapses on its own. People routinely pick a fortnight for something that turns out to take a day, and that is fine, because the failure mode we care about is not a grant that is slightly too long but a grant that outlives its purpose by years. Renewals are cheap and are approved by the same person in the same channel, so nobody has an incentive to inflate the estimate. The question about existing tools does more work than we expected. Roughly a quarter of requests get answered without a grant at all, usually by pointing at a report the requester did not know existed, and a handful have turned into small tools because the same request kept arriving.

The query proxy refuses to return more than five thousand rows from any table in the customer or payments schemas to an interactive session, and it will not serve a statement containing COPY TO at all. Exports above that ceiling go through `tools/data_export.py`, which requires a ticket reference, writes the file to a bucket with a seven-day lifecycle rule instead of to the requester's laptop, and notifies the owning team. The distinction we are drawing is between looking something up and taking a copy. A support engineer reading one customer's order history is routine and should stay frictionless; the same engineer pulling every order from the last quarter into a spreadsheet is a different act with different consequences, and until this existed the two were indistinguishable to us. The specific event was a departing employee who ran a broad SELECT into a CSV on their last week. We caught it, it was not malicious, and they deleted it when asked. But the reason we caught it was that someone happened to be watching a dashboard, which is not a control.

Sharing your screen while a production console is open, in any meeting with anyone outside the team, needs a second engineer present who has agreed to watch the screen rather than the conversation. It sounds like theatre and it is not. Two things go wrong in demos. The first is that a console window shows real customer records to whoever happens to be in the call, including vendors, candidates and people from other companies, and the presenter is concentrating on explaining something rather than on what is visible behind the dialog they just closed. The second is that a person narrating while typing runs commands they would not run while thinking, and we have one incident where a demonstration of a maintenance script executed it against the wrong environment because the presenter was talking through what the flags meant instead of reading them. The watcher's job is narrow: say something when customer data is visible, and say something before a destructive command runs. Recording such a session is separately forbidden, because a recording of a console outlives everyone's memory of what was on it and ends up in a shared drive that nobody reviews.

Group memberships are defined in the infrastructure repository and applied by the pipeline, and the cloud console's user management pages are read-only for everyone including the platform team. A change to who is in a group is therefore a pull request with a reviewer, a diff, and a permanent record of who asked and who agreed, rather than a click that leaves nothing behind but a line in an audit stream nobody reads. Click-driven changes had two problems we could never solve. They drifted, because someone would add a person in a hurry during an incident and the intent was never written down, so the state of the world diverged from anything you could reason about. And they were unreviewable in practice, since the audit stream tells you a membership changed but not why, and by the time anyone asks, the reason lives in one person's memory. Making the repository the source of truth means drift is detectable by definition: the plan runs on a schedule and anything applied out of band shows up as a diff the next morning. The cost is that an urgent grant during an incident takes a few minutes longer, which we decided we could live with, and the break-glass path exists for the case where we cannot.

Renewal is automatic, overlapping, and never requires a restart. `cert-manager` in the `platform-system` namespace holds a `Certificate` resource per hostname and begins the ACME order when the current leaf has thirty days of life left, which on a ninety-day certificate leaves two months of slack. The new material is written into the same Kubernetes secret, and because the edge proxy watches that secret and reloads its TLS configuration in place, connections in flight are unaffected and no pod is replaced. The overlap is the part people get wrong: the old certificate stays valid throughout, so at every instant there is a working chain, and the cutover is the proxy picking up a file rather than a coordinated swap. Verification is DNS-01 against a delegated zone, chosen over HTTP-01 so that wildcards work and so renewal does not depend on the ingress path being healthy, which matters because the times you most need to renew are the times something else is broken. `certificate_expiry_seconds` is scraped from the proxy itself rather than from cert-manager's status and pages at twenty-one days remaining, because we once had a controller reporting a successful renewal while the proxy served the old file. All of this replaced a calendar reminder and a manual upload, which failed at three in the morning on a wildcard nobody had been assigned.

Traffic between services inside the cluster is mutually authenticated, not merely encrypted. Each workload gets an identity from the mesh's own certificate authority, presents it on every connection, and the receiving side checks it against an authorisation policy that names the specific callers allowed to reach that service. The policies live beside the service's Helm values so the list of legitimate callers is reviewed with the code that serves them. What we were buying is not confidentiality on the wire, which the network already gave us, but the ability to say no. Before this, anything with a pod IP could call anything else, which meant an internal tool with a template injection bug could reach the ledger service's write endpoints, and the only thing preventing it was that nobody had tried. The identity-based check also survives the thing network policy does not, namely a workload moving to a different node or a different address range mid-incident. The cost is real and we accept it: a new caller cannot simply start calling, someone has to add it to a policy, and roughly once a month somebody debugs a permission denial for ten minutes before realising that is the system working.

The public load balancer terminates the customer's TLS session and opens a fresh one to the backend rather than passing the original through. Terminating at the edge is what lets us do the things that need plaintext: routing on path, rate limiting per API key, request logging with a correlation identifier, and stripping the handful of headers that customers occasionally send by accident. Re-encrypting on the inside leg means the traffic crossing the VPC is still protected, with the backend presenting an internally issued certificate that the balancer verifies against the private root. We deliberately did not choose passthrough. It moves policy enforcement into every service, which is the arrangement we had before the gateway existed and which produced four different implementations of API key validation with three different bugs. We also did not choose plaintext on the inside leg, which was the shape for about a year, because a VPC is a trust boundary only until somebody peers it, attaches a transit gateway, or runs a third-party agent inside it, and all three of those have happened here without the network diagram being redrawn.

Private keys for workload certificates are generated inside the pod that will use them and never leave it. The workload creates the key in memory, sends a signing request to the internal authority, receives the signed leaf back, and the key material exists only in that process for the lifetime of that pod. Nothing writes it to a volume, nothing puts it in a secrets store, and consequently there is no copy for anyone to steal, no backup that quietly retains it, and no rotation problem for the key itself because a restart produces a new one. The previous design generated key pairs centrally and distributed them, which meant a single store held every workload's private key, and losing that store would have meant reissuing everything we run while assuming an attacker could impersonate all of it. It also meant the store's audit log became the only evidence of who had read what, and nobody was reading that log. The property that makes this workable is that a certificate is cheap to issue and short-lived, so losing the key on a pod restart costs nothing. When a key is expensive to replace, people copy it, and once it is copied you cannot say where it is.

Every image built from our base layers carries the internal root certificate in the system trust store, installed at `/etc/ssl/certs/aldercross-internal-root.pem` and registered with the distribution's trust tooling during the base image build. Applications therefore verify internal endpoints with their language's default trust configuration and no code goes near a custom trust path. The reason this is a rule rather than a convenience is what happened without it. Services that could not verify the internal authority worked around it individually, and the workarounds were exactly what you would expect: an environment variable disabling verification, a request library configured with `verify=False`, and in one case a wrapper function used across a whole codebase that silently swallowed certificate errors. Each was added under deadline pressure by someone who intended to fix it properly. Two survived for over a year. Putting the root in the image removes the motive, because the correct thing is now also the path of least effort. A test in the base image pipeline connects to an internal endpoint with an unmodified client and fails the build if verification does not succeed, so a change that breaks the trust store is caught before anything ships on it.

The edge refuses anything below TLS 1.2, and the cipher list is an explicit allowlist in `services/gateway/tls_profile.yaml` rather than whatever the library defaults to. Renegotiation is off, compression is off, and the ordering prefers the forward-secret suites. Getting to that configuration took a customer negotiation rather than a technical decision, because two integrators were still calling us from an application platform that could not speak anything newer than TLS 1.0. We gave them a nine-month notice, published the exact date, sent a monthly reminder listing the connection counts we were still seeing from their key, and moved them to a temporary hostname with the older profile for the final month so the cutover on the main endpoint could happen on schedule. Both finished before the deadline. The reason we did not simply keep the old suites available is that a protocol version is not negotiated by the honest client alone: leaving TLS 1.0 enabled means an attacker who can influence the handshake can ask for it, so the presence of the old option weakens every connection and not only the ones that use it.

Client certificates for partner callbacks are issued by hand and we have decided not to automate it. There are eleven of them, one per partner that signs its webhook deliveries to us with a certificate rather than a shared secret, and each issuance involves a person on their side sending a signing request through a channel we have agreed with them in advance and confirming the fingerprint on a call. That is slow and it is meant to be. The whole value of the arrangement is that we know which organisation is on the other end, and an automated issuance path means whatever proves identity to the automation becomes the real credential, which for most of these partners would be an email address. The manual step is also where the paperwork happens: the contact list gets confirmed, the expiry goes on a shared calendar with two owners, and the partner tells us which of their systems will present it. We have exactly one rule beyond that, which is that an expiring partner certificate is our problem to chase and not theirs, because the outage lands on our customers either way and blaming the partner has never once shortened it.

The legacy invoicer is the one host where a certificate swap still costs a maintenance window. It runs a bundled web server that reads its keypair once at process start from `/opt/invoicer/conf/ssl/`, has no reload signal that actually rereads the file despite what its manual claims, and sits behind a fixed IP that two banking partners have allowlisted, so it cannot be replaced with a new instance behind a name. The procedure is written down in `runbooks/invoicer-cert-swap.md` and takes about twenty minutes: announce in the status page the day before, copy the new bundle onto the host, verify the chain with `openssl verify` against the partner-supplied root, stop the service, move the files into place, start it, then confirm both partners' health probes are green before closing the window. It is scheduled on a Sunday morning because that is when the settlement file is not moving. This is a genuine exception and it is documented as one, kept alive only because the machine is scheduled for decommission with the billing cutover. Nobody has been asked to make it prettier in the meantime and nobody should be.

We watch the public certificate transparency feed for anything issued against our domains and alert on entries we did not ask for. The check runs hourly, compares what the logs show against the set of hostnames we know we manage, and posts to the security channel on a mismatch. It has fired for real twice. Once a marketing agency running a campaign microsite stood up a subdomain with their own hosting provider, which was harmless but was also the first anyone internally heard of it. The other time a hostname appeared under a certificate we could not attribute at all, and the two hours we spent establishing that it was a former employee's abandoned side project on a personal account were two hours of genuine anxiety. Both cases make the same point: the interesting failure is not somebody attacking us, it is us losing track of our own surface. A subdomain we do not know about is one nobody patches, nobody monitors, and nobody thinks to remove, and it will still be pointing at whatever it pointed at long after the person who created it has moved on. The feed is the only source that tells you about it without your cooperation.

Audit records are written into a cloud account that the production workloads cannot read, cannot delete from, and cannot administer. The producing accounts hold a role whose only permission is PutObject into the `sec-archive` bucket, with no ListBucket, GetObject or DeleteObject anywhere in the policy, and the bucket itself has object lock in compliance mode with a seven-year retention. Nobody in engineering, the platform team included, has a standing role in that account. The reason is the one that matters for evidence: if a person with production administrator rights can also delete or alter the record of what they did, the record proves nothing about that person. Encrypting the logs, making the bucket append-only in the same account, alerting on deletions: all of those leave the same principal on both sides of the boundary, and an audit trail has to be trustworthy precisely when the operator is not. The event that settled it was mundane, not malicious. A cost cleanup script written to remove old build artifacts matched a log group by prefix and deleted eleven months of API audit history in the middle of an afternoon, and nobody noticed for a week. It was recoverable only because a partial export happened to exist. It also answers the question an auditor always asks, who could have changed this: two named people who hold the break-glass path into the archive account.

Application logs are kept for fourteen days in the searchable index and then dropped entirely. There is no cold tier, no glacier copy, and no exception process, and the retention is set on the index template rather than on individual streams so nobody can quietly extend theirs. The number came from measuring how old a log line was when someone actually opened it. Ninety-five percent of queries in a sampled month touched data less than three days old, and the tail beyond two weeks was almost entirely people trying to reconstruct something a metric or an audit record would have answered better. Meanwhile the index was the third largest line on the infrastructure bill and was growing faster than traffic, because every new service arrived with debug logging left on. Fourteen days is deliberately short enough to be uncomfortable, which pushes teams to emit a metric or an event for anything they will need to answer in a month. It also caps our exposure: a log line containing something it should not is a mistake with a bounded lifetime rather than a permanent record. The trade is real and we say so out loud, since a slow-burning bug that surfaces after three weeks is harder to investigate now than it was before.

An action that requires an audit record does not commit until the record is durable. In practice that means the audit write and the business write share a transaction where they share a database, and where they do not, the service writes the audit row first, gets an acknowledgement, and only then performs the effect. It is the ordering that matters, not the atomicity: a record of something that did not happen is a confusing but harmless artifact that investigators can reconcile, while an effect with no record is invisible and unrecoverable. The previous design queued audit records asynchronously for throughput, and it worked until the queue backed up during a partial outage and roughly forty minutes of permission grants and refunds were performed with no trace, precisely during the window we most wanted to review afterwards. Asynchronous audit fails exactly when you need it, because the pressure that breaks the queue is the same pressure that produces the interesting actions. We pay for this with latency on the affected endpoints, measured at a few milliseconds for the shared-transaction cases and around twenty for the cross-service ones, and that ceiling is why the set of audited actions is a deliberate list rather than everything.

Every audit row carries the same five fields regardless of which service wrote it: the acting principal in a canonical form, the request identifier that ties it to the originating call, the target resource, the action, and the wall clock time in UTC with millisecond precision. The schema is defined once in `libs/audit/schema.py` and services cannot add columns, only structured detail inside a `context` object, which keeps the common fields queryable across every producer. The canonical principal form is the field that took longest to agree. A human acting through the console, a human acting through an API key they own, an internal service acting on its own behalf, and an internal service acting for a user all needed to be distinguishable, and the earliest version flattened the last two into the service name, which made an entire class of question unanswerable. Now the row carries both the immediate actor and the originating one when they differ. The request identifier is the other load-bearing choice, because most real investigations start from a customer complaint rather than from a record, and being able to pivot from one HTTP request to every audited effect it caused turns an afternoon of correlation into a single query.

Each morning a job walks the previous day's audit objects, computes a hash chain over them in order, and posts the resulting digest and the object count into the security channel. Anyone can recompute it from the archive and compare. That is the entire mechanism and it is deliberately simple, because the property we want is that a tampered or missing record becomes visible without anyone having to trust our own tooling to report honestly. The digest is also mailed to an address outside our infrastructure, which sounds paranoid until you consider that a digest stored only alongside the thing it protects can be rewritten by whoever rewrote the thing. Publishing it somewhere we do not administer makes yesterday's value fixed. We adopted it after a compliance review asked how we would detect modification and the honest answer was that we would not, since our confidence rested entirely on nobody having the access to try. The check has never found tampering. It has twice found gaps: once when a producer was misconfigured after a namespace rename and stopped writing for most of a day, and once when a retry loop wrote the same batch three times, which the count made obvious immediately.

Interactive sessions on production hosts are recorded in full, keystrokes and output, and kept for one year. The bastion runs the session through a recorder that writes to the same archive as the audit stream, and there is a visible notice on connect saying so, because recording people without telling them is both wrong and, in two of the jurisdictions we employ in, unlawful. The recording exists for reconstruction rather than for supervision, and we say that explicitly and have never used one in a performance conversation. What it is good for is the morning after an incident, when four people were typing in three terminals and the timeline in the incident document is a best guess assembled from memory and channel messages. Having the actual sequence has twice changed our understanding of what caused what, in both cases exonerating the change everyone assumed was responsible. The recordings are also the reason the interactive path can stay as open as it is; a tightly restricted shell would slow down every incident, whereas a recorded shell keeps the speed and moves the control to after the fact. Redaction is imperfect and we know it: the recorder masks obvious secret patterns in the stream, but anything typed into a prompt is captured, so credentials are never entered into a recorded session.

Personal fields never enter the audit stream in readable form. The target of an action is recorded as an internal identifier, and where a human-meaningful value genuinely has to be present, such as the email address that a change of contact details was made to, it is stored as a keyed hash and the plaintext stays in the operational database where the retention rules and the erasure tooling can reach it. The reason is a collision between two requirements we cannot compromise on separately. The audit archive is immutable for years by design, and a customer has the right to have their personal data erased. Those are irreconcilable if the archive holds their details, and the resolution everyone reaches eventually is to make sure the immutable record contains references rather than content. We reached it the hard way, during the first erasure request that turned out to touch audit data, where the legal answer took a fortnight to arrive and the engineering answer would have been to break the immutability guarantee. The hash is keyed rather than plain so that an investigator with a specific address can still confirm whether it appears, which preserves the one investigative use that mattered without making the archive a lookup table for anyone who obtains it.

Investigators do not query the raw audit objects. A nightly job compacts the previous day's newline-delimited JSON into partitioned Parquet under a `dt=` prefix and registers it in the catalogue as `audit.events`, and every dashboard and ad-hoc query reads that table instead. The compaction is a straight transformation with no filtering, so the Parquet is a view of the archive rather than a second copy of the truth, and the raw objects remain the authoritative record. This exists because the raw layout is optimised for writing and is miserable to read: hundreds of thousands of small objects per day, one per batch flush, and a question like which principals touched a given customer last quarter meant scanning tens of gigabytes and waiting twenty minutes. The same query against the compacted table finishes in a few seconds and costs a fraction of a cent, which changed how people use the data. The measurable effect was that ad-hoc audit queries went from a handful a month, all of them from compliance, to a routine step in ordinary incident review, because it stopped being an errand and became something you could do while talking.

An alarm watches the rate of incoming audit records and fires when it falls below a floor derived from the same weekday and hour a week earlier. Alerting on absence rather than on error is the point. Every failure mode we have actually experienced in this pipeline was silent: a producer that stopped emitting after a library upgrade changed a default, a role whose trust policy was tightened in a way that broke one writer, a namespace rename that left the exporter pointed at nothing. In none of those did anything log an error loudly enough for a human to see, because the writers were fire-and-forget by design and the collector cannot miss what it never receives. The floor is derived from last week rather than from a fixed threshold because our volume follows the business day closely enough that a static number is either useless at night or noisy at noon. It is a low bar deliberately, catching a producer disappearing rather than a modest dip, since we would rather have an alarm that never cries wolf than a precise one people learn to ignore. The alarm routes to the security oncall and not to the service owner, because the service is generally fine and it is the record that is missing.

Product events identify a person by `user_ref`, an opaque per-tenant identifier, and carry no address, phone number or name in any field. The collector enforces it rather than trusting authors: `schemas/events/*.json` is validated in CI against a rule that rejects any property whose name or example value matches the contact-detail patterns, and at runtime the collector drops a payload that fails the same check and increments a counter instead of forwarding it. Resolving a reference to an actual person happens only in the warehouse, by joining `analytics.user_ref_map`, which lives in a restricted schema with its own grant list. Three things forced it. Payloads fan out to places the author never considered: a third-party analytics product, a debugging log with fourteen-day retention, the warehouse, and each became a copy of the customer's address our erasure tooling did not know about. The second is that events are permanent by nature, so a personal detail written into one is written there forever. The third was the specific incident: a support engineer filtered a dashboard by a customer's address to debug a complaint, the filter value travelled to the vendor as query metadata, and we spent a week establishing what had been retained and where. An opaque reference makes the join a deliberate, grantable act instead of an accident of payload design.

Event names are `object_verb` in the past tense, lowercase with underscores: `invoice_issued`, `shipment_delayed`, `session_started`. Object first is the part people get wrong and the part that matters, because a name list sorted alphabetically then groups everything about invoices together, which is how anyone actually reads the catalogue when they are trying to find out whether the event they want already exists. Past tense encodes the other rule: an event records something that has happened and is therefore immutable, so `invoice_issue` or `issue_invoice` would be a command, and commands belong on the queue rather than in the event stream. A test in the schema pipeline checks the pattern and rejects new names that fail, with a small allowlist for the dozen legacy names that predate the convention and are not worth renaming. The convention came from a period when we had `user_signup`, `signed_up`, `UserRegistered` and `registration_complete` in the catalogue, at least three of which fired for the same action, and every funnel analysis started with a fortnight of establishing which one to trust. Renaming an event is a breaking change handled the same way as a schema change, with both names emitted for one full release.

Browser and mobile clients send events to `collect.aldercross.com`, a first-party endpoint we run, and never to a vendor domain directly. The collector validates, enriches and forwards onward to whatever destinations are configured. The immediate reason was that a growing share of traffic never arrived: content blockers and the tracker lists shipped in mainstream browsers dropped requests to vendor hostnames, and the loss was not random, it correlated with exactly the technically literate segment whose behaviour we most needed to understand. Measured against server-side records of the same actions, we were missing about a fifth of sessions on desktop. The second reason is control. With a collector in the middle we can change destinations without shipping a client release, drop a field that turns out to be sensitive without waiting for app store review, and replay a day of raw events into a new destination when somebody's pipeline loses data. The third is that vendor scripts running on our pages get to see whatever is on the page, and a first-party endpoint plus a payload we construct ourselves means the browser sends what we decided to send and nothing else.

The schema registry refuses a change that would break existing consumers. Adding an optional field is allowed and deploys without ceremony; removing a field, renaming one, narrowing a type or making an optional field required are all rejected by `tools/schema_gate.py` in the producer's pipeline, which compares the proposed schema against the registered version and fails the build with the specific incompatibility named. Getting past the gate requires registering a new major version of the event and emitting both until the consumers have moved, which the registry tracks by recording which consumer groups have read which version in the last thirty days. The gate exists because events are read by code that was written before the change and that nobody is going to update in the same pull request. A field rename in the checkout stream once broke a revenue model and two operational dashboards, and the person who made the change had no way of knowing they existed. Producers cannot be expected to know their consumers; that is the entire ergonomics problem of an event bus. So the compatibility rule is mechanical and the registry, not a human, is what remembers.

Page view events are sampled at the collector at ten percent, with the sampling decision keyed on a hash of the session identifier so that a sampled-in session is complete rather than a sequence of holes. Every other event type is unsampled. Two properties made this safe. Sampling on the session means funnels still work, because a session that appears at all appears throughout, and a partially sampled session would silently understate every step after the first. And the retained factor is written into the row as `sample_weight`, so aggregate counts are reconstructed by summing weights rather than rows, which puts the correction in one place instead of in every query someone writes. Page views were about eighty percent of ingest volume and close to nothing of the analytical value, since almost every question people asked was about actions rather than about navigation. The saving was around eleven thousand a year in warehouse storage and load costs. We revisit the rate annually and have raised it once, temporarily, during a redesign where the navigation itself was the thing under study, which is the correct way to use a knob like this.

Every event carries two timestamps: `occurred_at`, stamped by the client when the thing happened, and `received_at`, stamped by the collector when it arrived, both in UTC. Analysis uses `occurred_at`; pipeline monitoring and partitioning use `received_at`. Keeping both is not redundancy, it is the only way to survive client clocks, which are wrong far more often than anyone expects. In a sampled week, roughly one in four hundred mobile sessions carried a clock skewed by more than an hour, and a handful were off by years because the device had been factory reset and had not yet synchronised. If you partition on client time, those events land in partitions from a decade ago or in the future and quietly break every incremental job downstream. If you analyse on server time, you attribute an action to whenever the phone next found connectivity, which for an offline-capable app is meaningless. The collector also writes `clock_skew_seconds` as the difference between the two, and events beyond a day of skew are corrected onto server time with a flag rather than dropped, since the alternative is silently discarding exactly the offline sessions the mobile team cares most about.

The consent state that was in force at the moment of collection is stamped onto the event itself and travels with it forever. It is not looked up later against a current preference table, and that distinction is the whole design. Consent is a fact about a point in time: whether this person had agreed to this category of processing when this event was captured. A lookup at query time answers a different question, namely what they think today, which gives you the wrong answer in both directions. It retroactively legitimises data collected before agreement, and it retroactively invalidates analysis that was correct when it ran. The stamped state also means downstream consumers can filter without needing access to the preference store at all, so the marketing destination simply never receives rows whose stamp does not permit it, and nobody has to remember to apply a rule. We arrived at this after a regulator's questionnaire asked us to demonstrate the basis for a specific processing activity on a specific past date, and the honest answer was that we could show the current state and the change log and would have had to reconstruct the rest by hand.

The collector truncates the source address before the event is written anywhere, dropping the final octet for IPv4 and keeping only the first forty-eight bits for IPv6. Geographic and network lookups happen first, in memory, at the moment of receipt, so the row that lands downstream carries country, region and connection type but not an address that identifies a household. Nothing keeps the full value, including the collector's own access log, which is configured with the same truncation. The precision we gave up is smaller than it sounds. City-level geolocation from a full address is unreliable for a meaningful fraction of traffic anyway, and every analytical use we had, splitting adoption by country, spotting a regional outage, sizing a market, works identically on the truncated form. The one use that genuinely needed the full value was abuse investigation, and that now happens at the edge where the request is still live, which is a better place for it. What tipped the decision was noticing that the full address had leaked into a vendor destination through a field we had forgotten was included by default, which made it clear that the only reliable control is not to have the value in the pipeline at all.

The mobile SDK never sends an event immediately. Events accumulate in a small on-device queue and flush when the batch reaches a size threshold, when a timer expires, or when the app goes to the background, whichever comes first, and a failed flush retries with exponential backoff and jitter until the queue's cap is reached, at which point the oldest events are discarded first. The design is entirely about the network the app is actually on. A per-event request on a congested mobile connection costs a radio wake-up each time, which is the single largest avoidable battery drain in an app like ours, and it produces exactly the traffic pattern that fails when a stadium full of people share a cell. Backoff with jitter matters for our side rather than theirs: without jitter, an outage ends with every device in the installed base retrying in the same second, which is a self-inflicted denial of service, and we caused one that way. Discarding oldest first is the one choice people argue with, and the reasoning is that recent events describe the session someone is currently having, which is what an investigation needs, whereas the oldest ones are usually from a session already understood.

An erasure request is executed by one command against a registry of stores, never by hand. Once the requester's identity is confirmed by support, the ticket moves to the platform queue and an engineer runs `tools/erasure.py --subject <id> --ticket <ref>`, which reads `compliance/erasure_targets.yaml` and walks every registered store in order: the primary Postgres schemas, the warehouse, the search index, the object store holding uploaded documents, the two vendor systems that have delete APIs, and the support desk. Each target reports a row count and the run writes an evidence record into `erasure_runs`, which is what we produce if anyone asks us to demonstrate completion. Three rules make the rest work. Anything the registry does not know about is not erased, so adding a store that holds subject data means adding it to the file in the same change, checked by a test against the databases the platform account can see. Financial records are exempted rather than deleted: ledger rows stay, with the personal columns overwritten, because we are required to keep them for seven years. And backups are handled by expiry rather than surgery, so a subject can still appear in a snapshot until that snapshot ages out, which is written into the response we send. The trigger was a request that missed the search index, and the customer found their own name in an autocomplete two weeks later.

Every table that holds customer-derived data declares a retention window in `compliance/retention.yaml`, and a nightly job enforces it. The declaration is three fields: the table, the column that carries the clock, and the window expressed in days. A table with no entry fails the schema pipeline, which is the only reason the file is complete, since the honest version of this in most companies is a document written once and never updated. Windows range from thirty days for raw request traces to seven years for anything the ledger touches. The interesting part is the column choice rather than the number. For an order the clock starts at fulfilment, not at creation, because a cancelled order that sits unfulfilled for a year should not be aged out from underneath a dispute. For a support conversation it starts at the last message rather than the first. Getting those wrong deletes data while it is still in use, which we did once with an early version of the job and a partially populated timestamp column, losing several months of attachment metadata on tickets that were still open. The job now refuses to act on any table where more than a small fraction of rows have a null clock, and the whole run is dry-run by default with a separate flag to apply.

Closing an account in the product suspends the tenant rather than removing anything. The workspace goes read-only immediately, integrations stop firing, seats are released so billing stops on the next cycle, and a banner offers reactivation for thirty days after which the tenant is simply marked closed and stops appearing in any interface. Nothing is destroyed at any point in that flow, which surprises people until they see the numbers: about one closed workspace in nine comes back, most of them within a fortnight, and almost every one is the same story of an administrator closing the wrong workspace or a team that discovers a report they still needed. When closure destroyed data immediately, each of those was an escalation and a restore from backup, which is expensive, slow and occasionally impossible. Suspension turns a crisis into a click. An erasure request is a separate mechanism entirely and is not what this flow is for; closure is a billing and access state, not a privacy action, and support are trained to say so explicitly when a customer asks for one and means the other.

A subject access request produces a single zip generated by `tools/subject_export.py`, containing one JSON file per source system plus a manifest listing what was included and, importantly, what was deliberately excluded and why. The archive is uploaded to a bucket with a fourteen-day lifecycle and delivered as a link that requires the customer to authenticate, never as an email attachment, because an attachment goes wherever the mailbox goes and we have no way to withdraw it. The manifest turned out to matter more than the data. Our first few exports were a flat dump, and the follow-up questions were always about absence rather than content, along the lines of why there was nothing about a particular interaction, and answering them meant a fresh investigation each time. Now the manifest names every store consulted and states plainly when a store held nothing. Derived analytics aggregates are excluded and the manifest says so, since a bucketed count that includes one person among thousands is not their personal data and including it would be both misleading and enormous. The whole run takes about four minutes and the slow part is the object store, which we have not bothered to optimise because the deadline is measured in weeks.

Support replies to privacy correspondence come from a fixed set of approved macros and agents do not compose these messages freely. There are five: acknowledgement, a request for identity confirmation, a completion notice, a notice that the deadline is being extended with the reason, and a refusal explaining the narrow grounds on which we decline. They were written with counsel and any edit to them goes back through counsel, which is unusual for us and deliberate here. The reason is that a well-meaning agent writing in their own words makes commitments we cannot keep. In the months before the macros existed we had agents promise complete removal from backups, promise a turnaround faster than the process allows, and in one case volunteer a description of our internal systems that was both wrong and more detail than anybody needed. None of them did anything unreasonable; they were being helpful under time pressure about a subject where the precise wording carries legal weight. The macros also carry an internal note that never goes to the customer, telling the agent exactly what the next step is and who owns it, which removed most of the ambiguity that produced the improvised replies in the first place.

Test fixtures are generated, never captured. `tests/fixtures/` contains factory definitions that build records from a seeded generator, and a check in the pipeline greps for anything resembling a real address, a live payment token prefix or one of our internal customer identifier formats, failing the build if it finds one. The check exists because copying a real record is the fastest way to reproduce a bug and therefore the thing an engineer will do at four in the afternoon with a customer waiting. We found a genuine customer's full order history sitting in a test file that had been in the repository for two years, added while debugging exactly that kind of report and never cleaned up. It had been read by everyone who ever ran the suite, copied into every fork, and captured in every CI log. Deleting the file does not fix it either, since the history keeps it, so we had to rewrite that part of the repository, which is a bad afternoon nobody wants twice. The factories are now good enough that reaching for real data is rarely tempting, and where a bug genuinely depends on a specific shape, the practice is to write a fixture that reproduces the shape with invented values and put the customer reference in the ticket rather than in the tree.

Tables that support soft deletion are never queried directly by application code. Each one has a companion view, `<table>_live`, that applies the `deleted_at IS NULL` predicate, permissions grant SELECT on the view rather than the base table, and the ORM models are bound to the views. Getting at deleted rows requires the base table and an explicit grant, so it is possible and it is visible. Relying on callers to add the predicate does not work at scale, and the failure is silent in the worst direction: forgetting it shows deleted records to somebody, which is a customer-visible bug and occasionally a privacy one. We had three of them within a year, all in reporting code written by people who had never been told the convention existed, including a monthly summary that counted removed users as active for four months and made the retention numbers we were reporting to the board quietly wrong. A view makes the safe path the default and the unsafe path a deliberate act. The cost is that a couple of hot queries lost an index-only scan and needed a partial index to get it back, which is a fair price for removing an entire category of mistake.

Every external processor that touches customer data appears in a register with the categories of data it receives, the contractual paperwork on file, the internal owner, and a review date. Adding a vendor to the register is part of procurement rather than a separate compliance exercise, so the register cannot drift from reality by very much, and the review date forces a conversation about whether a tool bought for a six-week experiment is still in use two years later. Several were not. The register began as a legal requirement and turned out to be more useful operationally than we expected, because it is the only place that answers the question of who else has this data when something goes wrong at a vendor. When a widely used support product disclosed a breach, the register told us in minutes which of our data had ever been sent there, who owned the relationship, and what the contract said about notification. Without it that would have been a day of asking around, and the notification clock does not pause while you work out your own exposure. The awkward finding on first assembling it was a handful of tools nobody could account for, all bought on somebody's card for a good reason and never mentioned again.

When an enterprise contract ends, the wind-down follows `runbooks/tenant-offboarding.md`, which is a commercial procedure rather than a privacy one. The sequence is fixed: confirm the end date with the account team, disable outbound integrations first so we stop writing into the customer's systems, generate the contractual handover extract in the agreed format and deliver it through the channel named in the contract, then move the tenant to a dormant tier that keeps the data intact and stops all billing. The data stays for the tail period the contract specifies, usually ninety days, because that is the window in which a customer discovers they need one more export and because renewals happen late more often than anyone admits. Two details are there because of specific bad experiences. Integrations go first because on one occasion we kept pushing records into a departed customer's warehouse for a month after their access ended, which was awkward to explain. And the extract is generated before the tenant goes dormant, since generating it afterwards means reactivating, which needs an approval nobody is around to give on the day it turns out to be needed.

We looked at change-data-capture into the warehouse twice and turned it down both times, most recently last autumn, and the load still runs once a night starting at 02:30 UTC. Three reasons, in the order they actually weighed. Correctness first: the ledger closes the previous day at 02:00 and adjustments land right up to that boundary, so any figure computed before the close is provisional, and a streaming warehouse would have made provisional numbers continuously available on dashboards that people quote in meetings. Every finance conversation would then start by establishing which version of a number someone holds, which is what the nightly boundary removes. Second, cost: the managed connector prices per row changed, and at our volume the quote came to roughly nine times the nightly extract's compute, for data that nobody reads before morning. Third, operations: a streaming pipeline is a service that pages, and analytics has no oncall rotation and does not want one, whereas a failed batch is a morning ticket and a re-run that finishes before anyone is affected. The one exception is the operations dashboard the fulfilment team watches, which queries the read replica directly and is documented as not being a warehouse figure. We will revisit this if a business process genuinely needs sub-hourly analytical data; wanting a dashboard to feel fresher has never been sufficient.

Every stage of the load can be run again over the same window without producing a different result. Extracts write to a staging table keyed by the source primary key and the batch date, and the merge into the raw layer is a `MERGE` on that key rather than an insert, so a re-run overwrites rather than duplicates. The batch date is passed in explicitly instead of being read from the clock, which is the detail that makes a manual re-run of a failed night actually reproduce that night. Before this, recovering from a partial failure meant working out how far the job had got and hand-deleting rows, an operation performed at seven in the morning by whoever noticed, and we duplicated an entire day of order lines that way and did not catch it until a monthly revenue figure came out visibly wrong. Idempotence also makes backfills ordinary: pointing the same job at a range of past dates is the supported way to rebuild after a schema fix, rather than a special script written for the occasion. The cost is that the merge is slower than an append and needs the key to be genuinely unique in the source, which turned out not to be true for two legacy tables and had to be fixed there first.

All transformation models build in a single scheduled run with the dependency graph derived from the references between them, rather than as a set of independently scheduled jobs. There is one entry point, one run identifier, and one place to look when something is wrong. The previous arrangement gave each team its own schedule, which produced the failure everyone eventually gets: a downstream model reading an upstream table that had not been rebuilt yet, so the output was internally consistent, plausible, and silently a day stale in one branch. Nobody detects that by looking at it. Deriving the graph from the code rather than declaring it in the scheduler is the other half, because a hand-maintained ordering drifts the moment somebody adds a reference and forgets to update it, and the failure is again invisible. With the graph derived, adding a reference reorders the run automatically. We accept two costs. The run is as slow as its longest path, currently a little over forty minutes, and a failure early in the graph blocks everything behind it, which we deliberately do not work around with partial runs because a partial run is exactly the stale-mixture problem returning through a different door.

Every warehouse session sets a query tag naming the team, the tool and the model or dashboard that issued it, and the monthly spend report is grouped by that tag. Tagging is not optional: the connection helpers in `libs/warehouse/` set it from configuration, and untagged sessions are reported as a single line that teams find embarrassing enough to fix. Attribution changed behaviour in a way that a global cost target never did. When the bill was one number owned by the platform team, the response to it being high was a meeting. When it arrived as a per-team figure with the top five queries listed, three teams found their own runaway dashboard within a week, and the largest single item turned out to be an hourly refresh on a dashboard whose owner had left, which nobody had opened in five months. Total spend fell by about a third over the following quarter with no central intervention beyond publishing the report. The tag is also useful outside billing, since it is the fastest way to identify who is running the query that is currently saturating the warehouse, which used to require guessing from the SQL.

Incremental models do not trust yesterday's boundary. Each run reprocesses the trailing three days rather than only the newest partition, replacing rows by key, which costs a modest amount of extra compute and removes an entire class of quietly wrong data. Late rows are common in our sources for ordinary reasons: a shipment scan uploaded from a handheld device that was offline in a warehouse basement, a partner file that arrives a day late, a correction posted against an order after a dispute. With a strict boundary, all of those land after their partition has been built and are never picked up, so the figure for that day stays wrong forever and gets more wrong the further back you look. We measured it before choosing the window: on the order line stream, about one and a half percent of rows arrive after their event date, ninety-nine percent of those within two days, with a thin tail beyond that. Three days covers the tail we care about. Anything later than that is handled by an explicit backfill, which is rare enough to be a manual decision, and the models are built so that a backfill of an old range does not disturb anything newer.

The extract connects to a replica provisioned for it alone, not to the primary and not to the replica the application reads from. It is a separate instance with its own subscription, sized smaller than the primary since it serves one client, and configured with a much longer `max_standby_streaming_delay` so that a long analytical scan is not cancelled by conflicting replication. That last setting is the reason it cannot share the application's replica: the application needs its replica to stay close to the primary, and the extract needs its queries not to be killed mid-scan, and those two requirements are directly opposed. We learned this by running both on one instance for a year, during which the extract failed intermittently with query conflicts, always on the largest tables, always in a way that looked like a transient error and got retried into success often enough that nobody investigated properly. Isolating it also means an unusually heavy extract, after a big backfill for example, cannot add lag to the path serving customer reads, which had happened twice and both times looked like a mysterious site slowdown until somebody thought to check what analytics was doing.

The raw layer of the warehouse is append-only. Rows arrive, are never updated, and are never deleted except by the retention job dropping whole partitions; anything that looks like a change to a source record arrives as a new row with a later ingestion stamp, and the current state is a view that takes the latest per key. Keeping history rather than the latest value is what makes the layer worth having. When a transformation turns out to have been wrong, and they are, we can rebuild from what the source actually said at the time instead of from what it says now, which is a different thing for any table whose rows get updated in place. Mutable raw data quietly destroys that: a status column that gets overwritten leaves no evidence of what the status was on the day the number was computed, so a rebuild silently produces different history and nobody can explain the discrepancy. The obvious objection is storage, and the honest answer is that the raw layer is by far the largest thing we keep and it is still a small fraction of what the warehouse costs, because the expensive part of a warehouse is compute and not bytes at rest.

Before any model builds, the run checks that each source table has received data recently enough and stops the whole run if one has not. Stopping is the deliberate part. The instinct is to carry on with what you have and flag it, and we did that for a while, which meant dashboards were built from a source that had silently stopped feeding and looked entirely normal, since a missing day at the end of a series renders as a line that has not moved rather than as an error. People made decisions from those. Failing loudly means the dashboards show yesterday's data with a visible staleness banner, which everybody understands immediately, instead of today's data that happens to be wrong in one dimension. The thresholds are per source and set from the source's own rhythm rather than a global rule, so a partner file that only arrives on weekdays does not fire every Sunday. Getting those wrong in the first weeks produced enough noise that people started ignoring the channel, which was a useful lesson about the cost of a check that cries wolf, and we spent a fortnight tuning them individually before the check earned its trust back.

The job that pushes account health figures back into the sales tool is chained to the completion of the transformation run rather than given its own schedule. It waits for the run to report success and then starts; if the run fails, the push does not happen at all and yesterday's values stay in place. Sending nothing is much better than sending something stale in this particular direction, because the numbers land in front of account managers who are on calls with customers, and there is no banner or freshness indicator in a sales tool. A field simply shows a value and the person reading it assumes it is current. We found this out when a failed transformation left a churn risk score frozen for three days and two account managers had conversations based on it, one of which was awkward. The chaining also removes a race that used to produce a partial push, where the sales tool received a subset of accounts because the job started while the model was still being rebuilt, leaving half the fields updated and half not, which is the worst of both states and is invisible from either side.

`events` is range partitioned on `occurred_at` with one partition per calendar month, managed by `pg_partman` with `premake = 3` so three future months always exist before anyone needs them. Monthly rather than daily or weekly, for reasons that are all about the numbers rather than taste. Retention on this table is expressed in months, eighteen of them, so a monthly boundary means enforcing retention is `DETACH PARTITION` followed by a drop, which is instantaneous and produces no dead tuples at all. The prior arrangement was a single table and a nightly `DELETE` over a date range; the night it fell far enough behind to remove six weeks at once it ran for over forty hours, pushed replication lag past twenty minutes and bloated the table until we scheduled a rewrite. Daily partitions were the obvious alternative and we measured them: eighteen months of daily gives well over five hundred child tables, and planning time on the common query went from under a millisecond to roughly fifteen, which matters on a table that serves a few thousand queries a second. Monthly gives eighteen. The other half is that our access pattern is naturally monthly, since almost every read is either the last few days or a named billing month, so pruning eliminates all but one or two children in either case.
