Detached partitions are archived to object storage before being dropped, which is a separate job.

The `events` primary key is a bigint identity column, not a UUID, and this was argued about at length before it was settled. UUID version four keys distribute randomly across the index, so every insert lands on a different page and the working set of the index becomes the whole index rather than its right-hand edge, which on a table taking a few thousand writes a second is the difference between a hot index that stays in memory and one that thrashes. We benchmarked it on a copy of production at the volume we had then and saw insert throughput fall by a bit over a third with random keys, with the gap widening as the table grew. The bigint also costs eight bytes rather than sixteen, which matters more in the indexes that reference it than in the table itself. The usual argument for UUIDs is that identifiers can be generated by the client without a round trip, and we grant it, which is why the externally visible identifier on this table is a separate column holding a generated string with its own unique index. Internal joins use the bigint, external references use the opaque string, and nothing exposes the sequence value in an API because a guessable identifier tells a customer how many events we process.

Any query against `events` has to constrain `occurred_at`, and there is a check that enforces it. The repository layer refuses to build a statement against this table without a time predicate, raising rather than executing, and the review guidance is that a caller who genuinely wants everything must say so with an explicit wide range so the intent is visible in the code. Unbounded queries are the single most common way this table has been made to hurt. Someone writes a support tool that counts rows matching a status, it is fast in staging where the table holds a week of data, and in production it scans a table three orders of magnitude larger and takes the connection pool with it. That has happened four times, twice from the admin interface and twice from an analytics notebook, and each time the code was obviously correct in isolation. The check is crude on purpose and does not attempt to understand whether the predicate is selective, only that one exists, because a rule an engineer can evaluate in their head is worth more than a clever one that fails in surprising ways. `statement_timeout` on the application role is the backstop underneath it.

There are no foreign keys on `events`, which surprises people reviewing the schema for the first time, and it is deliberate. The table is an append-only record of things that happened, and the entities it refers to have their own lifecycles: an order can be removed as part of an erasure request, a workspace can be deleted, an integration can be torn down, and none of those should be blocked or cascaded by the existence of a historical record. A foreign key would force one of two bad choices, either preventing the deletion or destroying history as a side effect of it. Both are wrong for a record whose entire purpose is to say what the world looked like at a moment. There is a second, more practical reason: constraint checking on a table taking sustained high write volume costs a lookup per insert per constraint, and the referenced tables are precisely the busy ones. What replaces the constraint is an orphan report rather than nothing. A job walks recent rows against their referents and reports references that never existed, which distinguishes a genuine bug from the expected case of a referent that has since been removed, and in practice it fires perhaps twice a year.

The variable part of an event lives in a `payload` column of type jsonb, alongside a `schema_version` smallint that says which shape it is in. Columns were the alternative and they do not survive contact with sixty event types whose fields overlap by perhaps a fifth; you end up with a very wide table that is mostly nulls and a migration every time somebody adds a type. The version column is what makes jsonb tolerable rather than a swamp. Readers switch on it explicitly, so an old row is parsed with the code that understood it instead of being coerced by whatever the newest parser assumes, and a producer changing a shape bumps the version rather than quietly redefining a key. Without it, the meaning of a field drifts and every query becomes a small archaeology exercise. We index the payload sparingly and on purpose: two expression indexes on the specific keys that operational queries filter by, rather than a general GIN index across everything, because a GIN index on this volume was larger than the table and slowed writes noticeably for the sake of ad-hoc queries that belong in the warehouse anyway.

Autovacuum on `events` runs with per-table settings well away from the cluster defaults: `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` is set to 0.002 with a threshold of a thousand rows, and `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` is raised so the worker is not throttled to uselessness. The default scale factor of a fifth of the table is a sensible number for a table of thousands of rows and an absurd one for a table of billions, where it means waiting for hundreds of millions of dead tuples before a vacuum starts, by which point the vacuum takes hours and the visibility map is long stale. We noticed through the symptom rather than the cause: index-only scans on the hot path stopped being index-only, and query times on the customer timeline view roughly tripled over a fortnight with no change to the code or the data volume. The freeze settings matter as much as the vacuum ones on a table this size, since a wraparound-driven emergency freeze on a partition holding hundreds of millions of rows is an unplanned, unthrottled, non-cancellable vacuum arriving at whatever time it likes, and the one we experienced arrived on a Monday morning.

Application code does not insert into the events table one row per request. Each process holds a small in-memory buffer, appends to it, and flushes on a short interval or when the buffer fills, so the database sees a multi-row insert from each process a few times a second instead of a continuous stream of single statements. The gain is not in the write itself but in everything around it: one transaction, one round trip, one set of write-ahead log records, and crucially one connection held briefly rather than a connection acquired and released per event. Connection acquisition was the actual bottleneck before this, since the pool was saturating during traffic peaks and requests were queuing to get a connection to write an event that nobody was waiting on. The accepted cost is that a process dying loses whatever is in its buffer, and we decided that is acceptable for this table specifically, because these events are operational history rather than the record of a business action. Anything that must not be lost is written in the same transaction as the thing it records, and telling those two categories apart is a design decision made per event type when it is introduced.

The primary key on the events table is a composite that includes the partition key column, not the identity column alone. This is not a design preference, it is a requirement of the database: a unique index on a partitioned table must contain every partition key column, because uniqueness is enforced per child and the planner has no way to guarantee a global constraint otherwise. People rediscover this every time they try to add a plain unique constraint and get an error that reads like a bug. The practical consequence worth knowing is that a lookup by identity alone cannot use the primary key index to prune, so it visits every child. Code paths that fetch a single row therefore pass the timestamp along with the identity, and where a caller genuinely only has the identity, such as a support tool resolving an external reference, there is a lookup table mapping it to its time bucket. That indirection is ugly and we considered several alternatives, including a global index, which the database does not offer, and a non-partitioned mirror of the key columns, which we rejected because it introduces a second thing that can be inconsistent.

The index that serves almost all read traffic on this table is a composite over tenant and time with the three columns the timeline view renders included in the index payload, so the common query is answered without touching the heap at all. It was measured rather than guessed. The timeline endpoint accounted for the large majority of reads, the profile showed most of the time going to heap fetches scattered across pages rather than to the index descent, and including the rendered columns turned a scattered read pattern into a sequential one within the index. Latency at the ninety-fifth percentile improved by more than half. The trade is that a covering index is larger and every write updates it, and we watched write latency carefully afterwards to confirm the cost was where we expected. The rule that came out of this, which we now apply generally, is that adding columns to an index for coverage is worth it when the query is high volume and the included columns are narrow and rarely updated, and it is a bad idea when someone is trying to make one occasional report faster.

Notice travels through the producer's own pull request, not through a channel. Every table that the extract replicates is listed in `contracts/replicated_tables.yaml`, that file and the migration directories are owned by `@data-platform` in CODEOWNERS, and any migration touching a listed table therefore blocks on a review from someone on the analytics side. On top of that, `tools/contract_check.py` runs in the producing service's pipeline, resolves the column references of every downstream model from the compiled manifest, and fails the build by name when a change would remove or retype a column something reads: the error says which model, which column and who owns it. Additive changes pass without a human. Breaking ones need ten business days between merge and the destructive half, which is the same expand-then-contract shape we use for the application, with the analytics side confirming they have migrated in between. The weekly digest of merged contract changes still goes out but it is a courtesy, not the mechanism. We tried making the channel the mechanism first and it failed exactly as you would expect: `#schema-changes` was muted by most of the people it was meant to inform within a month. What proved it was a column rename that broke the revenue dashboard for three days, announced correctly in the channel by an engineer who did everything right, read by nobody.

Every model declares tests on its key columns and the run fails if they do not hold. At minimum that is not-null and uniqueness on the grain column, plus a relationship test wherever a model joins to a dimension, and the convention is that the grain of a model is stated in a one-line description and asserted rather than left for a reader to infer. The tests are cheap and they mostly pass, which is the point: they are there for the day a source changes shape underneath us. The one that has earned its keep repeatedly is uniqueness on the grain, because a duplicated row does not raise an error anywhere, it silently doubles a metric. We shipped a customer count that was eleven percent high for a week because a join fanned out against a dimension that had gained a second row per key, and every dashboard reading it looked entirely healthy. The relationship tests are the ones people are tempted to skip since they are the slowest, and we keep them on the models feeding finance and allow them to be dropped elsewhere. A failing test stops the run rather than warning, for the same reason a failing unit test stops a build.

Nothing downstream reads a raw table directly. Every source gets a thin staging model whose only job is renaming, casting and light cleaning: source column names become our conventions, timestamps are cast to UTC, the several ways the older services spell a boolean become an actual boolean, and identifiers get a consistent suffix. No joins, no business logic, one staging model per source table, always. The value is that the odd shapes of a source are dealt with exactly once, in one file, by whoever understood them. Before the layer existed, the same casting appeared in four models written by three people, two of which handled a nullable timestamp differently, and a discrepancy between two dashboards took most of a day to trace to that. It also gives a single place to put a comment explaining that a column called `status` on a legacy table has five values of which two mean the same thing for historical reasons. The discipline that keeps it useful is the prohibition on logic; the moment a staging model starts filtering or joining, it stops being a translation and becomes something with an opinion, and then people need to read it to know what a number means.

A warehouse column that is on its way out gets a comment applied with `COMMENT ON COLUMN` in the form `DEPRECATED <date>: use <replacement>`, and the date is when it will actually be dropped rather than when somebody noticed it was obsolete. The catalogue surfaces comments in the column browser, so the warning appears where people look for the column instead of in a document they would have to know exists. A monthly job lists columns past their stated date and posts the list to the analytics channel, and the honest state of things is that about half of those get extended once before they go. Extending is fine; the previous state of affairs was columns that were known to be wrong being quietly used for years because nothing about them said so. We started this after finding two columns with almost identical names, one of which had been superseded eighteen months earlier, both still populated, and a report that had been reading the abandoned one since the day the replacement landed. Nothing in the warehouse would have told anybody. The rule now is that superseding a column means commenting the old one in the same change, and reviewers ask for it.

There is one definition of active customer, one of monthly recurring revenue, and one of churn, and they live in `semantic/metrics.yml` rather than being written into each dashboard. Tools read the definition from there; a dashboard that computes a headline metric with its own SQL does not get approved. The reason is the meeting everybody has had, where two people bring the same metric with different numbers and the next forty minutes are spent on whose filter was right rather than on the decision at hand. We had a version of that at a board meeting, with two figures for active customers that differed by about nine percent because one excluded trial workspaces and the other excluded workspaces with no activity in the period, and both were defensible. Centralising the definition does not make the choice correct, it makes it singular and visible, and the file carries a comment for each metric explaining what is deliberately excluded and why. Changing a definition is a pull request that names the person who asked and the reason, so the history of a number is readable, which turns out to matter more than the definition itself when someone asks why a series moved.

The data catalogue is generated from the warehouse itself on every run rather than maintained by hand. Table and column descriptions come from the model definitions in the repository, lineage is derived from the references between models, and freshness and row counts are read live. Nothing in it is typed into a wiki. We had a hand-written catalogue before and it followed the usual arc: enthusiastic for a quarter, patchy for two, then actively harmful because the entries that were wrong looked exactly like the entries that were right. Somebody built a report on a table the catalogue described as current and which had been superseded before the description was written. Generating it means the worst case is a missing description rather than a false one, and missing descriptions are visible as gaps that we can count and chase. The one thing we do maintain by hand is the short paragraph at the top of each subject area explaining what the tables are for and what questions they are meant to answer, because that genuinely cannot be derived from anything, and it is also the part people actually read first.

Requests for analytical work come in through a short form and every one gets a written decision within the week, including the ones we decline. The form asks what decision the answer will inform, when it is needed, and what the requester will do differently depending on the result. That third question is the one that does the work, and a surprising number of requests fail to answer it, which is usually the moment the requester realises they wanted a number for reassurance rather than for a decision. Those get a friendly no and nobody minds. The form replaced a mixture of direct messages and hallway conversations, which had two failure modes: the analytics team's queue was invisible, so nobody could see that the request they were chasing was behind eleven others, and work was implicitly prioritised by who asked most persistently rather than by what mattered. Publishing the queue changed the tone of the conversation entirely, because a person who can see the queue argues about priority with the list rather than with the analyst. The commitment is a decision within the week, not delivery within the week, and keeping those two things separate is what makes the commitment keepable.

The core models are checked each run against their own recent history, and a row count that falls outside the band established by the preceding weeks opens a ticket automatically rather than paging anyone. The band is generous and accounts for the weekly rhythm, since our weekends are visibly quieter and a fixed threshold would either fire every Saturday or catch nothing. Automatic ticket rather than alert is a deliberate choice about what this signal is worth: an anomalous count is nearly always a real change in the business or a source doing something new, and almost never an emergency, so waking somebody would train them to dismiss it. A ticket in a queue that a person reviews each morning gets the same investigation with none of the fatigue. The check has caught a genuine pipeline fault perhaps three times, and each time the count went to zero rather than merely drifting, which is a case a much simpler rule would also have caught. Its real value has been the other direction: it has twice surfaced a real business change, once a partner silently halving their feed volume, before anyone on the commercial side noticed.

Analysts have read access to the replica and to the warehouse and no write access to any production database, and this has never been controversial on either side. The reason is not distrust, it is that the application's schema is owned by the service that writes it, and a row written from outside that service bypasses every invariant the code maintains, from the audit record to the derived counters to the queue message that would have been emitted. There is no way to write into an application table by hand and leave the system in a state its owners can reason about. Where analytics genuinely needs to write something, and it does, the destination is the warehouse or a schema the analytics team owns outright, and where a business process needs a value to flow back into the product, it goes through an endpoint on the owning service rather than through the database. The one time we bent this, for what was supposed to be a one-off correction of a mis-set flag on a few hundred accounts, the update did not fire the notifications that the normal path would have, and the discrepancy surfaced weeks later as a support mystery nobody could explain.

Every workload manifest sets `resources.requests.cpu`, `requests.memory` and `limits.memory`, and deliberately leaves `limits.cpu` unset. The asymmetry is the policy, not an omission. Memory is incompressible: a process that asks for another page either gets it or is killed, so an unbounded container grows until the kubelet evicts whatever else shares the node, and the victim is rarely the offender. A memory limit turns that into a contained OOMKill of the guilty pod, which is why it is mandatory and is written as the request plus fifteen percent of headroom. CPU is the opposite kind of resource. The CFS quota does not slow a container proportionally under contention, it stops it dead at the quota boundary for the rest of each hundred-millisecond period even when the node is three quarters idle, so a limit buys nothing on a healthy node and costs tail latency on every node. We learned that by adding CPU limits fleet-wide during a capacity tidy-up: checkout p99 tripled overnight while node utilisation sat near thirty percent, and `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total` climbed on pods nowhere near their request. Fairness under contention comes from the request instead. Admission policy `policy/resources.rego` rejects any manifest carrying a CPU limit; the standing exception is batch work on the spot pool, where a noisy neighbour costs more than a latency tail.

Request values are not chosen by hand any more. `tools/rightsize_report.py` runs every Monday, pulls fourteen days of `container_memory_working_set_bytes` per container from the metrics store, takes the ninety-ninth percentile, adds a quarter for headroom and opens a pull request against the owning team's chart when the current value differs from that figure by more than thirty percent. CPU requests come out of the same report using the ninety-fifth percentile of usage. Two details matter. The report reads working set, never resident set size, because RSS counts page cache the kernel would happily drop and sizing against it inflates every request in the fleet by a wide margin. And it only opens a PR, never applies: the team that owns the service still has to look at whether the fortnight it measured was representative before merging. What made this worth building was drift. Requests had been set once at service creation, always to a round number somebody liked, and then never revisited through two years of traffic growth and a runtime upgrade that changed the allocator's behaviour. Half the fleet was reserving multiples of what it used while three services were chronically under-requested and getting scheduled onto nodes that could not actually feed them.

A single OOMKill files a ticket against the owning team and appears on the weekly reliability review; it does not wake anybody. The pager fires when the same deployment records three OOMKills inside ten minutes, which is the shape of a real problem rather than one unlucky request. That threshold came out of a month where the on-call rotation was woken eleven times by the same import worker, which allocated a large buffer for one oversized customer file, died, restarted, and completed the job on retry every single time. The alert was accurate and completely useless. The rule that came out of the review is that a self-healing failure is not a page, it is a backlog item, and the way to tell the two apart is whether the restart actually resolves it. The alert carries the container name and the last recorded working set so the responder does not have to go find them, and it deliberately does not auto-resolve: the ticket stays open until somebody either raises the limit with a reason or fixes the allocation. The rule is `OOMKillBurst` in `alerts/workload.yaml`. Deployments in the batch namespace are excluded entirely, because an OOMKill there is an expected outcome of the sizing loop.

Every JVM service starts with `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70.0` and never with a hard `-Xmx`. The percentage form reads the cgroup limit the container was actually given, so changing the pod's memory allocation changes the heap ceiling with it, and the two cannot drift apart. Before that, heap size was baked into each service's entrypoint script, and raising a pod's memory during an incident bought nothing at all because the JVM went on using the old ceiling while the container sat with idle headroom; the reverse case was worse, because lowering the pod's allocation without touching the script produced a process that would confidently allocate past its own container and get killed. The thirty percent left over is not slack, it is metaspace, thread stacks, direct byte buffers, JIT code cache and the allocator's own overhead, all of which count against the cgroup and none of which live in the heap. Services that lean heavily on direct buffers for network IO run at sixty percent instead and say so in a comment next to the flag. Native memory tracking is enabled in staging only, since it costs a few percent of throughput.

Each team gets a namespace with a quota on it, and the quota is owned by the platform team rather than the team consuming it. Raising one is a ticket with a sentence about what changed, and it is almost always granted; the point of the ticket is not to say no, it is to make growth visible to the people who have to buy the hardware it lands on. Before the quotas existed, capacity was a shared commons and behaved like one. A team preparing for a launch scaled their staging estate up over a long weekend to rehearse load, which was entirely reasonable of them, and by Monday the cluster had no schedulable headroom left for anybody else; the first symptom anyone saw was unrelated deployments hanging with pods stuck pending. Nobody had done anything wrong and there was no mechanism that would have surfaced it. The quotas also gave us a number to plan against instead of an average, since the sum of what teams have asked for is a far better predictor of next quarter than what they are currently using. Namespaces used by the platform team itself are quota'd on the same terms, which was a deliberate choice about credibility.

The mesh proxy and the log shipper each declare their own requests in the pod spec instead of inheriting a cluster-wide default from the injector. The injector still supplies its default of `100m` CPU and `128Mi` memory when none is given, but every deployment above a modest traffic level overrides it. The default was tuned against a median service and the median service is not the one that matters: the proxy in front of the search API handles roughly forty times the request rate of the fleet median, and at the default it was the slowest thing in the pod while the application container beside it sat comfortably inside its own allocation. That failure is genuinely hard to see, because every dashboard attributes the latency to the service, and the service is innocent. The other reason for making it explicit is arithmetic. Scheduling decisions are made on the sum of every container in the pod, so an invisible injected block means the number a team believes they are requesting is not the number the scheduler uses, and capacity forecasts built on the deployment specs came out low by a consistent margin across several hundred pods.

An admission policy refuses any pod that omits `resources.requests` on any container, including init containers. A pod with no request is treated by the scheduler as costing nothing, so it will fit anywhere, and the node it lands on has no idea it is now oversubscribed. That is exactly what happened to the node running the two busiest gateway replicas: a debug pod someone left behind with an empty resource block was scheduled onto it, grew to several gigabytes over an afternoon, and pushed the node into memory pressure, at which point the kubelet evicted the gateway pods because they had lower priority scores than the thing that caused the problem. The bypass is an annotation naming a ticket, valid for seven days, and the policy logs every use of it into the platform channel. Init containers are included because they are counted in the pod's effective request as the maximum across them, and a large init container that requests nothing has produced the same scheduling lie twice. The policy runs in enforce mode in every cluster including development, since a rule that only applies in production gets discovered in production.

Kubelet eviction settings live in the node image configuration and are the same on every node in a pool; no workload can influence them. There is a soft threshold with a grace period, which gives pods a chance to terminate cleanly, and a hard threshold below it, which does not. Both sit further from empty than the defaults do, and the reserved allocation for system daemons and the kubelet itself is larger than the defaults as well. The reasoning is that the node has to stay reachable in exactly the conditions where it is under the most pressure. A node that runs itself down to the last scrap of memory loses the container runtime and the kubelet before it loses the workload, and once that happens the control plane cannot tell whether the node is busy or gone, so recovery goes from an eviction that takes seconds to a node replacement that takes minutes. Disk gets the same treatment for the same reason, since a full disk stops image pulls and log writes and turns a single unhealthy node into one that cannot be redeployed onto. Keeping these on the image also means the values are reviewed as part of the image rollout rather than adjusted live during an incident.

The vertical autoscaler is deployed across the fleet but it is configured never to act. It watches, it produces recommendations, and those recommendations show up in the weekly sizing report and in a column on the capacity dashboard, and that is the whole of its authority. It ran briefly in a mode where it applied its own suggestions, and the objection that ended that experiment was not that its numbers were bad, because on the whole they were better than the ones people picked. The objection was the mechanism: applying a new size means recreating the pod, and the controller has no notion of whether now is a sensible moment. It resized a stateful consumer in the middle of the busiest hour of the week, which was defensible on the metrics it could see and indefensible to anyone watching the resulting backlog. It also fought with the horizontal scaler on the same workload, each reacting to the other's effect on utilisation. Advisory output turned out to be most of the value anyway, since the hard part was never computing the right number, it was noticing that the current one had gone wrong.

There are four node pools and a workload lands in exactly one of them. `system` runs the control-plane adjacent things — ingress controllers, the metrics stack, cert renewal — on three small on-demand nodes per zone, tainted `dedicated=system:NoSchedule` so nothing else drifts onto them. `general` is the default and holds every stateless HTTP service; it is on-demand, mid-size, and has no taint, so anything without a nodeSelector ends up there. `memory` runs the search indexer and the report renderer on high-memory instance types, tainted `dedicated=memory:NoSchedule` because those instance types cost roughly three times per core and letting ordinary services land there was the single largest line on last year's compute bill. `spot-batch` runs queue consumers and nightly jobs on interruptible capacity, tainted `lifecycle=spot:NoSchedule`, and nothing with a customer-facing SLO is permitted on it. Placement is by nodeSelector plus the matching toleration, both written into the chart, and a chart with a toleration for a pool it has no selector for is rejected in review. The split exists because we ran one undifferentiated pool and the nightly reindex — legitimately memory-hungry, legitimately low priority — repeatedly caused the scheduler to evict API pods to make room for it. Separating the pools made that impossible rather than merely discouraged.

A DaemonSet on the interruptible nodes watches the instance metadata endpoint for the two-minute interruption notice, cordons the node the moment it sees one, and drains it with `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 90`. Consumers get a real shutdown window instead of a socket that simply stops existing. Before it was deployed, an interrupted node dropped every in-flight job on it, and the only recovery was the visibility timeout expiring several minutes later, which turned a routine capacity reclaim into a latency spike on the backlog every time capacity got tight. The handler also emits an event that the job runner uses to stop pulling new work immediately, since draining a consumer that is still accepting messages just means it gets killed holding more of them. The two minutes is not generous and the design assumes it will occasionally be missed entirely, because the notice is best-effort and a genuine hardware failure sends nothing at all. Everything that runs on that capacity therefore has to be safe to kill at any instant regardless, and the handler is treated as an optimisation on top of that property, not a substitute for it.

The base node image is rebuilt on the first of every month with current package versions and rolled through the fleet over the following week, one pool at a time, oldest nodes first. Nodes are replaced rather than patched in place: nothing runs an update on a live node, and no node is older than about five weeks at any point. The reason is that in-place patching produced a fleet where no two nodes were quite the same, and a kernel-level bug that only manifested on the older half took days to characterise because nobody could say what the older half actually had installed. Immutable images make the question answerable from the build manifest. The roll respects disruption budgets and stops automatically if the count of pending pods stays above zero for more than ten minutes, which catches the case where the new image has a defect that only appears under real scheduling pressure. Out-of-cycle rebuilds happen for security advisories rated high or above and follow the same replacement path, just faster. The image build in `packer/node-base.pkr.hcl` is reproducible from a pinned package snapshot so a rebuild of last month's image produces last month's contents.

Adding a DaemonSet requires platform team approval, and the current inventory is small and written down. The arithmetic is the argument: anything in that inventory runs once on every node in every cluster, so a modest request multiplies by the fleet size and comes straight out of the capacity available for actual workloads. We got to that rule after counting what was already there and finding several agents doing overlapping work, two of which nobody could name an owner for. Together they were consuming a meaningful fraction of every node before a single application container started. There is a second, less obvious cost. A DaemonSet is on the critical path of node startup in a way a Deployment is not, because a node is not usefully ready until its node-level agents are, so every addition slows down scale-out and therefore slows down recovery from a capacity shortfall. The bar for approval is that the thing genuinely needs node-level access — host networking, host filesystem, hardware — and cannot be a Deployment. Wanting to be near the workload is not sufficient reason.

Any Deployment fronting customer traffic has to declare a topology spread constraint across availability zones with `maxSkew: 1` and `whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway`. The soft form is deliberate; a hard constraint means a zone outage leaves pods pending rather than crowded, which is exactly backwards from what you want during a zone outage. Anti-affinity by hostname is set on the same deployments so two replicas of a service do not share a node. The constraint exists because replica counts are not distribution guarantees. A service running six replicas had five of them in one zone, purely because that zone had the most schedulable room the morning the deployment last rolled, and nobody knew until the zone went away and the service lost most of its capacity in one step. The dashboards showed six healthy replicas right up to the moment they showed one. Spread is checked continuously now rather than at schedule time only, and a weekly report lists deployments whose actual distribution has drifted, which happens naturally as nodes are replaced and pods are rescheduled one at a time.

Accelerator capacity is charged to the team that asked for it rather than absorbed into the shared platform budget, at the actual hourly rate plus the storage attached to it. Nodes are labelled with a cost-centre tag at creation and the monthly report joins node-hours against that tag. This is a billing arrangement, not a technical control, and it was introduced because shared budgets produce a specific failure: capacity requested for a two-week experiment stays allocated for months, since nobody who can release it has any reason to notice. Within a month of the charge appearing on their own line, two teams released capacity they had genuinely forgotten about. The report also breaks out utilisation next to cost, which turned out to be the more persuasive number of the two, because an accelerator sitting idle looks very different when the idleness has a price on it. Teams can still ask for as much as they can justify; the change is only that the justification is made to their own budget rather than to the platform team, which is a conversation they are better placed to have.

Every service carrying a stated availability target ships a PodDisruptionBudget with `minAvailable` set to fifty percent of its replica count, rounded up. Without one, voluntary disruptions — node drains, image rolls, autoscaler consolidation — are unbounded, and the eviction API will happily take every replica of a service at once if they all happen to sit on nodes being replaced together. That is precisely how a routine node roll took the notification service down for four minutes: it had three replicas, all three were on nodes in the same batch, and the drain was correct in every respect except the outcome. The fifty percent figure is a compromise. Set it higher and node rolls stall for hours waiting for room; set it lower and it stops protecting anything. Single-replica deployments are the awkward case and are handled by refusing to give them a budget at all, on the grounds that a budget of one out of one blocks maintenance forever, and the right fix is a second replica. A weekly check lists deployments with an availability target and no budget.

The clusters run one minor version behind the newest generally available release, and the upgrade is scheduled in the first full week after that version has been out for a quarter. This is not caution for its own sake. The things that break on a minor upgrade are rarely the control plane itself; they are the ecosystem components hanging off it, and those get fixed on their own schedule after the release lands. Being a version behind means somebody else has already found the incompatibility and published the patch. We paid for that lesson by upgrading promptly once and discovering that a critical controller had not yet published a compatible build, leaving a cluster on a version its own tooling did not support for eleven days. Node pools are upgraded after the control plane and never in the same change window, since the skew policy permits nodes to trail and mixing both makes attributing a failure guesswork. The last supported version's end-of-life date is tracked in `docs/platform/upgrade-calendar.md` so the lag never quietly becomes two versions.

When a node starts producing symptoms nobody understands — disk latency climbing for no visible reason, a container runtime that has begun to hang on pulls — the first action is to cordon and drain it, not to terminate it. The node stays in the cluster, empty, with a label naming the incident and the person who set it aside. Deleting is faster and it was what we used to do, and the cost of that habit only shows up afterwards: the evidence goes with the instance. Twice we lost the ability to explain a class of failure entirely, because every affected node was replaced during the response and by the time anyone had time to investigate there was nothing left to look at. A cordoned node costs one instance-hour rate for as long as it sits there, which is cheap against a recurring failure nobody can characterise. The convention is that quarantined nodes are reviewed at the reliability meeting and released or terminated then, so they do not accumulate silently; a node that has sat quarantined through two of those meetings without anyone looking at it gets terminated by default.

The worker fleet scales on backlog, not on CPU, and the metric the scaler reads is messages ready divided by current replicas with a target of thirty. CPU was the original signal and it was actively misleading, because these workers are almost entirely waiting: they call a third-party address validator, they write to the ledger, they wait on both. During the worst backlog we have had, CPU across the fleet sat at eighteen percent and never moved while the oldest unprocessed message aged past four hours, so the autoscaler saw a fleet with plenty of headroom and correctly declined to add capacity to it. Utilisation was telling the truth about the machines and nothing at all about the work. Queue depth is the thing the customer actually experiences, so it is the thing we scale on. The scaler is a KEDA `ScaledObject` per consumer group, and it also reads oldest-message-age as a second trigger set at ninety seconds, which catches the slow-poison case where depth stays flat because arrivals and completions match but every message is now taking far longer than it should. Scale-up is allowed to double the fleet in a single step; scale-down is capped at ten percent per minute, because the cost of being briefly overprovisioned is a few instance-minutes and the cost of being underprovisioned is a backlog that takes an hour to work off.

`maxReplicaCount` on every consumer is set from a division, not a guess: the pooler's transaction-pool size for that role divided by the connections a single worker holds, minus a margin for migrations and ad-hoc sessions. Right now that puts the largest consumer group at forty-eight. The ceiling exists because scaling out past it does not add throughput, it removes it. Each new worker opens its pool, the pooler starts queueing on connection checkout, every worker including the ones that were already running gets slower, and the backlog the scale-out was responding to grows faster than before. We watched that happen during an incident where the scaler was allowed to run free and went to well over a hundred replicas; the database was not saturated on CPU or IO, it simply had nothing left to hand out, and the fix was to scale the fleet back down. The number is written next to the pooler configuration it derives from, with a comment naming the relationship, so that raising the pool without raising the ceiling looks like an unfinished job to whoever reads it next.

Front-end request capacity gets raised manually the afternoon before an event we know about — a large customer's scheduled bulk import, the end-of-quarter close, the marketing send that goes out on the first Tuesday of the month — and dropped again the following morning. Any automatic scaler is reactive by construction; it can only respond after the load has arrived, and for a step change rather than a ramp that means the first minutes are served by the old capacity no matter how well it is tuned. Those first minutes are the ones people remember. Pre-scaling costs a modest amount of unused capacity for less than a day, which is a much better trade than a visible slowdown at the start of an event somebody planned. The practice is deliberately kept simple and human: whoever is aware of the event says so in the channel and someone sets the floor higher, with a reminder to put it back. It has been suggested more than once that this should read from the calendar automatically, and it has been declined each time, because the failure mode of a calendar-driven scaler is capacity that never comes back down and nobody notices.

Consumers are configured with `prefetch_count = 1`. A worker takes one message, finishes it, and only then asks for the next. The default was a batch of ten and it produced a specific, hard-to-see unfairness: a worker that happened to receive ten slow messages sat on all of them while its neighbours idled, and the ten were invisible to every dashboard because they had been dispatched and were therefore no longer counted as ready. Backlog looked healthy while a third of it was parked in a socket buffer. Prefetching one costs an extra round trip per message, which measured at a couple of milliseconds against jobs whose median is well over a second, so the throughput argument for batching never applied to this workload in the first place. It also makes shutdown honest: a worker asked to stop has at most one message in hand, so it can finish and exit inside the grace period rather than abandoning nine others. The one consumer that still batches is the metrics roll-up, which processes uniformly tiny messages where the round trip genuinely dominates, and it says so in a comment.

Nothing automatically retries out of a dead-letter queue. Messages land there after the redrive policy exhausts its attempts, and they stay there until a person runs `ops/queue/replay.py` with an explicit queue name and a count. The tool prints a sample of what it is about to move and requires confirmation. Automatic redrive was the original design and it was removed after a poison message went round the loop for nine days, failing, being redriven, and failing again, generating a steady trickle of errors that everyone had learned to ignore because it never got worse and never got better. A dead-letter queue with anything in it is a question for a human, and the whole value of the pattern is that it stops the loop. The alert is on the age of the oldest message rather than the count, since one message stuck for two days matters more than fifty that arrived in the last hour during a dependency outage. The tool records who replayed what into an audit log, which has twice been the fastest way to explain why a customer received the same notification a second time.

A scheduled job does not do the work. It enumerates what needs doing and puts one message on the queue per unit, then exits. The workers that already exist do the rest. This started as a way to stop the nightly statement run from being a single process whose failure at the end meant starting over from the beginning, and the properties it bought turned out to be worth more broadly. Work becomes retryable per item rather than per run, so one customer with malformed data no longer costs everyone else their statement. It becomes observable, since progress is a queue draining rather than a process that is either still going or not. And it becomes parallel for free, because the same fleet that handles everything else picks it up. The scheduler itself is now trivial enough to be uninteresting, which is the point: it holds no business logic, so it needs no special deployment, no special monitoring and no special knowledge to operate. The one rule that goes with the pattern is that the enumeration step has to be cheap and idempotent, so that running it twice by accident is harmless.

The identity the autoscaler assumes is scoped to `GetQueueAttributes` and `ListQueues` on the specific queue ARNs it watches, and nothing else — no receive, no delete, no send, no access to any other queue in the account. It cannot read a single message body. This came out of a review that noticed the scaler had been created with the same broad policy as the workers, purely because that policy already existed and was convenient to attach. Nothing had gone wrong, but a controller that runs cluster-wide, that everybody trusts to be boring, and that holds credentials able to consume production work is a bad shape to leave lying around. The narrow policy is also self-documenting: reading it tells you exactly which queues the scaler is responsible for, which turned out to be faster than reading its configuration. Adding a new scaled consumer therefore requires a policy change alongside the scaler definition, and that extra step has caught two cases where somebody pointed a scaler at a queue in the wrong environment.

Visibility timeout is set to two minutes across the board, and jobs that legitimately run longer extend their own lease by calling `ChangeMessageVisibility` every thirty seconds from a background thread. The alternative — setting the timeout to the worst-case duration — was what we did first, and it meant the longest job in the queue dictated recovery time for every job in it. A worker that died holding a short message left that message invisible for the full timeout, so a rolling deploy of the fleet produced a stall proportional to the slowest job type rather than to anything the failed message was doing. Heartbeating inverts that. A crashed worker stops heartbeating immediately, so its message becomes available again within the short timeout regardless of how long it was expected to take. The important detail is that the heartbeat runs on its own thread and does not depend on the job's own progress, since a job wedged on a network call that never returns would otherwise keep renewing forever. A hard ceiling of one hour of cumulative extension stops that case and sends the message to the dead-letter queue.

Every consumer keeps at least one replica running at all times, even the ones that see no traffic for most of the day. Scaling to nothing is available and we do not use it. The reason is what the first message after an idle period costs: image pull on a cold node, runtime start, connection pools opening, the first-request compile of everything the process touches. On the consumers where this was measured the first message after idle took most of a minute, and for a queue that receives a handful of messages an hour that is not an occasional cost, it is nearly every message. The saving was also smaller than expected, since holding a single small replica is a rounding error against the fleet, while the tail latency it removes is visible to customers waiting on a confirmation email. There is a second reason that matters more during incidents: a fleet at zero has no running instance to look at, so the first thing an on-call engineer does is start one, and starting one to debug a problem changes the conditions they were trying to observe.

Every record we own is declared in `infra/dns/` as Terraform and changed only by merging a pull request; the console has read-only credentials for everyone, including the platform team, and the write role is held by the CI apply job alone. Two things forced this. The first was an emergency: during a regional failure somebody repointed a CNAME in the console to the standby, which was the correct call and restored service in minutes. Eleven days later an unrelated apply — a routine TXT record for a vendor — reverted it, because the state file had never learned about the manual edit. The outage came back at half past three in the morning with a cause that made no sense to the responder, who had no reason to connect it to a change made a week and a half earlier. The second was that the console's history could tell us a record had changed and roughly when, but not why, not what it had been, and not who approved it. A pull request answers all three and is searchable years later. The mechanics: `terraform plan` output is posted as a comment, one approval from outside the requesting team is required, and merge triggers apply. Break-glass is a named role with console write access, obtainable by anyone on call, and using it opens an incident ticket automatically, because the point was never to block an urgent change, only to guarantee it gets reconciled back into the repository.

Any record about to be moved has its `ttl` dropped to 60 at least seven days ahead of the cutover, and raised back to 3600 once the new value has been stable for a week. Seven days is not arbitrary: it has to exceed the old TTL by a comfortable margin, since resolvers that cached the record just before the change carry the old TTL, not the new one, and lowering it on the morning of a migration accomplishes nothing at all for exactly those resolvers. We found that out during a mail provider move, where a long TTL had been shortened the same day and a meaningful share of inbound mail kept arriving at the old host for the rest of the afternoon. The cost of running short TTLs permanently is more query volume and a marginally higher sensitivity to resolver latency, both small; the reason we still raise them back is that a short TTL on a record nobody is migrating is a standing invitation for a transient nameserver problem to become a visible one. The lowering step is part of the migration checklist rather than something people remember.

The apex is an ALIAS record pointing at the load balancer's hostname, not a CNAME and not a hardcoded address. A CNAME at the apex is not legal, because the apex must also carry SOA and NS records and a CNAME cannot coexist with anything else at the same name; providers that appear to allow it are synthesising an A response behind the scenes. The other option, pinning A records to whatever addresses the balancer had that day, is legal and wrong: those addresses change without notice when the provider replaces capacity, and we ran for a year on a set that had been copied by hand into the zone. When one of them was recycled, a portion of traffic went to an address that belonged to someone else entirely, which is a considerably worse outcome than an outage. The `www` name is a plain CNAME to the apex and the redirect is handled at the edge rather than in DNS, so there is exactly one place that knows the balancer's identity. Zone files that try to put an A record at the apex are rejected in review with a link to this note.

Services inside the cluster find each other through the cluster's own discovery mechanism and never through a publicly resolvable name. There is no split-horizon view and no internal zone hanging off the public domain. The reason is partly disclosure — a public zone is enumerable, and a zone that names every internal service hands an outsider an accurate architecture diagram for free — but mostly it is about failure coupling. When internal traffic resolves through the public resolvers, an external DNS problem becomes an internal outage as well, and the two are extremely hard to tell apart while you are in the middle of one. We had a morning where a provider issue at the zone level was diagnosed as an application problem for the better part of an hour, because services could not reach each other and nobody thought to check name resolution first. Keeping the two planes separate means an external resolution failure degrades exactly what it should, which is inbound traffic, and leaves the inside of the system able to tell you so. The rule has one exception, the object storage endpoint, and it is written down as a known coupling.

Certificates renew through the DNS-01 challenge, and the challenge records are written into a delegated subzone that holds nothing else. The renewal role can write to that subzone and has no permission anywhere else in the account. Delegation is the whole trick: DNS-01 is the only challenge type that issues wildcards and the only one that works for hosts with no inbound path from the internet, but it normally requires giving an automated process write access to the zone that also contains the records pointing at production. That is a large amount of authority to hand a renewal daemon, and the failure mode is not subtle. Delegating a subzone and pointing the challenge at it keeps the capability narrow enough to reason about. Renewal runs at thirty days remaining, retries daily, and alerts at fourteen, so there is a fortnight of margin before anything customer-visible happens. The alert is on the certificate's own expiry as observed from outside, not on the renewal job's exit code, because a job that succeeds while writing to the wrong zone is a thing that has happened here.

Domain registration sits with one company and authoritative name service with another, and the separation is intentional even though a single vendor would be cheaper and involve one fewer account to administer. The concern is not vendor reliability, it is vendor account risk. A billing dispute, a compromised login, or an automated abuse suspension at a provider that holds both the registration and the zone takes the domain away in a single step, and recovery runs at the speed of that vendor's support queue. Split across two, the same event takes half of it, and the half that remains is enough to recover from: the registration can be pointed at new nameservers, or the zone can be recreated and pointed at from the registrar. Registrar lock is on, transfer authorisation codes are held in the secrets store rather than in anyone's mailbox, and the contact address is a distribution list rather than an individual, because the person whose name was originally on it left the company. Neither account shares credentials with anything else we operate.

`ops/dns/whois_check.py` runs weekly, querying WHOIS directly for every domain we own and alerts at ninety, sixty and thirty days before expiry, and it deliberately does not trust the registrar's own renewal notices or its dashboard. Auto-renew is enabled on everything, and auto-renew is exactly what makes independent checking necessary: it silently depends on a stored payment method that will expire on its own schedule, and the notification that it failed goes to whatever address was on the account, which is frequently a person rather than a team. The check is cheap and it caught a domain used for a partner integration whose card had been declined two months earlier, twenty-three days before it would have lapsed. The list of domains it walks is generated from the DNS repository rather than maintained by hand, so a domain someone registers for a launch and forgets about is still covered as soon as its zone exists. Expiry dates are also posted into the platform channel once a quarter, which is less about alerting and more about keeping the inventory in front of people.

No wildcard record is permitted in the production zone. The only one that exists is `*.preview.harborlane.dev`, covering per-branch preview deployments, and it points at a single ingress that refuses any host it does not recognise. Wildcards make every possible name resolve, which means a typo in a client's configuration, a stale hostname in an old integration, or a subdomain someone invented for a demo all get a working answer and land somewhere. Debugging that is unpleasant, because the request arrives and is served, so nothing looks broken until you notice the hostname. The worse case is takeover: a wildcard pointing at a shared platform means anyone who can claim a name on that platform gets traffic sent to them by our zone, and we found one such record left over from an old vendor. Every production name is written explicitly, which makes the zone file long and makes it an accurate inventory of what actually exists. Adding a name costs one line in the repository, which is a small enough tax that nobody has argued for reintroducing the shortcut.

After a record changes, verification is done from a resolver that sits outside our own network and outside our provider's, not from a laptop on the office connection and not from inside the cluster. Both of those have caches and forwarders in the path that will happily answer from something they already had, so a check run there tells you what a resolver near you believes, which is the least interesting question available. It also occasionally tells you something is fine when it is not, which is worse than telling you nothing. The check queries the authoritative nameservers directly to confirm the record is actually published, and then queries a couple of well-known public resolvers to see what a customer would get. The two answers differing is normal for a while after a change and is exactly the thing worth watching, because the gap between them is propagation and knowing its shape is what tells you whether to keep waiting or start looking for a mistake. This became routine after an afternoon spent hunting a record that had never been published at all, while the person checking kept getting the old cached answer and concluding it was merely slow.

Purges are by surrogate key, they are soft, and the blanket purge is a two-person operation. Every response leaves the origin with a `Surrogate-Key` header listing the entities it was built from — a product id, a pricing table version, the navigation revision — and `ops/cdn/purge.py` takes keys, never URLs and never a prefix. A pricing change invalidates one key and touches a few hundred objects instead of everything. Purges are soft by default, which marks the object stale rather than deleting it, so the first request after a purge is still served from the edge while a single revalidation goes to origin; every subsequent request waits on that one fetch rather than each becoming its own. The hard purge exists, requires the `--hard` flag and a reason string, and is logged. Purge-all is not in the tool at all. Running it requires the console, two people in the channel, and a window outside peak, because the last time somebody purged the whole zone at midday the origin took the entire cacheable request volume at once — about ninety times its normal load — connection pools filled, health checks began failing, and the API went down alongside the marketing site, which shares nothing with it except an origin group. Recovery took longer than the outage, since a cold edge stays cold until traffic refills it.

The edge normalises the cache key by dropping any query parameter matching `utm_*`, `gclid` or `fbclid` and keeping a short allowlist of others, keeping only the parameters the origin actually varies on. Before that, every campaign link was its own cache entry, so a send that went out with per-recipient tracking parameters produced hundreds of thousands of distinct keys for one page. Hit rate on the landing page fell below one in five during exactly the hour it mattered most, and origin saw the load it had been built to be protected from. The allowlist is the important half of the design; a denylist was tried first and lost, because the next campaign tool invents a parameter nobody has denied yet, and the failure is silent. Parameters not on the allowlist are still forwarded to origin so analytics and attribution keep working — they are simply not part of the key. The list lives beside the edge configuration with a comment per entry explaining what varies, and adding to it requires showing that the response genuinely differs, since every entry multiplies the key space.

Every edge location fetches through one designated shield location rather than going to origin directly. A cache miss at any of the edges becomes a request to the shield, and only a miss at the shield reaches us. The effect is on the miss path, not the hit path, and it is the miss path that hurts: without it, a newly published object is fetched independently by every edge that receives a request for it, so a popular page after a deploy generated dozens of simultaneous identical origin requests for the same bytes. With the shield in place that collapses to one. The shield sits in `eu-west-1`, close to the origin rather than close to the traffic, because the shield-to-origin hop is the one being optimised and the edge-to-shield hop rides the provider's own backbone. The trade is a single point that adds a hop when the shield itself misses, and a modest latency penalty on genuinely uncacheable responses, which is why the API routes are configured to bypass it. Origin request volume dropped by roughly two thirds the week it was turned on.

Documents come from origin every time; only static assets are held at the edge. This is not a performance decision anyone is proud of, it is a correctness one. Pages are personalised — the header knows whether you are signed in, prices are regional, and the beta banner depends on account flags — and a cached document served to the wrong visitor is not a stale page, it is somebody else's page. We shipped one for about ten minutes once, and the ten minutes were spent explaining rather than fixing. The alternative would be to vary on enough of the request to be safe, at which point the key space is large enough that almost nothing is shared and the caching buys nothing anyway. What we do instead is make the document cheap: it is small, it renders without waiting on data, and everything expensive on the page is an asset that does cache. The marketing site is the exception and caches its documents happily, because nothing on it varies by visitor, and the two sites are configured separately so that nobody can accidentally extend one policy to the other.

Built assets carry `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` and a content hash in the filename. The hash is what makes the year safe: a changed file is a different name, so nothing ever needs to be told that an old name is out of date. The `immutable` directive matters more than it looks — without it, browsers still send a conditional request on reload, and while the response is a small not-modified it is a full round trip on every asset for every user who hits refresh. On a page with several dozen assets that is a visible delay on a slow connection, for files that by construction cannot have changed. The rule holds only if nothing unhashed sneaks into the same directory, so the build fails if it emits a file into the hashed asset path without a hash in its name; that check exists because a font was once published unhashed with the year-long lifetime and was pinned in browsers long after it was replaced. Files that genuinely must keep stable names, like the site manifest and the service worker script, live outside that path and take a short lifetime.

Cacheable responses are configured with `stale-if-error=86400, stale-while-revalidate=60`. When origin returns a server error or fails to respond, the edge serves the last good copy it has rather than passing the failure through. That distinction has already earned itself twice: during a deploy that went bad and during a database failover that took eleven minutes, most visitors saw a site that was slightly out of date and entirely functional, and support volume was near zero for both. It changes what an origin outage means for anyone who is not signing in. The risk is the obvious one, that a broken origin becomes invisible, so the edge emits a metric counting stale-on-error hits and it is alerted on directly, independently of origin health checks. Nothing is allowed to depend on it as a design: the window is a grace period for recovery, not a tier of availability, and pages whose content is time-sensitive enough that a stale copy would be wrong opt out explicitly in their response headers.

Any response served out of the asset paths has its cookie headers removed at the edge, in both directions: cookies are not forwarded to origin on those requests, and any the origin sets on them are dropped before the response is stored. Forwarding them would make the cache key depend on a value that is unique per visitor, which quietly disables caching altogether for exactly the content that most benefits from it. Setting them is worse. A response stored at the edge carrying a session cookie is served to whoever asks for that object next, and the second visitor is handed the first visitor's session. That is not a theoretical shape; it is a well-known way to leak an account and it has happened to other people often enough to be worth designing against rather than trusting the origin never to do. The stripping is configured at the edge rather than in application code because it needs to hold regardless of which service or framework rendered the response, including ones added later by people who never read this.

Full edge logs are sampled down to one percent (`sampling_rate = 0.01`) before they leave the provider, and only the sampled stream is delivered to storage and indexed. Unsampled logs are retained by the provider for three days and can be pulled in full for a specific window during an incident. The reason is cost, and the numbers were not close: the delivery and indexing charge for complete edge logs came to more than the bandwidth they described, which is an absurd shape for an observability bill to have. One percent is enough for every question the logs are actually asked — hit rate by path, cache status distribution, geographic breakdown, error rate trends — because all of them are aggregate questions over a very large denominator. The place it fails is per-request investigation, tracing one customer's exact sequence, and that is precisely what the three-day full retention covers. Getting that ordering wrong is what the design is about: sample the routine, keep the recent complete, and never be in a position where the only copy of an incident's traffic was thrown away to save money.

Origin responses may vary on encoding and on nothing else; anything wider is stripped at the edge and flagged in review. Each additional dimension multiplies the number of stored copies of the same object, and the multiplication happens per edge location, so the practical effect is a lower hit rate everywhere rather than a bigger cache somewhere. Varying on the user agent string is the pathological case and we shipped it once by accident through a framework default: the string is close to unique across visitors, so effectively nothing was ever a hit, and we discovered it as an origin load increase rather than as a caching problem. Varying on the language header is the tempting one, since it looks harmless and is genuinely useful, but it fragments the cache along a dimension that is far noisier than the handful of languages actually served, and the localisation is better decided at the edge from a normalised value. Where content really must differ per audience, the difference goes in the path, which is visible, debuggable, and purgeable on its own.

A public version gets twelve months from the day it is marked deprecated to the day it stops answering, and the twelve months run on a published calendar rather than on judgement. Versions are dates sent in the `Api-Version` header and pinned per account at first call. The sequence is fixed. On announcement every response for that version starts carrying `Deprecation: true` and a `Sunset` header with the exact retirement timestamp, and the migration guide goes up. Notices go to the technical contact on every account still calling it at twelve months, three months, and four weeks, and each notice names that account's own top five endpoints on the old version, because a generic mail gets filed and a mail quoting their traffic does not. At four weeks and at two weeks we run brownouts — the old version returns `410 Gone` for one hour, then for four hours a week later, both announced in advance — the only mechanism that reliably finds integrations nobody was reading mail about. Shutoff is a config change, reversible for seventy-two hours. All of this exists because we once removed an endpoint on thirty days' notice sent to a billing address, and a customer's nightly reconciliation job failed silently for a week before anyone connected the two. The rule that came out of it: no version is retired while any account is still calling it without a human having spoken to that account.

Adding a field to a response is not a breaking change here and never triggers a new version. The contract we publish says clients must ignore properties they do not recognise, and the client libraries are generated to do exactly that, so a new field costs an existing integration nothing. This is stated plainly in the compatibility section because the alternative is a version for every product change, and a surface with that many live versions is one nobody can afford to keep working. What does count as breaking is narrower and worth knowing precisely: removing a field, renaming one, changing its type, narrowing what a value may be, making an optional request parameter required, tightening validation on something previously accepted, or changing the meaning of a value while keeping its name. That last one is the dangerous entry, because it looks additive in a diff and is the one that has bitten us. Adding a new value to an enumeration sits on the boundary and is treated as breaking for enumerations clients branch on, and additive for ones they only display, which is a judgement call made in review rather than by rule.

`openapi.json` is produced by a build step from the route definitions and response models, and the file in the repository is checked to be identical to freshly generated output on every pull request. Editing it by hand fails the build. It used to be maintained separately, and the gap between it and reality grew in exactly the way you would expect: the drift was never in the interesting places, it was in optional fields, error codes and default values, so the document was correct enough that people trusted it and wrong enough that the generated clients had bugs. One field documented as a string had been an integer in production for nine months. Generating from code also gives us the diff for free, since a change to the surface shows up as a change to a committed artifact that a reviewer can read, which turned out to be the more valuable half. Prose descriptions and examples live in docstrings on the models so they end up in the same output and go through the same review. The published documentation site renders that file directly rather than keeping its own copy.

Every error response, from any endpoint, is `application/problem+json` with `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and an `instance` carrying the request id, plus an `errors` array for field-level validation failures. The `type` is a stable URI that resolves to a documentation page and is the field clients are told to branch on; `detail` is human-readable and explicitly not stable. Before this there were four error shapes across the surface, all born of the framework or vendor that happened to produce them, and every integration had a function whose job was guessing which one it had received. That function was where their bugs lived, and it was our fault rather than theirs. Two rules keep it from eroding: the status code and the `status` member must agree, which a test asserts across every route, and no endpoint may invent a `type` that is not registered in the error catalogue. Adding one is a two-line change and a documentation page. Validation errors return `422` and list every failing field at once rather than stopping at the first, since a client fixing them one round trip at a time is a poor experience.

Each client library release records the API version its code was generated against, in the changelog and in the `X-Client-Api-Version` header the library sends on every request. That header is what the server sees, so support can answer what surface a customer is actually calling without asking them to check anything. SDK version numbers move on their own schedule — a bug fix in the retry logic is a patch release with no API change behind it — so the two numbers cannot be inferred from each other, and people assumed they could for a long time. A customer reporting a problem with a library release two years old was routinely diagnosed against the current surface, which wasted a good deal of everyone's time before the constant existed. Generation is automated from the published specification, and a release is cut whenever the specification changes in a way that alters the generated output, which keeps the libraries close behind the server without anybody deciding when. Hand-written code in the libraries is confined to the transport layer, so a regeneration never conflicts with it.

Endpoints not yet stable are reachable only when the request carries `X-Enable-Beta` naming the specific feature, and they are absent from the published specification until they graduate. Nothing behind that header carries any compatibility promise: it can change shape or disappear between deploys, and it does. Putting them on a separate version number was the first idea and it was wrong, because a version number is a promise, and a version that changes underneath people teaches them that the numbers mean nothing. The header makes the bargain explicit at the call site, so a client cannot arrive at a beta endpoint by accident or by copying a snippet. Enabling it is per-account and recorded, which means we can tell exactly who to talk to before a shape changes, and the list is short enough that talking to all of them is realistic. Graduation is the interesting part: the endpoint gets added to the specification and starts answering without the header, but the header keeps working for a grace period so nothing breaks in the moment of promotion.

Services inside our own network call the public surface through the same gateway, with the same headers and the same rules, and there is no privileged internal path with extra fields on it. There was one, and removing it is one of the better decisions this team has made. What it produced was a surface whose most-used features were invisible to customers and whose documented features were exercised only by outsiders, so the parts we tested hardest were not the parts we shipped, and every awkward edge of the public design survived because no colleague ever had to live with it. The change also gave us honest numbers: traffic on an endpoint now means demand for that endpoint, rather than demand plus whatever our own batch jobs happen to do overnight, and that has changed which things get invested in. The cost is real and we pay it knowingly, since internal callers now take the same rate limits and the same pagination and occasionally the same awkwardness. When something is genuinely too awkward, the fix is to improve the public design rather than to route around it.

A pull request that changes the public surface in a breaking way cannot merge without a written note in the customer-facing release notes, in the same change, reviewed by someone from support. Not a ticket, not a line in the commit history — the actual text a customer will read. The discipline is deliberate and slightly annoying, and it exists because writing the sentence is the cheapest way to find out that the change is worse than it looked. Several proposals have died at that step, not because anyone rejected them, but because the author sat down to explain the migration and concluded there was a better shape available. Support reviews it because they are the ones who will answer for it, and they consistently catch the thing engineers leave out, which is what a customer is supposed to do differently rather than what changed. The notes are written for someone who has never read our internal vocabulary, so they name endpoints and fields rather than services and modules. Non-breaking changes get a note too, but without the review requirement.
