For each of our nine largest integrations `tests/contracts/` holds a recorded suite of the exact request sequences that partner sends, captured from real traffic with identifiers replaced, replayed against every build in CI. It asserts on status codes and on the specific fields those partners read, not on the whole response body, so an additive change does not fail it and a removed field does. This was built after a change that was correct by every internal test and broke one partner's inventory sync, because they depended on a field being present and empty rather than absent, a distinction nothing on our side had ever considered meaningful. The suites are regenerated from live traffic each quarter so they track what partners actually do rather than what they did when the suite was written, and the regeneration diff is reviewed, since a partner's usage changing is itself worth knowing. A failure blocks the build and is routed to the integrations channel rather than to the author, because the person who broke it usually has no idea who that partner is.

Every POST that creates or moves money must carry an `Idempotency-Key` header; the gateway returns `400` without one. The reason is that a client cannot tell the difference between a request that never arrived and a response that never came back, and the two demand opposite reactions. A timeout on a payment is exactly that ambiguity, and a client on a poor connection resolves it the only way it can, by trying again. We required keys after a morning when an upstream became slow enough to trip client timeouts while still completing every request it received: three hundred and eleven accounts were charged twice and the balance report disagreed with the processor for a fortnight. Nothing was broken in the sense of a bug: two correct systems produced a duplicate because the protocol had no way to say this is the same intent as before. With a key, the first request records its result under it and a repeat replays the stored response, status code and body included, rather than doing the work twice. Keys are scoped per account and per endpoint, so a collision across customers is impossible, and they are honoured for twenty-four hours, well past any retry window a client should have. A repeat arriving while the first is in flight gets `409`, since answering it would mean guessing an outcome nobody knows yet. Reusing a key with a different body is an error, not a replay.

Creation endpoints answer `201` with a `Location` header pointing at the new resource and a body containing only its id and its current state, not the fully expanded object. Clients that want the whole thing follow the header. The full body was the original design and it caused a specific coupling that took a while to see: the creation response and the fetch response drifted apart, because people would add a field to one and forget the other, and integrations ended up depending on whichever they happened to have used first. Two shapes for one resource is one shape too many. Returning the minimal body also keeps the write path fast, since serialising a large object with its expansions frequently cost more than the write itself, and that work is wasted for the majority of callers who only wanted to know it succeeded. The exception is endpoints whose result contains something not retrievable afterwards, a one-time token being the obvious case, where the value comes back in the creation response because there is nowhere else it can come from. Those are listed explicitly in the documentation rather than left for a client to discover.

The gateway rejects any request body over one megabyte with `413` before it reaches a service, and the limit is enforced on the streamed byte count rather than on a declared content length, since the declared length is a claim the client makes. Application-level limits were what we had, and they were unevenly applied and always applied too late: by the time a service noticed a body was too large it had already read it into memory. A single fifty megabyte upload against a service with modest per-pod memory took out three replicas, which was not an attack, just an integration that had accidentally been pointed at the wrong endpoint. Enforcing at the edge means the rule is uniform and no service has to remember it. Bulk callers who legitimately need to send more are directed to the upload endpoint, which takes a signed URL and puts the bytes in object storage without them passing through the API at all, and that path has its own much larger limit. The number is on the gateway rather than in each service configuration so that raising it is a deliberate, visible act.

Stored request results live in Redis with the durable copy written to `idempotency_records` in the primary database, and the read path checks the cache first. The database write is synchronous and happens before the response is returned, which is the part that matters: the cache is an optimisation for the hot path and never the system of record. A cache-only design was the first implementation and it survived until the first Redis failover, when a few seconds of evictions produced exactly the duplicate work the mechanism exists to prevent, at the worst possible moment. The durable rows are cleaned up by a job that deletes anything past its retention window in batches of five thousand, running hourly, because the table grows at the rate of the entire write volume of the platform and unattended it became the largest table we had within two months. Redis holds a shorter window than the database, so a lookup that misses the cache falls through and still finds the row. Both stores key on the same tuple, and the schema puts a unique constraint on it so a race between two concurrent inserts loses cleanly rather than storing two answers.

A bulk request either applies every item or applies none of them. There is no partial success and no per-item status array in the response. Partial application was the original behaviour, and it produced a class of support case that was miserable to resolve, because the caller had to reconcile which of two hundred items had actually landed, using a response format they had usually not implemented carefully. Almost nobody handled it correctly, and the ones who did handled it by retrying the whole batch, which is what the transactional design gives them for free. The cost is that a single bad item rejects the batch, which callers occasionally complain about until it is pointed out that the alternative is not knowing what state they are in. Validation runs over the whole batch before anything is written, so the error response names every item that failed and why, rather than stopping at the first and making the caller discover them one round trip at a time. Batch size is capped so that the transaction stays short enough not to hold locks anyone else is waiting on.

Removing a record sets a deletion timestamp and the row stays; queries filter on it through a shared scope that is applied by default rather than remembered per query. Hard deletion exists in two places only: the audit log, which is append-only and never deleted at all, and the erasure job that satisfies data protection requests, which genuinely removes rows and records that it did so in a separate register. The reason for soft deletion is not sentimentality about data, it is that deletion is the operation customers get wrong most often and the one with no undo. Restoring a mistakenly deleted account used to mean a partial restore from backup, which takes hours and brings back everything else from that moment too; now it is clearing a column. It also keeps foreign keys intact, so historical invoices still resolve the customer they were issued to rather than pointing at nothing. The trap we hit early is that a unique constraint has to include the deletion column or a deleted record blocks the name being reused, which cost an afternoon before anyone worked out why a re-registration was failing.

Every response carries an `ETag`, and `PATCH` requires an `If-Match` header holding one; a stale value gets `412` and the caller re-reads before trying again. Without it the last writer wins silently, which is fine right up until two people are editing the same record, and in this product two people editing the same record is the normal case rather than the exception. The failure it removed was reproducible and quiet: a support agent and a customer both open an order, the agent changes the shipping address, the customer changes the quantity, and whichever saves second reverts the other's field without either of them being told. The tag is computed from the row's version column rather than by hashing the serialised body, so it does not change when the representation changes or when an unrelated expansion is added, and it is stable across API versions. Field-level merging was considered and rejected: it makes some conflicts disappear and turns the rest into ones nobody can reason about. Making the conflict visible and cheap to resolve is worth more than making it rare.

Between the start and end of the nightly close, write endpoints touching balances return `503` with a `Retry-After` naming the end of the window, typically a few minutes. Reads continue normally. Letting writes through during the close was the earlier behaviour and it meant the close ran against a moving target: totals were computed, a transaction landed mid-pass, and the closing balance disagreed with the sum of its own entries by an amount nobody could locate afterwards. Finance reconciled by hand for two months. Blocking is crude but it is honest, and a clear refusal with a retry hint is far better for an integration than a write that succeeds and lands in an accounting period nobody expects. The window is published in the developer documentation and announced when it moves, since a partner's own nightly job scheduled inside it will fail every night otherwise. Queued work does not have to care; the consumers pause on the same signal and resume afterwards, so the backlog drains rather than erroring. Shortening the window is a standing piece of work rather than a solved problem.

Operations that cannot reliably finish inside the request budget do not try. They validate, enqueue, and return `202` with a job id and a status URL the caller polls. Report generation, bulk imports and account merges all work this way. The rule for deciding is the ninety-fifth percentile of the operation's duration against the gateway's own ceiling: anything within a factor of two of that ceiling becomes asynchronous, because the alternative is an endpoint that works in testing and times out on the largest customers, which is the worst possible distribution of failure. Making it explicit also stops the pattern where a client's own timeout is raised to accommodate one slow endpoint, which then applies to every other call it makes. Job records are kept for seven days with their result, so a client that loses the handle can list recent jobs for the account rather than starting over. Failures are surfaced on the job record with the same error shape used everywhere else, since a caller should not need a second error vocabulary just because the work happened later.

Collections are paginated by cursor, never by page number or offset. A list response carries `data`, a `has_more` boolean and a `next_cursor`, and the caller passes that cursor back as `starting_after` with an optional `limit` that defaults to fifty and is capped at two hundred. The cursor is an opaque base64 string holding the sort key and the row id of the last item returned; clients are told not to decode it, and its contents have changed twice without anyone noticing, which is the point. Every list endpoint sorts on `(created_at DESC, id DESC)` — the id is there purely to break ties, because two rows created in the same millisecond are common and a sort with ties is not a stable boundary to resume from. Offset paging was what we shipped first and it failed in both directions. Reading a large account's records, `OFFSET 400000` made the database walk and discard four hundred thousand rows for every page, so the last pages of a long list took seconds each and the query showed up at the top of the slow log. Worse, offsets are not stable under writes: a row inserted while a client was on page three pushed an item onto page four, so the client saw one item twice and another not at all, producing a reconciliation mismatch nobody could reproduce on demand. Total counts are deliberately not returned, since counting a filtered set costs about as much as the query itself.

Aggregate counts shown in the dashboard are read from `account_daily_rollup`, populated by a job that runs at half past one and covers the previous day. They are explicitly labelled with the date they were computed for, and the interface never presents them as live. Computing them on demand was the previous behaviour and it was the single most expensive query pattern we had: the counts were on the account overview, so every page load ran several full scans over filtered sets, and a handful of large accounts made those scans expensive enough to affect everyone. Rollups turned that into a lookup by primary key. The design question that took the longest was what to do about the current day, and the answer is to show nothing rather than a partial figure, because a number that is wrong in a way that resolves overnight generates support conversations forever. Backfilling the table after a schema change is a documented procedure that runs in date order and is safe to re-run, since the job writes with an upsert keyed on account and date rather than inserting.

Any list endpoint over time-series data requires a date range and rejects one wider than ninety days with a `422` naming the limit. Omitting the range is not permitted either; it defaults to nothing and returns an error rather than defaulting to all of history, because a default of everything is how an unbounded query gets written by accident. Records older than the window live in the same tables and are perfectly readable, just not in one request. The limit exists because the partitioning is monthly, and a query spanning three partitions plans well while one spanning forty does not — the planner's estimates degrade, it stops choosing the index, and the query that worked in testing against six months of data behaves entirely differently against six years. Callers who genuinely need a long span are pointed at the export path, which is built for it. Ninety days was picked because it covers a full quarter, which is the longest span anybody had a real reason to ask for interactively, and the handful of requests to widen it have all turned out on inspection to be export use cases.

A list endpoint accepts filtering only on the fields named in its own allowlist, and each of those fields is backed by an index chosen for that access pattern. Anything else is rejected rather than quietly ignored, because silently dropping a filter returns the wrong data with a successful status, which is the worst combination available. The generic filtering layer we had before let clients express nearly anything, and the practical result was that our query shapes were designed by our customers' integrations rather than by us. Any filter on an unindexed column was a sequential scan, and there was no way to see one coming; the first symptom was always database load. The allowlist inverts that: adding a filterable field is a change we review, and reviewing it means deciding what index it needs before anyone can use it. It also makes the surface honest, since a client can read what a collection supports instead of discovering by experiment which combinations happen to be fast. Requests that need a shape we do not support get answered with either a new field or an explanation.

Each collection has one order and the caller cannot change it. There is no sort parameter anywhere in the public surface. Every ordering is an index that has to exist, be maintained on every write, and occupy memory, and an arbitrary sort parameter means committing to a set of indexes we did not choose and cannot retire. The version of this we had briefly accepted a field name and a direction, and within a month integrations were sorting on columns whose indexes existed for an entirely different reason, which made those indexes impossible to change. There is a correctness argument too. A cursor is only meaningful in the order it was issued for, so an ordering the client can vary between calls is one where resuming is undefined, and the bugs that produces are intermittent and blamed on us. Where an alternative order genuinely matters, it becomes its own endpoint with its own index and its own name, which is more typing and considerably easier to reason about. Client-side sorting of a fetched page is of course fine and is what most callers actually wanted.

Anyone wanting their whole history calls `POST /v2/exports`, which returns a job id; when it finishes, a signed URL valid for one hour points at a compressed file in object storage. The list endpoints are not the tool for that and are not tuned for it. An export runs against a read replica, streams straight to storage without materialising in memory, and takes as long as it takes, which for the largest accounts is several minutes — entirely acceptable for a file somebody will open in a spreadsheet, and entirely unacceptable inside a request. The path exists because integrations were emulating it by walking collections in a tight loop at the maximum page size, which worked, consumed most of an account's rate limit, and put steady read load on the primary for hours. Pointing them at a purpose-built path was better for them and for us. The file's schema is versioned and documented separately from the API surface, since the two change for different reasons, and the URL is single-purpose so possession of it grants nothing beyond that one file.

Free-text search does not touch the transactional database. It queries a search cluster fed by a change stream, and the documented freshness budget is thirty seconds from write to searchable, measured continuously by `search_index_lag_seconds`, which times a probe document from write to searchable. The separation is about failure isolation as much as performance: search traffic is bursty, expensive and driven by humans typing, and letting it share capacity with the write path meant a spike in one became latency in the other. Keeping them apart also let the index be shaped for retrieval, with denormalised documents and analysers per field, instead of contorting the relational schema to serve queries it was never designed for. The freshness budget is stated publicly because the alternative — implying it is instantaneous — generates a support case every time someone creates a record and immediately searches for it. When the pipeline falls behind, the interface says so rather than quietly returning results from a lagging index, which was the behaviour before and was much harder to explain after the fact.

A collection response contains ids for related objects, not the objects themselves, and expansion is available only on single-resource fetches. The reason is the multiplication: a page of a hundred orders each expanding a customer, a shipping address and three line items is several hundred additional lookups per request, and the version of this we shipped originally did exactly that inside a loop. Rewriting it to batch the lookups helped and did not solve it, because the response was then large enough that serialisation and transfer dominated. Most callers were discarding the expansions anyway; they wanted a list to display and fetched details on click. Clients that genuinely need the related objects for a whole page use `POST /v2/batch/get`, which takes a set of ids and returns them in one call, and that has proven to be a much smaller set of callers than the original design assumed. The rule has one carve-out for objects that are meaningless without their parent, such as a line item, which is embedded because there is no useful endpoint from which to fetch it alone.

Every collection query must resolve to exactly one account, and the layer that builds queries refuses to construct one without that predicate rather than trusting each endpoint to remember it. This is enforced in the data access layer, not in the handlers, because handlers are written by people in a hurry and there are a great many of them. Getting this wrong is the failure that ends companies, and we came close: an internal reporting endpoint was added without the scope, and although it was behind staff authentication and no customer ever saw another customer's data, it took a code review rather than any mechanism to catch it. The lesson taken was not to review harder. Queries that legitimately span accounts, of which there are a small number for platform operations, use a separate explicitly named path that logs every call with the operator's identity, so crossing the boundary is possible, deliberate, and permanently recorded. Tests assert that the ordinary path raises when the scope is absent, so the protection cannot be removed quietly.

A delivery is attempted for twenty-four hours and then abandoned. That works out to fourteen attempts on an exponential schedule starting at ten seconds and capping the interval at two hours, after which the event is marked `undeliverable` and stops being touched. Two things fix the budget at a day. The first is queue economics: retries are stored work, and an endpoint going down does not stop us generating events for it. We ran a seven-day budget once and a large integrator's receiver returned `502` for most of a week; by the time they fixed it, roughly four million deliveries were queued for one destination, the shared workers were spending most of their capacity on attempts guaranteed to fail, and everyone else's webhooks were minutes late. One broken consumer degraded everybody, which is the wrong shape of failure. The second is that the retries had stopped being useful long before that. An endpoint refusing deliveries for a full day is not having a blip, it is misconfigured or down, and the fix involves a person; a delivery that finally lands three days late is frequently worse for the receiver than one that never lands, because their processing assumes rough recency. Abandoned events are not deleted — they stay queryable through the events API for thirty days, which is the supported way to catch up, and it is a pull so the receiver sets the pace.

Every delivery carries `X-Harborlane-Signature`, an HMAC over the timestamp and the raw request body computed with the subscription's secret. Receivers are told to compare it in constant time and to reject anything whose timestamp is more than five minutes old, which is what stops a captured delivery from being replayed later. Rotation overlaps: a new secret is issued while the old one stays valid for seven days, and during that window the header carries two signatures so a receiver can cut over whenever suits them without coordinating a moment with us. Rotation without overlap was the first design and it required both sides to deploy simultaneously, which in practice meant nobody rotated. The detail that generates the most support traffic is that the signature covers the exact bytes we sent, so a receiver whose framework parses and re-serialises the body before verifying will fail every time, and the documentation now says so before it says anything else. Secrets are shown once at creation and stored hashed, so a lost one is regenerated rather than recovered.

Adding an event type to a subscription, or creating a subscription outright, affects only events generated after the change; nothing is backfilled and there is no option to ask for it. This surprises people often enough that it is called out in the setup flow rather than left in the reference. The reasoning is that a backfill is indistinguishable from a flood at the receiving end — a subscription created against a busy account would immediately deliver whatever history was chosen, at whatever rate the fleet could manage, to an endpoint that has never received anything before and has been tested against a trickle. The first thing it would do is fall over, and the second thing it would do is trigger the retry machinery. The correct tool for catching up is the pull-based events listing, which the receiver drives at its own pace and can stop, and pointing people there during setup has proven to be the moment they actually build the reconciliation path, rather than discovering they need one later. Removing an event type takes effect immediately, since stopping is never harmful.

Each attempt writes a row in `webhook_delivery_attempts` recording the destination, the status code, the round-trip duration, the attempt number, and the first two kilobytes of the response body. Everything beyond that is discarded. Keeping the body at all is the point: nearly every support conversation about webhooks turns on what the receiver actually returned, and without it the exchange is one side describing symptoms to the other for a day before anybody looks at the same thing. The truncation exists because a misconfigured endpoint returning a full HTML error page on every attempt wrote more log volume in a week than the deliveries themselves, and two kilobytes covers any structured error and the opening of any stack trace, which is where the useful part invariably is. Bodies are redacted for anything matching the credential patterns before storage, since receivers do occasionally echo headers back. The rows are kept for thirty days and are exposed to the customer in the dashboard for their own subscriptions, which has removed a good deal of back-and-forth by letting them see the failures themselves.

All deliveries leave through a NAT gateway with a small, stable set of public addresses, published in `docs/webhooks/egress.md` and changed only with ninety days' notice. Customers behind corporate firewalls allowlist them, and without that guarantee a meaningful share of enterprise integrations simply cannot be set up. The commitment is more constraining than it sounds. It means delivery workers cannot run on arbitrary capacity with arbitrary egress, so they are pinned to a subnet that routes through the gateway, and it means a provider or region change becomes a customer-facing announcement rather than an internal migration. We accepted that after losing a deal to it. The addresses are also what lets a receiver do a cheap first-pass check on authenticity, though the documentation is careful to say the signature is the real control and the address list is convenience, because addresses can be spoofed at the network layer and a receiver treating them as authentication has built something weaker than it thinks. The published list lives in the same place as the signature documentation.

Webhooks arrive in whatever order they arrive in, and the documentation says so plainly rather than describing a best effort. Deliveries are distributed across a worker fleet, retries reorder by construction, and the network does what it does, so anything that looked like ordering would be a coincidence a receiver would come to depend on. Every payload carries a sequence value and the timestamp of the state it describes, and receivers are told to compare that against what they hold and discard anything older. That instruction is the whole design, because it turns ordering from a delivery problem into a receiver-side comparison that is trivial to implement and impossible to get subtly wrong. Guaranteeing order was considered seriously and would have required serialising deliveries per subscription, which makes one slow receiver the pace of every event for that account and makes a single failing delivery block everything behind it. The failure it would introduce is far worse than the one it removes. The compare-and-discard pattern is shown in the documentation in the first example rather than buried in an appendix.

Every subscription has a control that sends a synthetic event of any type it is subscribed to, with representative but obviously fake data and `"livemode": false` on the payload. It goes through the identical delivery path, signing included, so a signature that fails on a test event will fail in production. Before it existed, the only way to verify an endpoint was to perform the real action in the product, which for some event types meant creating an actual order or triggering an actual refund, and support had a documented procedure for cleaning up the resulting test records. Integrators were doing this against production because there was nothing else, and the test flag exists so a receiver can safely ignore or route them. Test deliveries are visible in the attempt log alongside real ones and are excluded from the failure statistics that drive alerting, since a developer iterating on an endpoint would otherwise generate exactly the pattern that looks like a broken integration.

`delivery_timeout_ms` is 5000, so a delivery fails if the receiver has not returned a status within five seconds, and the connection is dropped at that point. The documentation is explicit that a receiver should acknowledge and then do its work, not do its work and then acknowledge. The timeout is short on purpose. A worker blocked on a slow receiver is a worker not delivering anybody else's events, and with a generous timeout the fleet's effective capacity is set by the slowest endpoint subscribed to it. At thirty seconds, which is where it started, two customers whose receivers processed synchronously were consuming a disproportionate share of delivery capacity during their busy periods. There is a second reason that matters to the receiver more: a long timeout encourages doing real work inside the request, and any receiver built that way will eventually time out under load and get sent a duplicate, at which point they discover they needed idempotency after all. Five seconds pushes that discovery into their first day rather than their worst day. Connect timeout is one second and is counted separately.

Deliveries to any single subscription run at a bounded concurrency, set per subscription and raised on request once a receiver has demonstrated it can take more. The default is deliberately modest. Without the cap, an account generating a burst of activity produces a burst of simultaneous requests at their endpoint, and the receiver that has been working fine for months falls over precisely when its owner is busiest — which is a failure we caused, arriving disguised as a failure they caused. The cap also protects the fleet, since it bounds how much of the worker pool any one destination can occupy, and that is what keeps a single popular integration from starving the rest. Raising it is a conversation rather than a form, because the useful part is asking the customer what their receiver actually does per event; more often than not that conversation ends with them making the handler asynchronous instead, which solves their problem better than more concurrency would. The current value for a subscription is visible in the dashboard so nobody has to guess why deliveries are paced the way they are.

The numbers in the mobile networking layer were negotiated in a joint session after an incident, and both sides came away with obligations. What forced it: a dependency slowed down, the app's connect and read timeouts both sat at sixty seconds inherited from a framework default, and users watched a spinner for a minute before tapping retry, often twice, so the app generated roughly three times its normal volume against a backend already struggling and the slowdown became an outage. Neither team could fix that alone. The agreement is a budget, not one number. Mobile connects in five seconds and reads in fifteen for anything a person waits on; a short named list of known-slow endpoints gets thirty, and that list is the interesting artifact, since adding to it requires the backend team to accept it publicly. In exchange the server side commits that any endpoint not on the list keeps its ninety-fifth percentile under six seconds, and the gateway hard-caps at twenty seconds, returning `504` with a `retryable` flag so the client is told whether trying again is sensible. Mobile commits to at most two automatic retries, only on that flag, with jittered backoff, and to showing the user something before the timeout expires. The list and the percentile are reviewed together each quarter; an endpoint on the list for two reviews becomes a backend work item, not a permanent exception.

The minimum acceptable app build is `min_supported_build` in remote configuration, not something compiled into a release, and the app checks it on launch. Below the soft threshold it shows a dismissible prompt; below the hard one it shows a blocking screen with a store link. Baking the threshold into a build cannot work, because the users who need to be told are precisely the ones not installing new builds. The mechanism gets used rarely and deliberately: twice for a client-side bug that corrupted local state, once when a protocol change genuinely could not be made backward compatible. The rule that came out of the second of those is that the hard threshold moves only with a written reason and sign-off from both the mobile lead and support, since a blocking screen is a total outage for whoever hits it and there is a long tail of users on old operating systems who literally cannot install the newer build. Analytics track the distribution of live builds continuously, and the soft prompt is normally enough to move the bulk of it within a fortnight.

A mobile release goes out at one percent of the install base on day one, ten percent on day two, and everyone on day three, with the crash and error dashboards checked at each step before the next is started. Staged rollout is the only meaningful safety mechanism a mobile release has, because there is no rollback: a build that reaches a device stays there until the user installs another one, and pushing a fix through review takes hours at best. The percentages exist because a serious crash is visible at one percent within a few hours, and one percent of the base is small enough that the support volume is manageable while it is happening. Halting a rollout is one toggle in `mobile/release.yaml` and an ordinary, blameless action taken by whoever notices, not a decision that needs a meeting, and it has been used more often for a suspicious metric that turned out fine than for a real defect, which is exactly the ratio you want. Server-side changes the release depends on ship and are verified before the rollout begins, never during it.

A build does not progress through its rollout unless the crash-free session rate stays above the agreed threshold, measured on the cohort that has the new build rather than on the whole population. Sessions rather than users is a deliberate choice: measuring by user hides a crash that happens on one specific screen, because a user who crashes once and then uses the app normally all week still counts as affected either way, while the session measure shows how much of actual usage is being ruined. The threshold is a gate rather than a target, which matters culturally — nobody is asked to improve it, they are asked to not ship below it — and it is the only automatic stop in the release process. Getting there required cleaning up the reporting first, since a meaningful share of what was being counted came from a single background task failing on one manufacturer's older devices, which was real but was drowning everything else. Non-fatal errors are tracked separately and are not a gate, because making them one produced pressure to catch and swallow exceptions.

Actions taken without connectivity are written to a local queue and replayed in the order they were made once the network returns, with the interface showing them as pending rather than complete. Replaying out of order was the first implementation and produced results that were individually correct and collectively nonsense, since editing a record and then deleting it means something entirely different in the other order. The queue is capped, and when it fills the app stops accepting new offline actions and says so, which is unpleasant but far better than silently discarding the oldest. Each queued action carries the identifier generated on the device at the time it was taken, so the same action replayed after an ambiguous failure is recognised rather than duplicated. The flush is serialised per record, not globally, so one stuck action does not hold up unrelated work, and anything that fails permanently surfaces to the user with the option to discard rather than retrying forever in the background where nobody can see it.

The mobile client has exactly one host in its configuration, `api.harborlane.com`, and reaches every backend capability through it. It holds no service addresses and no knowledge of how the backend is decomposed. The alternative surfaced during a period when several teams were splitting services out, and each split was proposing that the app learn a new host; the objection was not effort but permanence. A hostname that ships in a build is effectively immortal, since old builds keep calling it for years, so every internal boundary the app knows about becomes a boundary we can never move. Routing through the gateway means services can be split, merged, renamed and relocated with no client change at all, and it gives one place to apply authentication, rate limiting and request logging rather than a copy of each per service. The cost is a hop and a component that must not go down, which is accepted and is why it is the most conservatively operated thing we run. Even the health check the app uses on launch goes through it, so the answer reflects the path a real request takes.

There is a staging account reserved for the mobile team, with its own seeded data, which nobody else writes to. It is reset from a fixture set every night at two, so the state a manual tester or an automated run starts from is identical every morning. Sharing a staging tenant was the previous arrangement and it failed in the ordinary way: someone else's test run would change the data a mobile test depended on, the test would fail, and half a day would go into investigating a defect that did not exist. Worse, it made intermittent failures unattributable, which is corrosive, because a suite people do not believe is a suite people ignore. Isolation cost a modest amount of extra infrastructure and removed an entire category of argument. The fixtures live in `mobile/test/fixtures/` alongside the app's test suite so that adding a scenario is one change rather than a request to another team, and the nightly reset is deliberately destructive, which discourages anyone from treating the tenant as a place to keep something.

Backend and mobile hold a short standing meeting each week where anything changing on the surface gets walked through before it is built, not after. It is the only recurring meeting either team has that includes the other, and it survived several rounds of calendar pruning because both sides fought for it. The value is almost entirely in the questions asked at the whiteboard stage, where a design that is convenient on the server turns out to require three round trips on a phone, and that is cheap to change while it is still a drawing. Written specifications did not achieve this. They were read, they were approved, and the problems were still found during integration, because reading a specification does not put you in the position of implementing against it. The meeting also carries the reverse traffic, mobile explaining what a constraint on the device actually means, which has changed several backend designs. Notes are short and the decisions land in the relevant tickets rather than in a document nobody revisits.

When a request fails, the app keeps the `X-Request-Id` from the response headers, or the locally generated one if no response arrived, and pre-fills it into the in-app support form along with the build number, the operating system version and the connection type. The user sees a short reference code rather than the raw identifier. Before this, a support conversation began with a screenshot and an approximate time, and correlating that against server logs was slow and often impossible; with the id it is one query. The locally generated fallback matters more than it looks, because the failures worth investigating are disproportionately the ones where nothing came back at all, and those are exactly the cases the server has no record of. The client sends that id on the request, so a trace exists even for something that timed out. The form deliberately captures the last few failures rather than only the current one, since users tend to report a problem after trying several times, and the interesting attempt is usually not the last.

Nothing re-drives a dead-letter topic automatically. The broker-side redrive policy is set to zero on every `*.dlq` topic declared in `kestrel/topics/`, and the only way a message leaves one is an engineer running `kestrelctl dlq drain --group <group> --since <window> --rate 50` from the ops host. That is deliberate, and cost an afternoon to learn. The first version of the platform re-drove dead letters every fifteen minutes, so when the tariff service came back from a two-hour degradation the same forty thousand messages cycled out of the DLQ and back into it until someone noticed, adding steady load to a dependency that was trying to recover and draining the retry budget of everything sharing its pool. The second reason is evidentiary. A dead letter is usually the only surviving copy of what actually failed, and an automatic drain destroys the sample before a human has read it. So the drain refuses to start unless the operator passes `--reason` with an incident or ticket id, it prints ten randomly chosen messages and waits for a confirmation, and it stops at ten thousand messages per invocation so a wrong window is bounded. The rule the runbook states outright is that you do not drain before the fix that caused the failures is deployed and verified, because the messages come straight back and the second lap looks identical to the first in every dashboard we have.

Every dead-letter topic is named after the topic the messages came from, never after the consumer that gave up on them: `shipments.events` dead-letters to `shipments.events.dlq` no matter which of its four consumer groups failed. We started the other way round, one dead-letter topic per group, and ended up with names like `dlq.label-writer-v2` that stopped meaning anything the week the service was renamed and told you nothing about what shape of payload was sitting inside. Source-based naming means a message in a dead-letter topic can always be validated against the schema subject of its parent, and the retention and partition count are inherited from the parent topic by the same generator. The trade is that a single dead-letter topic mixes failures from several consumers, so the failing consumer group is carried in the `x-dlq-consumer` header instead of in the topic name, which is where the dashboards read it from. `kestrel/bin/lint-topics` fails the pipeline for any topic ending in `.dlq` whose prefix is not itself a declared topic, which catches the hand-created ones that used to appear during incidents and then live forever.

Dead letters are copied to object storage before the broker expires them. A small consumer tails every `*.dlq` topic and writes newline-delimited batches to `s3://kestrel-deadletters/<topic>/<date>/`, hourly, with the broker retention on the dead-letter topics themselves left at twenty-one days. The reason for the copy is that the interesting questions arrive late: a partner disputes a shipment three weeks after the fact, or a bug turns out to have been silently failing since a release two months back, and by then the broker has long since aged the evidence out. Object storage is cheap enough that keeping the raw bytes for a year is not worth arguing about, and the archive is lifecycle-tiered to infrequent access after thirty days. The archive is explicitly not an operational path — it is not indexed, it is not searchable without a scan job, and nothing reads from it automatically. It is the thing you go to when someone asks whether a particular payload ever arrived and the answer matters. Access is restricted to the on-call role because the archived payloads are unredacted at the point they land.

A dead-lettered message keeps everything it arrived with. The producer's original headers are copied verbatim, the original topic, partition and offset go into `x-dlq-source`, the consumer group into `x-dlq-consumer`, the attempt count into `x-dlq-attempts`, the exception class and message into `x-dlq-error`, and the wall-clock time of the final failure into `x-dlq-timestamp`. The payload bytes are untouched — not re-serialized, not pretty-printed, not wrapped in an envelope. That last part matters more than it sounds. An earlier version wrapped the payload in a JSON envelope so the metadata could live alongside it, which meant the bytes in the dead-letter topic no longer validated against the schema subject of the source topic, and every tool that could read normal traffic needed a special case. Keeping the body byte-identical means the same deserializer, the same schema, the same viewer. The trace id is preserved too, so a dead letter links back to the request that produced it even when that request finished successfully hours earlier.

Growth in a dead-letter topic opens a ticket; it does not page anyone. The reasoning is about what the on-call engineer can usefully do at three in the morning. A message that has already been dead-lettered has finished failing — it is at rest, it is not consuming resources, and nothing about it gets worse while everyone sleeps. The situations that genuinely need a human immediately show up in other signals first: consumers crash-looping, a dependency returning errors, work not getting done. Dead letters are the residue of those, and paging on residue meant the on-call rotation was woken by the aftermath of things that had already been handled. There is one exception that does page, and it is a rate rather than a count — when a consumer group starts dead-lettering nearly everything it touches, that is a broken deploy rather than a scattering of bad payloads, and the page fires on the ratio of dead letters to processed messages, not on the size of the topic. Everything else becomes a ticket for the owning team with the sample attached, and is expected to be triaged within the working week.

Customer identifiers are stripped from a payload on its way into a dead-letter topic. A redaction step in the consumer runtime walks the deserialized message and replaces the fields listed in `kestrel/redaction.yaml` — currently `consignee.email`, `consignee.phone`, `consignee.address_lines` and `payer.tax_id` — with a salted hash of the value, keeping the field present and the type intact so the message still validates against its schema. The hash is stable within a day, which is enough to tell whether five hundred dead letters concern one customer or five hundred. This exists because dead letters are read by more people, in more places, than normal traffic: they get pasted into incident channels, exported into spreadsheets and archived for a year. Nothing else in the pipeline redacts, and that is intentional — the live path needs the real values to do its work. The cost we accepted is that a dead letter cannot be replayed straight back into processing after redaction, so the corrected payload has to be rebuilt from the upstream system of record rather than from the parked copy.

One dead-letter topic has exactly one owner, and the owner is the team that owns the consumer group, not the team that owns the producing service. This was an argument worth having. Producers wanted the failures routed back to them on the grounds that most bad messages come from bad publishing, and consumers wanted them on the grounds that the decision to give up on a message is theirs. What settled it is that only the consumer knows why it failed — the producer's payload may be perfectly valid and the failure may be a missing row in the consumer's own database — so routing to the producer generated a stream of handoffs where the first responder could not diagnose anything. Ownership is recorded next to the consumer group declaration and is what the ticket router reads. When the failure really is a producer problem, the consumer team raises it as such, with the evidence already attached, and that turns out to be a much better shaped conversation than a topic full of failures landing on a team with no context for them.

A message is written to its dead-letter topic before the source offset is committed, never after, and the two happen in that order inside the same processing loop. Auto-commit is off across every consumer group — `enable.auto.commit=false` — and the loop is publish-to-dlq, wait for the broker acknowledgement, then commit. Reversing the order loses messages: a consumer that commits first and dies before the dead-letter publish has moved past the offset with nothing to show for it, and the payload is gone. The order we use duplicates instead, because a consumer that dies after publishing but before committing will process, fail, and dead-letter the same message again on restart. Duplicates in a dead-letter topic are cheap and visible; a silent hole in the record is neither. The duplicate is easy to spot because the envelope carries the source partition and offset, so two dead letters with the same coordinates are the same message twice. Consumers that cannot publish to the dead-letter topic at all — broker unavailable — stop rather than skip, and let the lag build.

Dead-letter counts are read out in the weekly service review, one line per consumer group, and that slot exists to catch the slow leak rather than the outage. The pattern it was created for is a group that dead-letters a handful of messages every day, forever, because of a payload variant nobody wants to handle — small enough that no threshold fires, persistent enough that over a quarter it adds up to a meaningful number of customer-visible things that quietly did not happen. In review the question asked of any non-zero line is whether the team intends to fix it or intends to accept it, and accepting is a legitimate answer as long as it is written down with a reason. Groups that have been non-zero for three consecutive reviews without a decision get raised with the owning manager, which sounds bureaucratic and has in practice been the mechanism that got two long-running payload bugs fixed. The review also catches the opposite signal: a group whose dead letters drop to zero after years of a steady trickle usually means its consumer stopped running.

Lag alerts fire on projected drain time, not on message count. The rule that came out of the calibration is that a backlog only matters if it is not going to clear, so the expression divides current group lag by the consumer group's throughput averaged over five minutes and compares the resulting seconds against a per-class budget: `interactive` pages at a projected two minutes, `standard` opens a ticket at thirty minutes, `bulk` says nothing until six hours. Every threshold also requires the projection to have risen across three consecutive windows, which is what stopped the flapping: a single slow batch used to trip a count threshold and clear before anyone opened a laptop. We started with raw counts and the numbers were unmaintainable: ten thousand messages is a crisis for the label consumer and a normal Tuesday for the export consumer, so every group needed a hand-tuned constant, and those constants got quietly retuned upward each time a nightly import woke someone. The projection also goes to infinity when throughput is zero, which was the real blind spot: a stalled group with a small backlog now alerts faster than a busy group with a large one. A separate stuck-partition check carries no throughput term at all: no offset movement for ten minutes on a partition with pending messages pages immediately, because one wedged partition disappears inside a healthy group total.

The `orders.events` topic was repartitioned from six to twenty-four partitions during the winter capacity review. Partition count is the ceiling on consumer parallelism — a group can never usefully run more instances than the topic has partitions — and at six the order consumer was pinned at six replicas while its per-message cost kept growing. Twenty-four was chosen as four times the expected steady-state replica count so there is headroom for a doubling without another repartition, and because the partition key is the account id, which distributes well enough that the busiest partition carries about one and a half times the mean. Repartitioning is not free and this is why we do it rarely: adding partitions rehashes the key space, so ordering guarantees within a key are broken across the boundary, and the migration ran during a maintenance window with producers paused for ninety seconds. New topics are now created with a partition count sized for two years rather than the current load, since over-partitioning costs a little broker memory and under-partitioning costs a migration.

Consumers commit offsets on a timer, every five seconds, rather than after every message. Per-message commits produced an offset write for each unit of work, which at peak was a few thousand small writes a second against the coordinator and showed up as a visible share of broker CPU for no benefit anyone could describe. The exposure the timer creates is bounded and understood: a consumer that dies mid-interval reprocesses at most five seconds of work on restart, which is fine because every consumer is already required to be idempotent for unrelated reasons. Two consumer groups opt out and commit synchronously per batch — the settlement writer and the customs document sender — because for those the reprocessing window is a duplicate outbound side effect rather than a duplicate database write. The setting lives with the consumer group declaration rather than in each service's own config, so the value is visible in one place, and changing it requires the same review as changing the group's partition assignment.

Lag is measured by a per-cluster exporter rather than by the consumers themselves. A small sidecar in each broker cluster queries the group coordinator every fifteen seconds for committed offsets and the log-end offsets of every partition, and publishes the difference on port 9308 for the metrics agent to scrape. Having consumers report their own lag was the earlier design and it had an obvious hole: a consumer that has crashed or wedged reports nothing at all, and a metric that goes absent is much easier to overlook than a metric that goes large. The exporter sees the same coordinator state regardless of whether any consumer is alive, so a dead group still produces numbers. It also gives per-partition granularity that consumers could not, since each instance only knows about the partitions assigned to it. The exporter is deliberately read-only against the coordinator and runs with a consumer-group-describe permission and nothing else, after an early version was found to be capable of resetting offsets it had no business touching.

Broker disk usage pages at eighty percent of the data volume, and it pages rather than ticketing because the failure past that line is not graceful. When a broker fills its disk it stops accepting writes for every topic it leads, which means producers across unrelated services start failing at once, and the recovery involves either expanding a volume under load or truncating retention on live topics and losing replay capability. Eighty percent gives roughly a day of headroom at the growth rates we see, which is enough to expand the volume in business hours. The signal that usually precedes it is a retention setting someone raised for a good reason and never lowered, so the alert message links straight to the per-topic retained-bytes breakdown rather than to a host dashboard. This threshold has nothing to do with how much work is waiting to be processed — a cluster can be perfectly caught up and still be filling its disks with retained history, and conflating those two was why an early version of the runbook sent people looking at the wrong dashboards.

The lag dashboard is organised by owning team first and topic second, which is the opposite of how it started. A topic-shaped dashboard reads well to the platform team and badly to everyone else: during an incident the person looking at it has to know which topics their service consumes before they can tell whether any of the red belongs to them, and in practice people simply did not know, so a wall of unfamiliar names got mentally filtered out. Grouping by team means the first screen answers the only question most viewers have, which is whether their own consumers are healthy, and the platform-wide view moved to a second tab for the people whose job it actually is. The change also made ownership gaps visible, because a consumer group with no team attached now renders in an ugly unassigned block at the bottom rather than blending into an alphabetical list. Two groups sat there for a month before they were claimed, which is roughly the argument for the layout in a sentence.

Session timeout on every consumer group was raised to forty-five seconds with a heartbeat interval of three, after a run of rebalance storms. The default was low enough that an ordinary garbage-collection pause or a slow local commit could miss a heartbeat, at which point the coordinator evicted the instance, triggered a group rebalance, stopped every other instance in the group while partitions were reassigned, and made the next heartbeat more likely to be missed because everyone was now busy catching up. That feedback loop took the export group offline for twenty minutes without a single instance ever actually crashing. The longer timeout costs detection latency on a genuinely dead consumer, which is the trade we accepted: a truly dead instance is now noticed up to forty-five seconds later, and the stuck-partition check catches the case where that matters. Cooperative incremental assignment was enabled at the same time so a rebalance no longer stops partitions that are not moving.

Every alert rule on a queue must carry a link to a runbook section, and the linter that builds the alert bundle rejects any rule where the annotation is missing or points at a page that does not exist. This started as a reaction to a night when someone was paged by a rule whose name meant nothing to them, spent the first fifteen minutes working out which service it belonged to, and then discovered the rule had been added months earlier by a person who had since changed teams. The requirement is not that the runbook be good — plenty of them are two sentences — but that there be a named place where the next person can add what they learned. The rule of thumb is that the section answers three things: what the alert actually measures, what the first useful command is, and what it looks like when it is a false alarm. Anything paged that has no runbook entry gets one written as part of the incident's follow-up, which is the mechanism by which the thin ones slowly get thicker.

A synthetic message is published into every topic on a fixed cadence and consumed by a dedicated verifier, which reports success or failure of the whole path. The reason is that a quiet topic and a broken topic look identical from the outside — no lag, no errors, no traffic — and we had one integration that stopped receiving partner events for the better part of a week without a single signal firing, because the absence of work is indistinguishable from work being absent. The synthetic messages carry a marker header that makes real consumers skip them, they are excluded from throughput dashboards so they do not inflate a quiet topic's numbers, and their payloads are constant so they compress away in retention. What the verifier measures is liveness of the pipe, not the health of the work: it will happily report green while a real consumer is failing every genuine message, so nobody is allowed to treat it as a substitute for the consumer's own error signals.

The ledger event stream no longer promises global ordering, and dropping that promise was the biggest design change of the year. The original stream ran on one partition because a total order was assumed to be a requirement of double-entry accounting, and one partition means one consumer instance: throughput topped out near twelve hundred events a second, and any slow consumer stalled the stream for everyone. Month-end close forced the decision: a slow reconciliation consumer held the shared stream far enough behind that settlement, payouts and the customer-facing balance all lagged by nearly an hour, and no amount of scaling helped because there was nothing to scale. What we promise now is per-account ordering and nothing more. Events are partitioned on `account_id`, so everything touching one account stays in order relative to itself, while two unrelated accounts have no defined order at all. Consumers carry an explicit monotonic `seq` per account and reject anything they have already applied, so redelivery and interleaving are ordinary rather than exceptional. What was given up is any question of the form "what happened across the whole system, in order", which is now answered from `ledger_entries` by transaction time rather than from the stream. Nightly reconciliation catches gaps in per-account sequences, the safety net that made the trade acceptable to finance.

Every event on the ledger stream is published against a registered schema subject named after the topic with a `-value` suffix, and the producer library refuses to publish a payload that does not validate. Compatibility is set to backward on every subject, so a new version may add optional fields and may not remove or retype existing ones; a producer trying to register an incompatible schema fails in CI rather than at runtime. This came out of a week where a field changed from a string to an object and four consumers deserialized garbage for two days without erroring, because their parsers were tolerant in exactly the wrong way. The schema id travels in the message header rather than being inferred, so a consumer reading old retained data resolves the version that payload was written with instead of the current one. Retiring a field is a two-release job: stop writing it, wait until nothing reads it, then remove it from the schema. The registry itself is treated as production infrastructure, backed up with the databases, because losing it makes every retained message unreadable.

Nothing publishes to the ledger stream directly from application code. A row is written to `ledger_outbox` inside the same database transaction as the business change, and a relay process reads that table and publishes. The reason is the failure mode that pure dual-writes cannot avoid: a service that commits its transaction and then crashes before the publish leaves the database and the stream permanently disagreeing, and the disagreement is silent. With the outbox, the event is committed atomically with the fact it describes, so the worst case is a publish that happens late or twice rather than never. The relay claims rows in batches of five hundred ordered by primary key, publishes, then marks them sent; rows stay in the table for twenty-four hours after sending so a mistaken publish can be investigated, and a partial index keeps the unsent scan cheap as the table grows. The cost is one extra write per event and a small publish latency, typically well under a second, which nobody has ever complained about.

Retention on the ledger stream is ninety days, which is considerably longer than any consumer needs to keep up and is set for a different purpose. Replay is the actual reason: when a consumer has a bug that computed something wrong, the fix is usually to correct the code, reset that consumer group's offsets and let it rebuild its own state from history, and a retention window shorter than the time it takes to notice a bug makes that impossible. Ninety days was chosen because it comfortably covers a quarter, and most of the miscalculations we have had were found during quarterly reporting. It is not an archive and it is not the system of record — anything needed beyond the window is reconstructed from `ledger_entries`, which is retained for years under the finance policy. The storage cost of ninety days is modest because the events are small and compress well. Consumers are still expected to keep up in seconds; the long retention exists so that a rebuild is a routine operation rather than a project.

The balance snapshot topic is compacted rather than time-retained: `cleanup.policy=compact` with the account id as the key, so the broker keeps the most recent snapshot for every account forever and discards the superseded ones. That gives a consumer bootstrapping from scratch a complete picture of current balances by reading the topic once, without any consumer needing to query the ledger service, which is what the topic exists for. Compaction is a poor fit for the event stream itself and we do not use it there — events are facts and a later fact does not supersede an earlier one — but a snapshot is a value, and only the latest value is interesting. Two things had to change to make it work: snapshots must be published with a null payload to delete an account rather than being silently dropped, and the producer must publish a snapshot even when the balance is unchanged at least once a quarter, otherwise a dormant account's key eventually becomes the only evidence of a value nobody has re-verified. Segment settings were tuned so compaction actually runs on low-volume partitions.

Event type names are past tense, describe something that happened, and are never renamed once published. So `entry_posted`, `payout_settled`, `adjustment_reversed` — not `post_entry`, which reads like an instruction to somebody and invites consumers to treat the stream as a command bus. The naming rule and the immutability rule are really the same rule: the name is part of the contract, and consumers filter on it, so renaming one silently stops delivery to everything that subscribed under the old name. When a meaning genuinely changes, a new type is introduced alongside and the old one is deprecated on the usual schedule, with both published during the overlap. We also refuse names that encode the producer or the consumer, because a name like the one an early integration used told you which service emitted it and nothing about what occurred, and the moment that service was split the name became a lie. Names are reviewed at the same time as the schema, which is the only gate that catches this before it is permanent.

The ledger stream is mirrored asynchronously into the secondary region by a replicator that runs continuously and typically sits under two seconds behind. The mirror exists for disaster recovery, not for serving reads: no consumer subscribes to it in normal operation, and the topics on the far side carry a `mirror.` prefix specifically so nothing can point at them by accident. Offsets do not survive the crossing, since the mirrored topics have their own offset space, so a failover would restart consumers from a timestamp rather than from a committed position, and every consumer is required to tolerate that — which in practice means the same idempotency work that everything else already does. The replicator is bandwidth-capped so a backlog cannot saturate the inter-region link and take out the database replication that shares it, a lesson from a resync that did exactly that. Failover has been exercised twice in game days and both times the slow part was consumer configuration, not the data.

A team that wants to consume the ledger stream registers as a subscriber before it starts, rather than simply pointing a consumer at it. Registration is a short entry naming the team, the consumer group, the event types they care about and what they do with them, and it is reviewed by the ledger owners. This is unusual for us — most internal data is self-serve — and it exists because the stream carries financial facts and the consequence of a wrong reading is a wrong number in front of a customer or an auditor. The review catches the predictable misunderstandings, mostly people intending to derive balances by summing what they see rather than reading the published snapshot. The register is also what makes deprecation possible: when an event type has to change, the owners know exactly who to talk to instead of announcing into a channel and hoping. Nothing technically prevents an unregistered consumer, and once in a while one appears, at which point the conversation happens after the fact rather than before it.

Replaying the stream is done with a fresh consumer group name, never by resetting the offsets of the group that is running in production. Resetting in place looks like the obvious move and it takes the consumer offline for the whole replay, which for anything customer-facing means a rebuild becomes an outage, and if the replay turns out to be wrong there is no clean way back because the original position is gone. A new group starts wherever you point it, runs alongside the live one, writes into a shadow set of tables, and gets compared against production output before anything is switched. The convention is to suffix the group name with the date the replay started so the abandoned ones are obvious later; a stale group holding a position on an old offset is otherwise invisible until someone wonders why retention is not freeing space. Cleaning up finished replay groups is part of the same task that started them, and the ones nobody cleaned up are the reason that sentence is in the runbook.

An inbound partner event that the ingest worker cannot handle at all — it fails schema validation, or it crashes the handler twice in a row — is written whole into `parked_events` and the worker moves on. It is never discarded, and that word is doing real work: the obvious implementation, which we shipped first, logged the payload at error level and skipped it, and log retention meant the evidence was gone in two weeks. Two things changed our mind. The first was a partner who sent a malformed batch and then asked, six weeks later, which of their four thousand shipments we had received; the honest answer was that we had no idea, and reconstructing it from their side took two people most of a week. The second is that most poison is our fault, not theirs — an enum value we did not know about, a field that arrived as a string one day — so the payload is the only reproduction case that exists, and parked rows are now where the regression fixtures come from. A parked row keeps the raw body bytes, the request headers, the partner id, the validation error and the first-seen timestamp, and lives for one hundred and eighty days before it is reduced to a hash and a size. Parking is capped rather than unbounded: if more than two percent of a partner's events park inside ten minutes, ingest for that partner is paused, because at that point the sensible action is to stop and call them.

Every inbound partner payload is validated against a JSON Schema at the gateway edge, before it is queued and before any handler sees it. The schemas live in `gateway/schemas/partners/<partner>/<event>.json` and are versioned alongside the partner's integration contract. Validating early means a bad payload produces a clear response to the sender at the moment they sent it, with a pointer to the offending path, rather than becoming an asynchronous failure that they learn about through a support ticket days later. It also keeps handler code honest: because the shape is guaranteed by the time work is dequeued, handlers do not carry defensive branches for fields that cannot be absent, and the ones that had accumulated were deleted when this landed. Validation is strict about types and required fields and deliberately permissive about extra properties, so a partner adding a field of their own does not break the integration. Schema changes ship behind a per-partner flag so a new version can be enabled for one sender before it applies to all of them.

The gateway refuses any inbound request body over one megabyte with a 413 before reading the rest of it, and the limit is enforced at the proxy rather than in application code. The number came from measuring real partner traffic: the largest legitimate manifest we have ever received was around three hundred kilobytes, so a megabyte is generous by a factor of three and still small enough that a thousand concurrent uploads cannot exhaust memory. Before the limit existed, one partner's retry loop sent the same forty-megabyte document repeatedly after a bug on their side, and the ingest workers spent an afternoon deserializing it into memory over and over. Partners who genuinely need to send bulk data use the file-drop path instead, where the payload goes to object storage and the event carries a reference, which is a better shape for that work anyway. The limit is documented in the partner integration guide with the exact status code and error body, because the first version returned a generic error and the partner in question spent a day assuming it was authentication.

Partner events are deduplicated on the `delivery_id` header that the sender supplies, with the seen ids held in a Redis set for twenty-four hours and backed by a unique constraint on `inbound_events.delivery_id` for anything that gets persisted. Retrying senders are the norm rather than the exception — most partner platforms retry on any non-2xx, and several retry on a slow 2xx as well — so the same event arriving three times is ordinary traffic. Collapsing on the sender's own id rather than a hash of the body matters because two genuinely distinct events can be byte-identical: the same shipment scanned twice at the same location in the same second is two real facts. Where a partner does not send a delivery id at all, and two still do not, the gateway synthesizes one from a hash of the body plus the receipt minute, which is a compromise that loses genuine duplicates in that window and is documented as such in their integration notes.

An inbound event whose type we do not recognise is accepted, acknowledged and ignored, which is a different decision from what happens to a payload we cannot parse. Partners add event types on their own release schedule and tell us afterwards, or never; rejecting an unknown type would mean their new feature starts producing errors on our side and eventually pages someone, for something we have simply not implemented yet. So the gateway records the type in its counters and drops the body. The counter is the point: an unknown type showing up in volume is a strong signal that a partner has shipped something new, and it has twice been how we found out about an integration change before the account manager did. Unknown types are reviewed in the same weekly pass as the rest of the ingest metrics, and each one gets an explicit decision, either to implement it or to say plainly that we do not want it. What makes ignoring safe here is that the sender does not consider the event a request for anything — it is a notification, and their contract does not oblige us to act on all of them.

Every partner credential is scoped to exactly one event source and cannot post anything else. The keys are issued per integration rather than per partner, so a logistics partner sending both scan events and customs declarations holds two credentials, each accepted only on its own path and for its own event types. This came out of a review after a partner's integration vendor was found to be using one shared key across several of their customers, which meant a leak at the vendor exposed a credential that could write into more than one of our tenants' data. Scoping narrowly makes rotation possible without a coordinated outage: one integration can be re-keyed while the others keep running, and revoking a compromised key stops one flow rather than the whole relationship. Keys carry an expiry and the gateway warns in the partner's monthly report from thirty days out. Requests presenting a valid key on the wrong path are rejected and counted separately from ordinary authentication failures, because that particular pattern is almost always a misconfiguration rather than an attack.

The ingest endpoint returns 202 as soon as the payload has been validated and durably enqueued, never after the work is done. Processing takes anywhere from milliseconds to a couple of minutes depending on what the event triggers, and partners' HTTP clients almost universally time out well before the long end, so a synchronous design meant senders retried work that was actually still running, which produced duplicates for exactly the events that were most expensive. The 202 body carries the assigned `event_id` and a status URL, and partners who care about the outcome poll it or subscribe to a callback. The contract we publish is explicit that 202 means received and durable, not processed and accepted, since a partner integration team once read it the other way round and stopped reconciling entirely on the assumption that a 202 was a business acknowledgement. Durable means the enqueue has been acknowledged by the broker before the response is written; if that acknowledgement does not arrive, the gateway returns 503 and the sender's own retry does the right thing.

Each partner gets its own ingest queue rather than sharing one. The queues are created from the same template with the same settings, so this costs almost nothing operationally, and it buys isolation that matters in exactly the situations where everything else is going wrong. A partner that suddenly sends ten times its usual volume — a backfill on their side, a retry storm, a new customer they onboarded without telling us — fills its own queue and delays only its own events. On the shared queue we used to run, that scenario meant everyone waited behind one sender, and the partners who noticed were never the one causing it. Per-partner queues also make the metrics obvious without any extra tagging: the depth graph names the partner, and the on-call engineer can pause exactly one flow without touching the others. The obvious cost is a longer list of queues to look at, which is handled by rolling them up in the dashboard, and the less obvious one is that a brand new partner needs its queue created before its first event, which is now part of the onboarding checklist rather than something discovered on the day.

Changes a partner makes to their own payloads are recorded in a per-partner changelog that we maintain, not one they publish. Almost none of our senders version their integrations formally, and the ones that do tend to version the documentation rather than the wire format, so the only reliable record of what arrived and when is ours.
