An entry goes in whenever we notice a shape change — a new field, a value that used to be absent, a type that shifted — with the date first observed and where it was noticed. The value is entirely in hindsight: when a handler starts behaving oddly, the first question is what changed on the way in, and before the changelog existed that question was answered by guesswork and by scrolling through payload samples. It has also settled two commercial conversations where the partner sincerely believed nothing on their side had moved. Keeping it is a small ongoing tax paid by whoever is triaging, and it survives because the entries are short and nobody is asked to write prose.

Consumer replica counts follow queue depth automatically, through the scaler definitions in `deploy/scaling/consumers.yaml`. Each group declares a target of five hundred pending messages per replica, a floor of two replicas so a cold queue keeps warm workers, and a ceiling of its own. Scale-up and scale-down are deliberately asymmetric: the controller may add replicas every thirty seconds, but may only remove them after ten minutes below target. That asymmetry fixed the thrashing: the symmetric version added workers on a burst, removed them as soon as it cleared, and paid the cold-start cost again ninety seconds later, so a spiky afternoon left the pool starting more than working. The ceiling is what people get wrong when adding a consumer. It is not a cost limit; it comes from what the slowest dependency absorbs. Each replica holds four Postgres pool slots, so a ceiling of forty replicas promises no more than one hundred and sixty connections. We learned that in April: a backlog on the rating consumer was answered by raising its maximum, the extra workers exhausted the database pool, and a queue backlog became an outage on the synchronous API sharing that database. So the standing instruction during a large backlog is not to raise the ceiling: reroute the work to the bulk queue or throttle the producer, and let it drain at the rate the dependency survives.

Consumer prefetch was lowered from two hundred and fifty to thirty messages per instance. Prefetch is how many messages the broker hands a consumer before it has acknowledged anything, and a large value looked like an obvious throughput win until we watched what it did to distribution: a consumer that grabbed two hundred and fifty messages and then processed them slowly was sitting on ten minutes of work that idle instances next to it could not touch, so the queue looked deep while half the pool had nothing to do. Thirty is roughly one second of work at the median message cost, which keeps the network round trips amortised without letting any single instance hoard. The change also improved shutdown, since a rolling deploy now has to finish or return far fewer in-flight messages. Two groups override it: the export consumer prefetches one, because its messages take minutes each and fairness matters more than anything else, and the metrics forwarder prefetches a thousand because its per-message work is trivial and round trips dominate.

Consumer processes run single-threaded, one process per container, with concurrency achieved by running more containers rather than more threads inside one. `WORKER_CONCURRENCY` is fixed at one and the setting is not exposed in the service chart. The reasoning is that in-process concurrency made every capacity number a lie: an instance with eight threads reported one set of resource requests to the scheduler while its actual footprint depended on how many of those threads happened to be doing something expensive, and the noisy-neighbour effects were entirely inside a process where no scheduler could see them. One unit of work per process means the container's limits mean what they say, an OOM kills one message rather than eight, and the profiler output is readable. The obvious cost is memory: each process carries its own interpreter and its own copy of the job registry, which for the smallest consumers is a real fraction of the container. We accepted that, and the imports were trimmed instead.

Consumers stop taking new messages the moment they receive SIGTERM and are given one hundred and twenty seconds to finish what they are already holding, which is set as `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` on every consumer deployment. Before that, the grace period was the platform default of thirty seconds, and any message whose handler ran longer was killed mid-flight during every rolling deploy; because delivery is at-least-once those messages came back, so the visible symptom was not lost work but a burst of duplicate side effects clustered around each release. The handler contract that goes with the timeout is that no single message may take longer than the grace period, and the two job classes that legitimately do — the customs export and the monthly statement build — checkpoint their progress so a killed run resumes rather than restarting. Drain behaviour is exercised in staging on every release by killing a pod under load, because it is the kind of thing that silently regresses when a library changes its signal handling.

The bulk consumer pool runs against a nightly compute budget rather than being allowed to grow freely. The budget is expressed in replica-hours per night, currently four hundred, and the scheduler that starts bulk work checks the remaining allowance before it dispatches; when the allowance is exhausted, queued bulk work waits for the next window instead of running. This exists because bulk work is elastic in a way that hides its cost — a backfill that could take two hours across ten workers can take twenty minutes across sixty, and nobody choosing the number is looking at the invoice. Two consecutive months of surprise overruns, both traced to well-intentioned parallelism on one-off migrations, made the budget easier to justify than a policy asking people to be thoughtful. Exceeding the budget deliberately is possible and requires an approval in the change ticket, which happens a few times a quarter for genuine deadlines. The allowance resets at midnight UTC and unused hours do not carry over.

Bulk consumers may run on interruptible instances; interactive and standard consumers may not. The distinction is not about how important the work is but about how it behaves when the machine disappears with two minutes of warning. Bulk jobs are long, idempotent and checkpointed, so an interruption costs a partial batch that will be redone, and the discount on that capacity is large enough to be worth the disruption. Interactive consumers are the opposite: their whole value is the tail latency, and an eviction that redistributes partitions mid-burst is felt by someone waiting on a page. We tried mixing them and the incident that ended the experiment was not a capacity shortage but a rebalance cascade, where a handful of evictions in a shared group triggered reassignments that briefly stopped the healthy instances too. The pools are now separate deployments with separate node selectors, and the placement rule lives in the chart rather than in anyone's head. When interruptible capacity is unavailable, bulk work simply waits, which is the behaviour we want anyway.

Consumer containers preload the job registry at image build time instead of discovering handlers at boot. Startup used to walk the package tree importing every module to find decorated handlers, which took between eight and eleven seconds on the larger services, and that time is paid by every new replica exactly when the system is under pressure and wants workers immediately. The build now emits `registry.lock.json`, a manifest of handler names and their import paths, and boot imports only what it needs to serve the groups it is assigned. Cold start is down to about one and a half seconds. A CI check regenerates the manifest and fails if it differs from the committed one, which catches the case where a new handler is added and never registered — the failure mode there used to be a message sitting unhandled in a queue with no error anywhere, which took an embarrassingly long time to diagnose the first time it happened.

Consumer replicas are spread across availability zones by topology constraints rather than left to the scheduler's own packing preferences. Without the constraint the scheduler tended to pack a group's replicas onto whichever nodes had room, which on a quiet afternoon meant most of a consumer group landing in one zone, and a zone-level disruption then removed most of the pool at once. The constraint is a soft one, so during genuine capacity pressure the scheduler is allowed to violate it rather than leave work unscheduled — a badly balanced consumer group is much better than one that cannot start. Alongside it there is an anti-affinity rule keeping any two replicas of the same group off the same node, which matters more than the zone rule in practice because node replacement is a routine and frequent event. Neither rule applies to the bulk pools, where losing a chunk of capacity is not interesting and packing tightly is cheaper.

A queue declared in the manifest with no consumer group pointing at it fails the deploy check. It seems like a trivial rule and it exists because of a class of silent failure that is genuinely hard to see: work published into a queue nobody reads goes nowhere, produces no error, and shows up only as a customer noticing that something did not happen. We shipped exactly that twice — once when a consumer was renamed and its old group was left behind, once when a queue was created ahead of a service that then slipped a release — and both times the gap was measured in days. The check runs over the same manifest that creates the queues, so it compares intent to intent rather than reaching into a live cluster, which keeps it fast and deterministic. A queue that is genuinely meant to have no consumer yet, which happens during a phased migration, is marked as such with an expiry date, and the check fails again once that date passes.

Every cache key carries a schema version segment, so keys read `hl:v7:shipment:8831` rather than `hl:shipment:8831`, and the number comes from `SCHEMA_VERSION` in `app/cache/keys.py`. It is bumped whenever the serialized shape of a cached value changes: a field added, removed, renamed or retyped. The reason is that the cache outlives the deploy. When a `customs_status` field was added to the serialized shipment, new code read entries written minutes earlier by old code, found the field missing and raised, and about a third of detail-page requests failed for forty minutes until the TTLs aged out. A version segment makes a deploy atomic with respect to cached data: new code cannot see old-shaped entries because it never looks for them, and old code cannot see new-shaped ones if we roll back, which is the half people forget. Flushing the cache on every deploy was rejected outright: it drops the whole read load onto Postgres exactly while a release is in flight, and a rollback would need a second flush. Old-version keys are abandoned and expire under their own TTL, costing a little memory for an hour and nothing else. A CI check, `tools/cache_schema_check.py`, hashes the field names and types of every cached dataclass and fails the build when that hash changes without the version constant changing, because the thing that reliably goes wrong is a shape change nobody noticed was one.

Keys are namespaced by the service that owns them, using a two-letter prefix registered in `platform/cache-namespaces.yaml`: `hl` for the shipment API, `bl` for billing, `gw` for the gateway. Everything a service writes begins with its prefix, and the shared client refuses to build a key that does not. This exists because the cache cluster is shared and, before the registry, two services independently chose `user:<id>` for entirely different objects, which produced a genuinely confusing bug where one service's reads intermittently returned another's payload and deserialization sometimes succeeded because the shapes overlapped. Prefixes also make everything else measurable: the per-namespace memory report is a straight scan of the registry, eviction can be attributed to an owner, and when the cluster is under pressure there is a clear answer to which team is using it. Reserving a prefix takes a pull request against the registry file and is one of the few things where a two-character bikeshed is genuinely faster than the alternative.

Cached values are serialized with MessagePack rather than JSON. The measurement that decided it was on the shipment detail payload: about thirty percent smaller on the wire and in memory, and deserialization roughly twice as fast, which mattered because at peak the API deserializes a few thousand cached objects a second and that work was visible in the CPU profile. Compactness has a second effect that we cared about more than the speed — the cluster holds meaningfully more of the working set in the same memory. The cost is debuggability, since you cannot read a value with a command-line client any more, which is why `tools/cache_peek.py` exists and prints a decoded value for a given key. Datetimes are encoded as integer epoch milliseconds by an explicit hook rather than left to a default, after an early bug where a timezone-naive value round-tripped as something an hour off during a daylight-saving change. Nothing outside the application reads these values, so the format is an internal detail and can change with a deploy.

Entity caches default to a fifteen-minute time to live, set as `DEFAULT_TTL = 900` in the cache client, and a handler that wants something different passes it explicitly at the call site so the choice is visible in review. Fifteen minutes came from the shape of the traffic rather than from a principle: the median shipment detail page is viewed several times within a few minutes of a status change and then not at all, so most of the benefit is captured in the first minute or two, and the tail beyond a quarter of an hour is almost entirely wasted memory. Short TTLs also cap how wrong we can be. Nothing here invalidates on every possible upstream change, so the TTL is the backstop that guarantees a stale value cannot persist past a bounded window, and being able to say to support that data is at most fifteen minutes old is worth more than the extra hit rate. Reference data that genuinely does not move — country lists, service codes — sets hours instead, and the few values that must never be stale are not cached at all.

Invalidation is always by exact key. The client exposes a delete that takes fully-specified keys and nothing else, and pattern deletes are unavailable — `KEYS` is disabled on the cluster and `SCAN`-and-delete loops are rejected in review. The prohibition is not theoretical: a cleanup script running a scan-and-delete over a few million keys during business hours held the server busy long enough that unrelated requests timed out, and the same shape of mistake was subsequently attempted twice by people who had not heard about the first time. Making invalidation exact forces the writer to know what it wrote, which is a healthy constraint. Where one change genuinely affects many entries, the answer is a version segment in that key family, so bumping one number abandons the whole set at once and the old entries age out on their own instead of being deleted in a burst. The rare genuine need for a mass delete is a scheduled maintenance task with a rate limit, run by the platform team, and it has been used twice.

Nothing is written to the cache from inside an open database transaction. The rule is that the transaction commits first and the cache write happens after, in the calling code, never in a callback attached to the session. The reason is the obvious one made concrete: a cache populated inside a transaction that later rolls back leaves a value describing something that never happened, and because the cache has no rollback of its own, it is authoritative for its whole lifetime as far as every reader is concerned. We had that on the address-change path, where a validation failure late in the request rolled back the write while the cache happily served the new address until it expired, which support experienced as the system disagreeing with itself. Reading inside a transaction is allowed and is common, though even there the ordering is worth thinking about, since a value read from cache is not part of the transaction's snapshot and can be older or newer than everything around it. The linter flags cache writes inside a transactional block and the exceptions are argued in review.

The cache client applies a fifty-millisecond timeout to every read and treats a timeout as a miss. A cache exists to make things faster, so a slow cache read is worse than no cache read at all — it adds latency and then still costs a database query. Before the timeout was in place, a brief network problem in front of the cluster turned into a full outage of the read path, because every request blocked on a socket that eventually failed, and the connection pool filled with requests waiting on a service that was supposed to be optional. Writes get a slightly longer budget and fail silently, since a write that does not land only means a future miss. The timeout is deliberately below the point where a user would notice, which also means it occasionally converts a genuinely slow but successful read into a miss during a cluster hiccup; that trade is fine, and the miss rate spiking is itself a useful signal that gets its own dashboard panel.

All cache access goes through one thin wrapper rather than services holding a client directly. The wrapper is boring by design: it builds keys, serializes, applies timeouts, and emits a metric on every call tagged with the key family and whether it hit. That instrumentation is the whole reason it exists. Before it, the only cache metrics available were cluster-wide, which told us the overall hit ratio and absolutely nothing about which of the dozens of things being cached were pulling their weight, and two key families turned out to have hit ratios so low they were pure overhead. It also gives one place to change behaviour — a timeout, a serialization detail, a circuit breaker — instead of a search across services for direct client usage. The constraint that keeps it honest is that the wrapper exposes no clever features: no automatic refresh, no tiering, no magic decorator that caches whatever it wraps. Every one of those was proposed, and each would have hidden exactly the thing the metrics were added to reveal.

A cache miss is never an error, and code is written so that the cache being entirely absent changes nothing except latency. In practice that means no handler branches on whether a value was cached, no response includes a field derived from cache state, and no test asserts that a particular call was a hit. The discipline came from a period when it was not true: a listing endpoint had been written against the assumption that a warm cache was normal, and its uncached path did a query per row, so the first request after any invalidation was slow enough to time out and the timeout prevented the cache from ever being repopulated. The endpoint effectively could not recover from a cold start. Since then, every cached path is load-tested with the cache disabled entirely, and the requirement is that it stays within its latency budget with headroom rather than merely completing. Where that is impossible the answer is to fix the underlying query, not to declare the cache mandatory.

Recomputation of an expired key is single-flighted through a Redis lease. On a miss the caller attempts `SET <key>:lock <token> NX PX 5000`; the winner runs the query, writes the value and deletes the lock, while everyone else polls the key every twenty-five milliseconds for up to three hundred, then gives up and queries the database directly. The fallback is deliberate: it bounds the damage if the lease holder dies, so a slow query degrades into the old behaviour rather than a wall of blocked requests. The problem it solved was concrete. The rate-card key expired at nine in the morning, at the daily traffic peak, and every in-flight request missed at once: about three thousand four hundred identical queries hit Postgres inside a second, the pool was exhausted, and the API was down for ninety seconds. It repeated on three consecutive mornings before we understood it, because a warm cache the rest of the day made the graphs look fine. Locks are per key, never global, and the lock TTL sits below the query's statement timeout so a dead holder cannot block longer than it could have run. Two alternatives were tried and dropped: raising the TTL, which only moved the hour of the pile-up, and cron warming, which cannot cover keys whose identity depends on the request. `cache_singleflight_wait_seconds` and `cache_lock_timeouts_total` are the two metrics that tell us it is working.

The Redis client connects with a two-hundred-millisecond connect timeout and does not retry the connection inside a request. The distinction that matters is between a connection attempt and a command: a command against an established connection is fast or it is broken, while a connection attempt to a node that is being replaced can sit in a TCP handshake for the operating system's default, which is measured in tens of seconds. During a failover we watched request threads pile up in exactly that state while the cache node was gone but the socket had not yet failed. Two hundred milliseconds is far longer than a healthy connect within the same availability zone, which is well under five, so it is generous while still failing before anyone notices. Reconnection is handled by the pool in the background with its own backoff, so a request that arrives during the gap takes the miss path rather than waiting for the pool to heal. The same reasoning gives the client a short socket timeout on the read side, set independently.

The cache cluster runs three shards, each with one replica, and the shard count is fixed rather than elastic. Three came from memory headroom rather than throughput: the whole working set fits comfortably in two, and the third gives room to lose a node without the remaining ones going over their eviction threshold. Replicas exist for failover, not for read scaling — reads are never directed at a replica, because the replication is asynchronous and a read from a lagging replica after a write produces exactly the kind of inconsistency that is nearly impossible to reproduce later. Resharding is disruptive because the key distribution changes, so a substantial part of the cache is effectively cold afterwards, and that is one of the reasons the count is treated as a long-lived decision made with headroom rather than something to adjust each quarter. Client-side sharding was rejected in favour of the cluster protocol, so adding a node does not require a coordinated application deploy.

A key family whose hit ratio drops below eighty percent over a rolling day opens a ticket for its owner. The threshold is not about performance directly; it is a design smell detector. A cache that misses more than one time in five is usually caching something whose key space is far larger than its traffic — per-request query parameters folded into the key, or a per-user object for users who visit once a month — and in those cases the cache is costing memory, network round trips and code complexity to serve a small minority of requests. Two families were deleted outright after this alert pointed at them, and one was fixed by narrowing the key. The ratio is measured per family rather than per cluster because the cluster-wide number is dominated by a handful of hot families and stays comfortably high while individual ones are useless. Ratios can also fall for legitimate reasons — a deploy that bumped a version segment, a traffic-shape change — so the ticket asks for an explanation rather than a fix.

Hot keys are found by a weekly sampled scan rather than by guessing. The job runs `redis-cli --hotkeys` against a replica during a quiet window and posts the top twenty by access frequency into the platform channel, with the previous week's list alongside for comparison. The reason for doing it on a schedule instead of only during incidents is that hot keys arrive gradually: a key becomes hot because a feature became popular or because someone put a cache read inside a loop, and neither shows up as a problem until the day it does. The sampling is cheap and runs against a replica, so it costs nothing that anyone notices. What we do about a hot key depends on what it is — a genuinely shared value gets promoted into an in-process cache with a short lifetime, a key that is hot because of a code path is usually a bug in that path. The list has caught a per-request key built from a timestamp that changed every second, which was creating tens of thousands of single-use entries an hour.

When Redis is unreachable, the application serves everything from Postgres and keeps running. That sounds obvious and it was not always true: the first version treated a cache error as an exception and let it propagate, so a cluster maintenance window that should have been invisible produced a full outage of the read path. The behaviour now is that every cache operation is wrapped so a failure is logged and counted, reads return a miss and writes do nothing. The important part is what makes this survivable, which is a capacity decision rather than a code one — the database is provisioned to carry the full uncached read load for a limited period, and that assumption is verified in a game day twice a year by cutting the cache off in staging under production-shaped traffic. Without that verification, degrading gracefully in code is a story rather than a property, since the graceful path leads straight to a database that cannot take the load. The circuit breaker stops attempting the cache after a run of consecutive failures and probes occasionally, so a dead cluster does not add its timeout to every request.

The cache wrapper refuses to store a serialized value larger than one hundred kilobytes and counts the rejection instead. Large values are a bad fit for a shared cache in several ways at once: they crowd out many small entries that would each have been used more often, they make every transfer slower for other clients on the same connection, and a single big value being read frequently can saturate network bandwidth on one node while the cluster looks otherwise idle. The limit was introduced after a listing endpoint began caching an entire unpaginated result set, some of which ran to several megabytes for the largest accounts, and the cluster's outbound traffic tripled without any change in request volume. The rejection is deliberately silent to the caller, since a cache write failing is not an error, but it emits a metric tagged with the key family so the pattern surfaces rather than hiding. Endpoints that genuinely need a large derived object build it into object storage and cache the reference.

Caching lives behind the repository layer, not in the handlers. A handler asks the repository for a shipment and does not know or care whether the answer came from memory, from the cache or from a query, and the caching decision for a given entity is made in exactly one place. The alternative, which is what we had, put decorators on handler functions, and the result was that the same object was cached under different keys with different lifetimes depending on which endpoint you arrived through, so invalidating after a write meant knowing every endpoint that might have cached the thing. That is not knowledge anybody reliably has. Putting it in the repository also means the write path and the read path are neighbours in the same file, which makes it much harder to add a write that forgets to invalidate. The rule has one carve-out for aggregate views that are genuinely computed across repositories, and those are cached in a dedicated service object that owns its own invalidation and is reviewed as a unit.

A service may only read cache keys inside its own namespace, and reaching into another service's keys is treated the same way as reading another service's database tables. The temptation is real, because the cache is shared infrastructure and the data is right there, and it happened once: a reporting job read the shipment service's cached objects directly to avoid a slow API call, which worked until the shipment service changed its serialization and the reporting job started failing on data it had never been promised. Nobody had done anything wrong from their own point of view, which is precisely the problem with the pattern. Cached values are an implementation detail with no compatibility guarantee — they change shape at whatever pace the owning team finds convenient, and the owning team has no way to know who else is reading. If another service needs the data, the answer is an API call, and if that call is too slow, the answer is to make it faster or to publish the data as an event.

The rule is one sentence: a response may be cached at the edge only if it is byte-identical for every anonymous visitor. Anything that varies by session, account, tenant or entitlement is not eligible, full stop, and is sent with `Cache-Control: private, no-store`. The CDN is configured default-deny to enforce it — the edge caches only the path prefixes listed in `edge/routes.yaml`, currently `/assets/*`, the public tracking pages under `/p/*`, and `/api/public/v1/rates`; everything else is a pass-through no matter what headers the origin sends. Default-deny exists because the origin cannot be trusted to be right on every route. A framework upgrade once changed the default cache header on authenticated HTML, the edge honoured it, and for six minutes one customer's shipment list was served to other visitors. Two supporting rules fall out of it. Responses carrying `Set-Cookie`, or whose content depends on an `Authorization` header, may never be cached, and middleware asserts this in staging and fails the request rather than warning. And `Vary` is restricted to `Accept-Encoding`, because a wide `Vary` on something like `User-Agent` fragments the cache into near-uselessness while still appearing enabled, which is worse than not caching since nobody notices. Adding a prefix to the allow list needs platform review and proof the response is identical logged in and logged out.

Static assets are content-addressed at build time and served with a one-year lifetime: filenames carry an eight-character hash of their contents, and the edge sends `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`. Because the name changes whenever the bytes change, there is never a reason to expire an asset early, and there is nothing to purge on deploy — a release simply starts referencing new filenames while the old ones stay valid for anyone still on the previous page. The `immutable` directive is what stops browsers revalidating on reload, which used to produce a burst of conditional requests every time a user refreshed. The one thing this arrangement demands is that the HTML referencing the assets is not cached under the same terms, since an old page pointing at deleted files is the failure mode people actually hit. Old asset builds are retained for thirty days in the origin bucket so a client sitting on stale HTML keeps working, and the cleanup job that removes them checks the last-accessed timestamps before it deletes anything.

The deploy pipeline issues the CDN purge, as a step after the origin is confirmed healthy and before the release is marked complete. It purges by surrogate key rather than by URL: responses are tagged at the origin with keys like `html`, `rates`, `tracking`, and the pipeline purges the tags affected by the release, which is derived from which services were deployed. Purging by URL was the earlier approach and it did not survive contact with a site where the URL space is generated, since nobody could enumerate the pages that a template change affected. The ordering matters and was learned the hard way: purging before the new origin is live simply refills the cache with the old response and produces a much longer window of stale content than doing nothing. Purges are also rate-limited by the provider, which is why a full-property purge is not the answer to everything, and using one is a decision an engineer makes deliberately rather than a step in any pipeline.

Origin shielding is enabled for the image service, so every edge location fetches through one designated shield region instead of going to the origin directly. The number that made the case was the origin request rate: without a shield, a cold object requested from a hundred edge locations produced a hundred origin fetches, and for image derivatives, which are generated on demand, each of those was expensive CPU work rather than a cheap byte copy. With the shield, the first request populates one intermediate cache and the rest are served from it, and origin fetches for the image path fell by roughly eighty percent. The trade is an extra network hop for anything not already at the edge, which adds a few tens of milliseconds to a cold request from a distant region, and a dependency on the shield region's availability that we accepted after checking the provider's failover behaviour. Shielding is enabled only for the image path; for ordinary HTML the origin request volume was never the constraint and the extra hop is not worth paying.

Marketing query parameters are stripped at the edge before the cache lookup, so `?utm_source=`, `?utm_campaign=`, `?gclid=` and the rest of the list in `edge/strip-params.yaml` do not fragment the cache. Every distinct query string is a distinct cache entry by default, and a campaign that appends a unique click identifier to every link means every visitor requests a URL nobody has ever requested before — a page with an eighty percent hit ratio dropped into the twenties during a large campaign, and the origin took the load. The stripping happens only for the cache key: the full original URL is still passed to the origin and still reaches the analytics beacon in the browser, so no measurement is lost, which was the objection the growth team raised and it was a fair one. Parameters that genuinely change the response, like pagination or a tracking number, are on an explicit keep list, and adding to the strip list requires checking that the origin ignores the parameter as well.

Compression is negotiated and applied at the edge, and the origin returns uncompressed bodies. Doing it in both places was the state we inherited and it was worse than either alone: the origin spent CPU compressing responses that the edge then had to decompress to apply its own transformations, and because the two disagreed about which content types were worth compressing, whether a given response arrived compressed depended on the route. Moving it entirely to the edge means one place decides, the origin's CPU goes to generating pages, and the edge can pick the best encoding the client actually advertised rather than being limited to what the origin chose to produce. It also removes a whole class of confusion in which a header appeared to promise one encoding while the body was in another. The origin still compresses for the internal path where a service calls another over the network without passing through the edge, which is a separate setting and is left alone on purpose.

Error responses from the origin are held at the edge for ten seconds. Not longer, because serving a stale error after the origin has recovered is a self-inflicted extension of an outage, and not zero, because during an origin problem every edge location otherwise forwards every request straight into whatever is already struggling. Ten seconds turns a flood into roughly one request per location per ten seconds, which was the difference between an origin that recovered on its own and one that stayed down under retry pressure — we watched exactly that during a database failover, where the origin was healthy within a minute but did not stop being hammered for five. The rule applies to 5xx responses only. A 404 is a legitimate long-lived answer and is cached under the normal rules for its route, and 429 is passed through untouched because the limiter's own headers already tell the client what to do and a cached rate-limit response would go on rejecting a client whose budget had refilled.

The edge configuration is versioned in the frontend repository, next to the code whose behaviour it modifies, and is applied by the same pipeline that deploys the site. For a long time it lived in the provider's web console, which meant the actual routing and caching behaviour of the site was a thing you had to log in to read, changes had no review and no history beyond an audit log nobody consulted, and twice we spent the opening minutes of an incident discovering that somebody had changed something days earlier for a reason they had since forgotten. Keeping it in the repository gives the ordinary things — a diff, an approval, a revert that takes as long as any other revert. It also lets a change to a route and the change to how that route is cached arrive in the same commit, which is the pairing that used to drift. The console is now read-only for everyone except two break-glass accounts, and using one of those creates a follow-up ticket to reconcile the state back into the repository.

A second CDN was evaluated for redundancy and we decided against it. The case for was real — the provider has had two multi-hour incidents in three years, and during both the site was effectively unreachable regardless of how healthy the origin was. What sank it was the cost of correctness rather than the invoice. Everything we depend on at the edge would have to exist and behave identically in both providers, and the interesting parts are precisely the ones where providers differ: how the cache key is computed, how surrogate keys and purges work, how the request transformations are expressed. Maintaining both would mean every edge change is written twice and verified twice, by a team that ships edge changes most weeks, and a failover to a configuration that has been drifting quietly is not redundancy, it is a second outage waiting for its moment. The decision was recorded with a trigger for revisiting it: another incident of that length inside a year, or the point at which our edge logic becomes simple enough to express portably.

The `cache-prod` cluster runs `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru`; it used to run `noeviction`, and the change came out of an outage. At 11:20 on a Tuesday the cluster reached its `maxmemory` of 6gb and, under `noeviction`, every write started returning an OOM error. The client treated write failures as errors rather than no-ops, so requests failed across the read path and an optional component took the site down for eighteen minutes. The fix was not more memory, though it was raised to 12gb afterwards; it was accepting that a cache may forget things. Under `allkeys-lru` the cluster discards what was used least recently and writes keep succeeding, which is how a full cache should behave. We rejected `volatile-lru`: about eighteen percent of keys were written with no TTL by older code paths, and a volatile policy cannot evict those, so the cluster would have filled with exactly the entries nobody had thought about. Making it safe meant auditing every write first. The policy applies only to the cache cluster. `state-prod`, which holds rate-limiter counters and lease keys, stays on `noeviction` and pages on memory, because silently forgetting one of those is a correctness problem rather than a slower request. `maxmemory-samples` is raised to 10, and a sustained `evicted_keys` rate above five hundred a second is a sizing ticket, not an incident.

Persistence is switched off completely on the cache cluster: `appendonly no` and an empty `save` directive, so nothing is written to disk. The forking behaviour is why. A background save on a multi-gigabyte instance forks the process, and under write pressure the copy-on-write cost is a memory spike large enough to be dangerous on a node already sized close to its ceiling — we hit that once and the spike, not the working set, was what pushed the node over. Since everything in this cluster is reconstructible from Postgres, the value of a snapshot is close to zero: restoring a cache from an hour-old dump gives you an hour-old cache, which is barely better than an empty one and carries the risk of serving values whose schema no longer matches the code. A restart therefore comes back empty, which is a load event for the database rather than a data-loss event, and is why restarts are done one node at a time with a gap between them. The state cluster is configured differently, with persistence on, because its contents are not reconstructible from anywhere.

Failover is handled by three Sentinel processes with a quorum of two, deployed one per availability zone on nodes that host nothing else. Three is the smallest count that tolerates losing one and still forms a majority, and spreading them across zones is what makes a zone failure a failover rather than a split brain. `down-after-milliseconds` is set to five seconds, which is long enough to ride out a garbage-collection pause or a brief network blip and short enough that a genuinely dead primary is replaced before request timeouts pile up; we started at one second and spent a fortnight promoting replicas over nothing. Clients discover the current primary by asking Sentinel rather than holding a configured address, which was the change that made failovers invisible to the application instead of requiring a rolling restart. Failover is exercised deliberately once a quarter in production during a low-traffic window, because the failure we are actually worried about is the configuration having drifted since the last time anyone tried.

Redis version upgrades are done by building a new cluster and moving traffic to it, never in place. In-place upgrades on a cache mean a rolling restart, and a rolling restart of a cache is a series of partial cold starts where each restarted node arrives empty and the database absorbs the difference. Doing it that way once, during business hours, is what produced the rule. The replacement approach starts an entirely new cluster on the target version, lets it warm from normal traffic in a shadow mode where the application writes to both and reads from the old one, and then flips reads over when the hit ratio on the new cluster has converged. The flip is a configuration change and reverting it is the same change backwards, which means an upgrade that goes wrong is a minute of work rather than a recovery. The old cluster is kept for a day and then destroyed. It costs double capacity for a couple of days, which is a small price for making a version bump boring, and the same procedure is used for changing instance types.

Keyspace notifications are disabled on every cluster — `notify-keyspace-events` is empty and stays that way. The feature is genuinely useful and was used briefly to invalidate an in-process cache when a shared key changed, which is how we learned what it costs. The events are fire-and-forget over pub/sub, so a subscriber that is restarting or briefly disconnected misses them with no way to know, and a cache invalidation that is missed silently is the exact failure that is hardest to notice; ours ran for a week with one instance serving values that had been superseded. There is also a throughput cost, since every write on a busy cluster produces an event whether anyone is listening or not. What replaced it is a short in-process TTL, on the reasoning that a bounded staleness you can state is better than an unbounded one you believe is zero. Where an invalidation genuinely must be reliable, it goes through the message broker, which has delivery guarantees and a dead-letter path.

The state cluster is sized by peak connection count rather than by working-set memory. Its data is small — rate-limiter counters, lease keys, short-lived tokens — and it will comfortably fit in a fraction of the smallest instance we can buy, so memory tells you nothing about how big it needs to be. What actually constrains it is that every application process holds connections, and connection handling is where its CPU goes: at peak we run enough processes across services that the count reaches the low thousands, and the instance has to have headroom above that because a deploy transiently doubles connections while old and new pods overlap. That overlap is what caught us out originally, when a routine deploy pushed the cluster past its connection limit and new connections were refused, which surfaced as rate-limiter failures rather than anything that pointed at connections. The sizing note is written down next to the terraform, because otherwise the next person looks at the memory graph, sees it flat and low, and concludes the instance is oversized.

Server-side Lua is not used anywhere except the rate limiter, and adding a new script requires platform review. The limiter's script is there for a good reason: check-and-decrement has to be atomic, and doing it in three round trips from the application is both slower and wrong under concurrency. Everything else that reached for Lua was reaching for convenience, and the cost is that a script runs on the server single-threaded and blocks every other client for its duration, so a script with an unbounded loop over a key set is a cluster-wide stall — one such script, iterating over a set that had grown to a few hundred thousand members, held the server for over a second at a time. Scripts are also invisible to the usual tooling: they do not show up as the individual commands they perform, so the slow log points at the script and not at the operation inside it that got expensive. The limiter's script is pinned by hash, is under a hundred lines, and touches a fixed number of keys per invocation.

The destructive administrative commands are renamed in the managed configuration, so the ones that flush a database or terminate the server do not exist under the names anyone would type. This is not about defending against an attacker who has already reached the cluster — such a person can do plenty regardless — it is about the engineer with a legitimate connection, a shell open on the wrong environment, and muscle memory. Cache clusters are a particularly easy place to make that mistake, because the equivalent commands are single words with no confirmation and no undo, and because people connect to them casually while debugging in a way they never would with a production database. Someone did flush a staging cluster meaning to flush their local one, and the only reason it was a story rather than an incident is which environment it was. The renamed forms are documented in the runbook for the rare genuine need, which is essentially only rebuilding a cluster after a schema-shaped change, and each use is announced in the platform channel first.

A period of unexplained memory growth on the cache cluster turned out to be fragmentation rather than data, and the cause was a single hash that a reporting feature grew and shrank in large steps every hour. The allocator does not return freed memory to the operating system when the freed regions are interleaved with live ones, so the resident size kept climbing while the reported dataset size stayed flat, and the gap between those two numbers is the thing nobody was looking at. Once we knew what to look for it was obvious in the ratio metric, which now has a panel of its own. The fix was to stop using one enormous key for something that was logically many, and to write the reporting data with per-entry keys instead, which changed the allocation pattern into many similarly-sized objects. Activated defragmentation was enabled afterwards as a safety net rather than as the solution, on the grounds that it treats the symptom and costs CPU. The lesson we wrote down is that resident memory and dataset size are different questions.

Two numbers, arrived at by measurement rather than by taste. Public HTML goes out as `Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=600`, and the public rates endpoint as `s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=60, stale-if-error=86400`. The tuning story is the useful part. We started with an hour of stale window on HTML because it looked free, then shipped a bad marketing page: the fix was live at the origin in four minutes and the edge kept handing out the broken version for most of the following hour. That is what the stale window buys you when it is too long — a fix that has already landed but has not arrived. Cutting it to ten minutes came from measuring the revalidation, which finishes in under two seconds at the ninety-ninth percentile, so the window need only cover a burst of concurrent requests during a refresh. The rule we wrote down afterwards is that the stale window covers the revalidation and nothing else, while surviving an origin outage is what `stale-if-error` is for, and conflating the two is exactly how you end up with an hour of stale HTML. Anything where staleness is visibly wrong to a user gets no stale window at all: the shipment tracking page revalidates synchronously, because showing a delivered parcel as in transit is worse than a slow page. Releases purge the HTML tag, so the window never argues with a deploy.

HTML responses carry an ETag derived from the build identifier and the rendered content hash, in the form `W/"<build>-<hash8>"`. It is a weak validator on purpose, since the pages contain a request identifier in a comment and are therefore not byte-identical between renders, and a strong validator would never match. What this buys is cheap revalidation: a client with a copy sends the tag, the origin compares and returns 304 with no body, and for the larger pages that is a few hundred bytes instead of eighty kilobytes. Including the build identifier means a release invalidates every page whether or not its content changed, which is deliberate — it is cheaper than trying to reason about which template edits affect which pages, and a release is exactly the moment we want clients to re-check. The hash comes from the rendered body, so a content change without a release also invalidates. Generating it costs a hash over the response body, which is measurable but small, and it is skipped for anything streamed.

The service worker was removed from the customer portal and there are no plans to bring one back. It was added for offline support that nobody had asked for, and what it actually produced was a class of bug we could not reproduce and could barely explain: users running an application version that had been superseded weeks earlier, because the worker had cached the shell and its update path only ran under conditions that a long-lived tab never met. Support requests where the fix was to clear site data became routine, and the instruction to do so is not something we want in a support script. Removing it required shipping a worker whose only job was to unregister itself and clear its caches, and keeping that in place for a full quarter so that even rare visitors picked it up. The trade we consciously made is that the portal now needs the network, which for a logistics tool used in warehouses with patchy connectivity was debated at length; the conclusion was that a stale-but-working application is a worse experience than an honest failure.

The client-side query cache keeps fetched data for thirty seconds before it is considered stale, set once as `staleTime: 30_000` in the shared query client rather than per hook. Under the library's default of zero, every remount refetched, which in a tabbed interface meant switching away and back re-issued the same requests, and the portal was generating several times the API traffic its actual usage justified. Thirty seconds matches how people use the tool: they move between views within a task, and a task takes a couple of minutes. Data that must always be current opts out explicitly at the call site, which is currently three queries — live tracking, the outstanding-balance widget and the pending-actions count — and each of those carries a comment saying why. Mutations invalidate the queries they affect rather than relying on the window expiring, so the stale time is a floor on freshness for untouched data, not a delay after your own edits. Cached data survives a route change and does not survive a full reload.

Web fonts are self-hosted and preloaded rather than fetched from a third-party service. Two subset files are served from our own origin, referenced with `<link rel="preload" as="font" crossorigin>` in the document head, and declared with `font-display: swap`. Self-hosting removes a connection to another origin from the critical path, which on a cold visit over a mobile connection was costing a couple of hundred milliseconds of DNS and TLS before a single glyph was requested, and it removes a third party from the list of things that can make our site slow. Preloading matters because a font referenced only from a stylesheet is not discovered until the CSS has been parsed, so the browser starts fetching it late in the load; the preload hint moves that to the start. The subsetting is what keeps it affordable — the full family was several hundred kilobytes and the latin subset we actually render is a fraction of that. The files are fingerprinted like any other asset, so they inherit the long-lived asset caching.

Cache-Control headers are set in one middleware, `web/middleware/cache_headers.py`, which maps a route to a named response class, and never by individual handlers. Handlers setting their own headers is how we ended up with three different opinions about the same kind of page and a couple of routes that sent contradictory directives, which browsers and the edge resolved differently from each other. Centralising it means the whole caching posture of the site is one file you can read in a minute, and a new route that matches no class gets the conservative default rather than whatever the framework felt like. The classes are named for what a response is — public document, public data, private data, asset — rather than for the numbers they carry, so changing a policy is one edit in one place and the review is about the class rather than about a header. A test asserts the header for every registered route, which is what catches a handler that reaches for the response object directly and sets something of its own.

Image derivatives are generated on the first request for a size and then persisted, rather than being pre-generated for every source image at upload. Uploads arrive faster than anyone looks at them and most are never viewed at any size beyond the thumbnail, so pre-generating the full ladder meant doing expensive work for images nobody would ever request; the storage bill for the unused variants was the thing that made it visible. On-demand generation makes the first request for a given size slow, in the region of a second for a large source, and every request after that is a straight read. The derivative is written to object storage under a deterministic path, so the edge and the browser both cache it under the normal asset rules and the generator is only ever consulted once per size. The set of allowed sizes is a fixed list rather than free parameters in the URL, because an open-ended size parameter is an invitation to fill storage with variants nobody asked for, which happened during a week when it was open.

The marketing site and the application are served from one CDN property under a single hostname, rather than being split across two. Two properties is the tidier architecture and we ran it that way for a year; what it cost was a redirect on the transition between them, cookie scoping that had to be reasoned about carefully, and two sets of edge configuration that drifted apart in small ways nobody noticed until behaviour differed between them. Consolidating meant the route rules for both live in one place and are reviewed together, and the boundary between marketing and application is a path prefix rather than a hostname. The objection at the time, which was reasonable, is that a mistake in the shared configuration now affects both, where before an error in the marketing rules could not touch the application. We accepted that in exchange for there being one configuration to get right, and mitigated it by requiring the same review for edge changes as for application code.

Pages are rendered on the server for anonymous visitors and hydrated on the client only for interactive regions. The split is by whether a region has state a user can change, so the tracking view, the marketing pages and the public rate table ship as HTML with no accompanying component tree, while the booking form and the account areas hydrate normally. The reason is that a fully hydrated page has to ship and execute its own rendering logic to reproduce what the browser has already painted, and for read-only content that work is pure cost — measurable in the interaction delay metric on mid-range phones, which is the population most of our anonymous traffic comes from. It also makes the cacheability question simpler, since a page with no per-user client state has nothing to leak into a shared response. The rule that keeps it from eroding is that adding interactivity to a static region requires moving it explicitly into the hydrated set, which is a visible change in review rather than an incidental one.

No session talks to the primary without a bound on how long a single statement may run, and the bound is attached to the database role rather than to the application, because roles are the one place a careless caller cannot forget it. `web_app` gets `statement_timeout = 5s`, `worker` gets 60s, the reporting role `analytics_ro` gets 15 minutes, and the `migrator` role runs with statement timeout disabled but `lock_timeout = 3s` so a schema change waits for nothing. Anything that legitimately needs longer wraps its query in the `long_query()` context manager in `db/session.py`, which issues a `SET LOCAL statement_timeout` for the transaction, requires a reason string, and logs the pair so a grep tells you every place we chose to wait. When the limit trips Postgres raises SQLSTATE 57014, the driver maps it to `QueryTimeout`, and the request layer answers 503 with a retry hint instead of hanging the caller. The habit exists because of one afternoon: a support tool ran an unindexed `LIKE` scan over `shipment_events`, someone retried it a dozen times, and thirty pooled connections sat occupied until the pool was exhausted and every request queued behind it. Twelve minutes of full outage came from a query nobody thought was dangerous. The framing that stuck: an absent timeout is not neutrality, it is a decision to wait forever on behalf of everyone else sharing the pool.

The pooler in front of the primary runs in transaction pooling mode, not session mode, and that choice constrains what application code may assume. A backend is handed to a client for the duration of a transaction and taken away at commit, which is what lets roughly nine hundred application connections sit behind ninety server connections. The price is that anything with session lifetime breaks: server-side prepared statements, `SET` outside a transaction, advisory locks held across statements, `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY`, and temporary tables. The ORM is configured with prepared statement caching switched off for that reason, and the one service that wanted advisory locks for leader election was moved onto the queue instead. Server-side cursors were the last casualty and the export path was rewritten to keyset pagination. When a new service reports a mysterious `prepared statement does not exist`, this is why, every time. Session mode was measured before the switch and it did not survive contact with traffic: connection counts tracked application replicas, and each replica scaling event added backend processes on a machine already spending real memory per connection.

`idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` is set to two minutes on every application role, and it is not negotiable per service. An open transaction sitting idle is worse than a slow one: it pins its snapshot, so autovacuum cannot clean up rows newer than it, and on a table taking heavy updates that means bloat grows for as long as the session sleeps. We found this the slow way, when the transaction table had tripled in size over a week and the culprit was a debugging shell somebody left open inside a `BEGIN` on a Thursday. The two minute figure was chosen to be far above any real request and far below the point where bloat matters. Killed sessions surface as `57P01` in application logs and the job retries the whole unit of work, which is safe because every writer is already written to be re-runnable. There is a companion dashboard panel showing the oldest transaction age across the fleet, and anything above thirty seconds is treated as a bug in the code that opened it rather than a tuning problem.

Pool sizes are not tuned by feel. Each service declares `pool_size` and `max_overflow` in its chart, and both come out of one formula: pool size equals expected concurrent in-flight requests per replica, rounded up, capped at eight; overflow is two. Total backends across the fleet must stay under sixty percent of `max_connections`, which is 400 on the primary, leaving headroom for migrations, the pooler's own admin connections, and a human with psql during an incident. The reason for the cap is counter-intuitive and worth stating plainly: a bigger pool does not make a saturated database faster, it just moves the queue from the application, where it is visible and shed with a timeout, into the database, where it turns into lock contention and context switching. We raised a pool from eight to thirty during an incident once and made throughput measurably worse. Changes to these numbers go through the platform team because the budget is shared, and the chart schema rejects a pool size above the cap outright.

Every connection sets `application_name` at connect time to `service/version/role`, for example `harborlane-api/2481/web`, and the pooler is configured to pass it through rather than replace it. It costs nothing and it is the difference between a diagnosable incident and a guessing game. During saturation the first query anyone runs is a group-by over `pg_stat_activity` on that column, and it names the guilty deployment in seconds rather than requiring somebody to correlate query text against a code search. Before this existed every session showed up as the pooler, which meant that identifying which of eleven services was hammering the primary involved reading query shapes and arguing. The value is set in the shared `db/session.py` connect hook, so a service gets it by using the standard client and cannot get it wrong; a service that builds its own DSN and skips it is treated as a review finding. The same string is stamped into the slow query log lines, which is why log lines and live sessions can be joined without a translation table.

Transactions at `REPEATABLE READ` can fail with a serialization error, and the shared client retries them, but only three times with jittered backoff at 20, 60 and 180 milliseconds, after which the error reaches the caller. The cap is the interesting half. An earlier version retried until it succeeded, which was fine at low contention and catastrophic during the month-end settlement run, when two writers contending on the same ledger rows produced a retry storm that fed itself: every retry lengthened the contention window that caused the next failure. Capping the retries converted an unbounded amplification into a small number of clean errors that the queue could redeliver later at a calmer moment. The retry wrapper only applies to code paths marked as pure recomputation; anything that has performed an external side effect inside the transaction is excluded from retry by construction, because replaying it would double the effect. That exclusion is enforced by making the side-effect helpers refuse to run inside a retryable block.

Roles on the primary describe workloads, not owners. There is a web role, a worker role, a reporting role and a migrator role, and eleven services share them according to what they are doing rather than who they are. The tempting alternative — a role per service, so grants can be revoked individually — was tried early and abandoned. It produced a permissions matrix nobody could hold in their head, drifted constantly because new tables were granted to whichever roles the author remembered, and gave no operational leverage during an incident, since the question under pressure is never which service may read a table but which class of traffic to shed. Workload roles carry their own resource settings and their own grants, and shedding is a one-line change. Attribution, which is the thing a per-service role would have given us, comes from the connection label instead, at no cost to the grant structure. The rule that keeps this from rotting is that a new table's grants are written in the same migration that creates it, to the four roles by name, and a migration granting to anything else fails review.

Nightly batch work connects straight to the primary on the direct port rather than through the pooler, using a separate host entry that exists only in the batch chart. Batch jobs want the things transaction pooling takes away — a session that lives for the length of the job, server-side cursors over large result sets, temporary tables for staging — and they have the opposite connection profile from web traffic: a handful of connections held for a long time rather than many held briefly. Routing them through the pooler gave the worst of both, since a long-lived session in transaction mode occupies a backend anyway while forfeiting the session features. The number of direct connections is deliberately small and fixed, so the batch fleet cannot expand into the connection budget the interactive path depends on. The tradeoff accepted here is that a batch job cannot be scaled out by simply adding replicas; parallelism has to come from partitioning the work by key range, which is how those jobs are written anyway.

The session factory is configured so that a plain read does not open a transaction. Reads run in autocommit and only the first write in a request promotes the connection into an explicit transaction that commits at the end of the handler. This started as a fix for the pooler, which was handing backends back and forth far less often than expected because every request was nominally transactional from its first select, and it turned out to matter more for reasoning than for throughput: with the old arrangement, a request that read something and then did nothing still held a snapshot for its whole life, including the time it spent waiting on an external HTTP call. The consequence people trip over is that two reads in one request may see different states, which is correct for our workload but surprising if you came from a codebase where request equals transaction. Anything needing a consistent view across several reads asks for it explicitly with a read-only transaction block, and that block is the documented tool rather than an accident of framework defaults.

A slow query becomes work through a job, not through somebody noticing. `tools/slowlog_digest.py` runs at 07:00 on Mondays, reads the week's `pg_stat_statements` snapshots, ranks fingerprints by total execution time rather than by mean, and takes anything holding more than two percent of database time or sitting above 400ms at p95. For each surviving fingerprint it looks for an open ticket carrying the same `dbq-<fingerprint>` label; if there is none it files one in the DB project with the normalised statement, the week-over-week trend, a captured plan, and the owning team resolved from the connection label on the sessions that ran it. Tickets are assigned to that team, not to a database group, because the fix is nearly always in application code. A ticket closes itself when its fingerprint has been out of the top twenty for three consecutive weeks, which keeps the list honest without anyone doing triage bookkeeping. Before this the same information lived on a dashboard, and the dashboard was read after incidents and never before them — one query spent five months in the top three and was fixed in an afternoon once it had a number and an owner. Deliberately, the digest files at most eight tickets a week; a flood of them would be ignored exactly like the dashboard was.

`auto_explain` is loaded on the primary with `auto_explain.log_min_duration = 200ms`, `log_analyze = on`, `log_buffers = on` and a sample rate of one in ten. Everything below that threshold is invisible on purpose. The setting is the outcome of an argument: analyze mode adds instrumentation overhead to every statement it captures, so capturing everything would tax the fast path to learn about it, and the fast path is not what anyone needs a plan for. Sampling at ten percent keeps the overhead under a percent of CPU while still producing several plans a minute for anything that matters. Plans land in the standard log stream and are parsed out by the shipper into their own index with a fourteen day retention, shorter than ordinary logs because they are bulky and only useful while the query is still under investigation. The one thing to remember when reading them is that the plan captured is the one that ran, with the parameters it ran with, which is exactly why the captured artefact beats re-running `EXPLAIN` by hand with parameters you guessed.

`pg_stat_statements` is configured with `max = 5000` and `track = top`, and a cron job copies the whole view into the `db_stat_snapshots` table at 03:00 every Sunday and then calls the reset function. The reset is the part that surprises people, so here is why. The view accumulates from the last reset, which means without one it eventually describes a mixture of every release since the last failover, and a query that was terrible for two days in March keeps outranking one that is terrible right now. Weekly resets give a comparable window and let anyone diff two consecutive Sundays to see what a release changed. The snapshots are kept for a year, which costs a few hundred megabytes and has repeatedly answered questions about when a regression started. The one operational rule attached to this: never call the reset function by hand during an investigation, because you destroy the accumulation the investigation is standing on. If you want a clean window, take a snapshot first and diff against it.

Every statement the ORM emits carries a trailing SQL comment with the route, the deploy version and the trace id, in the form used by sqlcommenter, and it is injected by a session event hook so no call site has to remember. The comment is invisible to the planner, survives into `pg_stat_activity`, and is what lets a database-side observation be joined back to a request-side one without a shared identifier being threaded through the application by hand. The concrete payoff turns up when a single statement shape is emitted from four places and only one of them is slow — the shape alone cannot distinguish them, the route tag can. There is a subtlety worth knowing: the comment is part of the statement text, so a naive fingerprinting that does not strip comments will treat every route as its own entry and blow through the statements limit. Our normaliser strips them before fingerprinting and keeps them alongside, which took an afternoon of confusion to work out and is now covered by a test.

`log_lock_waits` is on and `deadlock_timeout` sits at one second, so the log carries the full detail of both sides of any deadlock, including the statements and the relations involved. None of it pages anyone. Deadlocks are detected and resolved by the database in about a second, one transaction is killed with `40P01`, and the caller retries; from the user's point of view nothing happened. What matters is the trend, so the count is graphed by relation and reviewed with the rest of the weekly database numbers, and a sustained rise gets looked at as a code shape problem rather than an incident. Almost every deadlock we have had traced back to the same cause: two writers touching the same set of rows in different orders, usually because one iterated a list in the order it arrived from an API. The standing fix is to sort the keys before locking, which sounds trivial and has resolved four separate outbreaks. Paging on deadlocks was tried for one quarter and produced nothing but interrupted sleep.

A comparison job runs after each release, taking the twenty highest-cost fingerprints from the two hours before the deploy and the two hours after, and posting a diff of mean execution time into the release channel. It is a signal, not a gate, and it does not open anything or block anything. The reason it exists is that plan changes are the least visible kind of regression: the code did not change, the statement did not change, but the planner picked something else because the statistics moved or a new index gave it a worse option. Two of our worst afternoons started that way and in both cases the change had been visible in the data for an hour before anyone connected it to the deploy that preceded it. Reading the diff takes a minute and has become part of the release checklist by habit rather than by rule. False positives are common when traffic mix shifts, so the convention is to look at the ratio and ignore anything under a doubling, which keeps the thing usable.

On the first working day of each month a short report goes out with the size of every relation over a gigabyte, its growth over the previous three months, and a straight-line projection of when it will cross the current disk allocation. Nobody is required to act on it, and that is deliberate: it exists so that capacity conversations happen while there is time to have them calmly, rather than during the week a volume fills. The projections are crude on purpose, since a fancier model would invite arguing about the model instead of about the table. Two useful things have come out of it that would not have come out of an alert. One is noticing that an audit relation was growing faster than the entity it audited, which turned out to be a retry loop writing duplicate rows. The other is a standing habit of asking, when a new relation is designed, roughly how large it will be in two years, and being unhappy with the answer often enough that designs change.

A panel tracks sequential scan counts and tuples read per scan for the fifteen relations above a gigabyte, pulled from the statistics collector. It is watched rather than alerted on, because a sequential scan is not by itself a problem — on a small table it is the right plan and the planner knows it. What the panel is for is spotting the shape change: a relation that has always been scanned sequentially at a steady low rate suddenly being scanned thousands of times an hour, which usually means a query that used to be selective stopped being selective, or an index stopped being chosen. Reading it requires knowing which relations are supposed to be scanned, and that knowledge lives in the panel description rather than in anyone's head. The one absolute rule is that the number alone never justifies adding anything to the schema; it justifies going and looking at what changed. The panel is pinned next to the write-throughput one because the two are usually read together, and the pair of them is the first place anyone looks when the primary feels slower than it did last week.

The only database alert that pages is saturation: `connections_in_use / max_connections` above 0.8 for five minutes, or replication apply lag above the standby threshold. Latency does not page, and that was a deliberate reversal. We used to page on mean statement duration crossing 50ms and it woke people for things that were not actionable — a nightly report starting, a cache warm after a deploy, a customer running a large legitimate import. Every one of those pages ended with the on-call engineer looking at a graph and going back to bed, which is the definition of an alert that should not exist. Saturation is different because it is the state in which every other request begins to suffer, and because there is something to do about it at three in the morning: shed the workload class that is consuming the pool. Latency still matters, it just belongs to whoever owns the endpoint during working hours rather than to whoever is holding the pager. The threshold of 0.8 was picked because the pooler needs headroom to open connections during a failover, and at 0.9 we found it could not.

An index is a write tax paid forever to make one read faster, so adding one is a reviewed decision rather than a reflex. The pull request that introduces an index has to carry four things in its description: the exact statement it serves, the `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` output before and after, the estimated write amplification from `tools/index_lint.py`, and a sentence on why the query cannot be made selective without it. The lint runs in CI and hard-fails on two conditions — an index whose leading columns are a prefix of an existing one, which is almost always redundant, and any index on a relation that already carries six, which needs a named reviewer from the platform team to approve rather than being forbidden outright. Creation is always `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` in its own migration file with no other statements in it, because concurrent builds cannot run inside a transaction block and mixing them with other DDL is how you get a half-applied revision. The six-index threshold has a history: `shipment_events` accumulated fourteen indexes over two years, each individually defensible, and the nightly import went from forty minutes to just under three hours while WAL volume doubled. Nobody had added a bad index; the cost was in the sum, and nothing in the process had ever looked at the sum.

Once a quarter someone reads `pg_stat_user_indexes` across the fleet and proposes drops for anything with zero scans since the last reset, excluding unique constraints and anything backing a foreign key. The proposal goes out as a single pull request listing each index, its size, and the date it was created, and owners have a week to object. Objections are usually about a quarterly job that has not run yet in the window, which is exactly the kind of thing the review period is there to catch. Drops themselves are trivial and reversible in the sense that the index can be rebuilt, though rebuilding a large one on a busy table is an hour of concurrent build, so nobody enjoys being wrong. The last sweep reclaimed about ninety gigabytes and shaved a noticeable amount off the bulk import. There is one standing exception, an index on the reconciliation relation that shows zero scans because it exists for a yearly audit query, and it is annotated in the schema comment so the next sweep does not propose it again.

Bloat is measured monthly with the estimate query in `ops/db/bloat.sql`, and any index above forty percent estimated bloat and larger than a gigabyte gets a `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY` scheduled into the quiet window between 02:00 and 05:00 UTC.
