Concurrent reindexing is what makes this routine instead of an outage; the non-concurrent form takes an access exclusive lock and would stop writes to the relation for the whole rebuild. Two operational notes have earned their place in the runbook. A concurrent reindex that fails leaves an invalid index behind with a suffix, and it must be dropped explicitly or the next attempt inherits the mess. And the rebuild needs disk headroom equal to the index size, so the check refuses to start when free space on the volume is below fifteen percent. The relations that need this are the ones taking constant updates on indexed columns; a mostly-append relation almost never bloats and is not worth the maintenance window.

Names are generated, never chosen: `ix_<table>_<columns>` for a plain index, `uq_` for unique, `fk_<table>_<referenced>` for foreign keys, `ck_<table>_<rule>` for checks, and the ORM's naming convention dictionary in `db/base.py` produces them so autogenerated migrations come out consistent. This is not aesthetics. Before the convention, constraint names were whatever the database assigned, they differed between environments because they had been created in a different order, and a migration that dropped a constraint by name worked on staging and failed in production. That failure happened during a deploy and cost an hour of rollback. With generated names the same DDL applies everywhere and diffs of the schema dump are readable. There is one migration in the tree that exists purely to rename several hundred legacy constraints into the convention, and the rule since then is that anything created outside it is a review finding, including things created by hand during an incident, which get renamed the following day.

New relations get `bigint generated always as identity` for their primary key, and random UUIDs are not used as keys even where a public identifier is needed. Where an opaque external identifier is required, a separate indexed `public_id` column holds a prefixed base32 value and the internal key stays numeric. The reason is index locality. A random UUID key means every insert lands in a random leaf of the B-tree, which turns a sequential write pattern into scattered page dirtying, inflates the working set, and bloats the index far faster than a monotonic key does. We measured this on the events relation during a spike and the difference in write throughput was large enough that nobody argued afterwards. The counter-argument, that sequential keys leak volume information and let people enumerate resources, is real and is what the separate public identifier answers. Relations created before this decision keep their UUID keys; converting them is not worth the migration, and mixed conventions in the schema are the visible cost of having decided this late.

The cluster-wide autovacuum settings are left alone and the six busiest relations carry their own storage parameters instead, with a much lower scale factor and a raised cost limit so the worker is not throttled into irrelevance on a table taking thousands of updates a minute. The default scale factor of twenty percent means a relation with two hundred million rows waits for forty million dead tuples before a vacuum starts, which by then is a long and disruptive vacuum rather than a series of short ones. Setting it low on the hot relations converts one big event into continuous background work, which is what the mechanism was designed for. The settings live in the migration that creates the relation, not in a config file, so they travel with the schema and cannot drift between environments. Getting this wrong in the other direction is possible and we did it once, tuning a relation so aggressively that the workers were permanently busy on it and starved everything else.

Text search left the database three years ago and lives in a dedicated search cluster fed by a change stream. The database side keeps only the identifiers and the canonical rows. The version with a text search column and a trigram index worked well enough at first and then stopped scaling in a specific way: the maintenance cost of the search structures dominated write time on the exact relations taking the most writes, and every improvement to search quality meant more of that cost. Ranking, synonyms and typo tolerance were also being reimplemented badly in SQL. The tradeoff we accepted going out is eventual consistency of about two seconds between a write and its appearance in results, plus an entire additional system to operate. What made it worth it is that search relevance work no longer touches the primary at all. Anyone proposing to bring search back into the database is asked to say what has changed about that maintenance cost, and so far nothing has.

We tried `INCLUDE` columns on several hot lookups to get index-only scans and kept exactly one of them. The idea is sound: put the payload columns in the leaf so the query never touches the heap. In practice two things spoiled it for us. The visibility map has to be current for an index-only scan to actually avoid heap fetches, and on relations taking constant updates it rarely is, so the plan claims index-only and does heap fetches anyway. And the wider leaves meant fewer entries per page, which made the index bigger and the cache less effective for every other query using it. The one that survived is on a nearly append-only reference relation where the visibility map stays clean and the payload is two small columns. The general shape of the finding is worth remembering when the technique gets proposed again: it pays off on stable data and quietly does nothing on churning data, and the plan output does not make the difference obvious unless you read the buffer counts.

Foreign keys are added in two steps and never in one. The migration that introduces the constraint declares it `NOT VALID`, which makes the database enforce it for new rows immediately while skipping the full scan of existing ones, and a second migration in a later release runs `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`, which takes only a share lock and lets writes continue. Doing it in one step takes a lock that blocks writes for the length of a full relation scan, and on the larger relations that is several minutes of a table nobody can write to, in the middle of a deploy. We learned the shape of that during an evening release that stalled for six minutes and looked exactly like an outage to everyone watching. There is a corollary that catches people: `NOT VALID` means the planner will not rely on the constraint until it is validated, so any optimisation you were expecting from declaring it does not arrive until the second half ships. The two migrations are written at the same time by the same author, and the second is not allowed to be a follow-up ticket that never gets done.

Anything a person can see comes from the primary. The three standbys exist for failover, for backups, and for the analytics extract, and the routing layer will only send a statement to one of them if the calling code has explicitly asked for the reporting session. There is no automatic read splitting, and the flag that used to enable it, `DB_READ_REPLICA_ENABLED`, was deleted from the chart rather than left switched off, because a flag like that gets turned on again by someone who does not know the history. The history is three weeks in the spring: we routed all GET traffic to the replicas, and support volume climbed for a fortnight before anyone connected the two, because a customer would save an address and the confirmation page would render from a standby eleven seconds behind, showing the old value. Lag is not the steady two hundred milliseconds the dashboard averages — it spikes into the tens of seconds whenever the bulk import or a large delete runs, which is exactly when reads follow writes. Fixing that properly means read-your-writes routing, session pinning after a write, and a story for every cross-request case, which is a lot of subtle machinery for a capacity problem we do not have. The primary is sized with headroom and the read path leans on caching instead, and the revisit condition is written down: sustained read CPU above sixty percent for a month.

The alert on `pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp` age fires as a warning at ten seconds and pages at thirty, evaluated per standby over a three minute window. The thresholds are about failover readiness, not about read correctness. A standby thirty seconds behind is a standby that would lose thirty seconds of transactions if we promoted it right now, and the whole reason the standbys exist is that promotion is the recovery path. The three minute window exists because short spikes during the nightly import are normal and paging on them taught everyone to ignore the alert, which is worse than not having it. When it does fire the runbook is short: check whether a long transaction on the primary is holding the standby back, check whether the standby is CPU-bound replaying, and if it is the import, wait. The one case that is genuinely urgent is lag that grows monotonically without a matching write spike, which historically has meant a stuck recovery process rather than a load problem.

Promotion is manual. There is no automatic failover controller, and the procedure in the runbook is two commands: fence the old primary by revoking its network policy, then promote the chosen standby and repoint the pooler's config map. It takes about four minutes with a calm operator and has been rehearsed quarterly since the second one of these went badly. The argument for automating it is obvious and we keep declining it, because the failure mode of an automatic controller is worse than the failure mode of a slow human: a controller that promotes on a network partition gives you two primaries accepting writes, and reconciling a split brain across a ledger is not an operation anyone wants to be performing. Our availability target has room for four minutes; it does not have room for reconstructing which of two divergent write streams was real. The rehearsal matters more than the automation debate. Each one has found something stale — a hard-coded host in one service, a monitoring check pointed at the old node by name.

One standby is not a physical replica at all but a logical subscriber, and that difference exists so it can carry indexes the primary does not. Physical replication forces an identical structure, so any index the analysts wanted would have been paid for on every write to the primary. The logical subscriber applies the same rows and then maintains eleven additional indexes locally, mostly wide composite ones supporting the cohort queries that would be absurd on the write path. The costs are honest and worth stating. Logical replication does not carry schema changes, so every migration needs a matching step on the subscriber and a CI check verifies that the two schemas are compatible before merge. It falls behind more easily under bulk writes, and it cannot be promoted to serve as the primary. It is a query surface, not a spare. When it breaks, the fix is usually to reseed a single relation rather than to rebuild the subscription.

The search cluster is fed by a replication slot rather than by application-level dual writes. A small consumer reads the decoded change stream, maps rows to documents, and writes them in batches of five hundred with a two second flush interval. Dual writes were the original design and they drifted, exactly as everyone warns: any code path that wrote to the database without going through the one blessed helper produced a document that never existed, and reconciliation jobs became a permanent fixture. Reading the change stream means the database is the only source of truth and anything committed will eventually be indexed. The operational hazard that comes with it is specific and needs to be understood by whoever is on call: an unconsumed replication slot pins WAL on the primary, so a consumer that has been down since Friday is a disk-full incident by Sunday. There is an alert on slot lag in bytes for that reason, set at twenty gigabytes, and the documented emergency action is to drop the slot and reseed rather than to let the volume fill.

Most writes commit asynchronously, meaning the primary acknowledges before a standby has confirmed the record, and one class of writes does not: anything in the ledger schema runs with synchronous commit against one named standby. The distinction is about what a loss of the last few hundred milliseconds would mean. For a page view, a preference change or a search log, losing the tail of the write stream during a failover is an annoyance nobody would ever notice. For a posted financial entry it is a discrepancy that has to be found and explained to someone, and the cost of finding it dwarfs the latency we save. The cost of the setting is real — those commits carry the network round trip, which shows up as a few milliseconds on the write path and considerably more when the chosen standby is having a bad day. That last part is why the synchronous standby is named explicitly rather than being any available one, and why its health is treated as a production dependency of the ledger service.

There is a standby in a second region that no traffic ever touches. It is not part of the failover plan for ordinary problems, it is not a read target, and its lag is routinely worse than the local ones because it is streaming across a longer path. It exists for the scenario where the primary region is gone, which has never happened to us, and it is kept because the alternative is restoring from object storage into a cold cluster, which we have timed at somewhere between five and seven hours. The recovery objective it buys us is written into the continuity document and reviewed annually with the compliance work. What keeps it honest is that it is exercised: twice a year it is promoted in an isolated network, a subset of services is pointed at it, and someone confirms that they start. Both exercises so far have found configuration that assumed the home region, which is the entire point of doing them.

When a standby has diverged or has been down long enough that the primary no longer has the WAL it needs, we rebuild it from a fresh base backup rather than trying to bring it back with the rewind tool. Rewinding is faster and works most of the time, and that is precisely the problem — the failure mode when it does not work is a subtly inconsistent replica that streams happily and serves wrong data, which is far harder to detect than a node that is plainly absent. A rebuild takes about ninety minutes on the current data size, runs from the backup rather than from the primary so it costs nothing on the write path, and finishes in a state we can reason about. The old node's data directory is kept until the new one has caught up, in case anyone wants to look at it. This is the sort of rule that feels wasteful right up until the once where it saves you, and the once was a rewound node that silently missed a range of transactions.

The warehouse extract runs at 02:10 UTC against `pg-standby-c` and nothing else runs there. Pinning it to one named node rather than to whichever standby is available was a lesson from an early version that picked the least-lagged one at start time and occasionally picked the node the backup was about to start on, producing two heavy sequential workloads on the same disks and an hour of replication lag on a node we might have needed. The extract itself is a set of statements with a fixed watermark: it reads rows whose updated timestamp falls in the previous full day, so re-running it produces the same output and a failed run can simply be run again. It emits a row count per relation into the job log, and a deviation of more than fifteen percent from the trailing week fails the run rather than loading a suspicious file, which has caught two upstream bugs before the analysts saw them. If the pinned node is unavailable the job fails loudly and waits for a human rather than falling back to another one.

The detector is a pytest plugin, `tests/plugins/query_guard.py`, that hooks the ORM's cursor execute event and counts statements inside each test, normalising them so that the same shape with different parameters collapses to one fingerprint. Two conditions fail a test. The first is exceeding the recorded budget for that test, held in `tests/query_budgets.json` as a plain map of node id to integer. The second is repetition: the same fingerprint executed more than five times inside one request scope, which is the signature of a loop issuing a query per row regardless of what the total happens to be. The pipeline job `query-budget` runs the API suite with `QUERY_GUARD=strict` and is a required check; the nightly runs the same plugin in `report` mode over the endpoints that have no budget yet and posts the counts, which is how new routes acquire one. Raising a budget is allowed but the diff shows it, and reviewers ask why, which is the social mechanism the tool provides. It exists because a list endpoint shipped issuing one query per row and nobody noticed at ten rows in development; a customer with two hundred and four saved views produced two hundred and five queries and a nine second response, and it had been that way for two releases. The counts were visible in production traces the whole time, which is why the check lives in CI, where somebody has to look before merge.

Relationship attributes are configured with `lazy="raise"` rather than the default, so touching an unloaded relationship throws instead of quietly emitting a query. It is a blunt instrument and that is the point: the failure happens at the line that caused it, with a stack trace naming the attribute, instead of somewhere later as a performance mystery. The cost is that every access path has to be declared up front with a join or a selectin load, which makes some query construction more verbose and occasionally forces a second explicit fetch where the old code would have wandered off and got the row itself. That verbosity has been a fair trade. Converting the existing code took about two weeks of a rolling migration, relationship by relationship, with the setting applied per relationship until the last few were done. Two places still opt out with an explicit override and both are annotated with the reason, both being admin tooling where the shape of the access is genuinely dynamic and the volume is a handful of rows.

Every serializer class carries a `required_loads` tuple naming the relationships it will touch, and the repository layer refuses to serialise an entity that was not loaded with at least those. It reads as bureaucracy until you have seen the alternative: the query lives in the repository, the access lives in the serializer, and the two drift apart every time either is edited, because nothing connects them. Making the serializer state its needs puts the dependency in one place and makes it reviewable in the same diff as the field that introduced it. Adding a field that reaches through a new relationship is therefore a two-line change rather than a one-line change, and the second line is the one that keeps the endpoint fast. New serializers inherit a base that asserts the tuple is non-empty when any relationship field is declared, so forgetting it is not possible by accident. The rule was written after a release where three separate endpoints regressed from the same refactor, all because a shared serializer grew a nested field.

In development the server prints a one-line summary after each request — total statements, total database time, and the three most repeated fingerprints — coloured red when the count is above thirty. It is not a gate and it cannot fail anything, it exists so that the feedback arrives while you are still holding the code in your head. Watching the number climb as you add a field to a response teaches the shape of the problem better than any amount of documentation, and several people have described it as the thing that made them internalise how the ORM actually behaves. The middleware is registered only when the debug setting is on and is excluded from the production image entirely, since the counting overhead is small but the log volume would not be. There is a companion flag that prints the statements themselves, off by default because it drowns the console, and a habit of turning it on for one endpoint when the summary says something surprising.

The graph layer routes every relationship fetch through a per-request dataloader that collects keys within a tick and issues one query per relationship per level. Without it a nested query for fifty objects with three levels of relationship produces a query per object per level, because a resolver by construction has no idea it is being called fifty times. This is a property of the execution model rather than a mistake anybody made, so the fix has to be structural. Loaders live in `graph/loaders.py`, are constructed once per request in the context factory, and the convention is that a resolver never touches the repository directly; that convention is the whole safety property, since one direct call reintroduces the pattern for the field it serves. Cache lifetime is exactly one request, deliberately, because a longer-lived loader cache would start returning stale rows across mutations and produce a much more confusing class of bug than the one it was solving.

After each deploy to staging a smoke run exercises twenty-two representative endpoints against a seeded dataset and compares p50 and p95 against budgets held alongside the scenario definitions. Failing it does not block the promotion; it posts a comparison table into the release thread and the release manager decides. The soft gate is a considered choice: staging traffic is synthetic, the dataset is a fraction of production size, and a hard gate on those numbers would have been overridden so often that it would have taught everyone to override it. What the run is good at is catching the large regressions, the ones where something went from milliseconds to seconds, and those show up unambiguously against any budget. It is bad at small ones, and nobody should read a fifteen percent move as signal. The seeded dataset is refreshed quarterly from an anonymised sample so the row counts stay in the right order of magnitude.

Each request emits its statement count and total database time as attributes on the trace span, and there is a dashboard panel ranking routes by mean statements per request over the last day. It is the production view of the same property the test suite constrains, and it exists because production has the data shapes that development never does: the customer with four thousand rows in a collection that everyone assumed would hold ten. Nothing alerts on it. The panel is read during the weekly review and when someone is already investigating a slow route, and its main use in practice has been to argue for work rather than to detect it — a route sitting at ninety statements per request is a much easier case to make than a vague sense that a page feels slow. The attribute is cheap because the counter already exists in the session for other reasons, and it is sampled at the same rate as the traces themselves rather than being recorded for every request.

The review checklist has one performance item on it and this is it: if the diff contains a loop, say out loud where the data for each iteration comes from. It is deliberately the only item, because a checklist of twenty things is a checklist nobody reads. The question is phrased as a request to the author rather than an instruction to the reviewer, since the author knows the answer and the reviewer is guessing. Most of the time the answer is obvious and it takes ten seconds. Occasionally the act of answering is where the author notices the problem themselves, which is the outcome the item is fishing for. It survives as a convention because it is cheap and because people found it genuinely useful rather than because anyone enforces it. The related habit that grew alongside it is asking what the collection looks like for the largest customer, which is the question that turns an abstract worry about a loop into a number somebody can check.

Raw SQL is legal, and it is legal in exactly one place: modules under `app/repositories/`. A flake8 plugin, `tools/lint_rules/no_raw_sql.py`, fails the build on a `text()` call or a driver cursor used anywhere else, and the allowlist is a directory pattern rather than a list of files so nobody has to maintain it. The reason is not purity about ORMs. It is that hand-written statements are where the parameterisation mistakes and the unindexed predicates live, and confining them to one directory means the set of files a reviewer has to read carefully is small and stable. Twenty-eight raw statements exist today; all of them are there because the generated query was measurably worse, and each carries a comment saying so with the plan cost that justified it. The rule also gives the search-and-replace a place to stand when a column is renamed, which used to mean grepping the entire tree and hoping. The one recurring argument is about analytics scripts, which are exempt because they are not part of the deployed application.

Decisions that are expensive to reverse get a numbered record in `docs/decisions/`, named `NNNN-short-title.md` and scaffolded by `make adr-new`. The template has five sections and no more: the context that forced a choice, the decision in the present tense, the consequences we are accepting, the alternatives that were rejected and why, and a status line. One page is the limit, and the rejected-alternatives section is the part that earns the file — six months later nobody needs to be told what we did, they need to know what we already considered and dismissed. A record is required for a new datastore or queue, a contract between two services, a vendor commitment, a change to the auth model, or anything that would take more than a week to undo; everything else is just a pull request description. They are written after the decision, not as a proposal, so they describe what was chosen rather than what someone hoped for. Superseding never edits the old file: the original keeps its text and its status becomes `Superseded by 0042`, so the trail of reasoning survives. The docs build fails on a file without a valid status header, which is the only mechanical enforcement there is. The habit came out of arguing about the same message broker three times in eighteen months, each time from scratch, because the reasoning from the first two lived in chat threads nobody could find.

There is a standing thirty minute slot on Thursday mornings for anything that needs several teams to agree, and the rule for using it is that a two-page pre-read goes out by Tuesday end of day or the item does not get on the agenda. Nothing is presented in the meeting; the first ten minutes are silent reading for anyone who did not manage it, and the rest is questions. That format replaced a presentation format that consistently produced polite nodding followed by objections raised a week later in a corridor, because listening to somebody talk through a design is a very poor way to notice what is wrong with it. Attendance is open and typically eight to ten people. The slot is often unused, which is treated as fine rather than as a problem to be filled — a standing slot that is empty half the time is what makes it available immediately when something does need it, and that availability is most of its value.

A page divided into adopt, trial, hold and avoid lists the technologies we have opinions about, and it is revised in January and July by whoever shows up to the session. Entries carry one sentence of reasoning and a date. It is advisory: nothing on the hold list is forbidden, it means bringing it in requires an argument rather than a preference, and two things on hold have moved back to trial after somebody made that argument well. The avoid list is short and is the only part with teeth, since everything on it got there by hurting us specifically. What the radar is really for is new joiners and cross-team work, where the alternative is discovering by accident that the company has three opinions about the same tool. Keeping the refresh to twice a year is deliberate — a continuously edited page would drift into a wiki nobody trusts, while a dated snapshot is at least honestly stale. Entries are removed once the debate is genuinely settled, since a list that only grows becomes a history of arguments rather than a description of what we use today.

`catalog/services.yaml` lists every deployed service with an owning team, a tier from one to three, a pager destination and a link to its dashboard. The deploy pipeline reads it and refuses to promote a service that is missing an entry, which is what keeps the file honest — a catalog maintained by good intentions is out of date within a quarter, and this one is out of date within a deploy. Tier drives the things that should follow from importance rather than from memory: tier one gets synthetic checks and a quarterly failover exercise, tier three does not page overnight at all. The file also answers the question that used to take twenty minutes at the start of an incident, which is who to talk to about a service nobody in the channel recognises. Ownership transfers are a pull request against that file and are expected to be accompanied by an actual conversation, because a merged change to a YAML file does not by itself transfer any knowledge.

Anything shipped as a named launch gets a short written review thirty days later, covering what was measured against what was predicted, what surprised us, and whether the thing is being used. It is half a page and it is not a retrospective of how the project ran; it is about the artefact and whether it did what it was supposed to. The reason it exists is that the honest answer is often no and nobody was collecting that answer. Two features have been withdrawn on the strength of one of these, which is the outcome that justifies the practice, and several have had their scope quietly reduced. The thirty day window is short enough that the people involved still remember the predictions and long enough that adoption numbers mean something. The reviews are filed next to the launch plan they refer to, so reading them in sequence tells you something uncomfortable and useful about how our predictions tend to be wrong.

One staff engineer each month is the designated reviewer for anything crossing team boundaries, and the rotation is published a quarter ahead. The role is not approval authority; it is a person whose job that month is to have read the things that touch more than one team, so that the question of whether two groups are about to build the same thing has an owner rather than depending on coincidence. Before the rotation existed this depended entirely on whoever happened to be curious, and it failed in the predictable way twice, both times producing two implementations of the same integration in the same quarter. The month is long enough to build context and short enough that nobody's own work stops. The person on rotation is explicitly expected to spend about a day a week on it and to say so when they cannot, and the rotation is skipped rather than half-done when the person is on call, since the two together is more interruption than anyone can absorb.

When an internal package or shared module is deprecated, the notice has to name a removal date and a successor, and both go into the release notes and the module's own docstring. A deprecation without a date is not a deprecation, it is a complaint, and we accumulated years of those before this became a rule — modules marked deprecated in comments that half the codebase still imported, with nobody able to say whether the mark meant anything. The date is allowed to move, once, with a note saying why. What follows from having a date is that the removal becomes schedulable work for the consuming teams rather than an ambient obligation, and the person doing the deprecating is required to have talked to those teams before publishing it. Removal day itself is undramatic when the process worked. Twice it has not worked and the module stayed, which was treated as a failure of the notification rather than as evidence that dates are unrealistic.

On the first Monday of the month someone writes three or four paragraphs about what changed across the platform and posts it where the whole company can read it, including support and sales. It is not a status report and it deliberately does not list every ticket; it picks the handful of things that someone outside engineering would notice or should know about, and explains them in language that does not assume our vocabulary. The writing rotates among the senior engineers, which spreads both the effort and the perspective. It started because support kept finding out about behaviour changes from customers, which is an embarrassing way to find out. The unexpected benefit has been internal: people on one team routinely learn from it what another team spent the month on, which the sprint reviews never achieved because nobody attends another team's review. Keeping it short is the discipline that makes it survive; the longer editions have been the less-read ones.

Internal systems get their names from a fixed list of coastal and nautical words kept in `docs/names.md`, claimed by adding a line to it, and never renamed once claimed. The list exists because descriptive names age badly: the service called `new-billing` was five years old and no longer new, `api-v2` sat beside a `v3` that was not its successor, and every one of those names had to be explained to every joiner. An arbitrary name carries no false promises and becomes meaningful through use. The rule that matters more than the list is the one about renaming — a rename touches dashboards, alert routes, runbooks, bookmarks and everyone's memory, and the cost is always larger than the discomfort of the old name. Two renames have happened, both because a name collided with a customer-facing product name and marketing asked. Public-facing names are a separate matter entirely and are chosen by people whose job that is; the internal name usually survives underneath and shows up in log lines forever.

In the narrative of a postmortem people appear as roles: the deploying engineer, the on-call, the reviewer, the support agent who escalated. Names appear in exactly two places, the author line and the action item owners, and the template in `docs/postmortems/template.md` says so at the top so nobody has to be corrected in review. The phrase "human error" is not accepted as a cause; a reviewer will send the document back and ask what made the error easy to make, which is the question the document exists to answer. There are two reasons. The first is the ordinary one about honesty — a document that assigns fault gets written defensively, and a defensive document omits the interesting details, which are usually the ones about how confusing the system was at 3am. The second is that these documents travel. One of ours went to a customer's technical account team with a name in it, and that engineer spent the next year avoiding the deploy tooling, so we lost both a contributor and every observation they would have made. That was the incident that turned a preference into a rule. Writing this way takes practice, because the natural sentence is "Priya deployed the config change"; the version we want is "the config change was deployed with a stale value, which the tool accepted without a diff". The second sentence is also the one that suggests a fix.

The write-up for a severity one or two incident is due five business days after the incident closes, and the clock is tracked on the incident ticket. Five days was chosen after trying two, which produced documents written while people were still exhausted and still missing information from other teams, and after watching an unbounded deadline produce nothing at all in about a third of cases. The document does not have to be finished to be shared; a draft with open questions circulated on day three usually attracts the answers faster than research does. If the deadline is going to be missed the incident commander says so in the channel with a new date, which is treated as entirely normal and happens perhaps a fifth of the time. What is not normal is silence, and a document that has slipped twice without a note gets picked up by the engineering manager. The completion rate has sat above ninety percent for six quarters, which is the only number anyone tracks about this.

Every action item leaves the postmortem as a real ticket with a named owner and a due date no more than thirty days out, and the review is not closed until they exist. Items without an owner were the standard outcome of the old format and none of them were ever done — a list at the bottom of a document is a wish, and a ticket in a backlog is at least visible during planning. The thirty day limit forces the item to be small; anything larger has to be split into the part that can be done in a month and the part that becomes a project with a sponsor. A monthly report shows the completion rate of incident actions, and it hovers around seventy percent, with the misses concentrated in items that were really infrastructure projects wearing a disguise. Owners are individuals rather than teams, because a team owns nothing in practice. Reassignment is fine and common; the point is that at any moment one person can say what the state of the item is.

The timeline section is generated, not remembered. `tools/incident_timeline.py` pulls the incident channel transcript, the deploy events, the alert firings and the status page updates for the window, merges them by timestamp and writes a first draft into the document. The author then prunes it, because the raw merge is far too long and includes every reaction and side conversation. Memory is unreliable about ordering under stress in a way that is well documented and that we have seen repeatedly: people consistently misremember whether the alert came before or after the deploy, and that ordering is often the entire finding. The generated draft also removes the tedium that was the main reason timelines were thin. One consequence worth knowing is that it makes the channel the record of the incident, so the convention is to narrate actions in the channel as you take them rather than in a direct message, even when it feels like noise.

If something would have been an outage and was not, only because a check caught it or somebody happened to be looking, it gets the same document as an incident that reached customers. These are the cheapest lessons available — the mechanism failed, the consequence did not arrive, and there is no pressure of angry customers distorting the analysis. Nobody is required to declare one, which is a deliberate weakness, so the practice depends on people being willing to write up something embarrassing that nobody would otherwise have known about. That willingness is fragile and is the main reason the reporting norms around these documents matter as much as they do. Roughly a quarter of the write-ups in the archive are near misses, and two of them prompted larger changes than any real incident did that year, including the rebuild of the deploy confirmation step. They are filed in the same place and carry a tag rather than living in a separate archive, because a separate archive is one nobody reads.

The postmortem review is run by an engineer who was not involved in the incident, drawn from a rotation kept in the same file as the on-call schedule. The chair's job is procedural: keep the discussion on the document, stop the conversation from becoming a design session for the fix, and make sure the questions that were not asked get asked. Someone who was in the incident cannot do that, not because of judgement but because they already know what happened and unconsciously skip the parts that seem obvious, which are exactly the parts an outsider stumbles over. The meeting is capped at forty-five minutes and the chair ends it on time even when items are unresolved; unresolved items become follow-ups rather than reasons to run long. Attendance is open and typically includes support, who ask the best questions about customer impact because that is what they spent the incident dealing with.

The archive is open to everyone, not just engineering, and support and account management read it regularly. The concern raised at the time — that non-engineers would misread technical detail and panic — has not materialised in three years; what happened instead is that support started answering customer questions about past incidents accurately without asking us, which saved an enormous amount of back-and-forth. There is a short summary at the top written for a reader who does not know the system, and writing it is a useful exercise because a cause you cannot state in three plain sentences is usually a cause you have not finished understanding. Documents that touch security details are the one exception and live in a restricted space with a stub in the main archive so the gap is visible. Sharing outward to customers is a separate decision made case by case, and those versions are rewritten rather than exported.

The template no longer has a root cause field. It has contributing factors, and it asks for at least three. Every serious incident we have had was a coincidence of several things, none of which would have been sufficient alone — a retry policy that was reasonable, a timeout that was reasonable, and a dependency that got slow rather than failing. Forcing that into a single root cause meant picking whichever one was easiest to describe, usually the last change in the chain, and the fixes that came out were correspondingly narrow. The three-factor minimum is artificial and occasionally produces a padded third entry, which is a cost we accept for what it does to the first two. A related change went with it: the document asks what stopped the incident from being worse, and the answers to that question have turned out to be worth protecting, since they are usually mechanisms nobody deliberately designed.

A third incident with the same tag inside ninety days stops being an ordinary write-up and becomes a deeper review: two weeks of scope, an explicit budget of engineering time, and a written answer to why the previous two sets of action items did not prevent this one. Tags come from a fixed vocabulary of about fifteen — `config-drift`, `dependency-timeout`, `capacity`, `deploy-order` and so on — chosen when the incident closes and revisable afterwards. The counting is done by a monthly job rather than by anyone noticing, because noticing is exactly what fails: three incidents spread over a quarter, handled by different people, feel like three unrelated bad days. The two that have gone through this treatment both concluded that the earlier actions had been correct but too small, which is a finding you can only reach by looking at the sequence. The ninety day window and the count of three were picked to fire a couple of times a year; a tighter rule fired on things that were genuinely coincidence.

Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday afternoons are meeting-free from 13:00 in each person's own local time, and everyone carries a recurring calendar block created by `scripts/focus_blocks.py` so the time shows as busy to anyone scheduling from outside the team. It is an agreement, not a control: the block can be booked over, and nothing rejects an invite. What makes it hold is that booking over it is visible and people say why. Three things are understood exceptions and nobody negotiates them — an active incident, an interview already committed to a candidate, and a customer call that cannot move. Everything recurring that violated it was moved to Monday or Friday morning when the agreement was made, which took one afternoon of calendar work. The measurement that prompted it: someone pulled a month of calendars and found the median engineer had four gaps shorter than forty-five minutes in a typical day, and almost no unbroken stretch over ninety minutes. The count of meetings was not the problem, their distribution was. A year on, the number of meetings is about the same and the afternoons are largely intact, which is exactly the outcome that was wanted. The failure mode to watch for is a slow accumulation of one-off exceptions that quietly become recurring, so the calendar gets audited at the start of each quarter and anything that has crept in is moved back.

Every recurring internal meeting is created with an end date on the last day of the quarter, and continuing it requires someone to recreate it. The asymmetry is the entire mechanism: a meeting that persists by default takes an act of confrontation to kill, while a meeting that ends by default takes a small act of will to continue, and the second act is much easier to skip when the meeting has stopped being useful. Of the eleven recurring meetings on the team calendar at the first expiry, four were not recreated and nobody missed any of them. Two came back a month later, which is the system working rather than failing. The rule does not apply to one-to-ones or to on-call handovers, which are exempt by name. The small cost is a burst of calendar admin in the first week of each quarter, and there is a script that lists what expired so the recreation is a decision rather than an oversight. The one thing that has needed guarding is the temptation to recreate everything in a single batch out of politeness, which would restore exactly the default the rule exists to remove.

There is no synchronous standup. Everyone posts into a thread before 10:00 local with what they are working on and anything blocking them, and the on-call engineer adds a line about the night. It is read asynchronously and answered in the thread. The switch happened because the team spans four time zones and the synchronous version was scheduled at an hour that was convenient for exactly two of them, which meant the two of them talked and everyone else attended. Writing it down also changed the content: a spoken update is performed for an audience and tends toward reassurance, while a written one is skimmed later by someone looking for a specific thing, and people write more usefully for that reader. The blockers get answered faster than they did in the meeting, because the person who can unblock you reads the thread rather than waiting to be asked. The thread is not archived anywhere special and nobody reads it after the day it belongs to.

If a meeting invite arrives with no agenda in the body, declining it needs no justification and causes no offence. This was written down explicitly because the social cost of declining is what made the previous norm useless — everyone agreed in principle that meetings should have agendas and nobody wanted to be the person who refused one. Making the decline explicitly acceptable moved the burden onto the organiser, where it belongs, and the practical effect was not a wave of declines but a sudden improvement in invite bodies. An agenda can be one line; the test is whether a reader can tell what would count as the meeting being finished. The norm has one asymmetry that people should know about: it applies to internal meetings between peers, and it is not an instrument for declining conversations you would simply rather not have. It also does not apply upward or to anything customer-facing, where the calculation is different and obvious.

The fortnightly demo runs for twenty-five minutes, not thirty, and it is recorded. The five minutes are given back deliberately so the next thing on people's calendars starts on time, which sounds trivial and is the difference between a day of meetings that fit and a day that runs late from ten in the morning onward. Recording it made attendance optional in practice, and about half the team watches later at speed. The format is strictly working software: something running, not slides about something that will run, and if it cannot be shown it does not go on the agenda. That rule removed the temptation to use the slot for status, which had been slowly consuming it. The demo is the one meeting nobody has ever proposed cutting, which is worth noticing given how many others have gone. Product and support are invited and usually come, and the questions they ask in the recording's comments have twice changed what got built next.

Nobody is scheduled for more than two interview loops in a week, and the recruiting coordinator enforces it against a shared availability sheet rather than asking each time. During the growth push before this cap existed, several engineers were doing five or six a week, which is most of a day gone once you count the preparation and the write-up, and the quality of the write-ups visibly degraded in proportion. The cap made scheduling harder for recruiting and made the panel wider, which turned out to be a benefit nobody predicted, since more people got trained to interview. Two loops is also roughly the point where interviewing stops feeling like a contribution and starts feeling like an imposition, and the difference in how a candidate is treated by someone in each of those states is not subtle. Debrief write-ups are due within twenty-four hours, and that deadline is the part most likely to slip when the cap is exceeded.

The team spans enough time zones that everyone is online together for about three hours a day, and the convention is that anything requiring a decision from more than two people happens in that window or in writing. Outside it, work proceeds on what has already been agreed. This is less about scheduling than about a failure we kept having: a discussion would start late in the European day, continue without the people who had gone home, and produce a conclusion those people first learned about the next morning as a fait accompli. Nobody intended that and it happened repeatedly. The written path is the important half, because a three hour window cannot hold everything, and the standard is that a decision taken asynchronously waits a full working day for objections before it is treated as settled. New joiners consistently underestimate how much this shapes the day, and the onboarding buddy is expected to spell it out in the first week.

Whoever is holding the pager is not assigned planned work for that iteration. They pick up interrupts, small fixes and whatever the week throws at them, and their capacity is simply removed from the plan. The version where on-call carried a reduced load looked more efficient on paper and failed in practice every single time: the planned work slipped, the person felt they were failing at both jobs, and the work that slipped was picked up by someone else halfway through, which cost more than it saved. Removing the capacity entirely also makes the true cost of the on-call load visible in planning, and it turned out to be about a fifth of the team's throughput, which was a considerably larger number than anyone had assumed and prompted real work on alert quality. A quiet week on call is treated as a gift to spend on whatever the person wants, and several of the better internal tools came out of exactly those weeks.

One-to-ones are thirty minutes every second week, and the agenda belongs to the report, not the manager. There is a shared document per person where either party drops items during the fortnight, and the manager's own topics go at the bottom on purpose. Weekly was tried and produced a lot of meetings with nothing in them, which taught people that the slot was skippable and then that lesson generalised to the fortnightly one for a while. What fixed it was the standing rule that the meeting is not cancelled, it is shortened — five minutes with nothing to discuss is a fine outcome and keeps the habit alive for the week when something matters. Status does not belong in it; that is what the written updates are for, and a one-to-one that turns into a project review is a sign something else is broken. The document is private to the two people and outlives the reporting line, which several people have found useful when they changed teams.

A fifth of each two-week iteration is reserved for sustaining work, and it is reserved as capacity in the plan rather than as an intention. Concretely: each team pulls one or two items labelled `sustaining` at planning, sized to about twenty percent of the iteration, and those items are committed alongside the feature work rather than listed underneath it as a stretch. The team chooses them, not product, on the argument that whoever pays the cost of the work not happening is best placed to rank it. Every candidate item carries one required line, what breaks or gets more expensive if we never do this, and items that cannot answer it are closed rather than left to age in the backlog. An item too large for one iteration is not a sustaining item; it becomes a project with a sponsor, a date and its own plan, which is how the query layer rewrite was run. Unfinished sustaining work may carry into the next iteration exactly once, then it goes back to the pool to be re-argued, because a half-done cleanup carried for three iterations is worse than one nobody started. Incident follow-ups are tracked separately and do not consume the allocation. The measured share over the last four quarters is around seventeen percent, which everyone regards as close enough. Before this, the policy was to do it when there was time, and across two full quarters the answer was that there was never time.

A change that touches more than about thirty files, or that is purely mechanical across a package, ships as its own pull request with nothing else in it. Mixing a rename across two hundred call sites with a behaviour change is a request nobody can review — the reviewer either reads all of it and finds nothing, or skims it and misses the four lines that matter. Splitting them makes both halves reviewable in minutes: the mechanical one gets checked by reading the tool invocation and the diff statistics, and the behavioural one is small enough to read properly. The convention that goes with it is that the mechanical pull request says which command generated it, so a reviewer can regenerate it rather than trusting the diff. Merge conflicts are the standing objection and the answer is to land the mechanical change quickly rather than to avoid it; one of these sitting open for a week is genuinely painful for everyone else.

One engineer per team per week handles escalations from support, ad-hoc questions from other teams and anything that arrives without warning. It is a different rotation from on-call, deliberately, because paging is about production being broken while this is about the constant low-grade demand for attention that used to land on whoever was most responsive and therefore most interrupted. Before the rotation, two people were absorbing most of it and both were quietly having their throughput halved without it appearing anywhere. The person on interrupt is expected to answer within the working day, not immediately, and to write down anything asked more than twice so that support can answer it themselves next time. That last part has slowly reduced the volume, which is the only real fix. Handover is a short thread on Friday listing what is still open, and the incoming person picks it up rather than the outgoing one finishing it over the weekend.

Nobody has more than two items in flight, and the second one is expected to be blocked rather than merely started. The limit is not enforced by the tracker; it is a norm that gets mentioned in planning when somebody's column is long. What it fixed was the specific pathology of a team where everything was ninety percent done and nothing shipped: five parallel items each waiting on review, each accumulating conflicts against the trunk, and each requiring its author to reload the context every time they returned to it. Finishing is worth more than starting, and the limit makes that concrete. The visible effect within a month was that review latency dropped, because someone blocked on their own work goes and reviews somebody else's rather than starting a third thing. The awkward case is genuinely long-running work with slow feedback loops, and the accommodation there is to split it into pieces that can each be finished, which is good practice anyway.

Quarterly planning ends with exactly three named bets per group, each with a sponsor and a written statement of what would count as it having worked. Three is a hard limit rather than a guideline. The previous format produced a list of eleven priorities, which everyone recognised at the time was not a list of priorities, and the effect was that mid-quarter arguments about what to drop had no answer because nothing had ever been ranked. With three, the answer to a new request is visibly either no or which of these three it displaces, and that conversation happens with the sponsor rather than by attrition. Work that is not one of the bets still happens — the ordinary flow of fixes, sustaining work and customer commitments continues untouched — and the bets are specifically the discretionary effort. The written success statement is the part most likely to be skipped and the part that makes the end-of-quarter review honest, because it was written before anyone knew how it would go.

A feature is not done when it merges. The checklist that has to be true before an item closes is short: it is behind a flag or fully rolled out, it emits at least one metric someone would notice moving, there is a panel showing that metric, and there is either an alert or an explicit note saying why one is not warranted. The last clause matters more than the alert itself, since forcing the question produces a considered answer either way. This came out of a run of features that shipped and then failed silently, in one case for six weeks, discovered when a customer asked why a thing had never worked. Nobody had done anything wrong; there was simply no way to tell the difference between working and broken from the outside. The checklist lives in the pull request template as four boxes, and the boxes are ticked by the author with the reviewer expected to spot-check the panel actually exists rather than taking the tick on trust.

If a defect is found in something shipped during the current or previous iteration, it goes to the front of the queue ahead of anything not yet started. The reasoning is about cost rather than about virtue: the author still has the context, the code is still fresh in review memory, and nobody has yet built on top of the broken behaviour. A bug in something six months old is a different animal and gets prioritised like any other work, on impact. This rule is one of the few places where prioritisation is not negotiable with product, and that was agreed explicitly rather than assumed. The boundary case that comes up regularly is a defect in something recent that is also low impact, and the convention there is to fix it anyway if it takes under an hour, on the grounds that the argument about whether to fix it costs more than the fix. Regressions in older code that were introduced recently count as recent for this purpose.

When support escalates a customer-affecting defect, it enters engineering with a named owner assigned that day and it displaces whatever that person was doing. Only support leads can escalate, and they are expected to have exhausted the workaround first, which keeps the volume at roughly two a week rather than at whatever the loudest account produces. The named owner is the important half. The previous arrangement put escalations into a shared queue where they were technically everyone's responsibility and practically nobody's, and the median time to a first response was measured in days, which support experienced as being ignored. What the customer is usually waiting for is an answer rather than a fix, and the owner's first obligation is to give support something to say within the same day. Escalations are reviewed monthly for patterns; a single account generating repeated escalations is usually a signal about a product gap rather than about a bug.

Anything in the backlog untouched for twelve months is closed automatically, with a comment saying it was closed for age and can be reopened by anyone in one click. The job runs on the first of the month and typically closes between forty and sixty tickets. The objection was raised and answered early: yes, some of those are good ideas, and no, they were not going to be done, because a backlog of nine hundred items is not a plan, it is a place where ideas go to avoid being decided about. Reopening happens perhaps twice a month and takes seconds, so nothing valuable is actually lost; what is lost is the false comfort of having written it down. Two categories are exempt by label, security findings and anything with a compliance date, and those are chased separately rather than being allowed to age quietly. The visible effect was that planning sessions got shorter, since the list people scroll through is now short enough to actually read.

Items carry a size of S, M, L or XL and there is no hours field in the tracker at all; the custom field was deleted rather than hidden, because a hidden field gets re-enabled by someone who thinks it was an oversight. The sizes mean roughly: S is under a day, M is a few days, L is most of an iteration, XL means we do not understand it yet and it must be broken down before it can be pulled. Two things killed hour estimates here. The first is that they were read as commitments by everyone outside the team no matter how carefully they were labelled, so a twelve-hour estimate became a promise about Thursday, and the ordinary variance of software work then looked like failure rather than like variance. The second is that they were not more accurate for the effort: a sample of forty completed items showed the hour figures off by a factor of two or more in over half of them, which is exactly the resolution a coarse size already gives you for a fraction of the argument. Sizing happens in one round in a thirty-minute session with the whole team, and disagreement of more than one size triggers a five-minute discussion, which is where the actual value is, since the disagreement almost always means two people are imagining different work. Forecasting is a separate question and does not use these numbers directly.

Any date communicated outside engineering is a quarter, never a week and never a day. Sales and support get told a feature is expected in the third quarter, and if they need something tighter the answer is a conversation with the sponsor rather than a firmer number from the team. The reason is that a specific date leaving the building comes back as a contract, and it comes back attached to whoever said it, months later, with all the context stripped away. Quarter granularity is honest about the resolution we actually have. It also gives an obvious escalation path: if a customer genuinely needs a date, that is a commitment decision with a sponsor and tradeoffs, and making it visible as such is better than an engineer being pressed into a guess in a call. Internally the team works in much finer increments, and nobody is pretending otherwise; the coarseness is about what crosses the boundary. The one exception is regulatory work with an externally fixed date, which is treated as a constraint rather than as a forecast.

The public roadmap has three columns and no dates. Now is what is being worked on, next is what starts when something finishes, later is everything we have decided is worth doing eventually. The version with a timeline was maintained for a year and was wrong within three weeks of every revision, and the maintenance of it consumed a meeting a fortnight. Worse, it invited planning against dates that were never real, so other teams built their own plans on top of ours and were surprised twice over. The three columns have a property the timeline lacked: moving something into now requires something else to leave, which makes the tradeoff explicit at the moment it is made. Items move backwards as well as forwards and that is treated as normal rather than as failure. The column contents are reviewed monthly with the sponsors, and the review is short because most of the argument is about a single boundary rather than about a whole chart.

Throughput numbers are visible per team and comparing them across teams is not done, and that has been said out loud in enough forums that it is understood rather than merely written. The numbers are not commensurable — the teams size differently, work on codebases of very different ages, and carry different amounts of operational load — so a comparison measures the sizing convention rather than the output. The deeper reason is what a comparison does to the numbers themselves: as soon as they are used to judge, they are gamed, sizes inflate, and the team loses its own planning instrument to get a better-looking chart. That has happened elsewhere to people here and the memory is vivid. Within a team, its own trend over time is genuinely useful for planning and is looked at every few iterations. Managers asking for a cross-team view are given cycle time distributions and a conversation instead, which usually turns out to be the thing they actually wanted.

An investigation is a spike, spikes are capped at two days, and the deliverable is a page of writing rather than working code. The cap is enforced socially by the fact that the spike is pulled as its own item with the timebox in its title, so exceeding it is visible at standup rather than being absorbed silently into a feature. What the two days are for is reducing the size of the thing that comes after: an XL that nobody can break down usually becomes an L and two Ms once someone has spent a day in the code. The written answer is the part people skip and the part that matters, because the alternative is that the knowledge lives in one person and the item is only breakable-down by them. A spike that ends with more uncertainty than it started with is a legitimate result and has happened twice, both times leading to the work being dropped, which is a very cheap way to not build something. The page is filed with the item it came from rather than in a separate space, so the next person to open that item finds it without knowing it exists.

Defects go into an iteration without a size on them. Sizing a bug means estimating how long it will take to find something you have not found yet, which is not an estimate but a guess dressed up, and the guesses were bad enough to distort the plan whenever a few landed in the same fortnight. Instead a fixed slice of each iteration is set aside for defect work and bugs are pulled from the top of the ranked list until it is used up. If a single bug is eating the whole slice, that is a signal to stop and talk about it rather than to have estimated better. The one thing that does get recorded is elapsed time once the bug is closed, which feeds nothing automatic but has been useful for arguing that a particular subsystem is expensive to own. The ranking of the defect list is done by support impact and is revisited weekly, which is more often than feature ranking because the inputs change faster.

When someone needs to know when a set of work will be finished, the answer comes from the historical distribution rather than from adding up estimates. `tools/forecast.py` takes the last ninety days of completed items, samples from that distribution, and reports the eighty-fifth percentile date for the remaining scope. It reports a range and refuses to print a single date, which has caused mild annoyance and is the entire point. The technique works because it captures everything the sum of estimates leaves out — the interruptions, the review latency, the half-week somebody was ill — and those are the things that actually determine when work finishes. It fails when the work is genuinely unlike anything in the sample, and the honest thing then is to say so rather than to produce a confident number from irrelevant history. The forecast is regenerated weekly, and watching the date move is more informative than any single run of it.

Iterations are two weeks long and begin on a Wednesday. The midweek start is not an aesthetic choice: with a Monday start, planning lands on the day with the most absences, the most weekend fallout and the most catching up, and the end of the iteration lands on a Friday afternoon, which is the worst possible time to be finishing anything given that deploys are restricted then anyway. Moving both to midweek made planning noticeably calmer and gave a natural two days at the end of the iteration for finishing work rather than for starting a weekend. The length was argued over more than the start day. One week produced too much ceremony relative to work; three weeks made the plan stale before it was finished. Two is unremarkable and works. The one thing that took adjusting to is that the iteration boundary no longer aligns with reporting periods, so the monthly numbers cut across iterations, which turned out not to matter to anyone.

Only the group's product lead can commit to a customer that something specific will be delivered, and that has been true since an account manager promised a bespoke export format in a renewal call that nobody in engineering heard about until the contract was signed. The rule is not about mistrust, it is about there being exactly one place where the tradeoff is visible, since every commitment displaces something and the person making it has to be able to say what. Engineers talking to customers is encouraged and happens constantly; what is off limits is a date or a feature promise, and the phrase people use is that they will take it back to the team. Commitments that are made get recorded in one document with the customer, the promise and the date, which is short and is reviewed at quarterly planning as a constraint on the bets rather than as an afterthought. Engineers who are asked directly are expected to say plainly that they cannot answer that, which sounds awkward written down and in practice takes one sentence and is never held against anyone.

Severity is assigned on customer impact as it stands at declaration time, never on cause and never on how alarming the graph looks. Sev1 means money or data: writes failing or landing wrong for any paying tenant, the checkout path down, or a suspected exposure of customer records. Sev2 is a whole capability unusable for a broad slice of accounts with no workaround. Sev3 is degraded but working, so elevated latency, a queue draining slowly, a report that is hours stale. Sev4 is a defect with a workaround and no clock on it, and it exists so small things stop being filed as Sev3 to borrow urgency. The declarer picks the opening number off the impact table in `runbooks/severity.md` and is expected to be wrong sometimes; when it is genuinely ambiguous the rule is to open at Sev2 and revise inside thirty minutes rather than debate it at the top of the incident. Anyone in the channel can raise a severity and it takes effect the moment they say it, while lowering one is the commander's call alone and gets a timeline entry saying what changed. Two inputs are excluded on purpose: the count of firing alerts, because a single bad probe lights up forty of them, and whether somebody senior is watching. The table exists because severity used to be whatever the loudest person felt, and the same failure was logged Sev1 in March and Sev3 in June, which made our trend data meaningless.

Any incident that closed at Sev1 or Sev2 owes a written postmortem within five business days, and the incident bot opens the document from `templates/postmortem.md` at close so nobody has to remember to start one. The commander owns delivery but rarely writes the whole thing; the convention is that whoever held a role during the incident writes their own slice of the timeline and the commander stitches it. Five days was picked because we tried two and got documents that were really just the channel transcript retyped, and we tried a fortnight and got documents that arrived after everyone had moved on and the details had gone soft. Overdue postmortems appear in the engineering weekly with the owner's name on them, which is the only enforcement there is and has been enough. A postmortem is considered done when the contributing factors section survives a read by someone who was not in the incident, not when the template is full. Sev3 incidents get a short note instead, a paragraph in the tracker saying what happened and whether anything needs following up, because forcing the full ritual on routine degradations was the fastest way to make people stop declaring them at all.

The pager routing rules key on the declared severity of the incident, not on which service raised it. Sev1 pages the primary immediately and pages the secondary in parallel rather than after a delay, because at Sev1 the fifteen minute wait we use elsewhere buys nothing. Sev2 pages the primary only, with the normal escalation ladder behind it. Sev3 does not page at all outside working hours; it lands in the team queue and gets picked up next morning. This was a deliberate move away from per-service routing, where every team had wired its own thresholds into its own alert rules and the result was that a Sev1 in a quiet service failed to wake anyone while a noisy service paged three people over a slow dashboard. The routing lives in one file, `oncall/routing.yaml`, and a service cannot override it; a service can only decide which of its alerts open an incident in the first place. The one exception is the payments path, which pages a named finance contact in addition to engineering whenever settlement is involved, because they hold relationships we cannot page our way into.

Every action item that comes out of an incident review leaves the room with a named person and a date, or it does not get written down at all. The rule sounds harsh and it is meant to be: for a long stretch our reviews produced lists of worthy improvements owned by a team, which is to say owned by nobody, and a year later we could point at the same contributing factor recurring in three separate incidents with an open unassigned ticket sitting next to each one. Ownership is personal even when the work is shared, because a person can be asked how it is going and a team cannot. Items that nobody will accept an owner for get deleted in the meeting rather than parked, and the deletion is recorded, because an honest empty list is more useful than a backlog that quietly signals we decided not to care. What actually changed after the rule went in was smaller lists. People stopped writing aspirational entries and started writing the two or three things that would genuinely have shortened the outage, which is what the review was for.

Vulnerability reports run on their own track and never enter the operational incident ladder. A finding from the bug bounty, a dependency advisory, or an internal review gets a CVSS base score, and the remediation clock comes from that score alone: critical is seven days, high is thirty, medium is ninety, low goes into the normal backlog. The two systems were merged once and it went badly in both directions. Reports of a stored cross-site scripting hole sat in an on-call queue for a week because nothing was on fire, and a routine dependency bump got declared an incident and pulled four people out of their afternoon for something with no exploit path. A finding converts into an operational incident only when there is evidence of exploitation or of data having actually moved, and at that point the incident is opened fresh with its own record and the finding is linked from it. The distinction people find useful: the incident ladder measures what is happening to customers right now, and the vulnerability score measures what could happen if someone bothered.

The review meeting has one written rule and the facilitator enforces it out loud: we describe what a person saw and what they did, and we never describe what they should have done. It is not politeness. The whole value of the meeting is that people volunteer the parts they are least proud of, the guess that turned out wrong, the command run against the wrong shell, the alert that was silenced last month by somebody who is sitting in the room. A single meeting where that got treated as a mistake to be corrected would cost us every future one, and we have watched that happen at other companies. The practical shape of it is that the facilitator rewrites questions in the moment. Why did you restart the wrong node becomes what did the console show you when you picked that node, and the answer is usually that both nodes looked identical in the list, which is a finding we can act on rather than a character trait we cannot. Managers attend as participants and do not chair. Nothing said in the room feeds a performance review, and that has been stated by the people who write those reviews rather than merely assumed.

The incident bot mints a record in the tracker the instant an incident opens, numbered sequentially as `INC-` plus a zero-padded counter that has never been reset and is now well past four thousand. The record is created before anyone knows whether the thing is real, and it is never deleted afterwards. Records that turn out to be a bad probe or a monitoring glitch are closed with a resolution of `not-an-incident` and stay in the sequence with a gap-free number. Two reasons we kept it strict. Gaps in a sequence are the first thing an auditor asks about, and the honest answer is much easier when there are none. And the false starts turn out to be data: the year we counted them, a third of the records closed as not-an-incident traced back to four alert rules, which is a much easier thing to fix than the vague sense that the pager is noisy. The number is what everything else keys on, so the channel name, the postmortem filename and the tracker record all carry the same id, and searching any one of them finds the others.

Each user-facing service publishes an availability objective and a monthly error budget, and burning that budget is what stops feature work, not a count of incidents. The gate is mechanical: if a service has consumed the whole month's budget, its team ships reliability work only until the window rolls, and the exemption for shipping anything else needs the head of engineering rather than the team lead. `slo/objectives.yaml` holds the targets, the burn is computed hourly from the same probes the pager uses, and the dashboard shows remaining budget in minutes rather than as a percentage, because minutes are a thing people can argue about concretely. What this replaced was a much worse conversation where a quarter with three noisy but harmless incidents felt worse than a quarter with one long silent one, and priorities followed the feeling. Budget burn does not care how many times the pager went off. A single ninety minute outage in a service with a tight objective can spend the month, and a week of flapping alerts that never actually broke a request spends nothing, which is the correct signal in both cases.
