Once a month somebody from the rotation walks the list of alerts that paged and marks each one as either having led to an action or not. An alert that fires repeatedly and never leads to anything is either deleted or demoted to a ticket, and the person doing the review has standing authority to do that without asking the owning team first, which was the change that made the exercise work at all. Before that, noisy alerts survived because deleting somebody else's alert felt rude and because every one of them had a story about the day it caught something. The ratio is the honest counter to that story. If an alert has woken people a dozen times and produced one action, the alert is not catching that failure, it is delaying it until someone happens to look. Teams can reinstate an alert they think was wrongly removed and a few have, but they have to say what the on-call person is supposed to do when it fires, and that requirement alone has killed more alerts than the review ever did.

The public status page goes up while we are still confused, and that is the intended order. The trigger is fifteen minutes of confirmed customer-visible impact, measured from the first alert rather than from the moment somebody thought to look, and the on-call engineer publishes at that mark whether or not there is a theory. Posting is not a statement that we understand the problem; it is a statement that we have seen it. The habit came out of the afternoon the ledger stalled for two hours while three of us chased a cause we wanted to be sure of before saying anything. By the time we published, support had taken over two hundred tickets, an integrator had posted a thread accusing us of dropping their webhooks silently, and two account managers had told customers it was on their side, because we had told them nothing and they had to say something. None of that was caused by the outage. All of it was caused by the gap. The other half of the reasoning is that silence is itself a claim. A green status page during a real outage reads to a customer as either we do not know or we are hiding it, and both are worse than an update that admits we are investigating. So the first post carries impact and a next-update time and nothing else, and the promised time is honoured even when the honest content is that there is still nothing new.

The status page runs on a third-party provider, on its own domain, under a separate cloud account with its own billing and its own DNS registrar login. Nothing about it touches our production estate, and that is the entire requirement. It was previously served from the marketing site behind our own edge, which worked perfectly until the afternoon a bad certificate rotation at the edge took down the marketing site and the status page together, so that for forty minutes the only channel we had for telling people the platform was broken was broken in exactly the same way and for exactly the same reason. The credentials for the provider are in the break-glass vault and are the one set of credentials the on-call engineer is expected to be able to reach from a phone with no laptop and no corporate network. Twice a year the disaster exercise includes publishing a test update from a phone, and both times we have run it we found something stale, once an expired seat and once a password nobody had migrated to the new vault.

The components listed on the public page are things a customer does, not things we run. Uploading documents, running a settlement, receiving webhooks, signing in. There is no component for the queue broker or the search cluster even though those are the pieces that actually fail, because a customer reading that our search cluster is degraded has to guess whether that means their reports are broken, and half of them guess wrong in each direction. Mapping happens on our side when we publish: the responder picks whichever workflows are affected, and the runbook carries the translation for the common failures so nobody is doing that reasoning under pressure. It also means our internal architecture is not on public display, which was a secondary benefit rather than a motive, though it stopped the recurring awkwardness of customers asking why we had renamed a component and whether that meant we had rewritten something. The list changes rarely and deliberately, and adding to it needs the same conversation as removing, because a long component list makes a partial outage look total at a glance.

Customers who subscribe to the status page get an email for two transitions only: a component moving into full outage, and the incident being marked resolved. Degraded performance updates and the running commentary in between are published to the page but do not send. We turned that down after an eleven hour incident where a responder was diligently posting progress every twenty minutes and every one of those posts mailed nine thousand subscribers, which generated more complaint volume than the degradation itself and taught a good number of people to unsubscribe permanently. The setting lives in the provider console under notification triggers, and the on-call engineer can override it for a single update when something genuinely needs pushing, such as a workaround customers should apply now. That override has been used four times in two years and each of those was the right call, which is roughly the rate we want it at. Integrators who want everything can subscribe to the webhook feed instead, which carries every update with no filtering.

Any maintenance that will visibly degrade or interrupt a customer workflow is posted to the status page at least seven days before the window opens, with the window given in UTC and in the two timezones where most of our volume sits. Seven days is not arbitrary. Our larger customers run their own change freezes and their own internal notices, and the feedback that produced the rule was from an operations team who needed five working days to tell their own users anything. The window itself is placed on a Tuesday or Wednesday and never on a Friday or the last two business days of a month, because month end is when settlement volume peaks and Friday evening is when we have the thinnest bench to recover with if the maintenance goes sideways. If the work finishes early we still leave the window open on the page until it expires, since customers plan around the stated end and quietly finishing early has caused a customer to start a batch into what they thought was a quiet period more than once.

Once an update is published it stays exactly as written. When something we said turns out to be wrong, the correction goes out as a new update saying what we now believe and that the earlier statement was mistaken, and the earlier statement stays visible above it. Nobody edits history to make the sequence read better. This came up the first time we published an impact estimate that turned out to be far too narrow, and the instinct in the room was to quietly widen the numbers in the original post so the record would be accurate. The argument that won was that a customer who read the original and made a decision on it deserves to see that the thing they read was what we said at the time, and that a status history which is silently improved after the fact is worth nothing as a record. The only permitted edits are typographical, and even those get avoided once an update is more than a few minutes old, because customers screenshot these posts and a mismatch between a screenshot and the live page costs more trust than a misspelling does.

The availability number in the enterprise agreements is computed from the third-party synthetic probe that hits `/health/deep` from four regions every thirty seconds, and not from how long incidents stayed open on the status page. The two are different instruments and they disagree routinely, which is fine and expected. A status page incident stays open through the tail while we watch for recurrence, and it often covers a degradation that the probe passes through happily. Conversely the probe has recorded minutes of failure that never became an incident because they resolved before anyone declared. Tying the contractual figure to the probe means the number is produced by something with no incentive and no judgement in it, which is what you want when a service credit hangs off it. Nobody on our side can edit the probe's history, and the vendor's report is what gets attached to the quarterly review. Support has standing instructions to answer uptime questions from the probe report rather than by counting status page entries, because customers who count entries always arrive at a worse number than the contract does and the conversation that follows is unpleasant for everyone.

There is an internal health view and it is not the public status page with more detail; it is a different thing built for a different reader. The internal view is per service, shows dependency edges, saturation and deploy markers, and is aimed at somebody trying to work out where a fault actually lives. The public page describes customer-visible workflows and is aimed at somebody deciding whether to file a ticket. We tried for a while to drive the public page automatically from internal signals and abandoned it, because the automation kept publishing outages that customers could not perceive and staying silent through ones they could, and each of those errors cost more credibility than the manual step cost effort. What survived from the experiment is the alerting link: when an internal component crosses the threshold that would matter to customers, the responder is prompted to consider publishing. Prompted, not committed. The decision to say something publicly stays with a person, because the machine has no way to know whether the thing it is watching is reaching anybody.

Marking an incident resolved on the public page requires thirty consecutive minutes of clean signal after the fix goes in, and the resolving update says what was wrong in one sentence and whether customers need to do anything, such as retry a batch or re-request a webhook. The waiting period exists because we twice published a resolution and then had to reopen within ten minutes, which reads much worse to a customer than a longer single incident and undermines every subsequent update we make during the same week. Thirty minutes was chosen as roughly two of our slowest recurring background cycles, so that anything which only fails on a periodic job has had a chance to fail again before we call it. The countdown is tracked by the incident bot and the responder is nudged when it completes rather than having to watch the clock. If the incident is reopened despite the wait, it reopens as the same incident with a new update rather than as a fresh entry, so the history stays honest about the fact that we called it too early.

Anybody with a login can declare, and that is the whole rule. Support agents, sales engineers, the office manager, a contractor in their first week: if you type `/incident declare` in Slack and describe what you are seeing in a sentence, an incident exists. No approval, no manager, no check that you are on the rotation, and no requirement that you know which service is at fault. The bot opens a channel, pages the primary, and the declaration stands until a commander closes it. Nobody but the commander can undo it, so there is no version of this where somebody senior arrives and tells the declarer they should not have. We arrived here the hard way. A support agent watched three customers report the same failed export within ten minutes, could not find anyone in the on-call tool who looked right, and spent the next fifty minutes asking in a team channel whether this was worth bothering someone about. It was. The postmortem's finding was not that she chose badly, it was that we had built a system where a person with the earliest evidence needed permission to use it. The second half of the rule matters as much as the first: declaring commits you to nothing. You are not the commander, you do not own the fix, and you can go back to your queue as soon as the primary acknowledges. False alarms are the expected cost and we have never once treated one as a mistake.

There is exactly one commander at a time and the transition is always spoken. The phrase people use is that they are taking command, and the person handing over says they are handing it over and names who has it, and neither of those is optional or implied by seniority. What this replaced was a common and dangerous state where two capable engineers were each quietly assuming the other was steering, so that nobody was tracking the whole picture and both were deep in their own theory. That happened twice in a month and the second time it cost us a good half hour of two people separately restarting things. Handoffs are most common at shift boundaries and after the first hour, when the person who has been holding it is tired and their judgement is worse than they think. Asking to be relieved carries no stigma at all and the people who do it most are the ones others trust most. The outgoing commander stays in the channel for a while afterwards to answer questions, but they answer as a participant, and if they start giving directions again somebody usually points out, cheerfully, that they handed it over.

Whoever is commanding is not also debugging. The commander asks questions, decides what gets tried next, keeps track of what has already been ruled out, and talks to everyone outside the channel. They do not have a shell open. This is the norm people push back on most, always with the same argument, which is that the commander is often the person who knows the failing system best and it is wasteful to sideline them. It is wasteful, and we do it anyway, because a person head-down in a log tail stops hearing the channel within about a minute. The night that settled it, the commander was also the only one who could read the replication state, and while they were reading it three people had drifted onto three separate theories and one had already restarted a node nobody had agreed to restart. If the deepest expert really is needed at the keyboard, the answer is to hand command to someone else and go be the expert. That trade is made openly and often, and it works far better than trying to hold both.

Any incident still open at the sixty minute mark gets a scribe, and the bot nudges the commander at that point rather than leaving it to memory. The scribe's job is narrow: keep a running list of what was observed, what was tried, what it changed, and what time each of those happened, posting it back into the channel every so often so everyone can see the same picture. They are not taking minutes of the conversation. The distinction that makes it useful is that a scribe records the state of the investigation, not the dialogue. This exists because long incidents develop amnesia. Around the ninety minute mark somebody invariably proposes an action that was already tried and rejected forty minutes earlier, and without a scribe the only defence is scrolling. It also makes handover survivable: a commander taking over at hour three reads one message instead of eight hundred. The scribe is usually somebody who joined late and has no context, which turns out to be a feature, because they ask what things mean and the answers end up in the record.

A page that is not acknowledged within ten minutes escalates to the secondary, and if that is also unacknowledged after another ten it goes to the team's manager and then to the head of engineering, with no further gaps. The tree is configured in the paging tool and cannot be edited by the person on call, which sounds distrustful and is actually a kindness: it removes the temptation to quietly extend your own grace period on a bad night. Ten minutes came from measuring actual acknowledgement times over a quarter. The median was under two minutes and the tail was almost entirely sleep, so anything longer than ten was overwhelmingly a phone that was face down or on silent rather than someone thinking. Managers in the tree are there to find a human, not to debug; the expectation on them is to start calling people. We have run the full tree to the top three times, and in two of those the primary's phone had installed an update overnight and reset its notification permissions, which is now a line in the onboarding checklist.

New joiners shadow the rotation for two full weeks before their name goes into it. Shadowing means they are paged alongside the primary, in parallel and for real, but nothing depends on them responding. They are expected to open the runbook, form an opinion, and say it in the channel, and the primary is expected to explain what they are doing and why while they do it. Two weeks is two on-call cycles here, which is enough to catch at least one genuine page for most people, and if somebody's shadow period passes with nothing happening at all we extend it rather than declare them ready on a technicality. The pattern we were fixing was people going straight onto the rotation after reading documentation, and then discovering during their first real page that the documentation described a system that had been reorganised eighteen months earlier. Shadowing surfaces that gap while somebody experienced is present. A useful side effect is that shadows file more runbook corrections than anyone else, because they are the only people reading the runbooks with fresh eyes and under real conditions.

When the failure is entirely a vendor's, we still run our own incident. It felt redundant the first few times and people asked why we were staffing a channel for something we could not fix, and the answer turned out to be that our customers do not have a relationship with our vendors, they have one with us, and everything downstream of the failure is still ours to manage. There are also almost always choices to make even when the fix is not ours: whether to fail open or closed, whether to queue and replay or reject, whether to switch a region, how long to wait before doing any of that. Those are decisions and they deserve a commander. The other reason is memory. Vendor status pages are frequently vaguer than the truth and disappear from history after a while, so our own record of what we actually saw, when it started, and how much it cost us is the only durable account, and it is what we take into the renewal conversation. Waiting for the vendor to confirm before we open anything just means the first thirty minutes are undocumented.

Incidents end with somebody saying so. The commander posts an all clear naming the time, what the resolving action was, and anything still being watched, and until that message exists the incident is running no matter how quiet the channel has gone. Before we made this explicit, incidents just faded out, and the failure mode was consistent: two or three people stayed up long after the thing was fixed because nobody had told them they could stop, while everyone else had drifted away an hour earlier assuming it was over. Both halves of that are bad, and the second half is worse, because it means the watching stops without a decision. The all clear also starts the clocks that hang off it, the follow-up window and the postmortem timer, so an incident with no all clear silently escapes both. The bot now asks the commander directly if a channel has been idle for forty-five minutes, which catches most of the ones that would otherwise have drifted, and the commander answers rather than the bot deciding.

Who is commanding, who is scribing, and who is talking to customers is written in the Slack channel topic and updated there as it changes. The tracker record has fields for all three and we leave them empty until the incident closes, at which point the bot copies the final state across. This looks like sloppiness and is deliberate. Under pressure, people look at the thing already in front of them, and every attempt at keeping the tracker current during an incident produced a tracker that was thirty minutes stale and therefore actively misleading, which is worse than blank. The topic is one click from the conversation and someone corrects it within seconds when it is wrong, because everyone can see it. A newcomer joining at hour two reads the topic and knows immediately who to direct a finding to instead of shouting it into the room. The rule people remember is that if the topic says you are commanding then you are commanding, regardless of what any other system claims, and the way to hand off is to change the topic and say so.

One person holds the comms role for the duration and every customer-facing word goes through them. They draft in a shared document seeded from `comms/templates/outage_update.md`, never in the incident channel, because text drafted in the channel is edited by six people at once and half-finished sentences escape. Two readers sign off before it leaves: the commander confirms the technical claims are things we actually know, and the duty support lead reads it as a customer would, routinely sending it back for using our internal names for things. The template forces four fields and forbids everything else. What a customer cannot currently do, in their words. Who is affected, as a boundary rather than a percentage. Whether anything they did is at risk, which is what they are all really asking. And the time of the next update. Cause is left out until confirmed, vendors are never named even when it is squarely their fault, and apology boilerplate is cut because it adds length without telling anyone anything. Once approved, that exact text goes to the status page, into the support reply macro and to the account managers in one action, and the single-source rule is the point of the whole arrangement. During the export outage, support told customers their data might be incomplete while the public update said nothing was lost, and untangling that publicly cost more than the outage did.

Nobody in an incident channel offers a customer money. Credit claims are handled afterwards by support against the contract, using the availability figure from the external probe report, and the calculation is the same for everyone whether they asked politely or escalated through their account manager. Agents can approve a credit up to twenty percent of one month's fee on their own; above that it goes to the finance queue. The reason this is kept out of the incident entirely is that we did it the other way once, and an engineer trying to calm an angry integrator at eleven at night promised a credit that did not match what the contract entitled them to, in a channel the customer could quote back at us. It was more generous than the contract, which made it harder rather than easier to walk back, and it set an expectation two other customers cited within a month. Support has a written response for the question when it comes up mid-outage, which acknowledges it and defers it, and it works because it is honest about the sequence rather than evasive about the money.

When an incident affects an identifiable subset rather than everyone, we generate the actual list of tenant ids from request logs with `tools/impact_query.py`, filtered on failed requests inside the incident window, and hand it to the account team. The list is produced from evidence, not from a guess about which accounts use the broken feature, and that distinction is the whole reason the tool exists. Estimating from feature usage was consistently wrong in both directions: it named accounts who had a retry succeed and never noticed anything, and it missed accounts whose integration hit the broken path from an unusual direction. Account managers were then confidently telling both groups the wrong thing. The query is deliberately conservative and includes anyone with a single failed request, because being told you might have been affected when you were not is a much cheaper error than the reverse. The list is internal and is never attached to anything public, since it is a list of customer names alongside a description of a failure.

The postmortem we publish to customers is written from scratch and is not a redacted copy of the internal one. It goes out within ten business days for any incident where customers lost data or lost more than an hour of service, and it passes legal review before publication, which is the only document in our incident process that does. The internal document exists to make us better and is full of things that would be misread outside the company, including honest speculation about contributing factors, names of individuals, and unflattering detail about systems we already know are weak. Redacting it produced something with holes that read as evasion. Writing separately produces something with a different job: what happened, what the impact was in terms a customer can check against their own records, what we changed, and by when. Legal review is not about softening language, and in practice their edits are mostly about avoiding statements that could be read as accepting liability for something we have not established. It has never once delayed publication past the window.

During a live incident the support queue stops running in arrival order and gets sorted by whether the customer is blocked. Somebody is watching the queue purely to reorder it, pulling out reports of stuck settlements and failed submissions ahead of questions about invoices and feature requests, and the ordinary response time targets are suspended for the duration and communicated as suspended. The reason for the explicit suspension is that agents were racing the clock on trivial tickets while blocked customers waited, not out of poor judgement but because the target was the thing being measured and nobody had told them it did not apply. Reordering has a second benefit that we did not anticipate. The person doing it is reading every inbound report as it lands and is usually the first to notice when the shape changes, that a second symptom has appeared or that reports have stopped, and passing that back into the incident channel has more than once been the earliest signal that a fix had landed.

Every ticket that turns out to be an instance of a live incident gets tagged with that incident's `INC-` id before it is answered. It takes an agent about three seconds and it buys two things that are hard to get any other way. First, the true customer-report count for the incident, which is the number that goes into the postmortem's impact section and is far more persuasive than a graph when arguing for prevention work, because it is people rather than percentiles. Second, a reliable way to go back afterwards and reply to everyone who wrote in, which we do once the resolving update is out. Before tagging, that follow-up was done by searching the queue for keywords and it missed people routinely, particularly anyone who described the failure in their own words rather than ours. The tag is also how we notice long tails: tickets carrying an incident id that arrive days after resolution almost always mean a customer whose retry never happened, which is a different problem needing a direct approach.

Announcement mail to a large list is sent from `notices.` on a separate subdomain with its own DKIM key and its own reputation, never from the domain the product uses for transactional mail such as receipts, password resets and webhook failure notices. The separation is about deliverability. A single bulk send to tens of thousands of addresses generates a spike of spam complaints and bounces no matter how welcome the content is, and if that lands on the transactional domain's reputation the next day's password reset emails start going to junk. We learned this on a routine product announcement and spent a fortnight recovering the sender score, during which support was walking people through checking their spam folders for reset links. The rule now is enforced by configuration rather than discipline: the bulk platform is only provisioned with the notices subdomain and physically cannot send as the transactional one. The two domains have separate warm-up histories and separate monitoring.

Scheduled marketing sends and outbound sequences are paused when a top-severity incident is open, and resumed by hand once it closes. The trigger is automatic, the resume is not, deliberately. What prompted it was a cheerful campaign about our reliability improvements landing in inboxes during the worst outage of that year, which several customers screenshotted and shared, and which turned an operational failure into a story about the company being either oblivious or dishonest. Neither was true; the send had been scheduled a fortnight earlier by somebody who was asleep. The pause covers campaign email, social posts from the company accounts and in-product announcement banners, all of which are scheduled ahead and none of which anyone thinks about during an incident. Manual resume exists because the right moment is a judgement call, and the wrong version of this is a system that unpauses everything the second an incident closes, sending the same cheerful message to people who spent the morning waiting for their exports to finish.

Customer notices are written in English and translated into the two locales where we have enough customers to justify a human translator on retainer. Everything else stays English, and we say so in the product rather than pretending otherwise. The temptation each time is to run the remaining languages through machine translation and cover everyone, and we tried it exactly once, on a notice about a data issue. The translated text of one sentence shifted the meaning from data may be delayed to data may be lost, which is the single most expensive translation error available to us, and it went out to every customer in that market before anyone who spoke the language read it. The rule that came out of it is that we do not publish text we cannot read. Where a market matters enough, the answer is to fund a translator properly rather than to approximate. The account managers covering the untranslated markets get the English text early enough to relay it themselves, which is slower and is the honest version of what was previously happening anyway.

Incident channels are archived seven days after the all clear and are never removed. They are exempt from the workspace retention rule that clears out dormant channels, the exemption is applied by the bot at creation time rather than remembered by a person later, and deleting one requires the security lead and a written legal reason. Only two have ever been deleted, both on advice about a dispute. The reason is that the channel is the primary record. The postmortem is a summary written afterwards by people who already know how it ended, and it inevitably smooths over the hour where everyone believed the wrong thing, which is usually the most instructive hour. The transcript preserves what was actually visible at each point, in what order, and how long it took someone to notice the thing that turned out to matter. You cannot reconstruct that from a document written in hindsight. The habit came from losing them. Somebody tidying the workspace deleted several dozen archived channels one quiet afternoon, entirely reasonably by the standards of the time, and four months later we hit the same replication fault. The postmortem said what we fixed but not how we found it, the engineers involved had left, and we spent two days redoing a diagnosis already done once. Searching old incident channels is now a normal first step, and it works because the search index still has them.

Channels are named `inc-` followed by the tracker id and nothing else, no description, no date, no service name, and the bot creates them so nobody gets a choice. Descriptive names were the obvious idea and they failed in a specific way: the name is chosen in the first two minutes when the understanding is worst, so we ended up with channels called after a symptom that turned out to be a side effect, and a search for the actual cause found nothing because the word never appeared in a title. Renaming afterwards breaks every link anyone has already pasted into a document or a ticket. A pure identifier ages well because it never has to be right about anything. The human-readable title lives in the channel topic, where it gets corrected freely as understanding improves and where being wrong for an hour costs nothing. People who want to find an incident by subject search the tracker, which is the system built for that, and then jump to the channel by id.

A project channel with no message for ninety days is archived automatically, and archived channels with no activity for a further year are removed entirely. This is a workspace hygiene policy rather than a legal one. We reached the point where searching for anything returned five plausible channels for the same project, four of them abandoned at different stages, and people were reading a stale conversation and acting on a decision that had been reversed in a channel they never found. Volume was the whole problem, so the policy targets volume. A channel that anyone actually wants to keep can be pinned as permanent by its owner in a single click, and roughly forty are. The nudge before archival goes to whoever created the channel and to anyone who posted in the last month, which catches the cases where the work is real but seasonal, such as the annual audit channels that go quiet for three quarters at a time. Nobody has complained about losing something they wanted since the reminder was added.

If two people work something out in a direct message or on a call during an incident, one of them pastes the conclusion back into the channel before acting on it. Not the whole conversation, just what was decided and why. This is a norm rather than a rule and it is enforced by people asking, cheerfully and constantly, where a decision came from when it appears without warning. Side channels are not the problem; they are unavoidable and often faster. The problem is a channel where the visible conversation stops making sense because three of the participants are also talking somewhere else, so that anybody joining reads a discussion that jumps to a conclusion with no path to it. That reader is usually the person who arrives with fresh energy at hour two, and they end up asking questions that were answered privately, which costs the tired people exactly the attention they have least of. The version that stuck is short: if you learned it somewhere else, say it here.

Postmortems are wiki pages under `/engineering/incidents/`, one per incident, and the tracker holds only a link. The tracker is good at workflow and bad at documents: comment threads interleave with status changes, formatting is poor, tables are painful, and there is no sensible way to revise a paragraph two weeks later when somebody works out what really happened. The wiki is bad at workflow and good at documents, so we let each do its job. Every page carries the incident id in its title, which is what makes cross-referencing work at all and is why the id gets typed into three systems. The follow-up actions are the deliberate exception and live in the tracker as real tickets rather than as a list at the bottom of the wiki page, because a list inside a document is not work and nobody's board shows it. The page links out to those tickets and their status renders inline, so the document stays readable as a record while the work stays visible where work is tracked.

Once an incident is open, the bot repoints the relevant alert webhooks so firing and resolving notifications land in the incident channel instead of the owning team's channel, and repoints them back at close. The mechanism is a routing key the alert manager reads at delivery time, so no alert definitions change and nothing needs redeploying. Two reasons. Alert traffic during a real incident is heavy enough to bury the team channel for everyone not involved, and more importantly the resolve notifications are evidence: seeing the exact moment a probe recovered, in line with the conversation, is far more useful than reading it later on a graph with a different clock on it. Before this, people were screenshotting alert notifications from one channel into another all night, badly and with gaps. The repointing covers only alerts that map to the affected services, which the bot resolves from the service tags on the incident record, so unrelated pages still reach their own teams normally.

On the all clear, the bot posts one message collecting the mechanical facts it already knows: declaration time, who held each role and when they took it, every deploy and feature flag change inside the window, the alerts that fired and when they cleared, and total duration. It makes no attempt to describe what happened. The summary exists because those facts were previously reconstructed by hand for every postmortem, badly, from four systems with slightly different clocks, and the reconstruction usually happened days later when the person doing it was guessing at timestamps. The machine has all of it accurately and instantly. What the machine cannot supply is the part that matters, which is what people believed at each moment and why they made the choices they did, and the template makes that separation explicit so nobody mistakes a complete timeline for a complete account. The message is also the thing people quote from most when writing up, because copying a line out of it is easier than looking anything up.

Inside an incident channel customers are referred to by account identifier rather than by company name, and nobody pastes in a raw record from a customer's data. This is not secrecy for its own sake. Incident channels are joined freely by people from across the company during a live event, including folks with no reason to know which named customer is having a bad day, and a channel where a name appears next to a description of failed payments is a thing that gets screenshotted and shared with the best of intentions. Referring to an id keeps the conversation just as precise while keeping it useful to a much wider group without a privacy review. Anyone who needs the mapping can look it up in the admin tool, which records that they did. The rule took a while to stick because using the name is natural and faster, and what made it stick was the account team asking us to, after a customer saw their own name in a screenshot pasted into a shared channel.

Every incident channel is open to the whole company and nobody is invited, they just come. Support, account managers, people from finance when money is involved, and quite often somebody with no involvement at all who is curious and learns something. The default was closed once, with the commander adding people as needed, and that produced a predictable failure: the people who could have answered a question fastest did not know the question was being asked, because the person asking did not know they existed. Openness has one cost, which is spectators asking well-meaning questions that pull the commander's attention, and the norm that handles it is that anyone who is not doing a job in the channel reads and does not ask. That works because it is said out loud rather than implied, and because the commander is allowed to say it again in the moment without it being rude. The channel that must stay small is a security investigation, and those are handled entirely differently.

A password change bumps one integer. Every user row carries `token_epoch`, every refresh token is minted with the epoch current at the time, and the auth service compares the two on every refresh and rejects anything stale. Changing or resetting a password increments that column in the same transaction that writes the new hash, so the instant the commit lands, every refresh token in existence for the account is dead. No fan-out, no session table walk, no cross-region delete, nothing to go wrong halfway. Access tokens are the deliberate exception. They are signed, self-contained and live for ten minutes, and we do not revoke them individually, so a stolen access token keeps working for up to ten minutes after the password changes. That window was argued over and accepted: making access tokens checkable per request puts a lookup on the hot path for every call, and ten minutes of residual access is a cost we can name. The device performing the change is re-issued a fresh pair before the response returns, so the person changing their password is not thrown out of the tab they are sitting in, which is the part everyone assumes is broken. The old design deleted rows from a `sessions` table, and after a takeover we found the attacker still signed in eleven days after the victim's reset, because the delete had run against one region's replica and quietly succeeded.

Services verify tokens locally against the signing keys published at `/.well-known/jwks.json`, which they cache for an hour and refetch on an unknown key id. Signing keys rotate every thirty days, and the retiring key stays in the published set for a further two days after it stops being used to sign anything, which is comfortably longer than any token's lifetime. That overlap is the entire trick and it means a rotation is invisible: nothing has to restart, no service needs the new key ahead of time, and there is no coordinated moment where a stale cache produces a wave of rejections. We got that wrong the first time by removing the old key at the moment the new one went live, and every service holding a warm cache started failing verification for a few minutes until it refetched. Verification is local by design so that an auth service outage degrades sign-in rather than taking down every already-authenticated request in the platform, which was the failure mode of the older setup where each service phoned home to validate.

A reset link carries a random token stored as a hash in `password_reset_tokens`, valid for fifteen minutes, and consumed on first successful use so a second click gets the expired page rather than a second chance. Requesting a new link invalidates any outstanding one for that account, which closes a small hole where a user who requested three links in frustration left two live tokens sitting in their mailbox indefinitely. Fifteen minutes is short and we get occasional complaints from people who start a reset, get distracted, and come back to a dead link, and the trade was made knowingly because reset mail sits in inboxes forever and inboxes are the thing most likely to be compromised in the first place. The response to a reset request is identical whether or not the address belongs to an account, including the timing, so the endpoint cannot be used to enumerate customers. The link lands on a page that never reflects the address back, since doing so turns a stolen link into a confirmation of who it belongs to.

Passwords are stored as Argon2id with the parameters recorded alongside the hash, and on every successful sign-in the verifier checks whether those parameters match the current settings in `auth/hashing.toml`. If they do not, the plaintext is in hand at that exact moment, so it rehashes and writes the upgraded value before responding. That is the only opportunity we will ever get, since we cannot rehash offline without the password. The mechanism exists so raising cost parameters is a normal change rather than a migration project. When we moved off the older scheme, active accounts converted themselves within a fortnight and the long tail was dormant accounts, which were left alone deliberately rather than being forced through a reset. Verification still accepts the legacy format and always will, because the alternative is locking out a customer who returns after two years. The parameters were tuned against real login latency on the smallest instance class we run, aiming just under a quarter of a second, which is where the cost stops being noticeable to a person signing in.

The security section of account settings shows a list of currently signed-in devices, each with a browser and platform description, an approximate city derived from the address, and a last-seen time. It shows a city rather than an address because the address is meaningless to almost everyone and actively misleading to the rest, since a corporate proxy or a mobile carrier will place someone hundreds of miles from where they are. We watched support handle a run of alarmed tickets from customers who read a raw address, looked it up, and concluded their account had been accessed from another country, when the truth was their employer's egress. Showing a city with a note that it is approximate cut those to almost nothing without hiding anything real, since a genuinely foreign sign-in still shows as a foreign city. The current device is labelled as such at the top of the list, because otherwise the first question every customer asks support is which entry is them.

Adding or removing a second factor sends a notification to the account address and to any recovery address on file, and it deliberately leaves existing signed-in sessions alone. The argument for ending them is obvious and we considered it seriously. What decided it was watching real enrolment behaviour: people add a factor on a laptop, then a phone, then swap a lost key for a new one, often three changes in one afternoon, and a policy that ends every session on each change means a person hardening their account is punished with repeated sign-ins across every device they own. That is precisely the friction that makes people give up halfway and end up in a worse state than when they started. The notification is the control that matters, because the threat is somebody else enrolling a factor, and the person who needs to know within seconds is the account owner. The mail says which factor changed and offers a direct path to lock the account, which is the action a victim actually needs and which does end everything.

Refresh tokens are single use. Every refresh returns a new one and retires the old, and each token records the id of the token it replaced, forming a chain we call a family. Presenting a refresh token that has already been redeemed is treated as theft rather than as a mistake: the entire family is revoked immediately, the account is flagged, and the user is sent back to sign-in. The logic assumes that if a token was redeemed twice, either the legitimate holder or an attacker has a copy, and there is no way from the server to tell which, so the safe move is to end both. This does produce occasional false positives, almost all from a client that retried a network timeout without knowing the first attempt had actually succeeded, and the fix was in the client rather than in loosening the rule. The retired token ids stay in `refresh_tokens` for thirty days after expiry precisely so a replay can be recognised as a replay instead of as an unknown token, which would otherwise be indistinguishable from ordinary garbage.

No agent can set or clear a password for a customer, and no amount of escalation produces someone who can, because the capability does not exist in the admin tool. What an agent can do is trigger the standard reset mail to the address already on file, which helps the honest caller and does nothing for anyone else. Changing the address on file is a separate flow that requires confirmation from the old address and a wait, and it is the flow attackers actually target. This was built after a run of calls with the same shape: a caller who knew the account name, the company, and a recent invoice number, who was locked out before an urgent deadline, and who was extremely persuasive about it. Every one of those facts is available to somebody who has read one email thread. The policy protects agents more than it protects the system, since an agent under pressure from a plausible and upset caller should not be the last line of defence, and the honest answer of I am not able to do that is much easier to give when it is literally true.

The stay signed in option issues a long-lived credential with a hard ceiling of thirty days from issue, and that ceiling does not move no matter how actively the person uses the product. Sliding expiry was the original behaviour and it meant a daily user was effectively signed in forever, which turned a convenience feature into a permanent credential sitting in a browser profile that may well be on a shared machine. At the cap the person signs in again and gets a fresh thirty days, which is a small annoyance once a month and is the point. The cookie is scoped to the app hostname, marked secure and http-only with strict same-site, and is never accepted for anything in the admin surface, which requires an ordinary interactive sign-in every time regardless of what the browser is holding. On a shared-device sign-out the cookie is cleared server side as well as in the browser, because clearing only the browser copy leaves a usable credential behind for anyone who can read the profile directory.

Nothing internal keeps its own user table. Every tool we run for ourselves sits behind the identity-aware proxy and authenticates through the company identity provider, and a service cannot get a record in `internal.zone` until it is registered with the proxy, which is what makes the rule stick rather than good intentions. Three reasons, in the order they actually mattered. First, revocation has to be one action. When somebody leaves, disabling their identity account must end their access to everything, and that is only true if nothing has a separate password. We learned this concretely: an engineer left in the spring, and during an access review that autumn we found their local account still active on a self-hosted dashboard that could query the production read replica, because that tool had been stood up with its own login two years earlier and had never appeared on anyone's list. Nobody had done anything wrong; the tool simply was not in the set of things offboarding knew about. Second, strong authentication gets implemented once, properly, at the identity provider, instead of ten tools each doing a mediocre version. Third, one access log covering everything, which is what an auditor asks for and what an investigation needs. The cost is real and we took it knowingly: an identity provider outage locks us out of our own tooling, which has happened twice.

The corporate VPN was decommissioned eighteen months ago and nothing sits on a private network perimeter any more. Access decisions now combine identity with device state, and the proxy requires a managed device reporting disk encryption on, screen lock under five minutes, and an operating system within two releases of current. The VPN was doing two jobs badly. It was granting broad network reach to anyone who connected, so a compromised laptop on the VPN could reach far more than the person using it ever needed, and it was a permanent capacity and support burden, being the single thing most likely to be blamed whenever anything was slow. Posture checks replace only the second half of what it did, the part about the machine being trustworthy, and identity handles the rest. What surprised us during the migration is how much was still reachable purely by being on the network, including three internal services with no authentication at all that had been quietly relying on the perimeter since before anyone currently here joined.

Two accounts exist that do not depend on the identity provider, one for the cloud root organisation and one for the proxy itself. Their credentials are split across sealed envelopes in two physical safes in different offices, and using either one pages the security lead and the head of engineering immediately and unconditionally, from a monitor that watches the provider's own audit stream rather than anything we control. They are tested twice a year in a scheduled exercise and rotated afterwards regardless of whether anything went wrong, because a credential that has been read aloud in a test is a credential that has been disclosed. The temptation each time is to keep a copy somewhere convenient, which would dissolve the entire control, so the exercise deliberately includes the inconvenience of travelling to the safe. Both times we have run it we found something rotten, once a recovery code that no longer matched after a provider migration and once an envelope that had been opened and resealed by somebody who never told anyone.

Every account created for somebody outside the company carries an expiry date set at creation, capped at ninety days, and it is a required field with no default and no option for none. On the date, the account disables itself. Extending is easy and takes a minute, and the person's sponsor gets a reminder a week out and again the day before, so nobody is surprised. The design principle is that the safe state has to be the one that happens when everyone is busy and nobody does anything, and the old arrangement had exactly the opposite shape, requiring somebody to remember to remove an account after an engagement ended, which is the moment they and everyone else stop thinking about that engagement at all. Ninety days is short enough that a forgotten account cannot linger and long enough that the average engagement needs one renewal rather than five. The reminders go to the sponsor rather than to the contractor, since only the sponsor knows whether the work is still happening.

Once a quarter every group in the identity provider is exported and sent to its owner, who confirms each member should still be there. The owner is a named person, never a team, and unanswered reviews escalate to their manager and then stop being polite. The exercise is boring and it consistently finds things: people who changed teams and kept the old access alongside the new, groups that accumulated members for a project that ended, and at least once a group whose owner had themselves left. What makes it work is that the default on no response is removal rather than retention. When the default was retention, reviews were approved wholesale in about the time it takes to click once, which produced a signed record that everything was fine and no actual scrutiny at all. Flipping the default made owners read the list, because now ignoring it breaks something for their own team. The review covers group membership only; what a group can reach is a separate question and is not decided in this exercise.

Anyone whose role touches production gets two hardware security keys, one to carry and one to leave somewhere safe, and app-based codes are not accepted for those accounts at all. Two keys rather than one because the failure everyone predicted was a lost key at the worst moment, and a spare in a drawer converts that from an emergency into an inconvenience. Codes from an authenticator app were dropped after a phishing exercise in which a convincing sign-in page collected a code and replayed it inside its validity window against nine people out of forty, none of whom did anything careless. A hardware key checks the origin as part of the protocol, so the same attack simply does not work, and that property is the entire reason for the cost and the shipping logistics. Enrolment happens on the first day, in person where possible, and the second key is registered at the same time because the account of somebody who has left the building with one key is much harder to fix later.

The proxy forwards identity to the service behind it in a signed assertion header, and every service verifies the signature against the proxy's public key rather than trusting the header's presence. This looks like belt and braces and it is not. A header can be set by anything that can reach the service's port, and services get reached from unexpected places: a debugging port left open, another service in the same cluster, a misconfigured ingress that bypasses the proxy for one path. If the only check is that the header exists, all of those become full authentication bypasses, and one of them was, on an internal tool that a health-check route had accidentally exposed. Verification is three lines in the shared middleware and the shared middleware is how services get it, so nobody implements it themselves. Assertions carry a short expiry and the service checks it, which stops a captured header from being replayed later from somewhere else.

A handful of vendors either do not offer federated sign-in at all or charge an extra tier for it that is out of proportion to what we spend with them. For those, everybody gets their own seat under their own work address, and shared team logins are not permitted no matter how much cheaper they would be. The point being protected is attribution. A shared login means a change in a vendor console is an event with no person attached, and the first time that mattered we spent an afternoon trying to work out who had changed a billing threshold, with the only honest answer being any of eleven people. Credentials for those seats live in the password manager under a group vault, they are unique per person, and removing somebody is a task on the offboarding list because there is no central switch that covers them. That manual step is exactly the sort of thing that gets forgotten, which is the argument we bring back to the vendor at every renewal.

A termination recorded in the HR system emits an event, and the provisioning service acts on it directly, disabling the identity account and closing out group memberships without waiting for anyone to file anything. The same pipeline handles joiners and, importantly, movers, which is the case checklists always miss because nobody feels that a person changing teams needs offboarding. The old process was a document with boxes to tick, owned by whichever manager remembered, and it worked well for planned departures and poorly for everything else. Departures that happen suddenly are precisely the ones where the manager is busy with something else and the checklist is opened two days later. The rule now is that the HR record is the trigger of record, so making a change means making it there, and there is no side door for a manager who wants access removed immediately without telling the people whose job that is. The one thing still done by hand is collecting hardware, because no system knows where a laptop physically is.

Internal authorization is a small fixed vocabulary of named roles bound to a subject and a resource, held in `role_bindings`, and we rejected the fine-grained scope model on purpose. There are eleven roles, they are named for jobs people actually have, and adding a twelfth is a design conversation rather than a pull request. The system we replaced granted individual capability strings, and the count reached something over three hundred before anyone counted. Two questions killed it. Nobody could answer what a given person could do, because the answer was a set of three hundred booleans with no shape to it, and nobody could answer who is able to issue a refund, because that required scanning every grant in the database and reasoning about which combinations added up. Access review had become a person clicking approve on a list they could not possibly evaluate, which is worse than no review because it produces a record saying somebody checked. Roles give up precision and buy comprehensibility. A support agent gets slightly more than the strict minimum for their work, and we accept that in exchange for a model where a manager can look at a person's roles and understand them in a few seconds. The public API is unaffected and still issues scoped tokens, because a third-party integration is a different kind of subject with a different question attached.

Tokens issued to third-party integrations carry scopes drawn from a closed list of nineteen strings, documented in the public reference, and customers cannot define their own. Requests for a custom scope come in every few months, usually from an integrator who wants read access to one field of one endpoint, and the answer is always no. A per-customer scope is a permanent bespoke branch in the authorization path that nobody outside that account will ever exercise and everybody will have to reason about forever, and the second one of those makes the first harder to remove. The list grows when a genuine new capability appears in the product, at which point it grows for everyone at once and gets documented as part of the release. Scope names are stable and never repurposed even when the underlying feature is renamed, since a token minted two years ago is still in use somewhere and the string in it must keep meaning what the integrator was told it meant.

Authorization happens in a single middleware that runs before any handler, driven by a declarative table mapping route patterns to requirements, and a route with no entry in that table returns 403 rather than falling through. That last part is the important one. The previous arrangement had each handler calling a check itself, which worked for every handler where somebody remembered, and the failure was always the same shape: a new endpoint added in a hurry, usually an internal-sounding one for a report or an export, with no check at all. We found three of those in a single sweep and one had been live for over a year. Centralising it means the question moves from did the author remember to is the route in the table, and a missing entry is loud and immediate rather than silent and permissive. Handlers can still make finer decisions on top, and some do for row-level rules, but they are refining a decision that has already been made rather than being the only thing standing between a caller and the data.

Any binding above the baseline tier carries an expiry stamped at ninety days when it is created, and the grant simply stops working on that date. Baseline roles that everybody needs to do their job are permanent; the ones that read customer records, move money, or touch production configuration are not. Renewal is a click by the grant's owner and takes seconds, and the reminder goes out a week ahead. The reason for expiry rather than review is that we had reviews and they did not shrink anything. People accumulate elevated access for a project, a migration, an incident, and it is nobody's job to notice afterwards, least of all the person holding it. Expiry makes accumulation cost effort continuously instead of once. The measurable outcome was that the count of people holding the billing administrator role dropped by more than half in the first two cycles, without a single conversation about whether anyone still needed it, because most of them simply let it lapse.

When an internal user is refused, the message says which role would have allowed the action and who owns granting it, rather than a bare not authorised. The instinct is that this leaks information, and for anything customer-facing it would, which is why external responses stay deliberately uninformative. Internally the calculus is reversed. The person being refused already knows the feature exists because they are looking at it, and the cost of a vague denial is a support ticket, a guess, and frequently somebody being granted far more access than they needed because whoever helped them could not tell which specific thing was missing and reached for the biggest role available. Naming the requirement turns a mystery into a request. The measurable change after we shipped it was in the shape of grants rather than their number: people started asking for the narrow role by name, because they had been told what it was called, and the broad catch-all role stopped being the default answer to any access problem.

There are no negative grants. Everything a subject holds adds capability and nothing subtracts it, so working out whether an action is allowed means asking whether anything permits it and stopping at the first yes. Explicit denials were proposed twice, both times for a real problem, which was wanting somebody to have almost all of a role except one dangerous part. They were rejected both times because evaluation order becomes load-bearing the moment they exist, and every system anyone in the room had worked with that supported denials had eventually produced an outcome nobody could explain without tracing the evaluator. Debugging an access question at speed matters more to us than expressing an unusual case elegantly. The answer to the real problem is to split the role so the dangerous part stands alone and is granted separately, which is more work up front and leaves you with something a person can read. It also forces the conversation about what is actually dangerous, which the denial approach lets you skip.

Which tenant's data you can see is not an authorization question and is never expressed as a grant. Every request runs inside a session that has set the tenant, and the data access layer appends the tenant predicate to every query itself, with a lint rule that fails the build on any raw SQL against a tenant-scoped table that does not go through it. The separation exists because the two concerns fail differently. Getting authorization wrong means somebody in the company sees something they should not, which is bad. Getting tenant scoping wrong means one customer sees another customer's data, which is the worst thing that can happen to us. Handling the second with the same mechanism as the first would mean the worst outcome depends on a role binding being correct. Instead it depends on a predicate that is added mechanically and cannot be forgotten, and the audit for it is a scan of the code rather than a scan of grants. The cross-tenant reporting job is the single exception and runs as a separate identity against a replica.

The roles designed for people are not grantable to a service identity, and the check refuses at grant time rather than failing later. Services get their own narrow role definitions, typically one per service, listing exactly the operations that service performs. The shortcut this prevents is well worn: a batch job needs to read something a support agent can read, so somebody gives the job the support role, and now a service with no session, no second factor and credentials sitting in a config store holds everything a support agent holds, including the parts nobody thought about. We found a reporting job holding the operations role in an audit, granted years earlier for one query it no longer ran. Service roles are also reviewed differently because their scope is knowable: you can read the service's code and enumerate what it calls, which is impossible for a person. When a service genuinely needs a new capability the answer is to extend its own role by one operation, which is a small readable change.

What each role means lives in `authz/roles.yaml` in the application repository and changes through the ordinary pull request path. The admin interface grants and revokes roles for people, which is a daily operational act, but it cannot alter what a role permits. Keeping definitions in the repository buys history that actually explains itself: every change to a role's meaning has a diff, an author, a date and a linked ticket, so the question of when the support role gained the ability to read payment metadata has an answer with a reason attached. In the previous system that was a row edit in a database with a timestamp and nothing else, and reconstructing intent afterwards was guesswork. There is also a genuine safety property, since a change to a definition affects everyone holding that role at once, which is a different magnitude of act from granting one person one role, and it deserves to move at the pace of a deploy rather than at the pace of a click.

Every machine client has two secret slots and rotation always overlaps them. The procedure is three staged commands, `ops/rotate_client_secret.sh --client <id> --stage mint`, then `--stage cutover`, then `--stage retire`, and both secrets authenticate successfully for the whole span between the first and the last. Mint writes a new secret into the empty slot and publishes it to the consumer's secret store. Cutover flips the consumer to the new value and restarts or reloads it. Retire clears the old slot, and it refuses to run until the usage counter for the old secret has been zero for twenty-four hours, which is what catches the consumer you forgot about. The cadence is ninety days, driven by a scheduled job that opens a ticket against the owning team, backed by a hard expiry at one hundred and twenty days: a secret older than that stops authenticating. That ceiling exists so a skipped rotation fails inside a known window with a ticket already open, rather than never happening at all, which is what used to occur. Before the two-slot design a rotation was a single atomic swap, and the night we swapped a partner's credential their nightly ingest failed from two in the morning until they woke up, because the new value could not reach their side until somebody there was awake to install it. Workloads that can federate hold no static secret and are outside this entirely.

A key created by a person carries that person's roles at the time of every request rather than a frozen copy from when it was issued, and disabling their identity account kills every key they hold in the same instant. Keys live in `api_keys` with the owner id as a non-null foreign key, so there is no way to create an ownerless one. This closes the gap that made personal keys dangerous: somebody leaves, their account is disabled correctly, and a key they generated for a script two years ago keeps working with the access they had on their last day. We found four of those during the audit that prompted the change, one of them still running a nightly job in a repository nobody maintained. The inherited-access half also matters. A key issued while somebody held an elevated role loses that capability when the role lapses, which means access reviews on people are automatically access reviews on their keys. Anything that must outlive a person is a service client instead, and the tooling says so when you try.

Outbound webhooks carry a header holding a timestamp and an HMAC over the timestamp joined to the raw request body, and receivers are told to reject anything whose timestamp is more than five minutes from their own clock. The timestamp is inside the signed material rather than beside it, which is the part integrators most often get wrong when they write their own verifier: signing only the body means a captured delivery can be replayed forever. Five minutes is generous enough to survive ordinary clock drift on a receiver that is not running time sync properly, which in our experience is a surprising share of them, and short enough to make replay impractical. Verification must compare in constant time, and the sample code in the documentation does, because the first three integrations we reviewed had all written a plain equality check. Retries reuse the original timestamp and signature rather than re-signing, so a delivery retried outside the window is correctly refused instead of arriving as something that looks fresh.

The build system exchanges its signed job token for short-lived cloud credentials through the identity provider's federation endpoint, and the trust policy pins the repository and the branch, so a workflow on a fork or a feature branch cannot assume the deploy role even with a valid token. Credentials last fifteen minutes and never touch a variable store. Before this there was a long-lived access key sitting in the CI settings, shared by every pipeline in the organisation, which meant every contributor with the ability to add a workflow file effectively held production deploy access, and the key was too frightening to change because nobody knew everything that used it. That fear is the real cost of a shared static credential, more than the exposure itself. The pinning is worth stating explicitly because a trust policy that only checks the provider and not the repository is the common misconfiguration, and it grants anyone on that provider the ability to assume your role.

A pre-receive hook scans every push against a pattern set and rejects the whole push when it matches a credential shape we recognise, so the commit never lands on the server at all. Anything that gets past the hook and is found later by the scheduled scan is treated as compromised immediately: the credential is revoked within minutes by automation, before anyone investigates whether the repository was private or whether the value was real. That ordering is the entire point and it was contested. Investigating first feels responsible and takes hours, during which the credential is still valid and, if the repository was ever public even briefly, already harvested. Revoking first costs an outage of one integration and an apology, which is recoverable. We have revoked four credentials this way and two of them turned out to be test values, which is a rate we are content with. Cleaning history afterwards is done, but as housekeeping rather than as remediation, because a value that has been pushed is disclosed regardless of what the history looks like later.

Every credential that exists for a machine has a person's name attached to it, not a team name, and creating one without an owner is not possible in the tooling. Ownership means answering two questions when they come up: what breaks if this stops working, and can it be retired. Team ownership sounds more robust and is in practice how credentials become orphaned, because a team is not a thing that reads a message and does something about it, and teams get reorganised while credentials do not. When somebody leaves, their credentials appear on a list that must be reassigned before the offboarding is closed, which is the moment the honest conversation about whether anything still needs them tends to happen. A good number get deleted right there. The inventory started as a spreadsheet compiled by hand and everyone agreed it would be out of date within a month, which it was, but even a stale list turned out to be enormously better than the previous state of nobody being able to name what existed.

A partner integrating with us receives distinct client identities for sandbox and for production, never one identity valid in both. This is more setup work for them and they say so, and we hold the line because of what happens otherwise. A single credential across environments means a misconfigured endpoint in their test harness sends test traffic to production and it authenticates perfectly, so nothing rejects it and the only signal is real records appearing that nobody meant to create. That happened during an early integration and produced a day of reconciliation work to unpick which entries were exercises. Separate identities turn that class of mistake into an authentication failure, which is loud, instant and self-explaining. It also gives us a clean way to see whether a partner is actually testing before they go live, and to apply completely different limits to the two, since sandbox traffic is bursty and unrepresentative by nature and should never be read as a signal about anything.

Anything with an expiry date, and that includes certificates, signing keys and partner agreements, is watched by a job that posts into the owning team's channel a fortnight before the date and again with rising urgency as it approaches. The warning names the thing, the owner and the date and nothing else, because a warning that requires reading a runbook to understand gets ignored. A fortnight was chosen after we tried a month, which was too early to feel real and got mentally filed as somebody else's future problem, and a week, which was not enough time for anything requiring a third party to act. The reason this exists at all is that expiry failures are uniquely unpleasant: they happen at a precise moment nobody is watching, usually a weekend, and they present as a total outage of something that was working perfectly a second earlier. The job reads the expiry directly from the live thing rather than from a record of what somebody entered, since the record is exactly what goes stale.

New credentials go to a partner as a link to a one-time secret service that destroys the value after a single read and expires by itself if nobody opens it. Nobody pastes a secret into an email, a shared document or a ticket, and the rule holds regardless of how much of a hurry anyone is in. Email is the specific concern because it is copied to places nobody tracks: it sits in two mailboxes indefinitely, gets forwarded to a colleague, is indexed by whatever the recipient's employer runs, and survives every subsequent rotation as a permanent record of a value that was once live. A ticket is worse, since ticket systems are read by more people than anyone expects and are often exported wholesale during migrations. The one-time link also gives a useful signal for free: if the link is opened before the intended recipient tries to use it, something is wrong, and if it expires unopened we know the handover never happened rather than assuming it did.

A short list of admin operations cannot be completed by one person. Issuing refunds in bulk, deleting a tenant, exporting a customer's full dataset, granting the billing or operations role, and editing pricing configuration for a named account all create a pending request instead of executing, and a second person has to approve it in a different screen before anything happens. Self-approval is impossible rather than discouraged: the approvals table carries a check constraint that the approver and the requester differ, so no amount of session juggling gets around it. Requests expire after thirty minutes, and the approver is shown a rendered summary of exactly what will change, including the row count the filter currently matches, because approving an opaque request is theatre. The reason is mistakes far more than malice. An operator ran a bulk refund with a date filter off by a month and reversed a little over three thousand invoices in under a minute; the money went back automatically, recovering it took six weeks of individual conversations, and two accounts did not renew. Nothing about that was dishonest and no additional care from that individual would have caught it, because the filter looked right. Approval is peer review, not hierarchy: anyone holding the same role can approve, since what we want is a second person reading the parameters, not a manager's blessing.

Nothing an operator deletes is actually removed at the moment they delete it. The record gets a `deleted_at` stamp, disappears from every ordinary query through the default scope, and a nightly job purges anything stamped more than thirty days ago. Recovery inside that window is a single command and takes about a minute, which is the entire point: the expensive part of a wrong deletion was never the data, it was the restore, which meant standing up a snapshot, extracting a handful of rows and reconciling them against everything that had happened since. Thirty days comes from how long it takes anyone to notice. Deletions of active things are reported within hours, but a customer coming back after a quiet period and finding a configuration missing is the case that decides the number, and a month covers almost all of those.
