The purge is genuinely a purge, since keeping soft-deleted records forever turns a deletion request into a lie, and the job's completion is monitored for exactly that reason.

Any admin operation acting on a selection refuses to run against more than five hundred records, and the tooling offers no override flag. Larger jobs are split into batches, which the interface will do for you, and each batch is a separate operation with its own record. The cap is a blast radius control rather than a performance one; the database would happily take a hundred thousand rows in one statement. What the cap buys is that the gap between intent and effect stays small. A wrong filter that hits five hundred rows is an unpleasant afternoon, and the same wrong filter unbounded is a company-level event, and the difference between them is entirely arbitrary rather than a matter of anyone's skill. Batching also means a mistake gets caught between batches: the first batch produces visible effects, somebody notices, and the rest never runs. Five hundred was picked because it is comfortably above what any legitimate manual operation has ever needed and comfortably below the number at which recovery stops being a matter of a few hours.

The administrative surface re-challenges for a second factor every four hours regardless of how recently the person signed in, and the challenge is on the hardware key rather than anything that can be read aloud. It also fires on first entry into the surface each day, so opening the console at nine in the morning always costs a tap. The interval is a compromise that took a while to settle: an hour was tested and was genuinely disruptive for the operations team who live in the console all day, and a full working day made the control almost meaningless for the case it protects against, which is an unlocked machine in a shared space or a session token lifted from a browser profile. Four hours means a stolen session has a bounded life measured in hours rather than days, and it costs the average operator two taps a day. Ordinary product surfaces are not re-challenged on a timer, because the risk profile is entirely different and the friction there would be paid by every customer.

Every write from the admin console records the actor, the target, the before and after values, and a free-text reason that the operator types and cannot skip. Rows land in the append-only audit store, not in the application database, so nothing the console can do will alter them afterwards. The required reason field was the contentious part and it earns its place. Reading an audit log six months later, the mechanical facts are almost never the puzzle; what is missing is why anybody did it, and the answer usually left with the person. A reason of asked by customer in ticket four thousand and twelve turns an alarming entry into an ordinary one in seconds. The field is not validated beyond being non-empty, because validating it would produce a dropdown and a dropdown produces the first option. In practice people write real sentences, which we did not fully expect, and the audit trail has become the first place anyone looks when a customer disputes what happened to their account.

The internal console is a distinct application on a hostname of its own, sharing no cookies, no session storage and no front-end bundle with the customer-facing product. It used to be a set of routes inside the main application, gated on a role, and that arrangement had a specific weakness worth naming. Every cross-site scripting hole anywhere in the customer product became a potential path into administrative capability, because the browser holding an operator's session had the console's origin and the product's origin as the same origin. A separated console means an issue in the product cannot reach it, and the console gets its own much stricter content policy, its own dependency budget and its own release cadence. Separation also made it possible to put the console entirely behind the identity proxy and off the public internet, which was never an option while it lived on the same hostname customers use, and it removed the recurring anxiety that a routing change might expose an internal path.

When somebody from our side acts inside a customer's account, the account owner gets a message saying who did what and when. It is not optional and there is no quiet mode, including for support acting on a request the customer made themselves. The uncomfortable version of this question is what a customer would think if they found out about an action from somewhere other than us, and the answer is always worse than the notification. Telling them proactively makes the whole category unremarkable: they see us fix the thing they asked about, and the message reads as evidence that we are careful rather than as an alarm. It also gives them a control we cannot give them any other way, since only they can tell whether an action was actually requested by someone at their company. Twice a customer has come back to ask who authorised something, and in both cases the answer was fine, and in both cases they said the notification was the reason they trusted the answer.

Payment instruments show as a brand and the last four digits everywhere in the internal tools, and there is no path to reveal more, for anyone, at any level. The full number is not held by us at all; it lives with the payment processor behind a token, so the capability does not exist to be granted. This started as a compliance requirement and turned out to be a considerable operational relief, because the most common awkward conversation in support is a caller asking an agent to read their card number back to them, and the honest answer that we simply do not have it ends the exchange without anyone having to make a judgement about whether the caller is who they say. Agents can trigger a re-authorisation, update the instrument through a link sent to the account owner, or refund against the original charge, all of which cover the real needs. What we gave up is the ability to help somebody who has lost their card and wants to know which one they used, and that has come up perhaps twice.

A direct connection to a production database is obtained by requesting one, which issues credentials valid for sixty minutes and opens a recorded session where every statement is captured with its timestamp. Read-only is the default and the write variant is a different request that shows up in a channel as it is granted. The recording is not there to catch anyone out; it is there because the question after something unexpected is always what exactly was run, and human memory of a debugging session an hour later is genuinely poor, particularly about the order things happened in. Having the transcript has more often exonerated the person than implicated them. The hour limit exists because open shells become permanent otherwise, and a terminal left connected overnight on a laptop is a credential with no expiry sitting in a session nobody is watching. Renewing is one command, so the limit costs almost nothing for the rare long investigation while making the ambient state of the world be that nobody is connected.

Every cloud resource carries three mandatory tags, `cost_center`, `service` and `owner`, and the Terraform provider's default_tags block fills them from workspace variables, so anything created through the module path cannot miss them. `finops/allocate.py` runs on the third of each month against the Cost and Usage Report landed in `atlas.cur_daily`, joins line items to the service registry, and writes a per-team rollup into `finops_allocation_monthly`. Untagged resources plus genuinely shared spend, meaning the NAT gateways, the shared cluster control planes, the transit gateway and the support plan fee, fall into a pooled bucket that is spread across teams in proportion to their tagged compute, which is crude and defensible and has never been the thing an argument was actually about. The output is showback rather than chargeback: no money moves between budgets, teams see their line in the monthly platform review, and a swing of more than fifteen percent against the prior month is expected to come with an explanation. This exists because the first year of the bill was one undifferentiated number that only the CTO could act on, so nobody acted on it. The working rule when a team forms is that they get a `cost_center` value before they get a Terraform workspace, since retro-tagging six weeks of resources is a day of work nobody volunteers for.

The anomaly detector watches daily spend per service and posts into `#platform-cost` when a service's rolling three-day average moves more than four hundred dollars a day above its trailing four-week band. It pages nobody. That was deliberate: the first version was wired to the on-call rotation, fired at two in the morning for a batch job that had legitimately doubled, and taught everyone to ignore it within a fortnight. A cost surprise is almost never something to fix at night, but it is something to notice within a day, which is what a channel post at nine in the morning does. Alerts are acknowledged by a thread reply naming the cause; an unacknowledged one gets picked up at the weekly platform sync. Two categories are suppressed outright, the annual commitment charge that lands on the first of the month and the one-off data migration jobs that are announced in advance with a suppression window. What the detector is not is a control. It has no ability to stop anything, and every attempt to give it one has been rejected, because the failure mode of an automatic shutdown on a spend signal is taking production down over money.

The cloud bill review runs for half an hour on the first Thursday and the agenda never changes, in that order: commitments coming up for renewal, the largest absolute movers since last month, anything flagged by the anomaly detector that nobody explained, and one deep dive chosen in advance. The fixed order exists because the meeting used to be a scroll through a dashboard, which meant it reliably spent its whole slot on whatever appeared first and ran out of time before the renewals, which are the only items with a deadline. Attendance is the platform lead, one person from finance, and the engineer who owns whatever the deep dive is about; nobody else is required and most months nobody else comes. Decisions taken in the room are written into the same running document as everything else and carry an owner, because the failure mode of a cost meeting is a room full of agreement that nothing needs doing and no record of who agreed. The deep dive rotates through the estate rather than always landing on the biggest line, since the biggest line is usually the one people already understand.

Accelerated instance families are capped through service quotas at two concurrent instances per non-production account, and raising that cap is a ticket to the platform team rather than a self-serve action. The cap is not about the technology, it is about the shape of the mistake: a GPU node left running over a long weekend costs more than the entire non-production estate does in a month, and it produces no signal at all while it happens because nothing is broken. We hit that twice within one quarter, once from a notebook nobody closed and once from an autoscaling group whose minimum was set during an experiment and never put back. Production accounts have their own ceiling set well above steady demand so a legitimate scale-up is never blocked, and the ceiling exists there only to bound a runaway loop. Requests to lift a non-production cap are approved routinely and usually within the hour; the point of the ticket is not gatekeeping but that somebody outside the experiment now knows the instances exist and can ask about them a week later.

Interactive warehouse queries are capped at two terabytes scanned and are killed at the limit with an error naming the offending table. Scheduled jobs run under a separate role with a higher ceiling that is reviewed when a job is registered. The cap came out of a single ad-hoc query that cross-joined the raw event stream against itself and cost more in one afternoon than the whole analytics workload does in a normal week. The limit does something more useful than saving that money, though: it converts an invisible cost into an immediate, legible error at the moment the person is still looking at the query, which is the only moment they can cheaply fix it. Almost every rejection is solved by adding a partition predicate on the event date, and the error message says so explicitly. The two exemptions are the nightly rebuild of the wide reporting tables and the backfill role, both of which run against partitions on a schedule and are watched by their owners. Anyone can request a temporary ceiling lift for a genuine one-off investigation and it is granted for the day, not permanently.

Software subscriptions are not tracked with the same tooling as infrastructure, and that split is on purpose. Every paid vendor has a row in the vendor register held by finance, carrying the owning engineer, the renewal date, the notice period and whether the contract auto-renews. The engineering side of that record is one named person whose job at renewal is to answer whether we would buy it again today. The register exists because two separate tools renewed for another year while nobody in engineering was still using either, and in one of those cases the notice period had already passed by the time anybody noticed the charge. Nothing about seat counts or usage is inferred automatically; the owner is asked, in a reminder that fires well before the notice window closes rather than before the renewal date, which is the mistake the first version of the reminder made. Consolidating vendors is a standing preference rather than a rule, because the real cost of a small tool is rarely the invoice, it is that it becomes load-bearing for one team and nobody else knows it exists.

Every design document has a run-cost section, and a document without one gets sent back the same way one without a rollout plan does. The expectation is deliberately low: an order-of-magnitude figure for steady state, the dominant driver behind it, and how the number moves if the feature is far more popular than expected. Nobody is held to the estimate afterwards and nobody is asked to be precise, because precision is not the point. The point is that the author has looked once, before anything is built, at whether the design has a cost shape that scales with usage or with data retained, and those are the two shapes that turn into a problem a year later when the design is expensive to revisit. The habit came from a feature that was correct, well built and quietly the second largest line on the bill within two quarters, entirely because it kept every intermediate result forever and nobody had ever asked what that would come to. Reviewers are told to challenge the driver rather than the arithmetic, since a wrong driver is the failure that matters.

The billing export is snapshotted at 06:00 UTC on the fifth of the month into `finops_export_frozen`, and every downstream report reads that frozen copy rather than the live table. Cloud providers restate the previous month's line items for days after it closes, applying credits, refunds and late usage records, so the same query run on the second and the ninth returns different totals for a period that everybody in the room believes is finished. That is survivable until a number is quoted in a board pack and then quoted again from a rerun, at which point the whole dataset loses credibility over a variance of a fraction of a percent. Restatements after the freeze are not merged into the frozen copy; they accumulate in an adjustments table and are picked up in the following month, which matches how the finance team already handles accruals. The fifth was chosen because provider restatements are substantially complete by the fourth and the internal reporting deadline is the seventh, leaving two days of slack. Reruns of the export against a frozen period are blocked by the job itself rather than by convention.

Each repository has a monthly ceiling on self-hosted runner minutes, defaulting to forty thousand, and crossing ninety percent posts a warning into the repository's own channel while the hard ceiling queues jobs rather than dropping them. Queueing instead of failing was the whole argument during the rollout: a hard stop on minutes means a repository that has an expensive week cannot ship a security fix, which trades a bounded cost problem for an unbounded availability one. In practice the warning is the mechanism and the ceiling has been reached three times in two years. Every one of those was the same root cause, a matrix that grew a dimension nobody priced, and the fix each time was pruning the matrix rather than raising the ceiling. Scheduled nightly jobs draw from a separate pool so that a noisy cron cannot consume the budget a team needs for pull requests during the day. Raising a ceiling permanently needs a look at what the extra minutes are buying, which usually surfaces a test suite that has been running on every push for a year with nobody reading the result.

The media and export buckets live in `eu-west-1` because that is where the services and the warehouse that read them run, and the decision was settled on transfer arithmetic rather than on latency or residency. The original layout was an accident: the first account defaulted to `us-east-1`, so the buckets were created there while the derivative pipeline and the analytics cluster were built in Ireland. Same-region reads inside one account cost nothing. Cross-region transfer was billed at two cents a gigabyte and we were moving roughly forty terabytes a month, because every uploaded original was pulled back across the ocean once for thumbnailing, again for the video probe, and again whenever a nightly job re-derived anything. The transfer line was larger than the storage line for the same bucket, which is what finally got it looked at, and internet egress at nine cents a gigabyte was a separate problem the CDN already covered. Moving the buckets took a weekend of replication and removed the line entirely. The rule that came out of it: a new bucket is created in the region of its heaviest reader, not the region of the team that owns it, and when readers genuinely straddle two regions the compute moves to the data rather than the data being copied to the compute. Residency rules were a real constraint too, but they agreed with the cheap answer and so never decided anything.

No bucket is exposed to the public internet directly. Everything customer-facing is served through the CDN distribution, origin access is locked to the distribution's identity, and objects are written with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` because every asset URL carries a content hash and therefore never changes meaning. The immutable directive matters more than the long lifetime: without it browsers still issue revalidation requests on reload, and a revalidation that returns a not-modified response still costs an origin round trip on a cold edge. Cache hit ratio sits above ninety-six percent for images and above ninety-nine for the versioned application assets, and the panel showing that ratio is the first thing to check when the origin request count moves, since a hit-ratio drop is almost always a cache key that grew a query parameter. Uploads bypass the distribution entirely and go straight to the bucket with a scoped credential, because pushing writes through a cache layer buys nothing and complicates the failure modes. The one directory served with a short lifetime is the runtime configuration blob, which is deliberately small and deliberately allowed to change under a stable name.

Exactly one bucket replicates across regions, the append-only audit store, and it does so because the retention obligation attached to it survives the loss of a whole region while nothing else in the estate does. Replication is configured with object lock preserved on the destination and a replication time control target of fifteen minutes, and the replication lag metric is alerted on rather than assumed. Every proposal to turn on replication for another bucket has been turned down with the same reasoning: replication is a copy, not a backup, and it faithfully reproduces a deletion or a corruption at the far end within seconds. What people usually want when they ask for it is either point-in-time recovery, which versioning plus lifecycle already gives them, or a faster failover story, which they should be getting from rebuilding derived data rather than from a second copy of it. The audit bucket is the exception precisely because its contents are neither derived nor deletable, so the failure mode that makes replication dangerous cannot occur there. The destination is owned by a separate account with no write path from production.

Object storage and queue traffic from private subnets goes through gateway and interface endpoints rather than through the NAT gateways. Before that change, every read a worker made from a bucket left the subnet, crossed a managed NAT, and was billed per gigabyte processed on top of the hourly charge for the gateway itself, which meant we were paying a data-processing fee to talk to a service sitting in the same region. The batch fleet alone was pushing enough through the NAT tier that the processing charge exceeded the compute the batch jobs ran on. The endpoints are declared in the network module so a new VPC gets them without anyone thinking about it, and the module also emits a policy restricting the endpoints to the accounts we own, which was the security team's condition for approving the shape. The remaining NAT traffic is genuine outbound internet, mostly package downloads during image builds and calls to a handful of partner APIs, and that residual is small enough that nobody has proposed the next optimisation of hosting an internal package mirror.

The artifact bucket has a lifecycle rule that transitions objects to infrequent access at thirty days and to archival storage at ninety, with expiry at one year for everything except tagged release builds, which are kept indefinitely. The rule was written after the bucket quietly became the third largest storage line in the account, holding every container layer and test artifact produced since the pipeline was built. The retrieval cost of the archival tier is the part people get wrong, so it is worth stating: pulling an archived object back is neither free nor instant, which is fine for the forensic case of wanting a build from eight months ago and wrong for anything in a recovery path. Nothing that a deploy or a rollback depends on is allowed in a tier below infrequent access, and the release tag exemption exists exactly so that rolling back to a nine-month-old release does not become an hour of waiting. Small objects are excluded from the transitions altogether, because the per-object overhead on a tier transition can exceed what the object costs to keep where it is.

When a customer asks for a full data export we generate the file into a private prefix and hand back a time-limited signed link rather than attaching it to an email or pushing it to a location they nominate. Two things drove that. Attachments failed constantly at the sizes people actually request, and the failure was silent from our side, so the first sign of trouble was a follow-up ticket days later asking where the export had got to. Pushing to a customer-nominated destination was worse, because it meant holding credentials to somebody else's storage for an indefinite period and being on the hook operationally when their bucket policy changed. A signed link expires on its own, needs no credential exchange, and leaves a clean access record on our side showing whether the file was ever collected, which turns out to be the question support asks most often. Links are single-purpose and scoped to one object; nobody hands out a signed prefix. Exports themselves are generated asynchronously and the requester is notified when the file is ready rather than holding a connection open.

The isolated backup copy sits in a separate account under separate credentials, and that separation was chosen over putting the copy in a distant region. The threat we are actually defending against is not a region disappearing, which has never happened to us and would be survivable, but an attacker or a mistake with production credentials destroying both the live data and everything reachable from those same credentials. A second region does nothing about that, because the same identity can usually reach both. A second account with a one-way push, no interactive access, and its own root contact does, and it costs nothing extra to arrange once the pipeline exists. The trade-off is honest and worth stating: we accept that a regional failure would mean a slower recovery, because recovery from the isolated copy is a restore rather than a failover either way. Access to the backup account is broken out of the normal single sign-on path and requires two people, which is deliberately inconvenient and has been exercised twice in drills.

Derivative images are generated when an original lands and stored beside it, rather than being produced on demand by a resizing service in front of the bucket. The on-demand shape is more elegant on paper and we ran it for about a year. What killed it was that a crawler or a badly behaved client could walk an unbounded space of size parameters and force a fresh render for every one, so the work was neither bounded nor cacheable, and the tail latency on a cache miss was long enough that product kept asking for a spinner. Rendering at upload makes the cost a known multiple of the number of originals, which is a number we can forecast, and it happens in a queue where a slow render inconveniences nobody. The cost of the choice is that adding a new size means a backfill over the existing corpus, so the set of sizes is deliberately small and adding one is a conversation rather than a config change. Requests for a size we do not hold fall back to the nearest larger one scaled down in the browser.

We hold a one-year, no-upfront compute commitment sized to cover roughly seventy percent of the trailing ninety-day baseline hourly spend, and we deliberately did not take the three-year term even though it discounts about twice as deeply, twenty-eight percent against fifty-two on the quotes we were given. The reasoning is that a commitment is a bet on the shape of the estate, not on its size. Over three years the shape changes: we were already part way through moving services to Arm instances, the legacy invoicer is scheduled to leave its own database class entirely, and two of the largest workloads are candidates for a different runtime. We had learned that concretely, having bought a three-year reservation on a database family we migrated off eight months later, leaving two years of commitment sold at a loss on the marketplace. No-upfront was chosen over all-upfront for the same reason in a different currency: the extra few points of discount are not worth pre-paying for capacity we might not want. Seventy percent rather than full coverage, because the top of the curve is the part that moves, and paying on-demand for the peak beats committing to a floor we might drop below. The position is reviewed each quarter by the platform lead and finance together, and the trigger to top up is coverage falling below sixty percent for two consecutive months.

Interruptible instances run the CI fleet, the nightly report builds and the media transcoding queue, and nothing else. The node pools are labelled and every workload that lands on them carries a toleration, so a request-serving deployment cannot drift onto them by accident. The rule is not about the discount, which is large and which we happily take, it is about what an interruption costs. A transcode that dies two minutes from the end restarts and nobody notices; a checkout request that dies two minutes from the end is a customer. The two-minute termination notice is consumed by a handler that drains the node and requeues in-flight work, and every job on those pools has to be safe to run twice, which is checked when a job is registered rather than assumed. We tried request-serving on interruptible capacity for one quarter behind a small traffic share. It worked most of the time, and the failure days were bad enough, and unpredictable enough in their timing, that the saving stopped being interesting. Capacity pools are diversified across three instance families so a shortage in one does not empty the fleet.

The horizontal autoscaler targets sixty percent average CPU for request-serving deployments. Eighty looks more efficient and was the original setting; it was lowered after two incidents that shared a mechanism. Scaling is not instant. A new pod needs image pull, start-up, warm-up and readiness before it takes traffic, which on our heaviest service is close to ninety seconds, and traffic can double in far less than that when a partner retries a batch. At eighty percent there is no headroom to absorb the ramp, so latency degrades while the replacement capacity is still booting, and the latency degradation itself increases concurrency, which increases CPU further. Sixty leaves enough slack that the ramp is invisible. The extra idle capacity is the price of that, and it is a much smaller number than it looks because the fleet is scaled down aggressively overnight. Services with genuinely fast start-up are allowed a higher target and two of them run at seventy-five. Minimum replica counts are set from observed weekday-morning demand rather than from a formula, because the scale-from-floor case is the one that hurts.

Every managed database instance is reviewed once a quarter against ninety days of peak CPU, peak connections and buffer cache hit ratio, and the review produces a decision to keep, shrink or grow rather than a report nobody reads. Shrinking is the outcome people resist and it is usually the correct one, because instance classes are chosen at project start when nobody knows the workload and are then never revisited. Two of the current fleet are two sizes below where they started with no measurable change in latency. The review deliberately ignores average utilisation and looks at peaks, since a database sized on averages falls over during the month-end run. Growing is allowed to happen out of band at any time and does not wait for the quarter. The one thing the review is not allowed to do is resize during a period of elevated replication lag, because the failover that a class change performs will extend the lag rather than clear it, which we learned during an otherwise routine resize that turned into forty minutes of stale reads on the reporting replica.

Moving to Arm instances was done one service at a time over two quarters, never as a fleet-wide flip, and each move ran both architectures side by side behind the same load balancer for a full week before the old node group was drained. The per-service pace was not caution for its own sake. Roughly a fifth of the services had a native dependency that did not have a multi-architecture image, and finding those by attempting a fleet migration would have meant discovering them all at once during a rollback. Container images are now built as multi-arch manifests by default in the shared pipeline, so a new service inherits the capability without asking. The measured saving was in the region of eighteen percent on compute for equivalent throughput, and two services showed no benefit at all because they were memory-bound; those stayed where they were, since a migration that buys nothing still costs the rebuild and the risk. The remaining holdout is the legacy invoicer, whose runtime is pinned to a version with no Arm build.

Staging deliberately runs on smaller instances and fewer replicas than production, and that is a policy rather than an oversight. Periodically someone proposes making it production-shaped so that performance results transfer, and the proposal is refused every time for the same two reasons. The first is cost, obviously, since a mirrored environment roughly doubles the compute line for something that is idle most of the day. The second is more important: a staging environment that is nearly but not exactly production-shaped produces performance numbers that people trust and should not, because the interesting differences are in data volume and traffic shape rather than in instance size, and neither of those is fixed by buying bigger machines. Load testing therefore runs against production behind a traffic-shadowing path with a clearly bounded blast radius, which is the only place a performance number means anything. What staging must match exactly is configuration, runtime version and the schema, and those are enforced; the hardware underneath is explicitly not part of the contract.

Cluster infrastructure, meaning the ingress controllers, the log shippers, the certificate manager and the metrics agents, runs on a small dedicated node pool of three on-demand instances per zone that nothing else is scheduled onto. Keeping them off the general pool costs a little idle capacity and buys two properties. Infrastructure pods stop competing for resources with the workloads they are supposed to be observing, which matters most during exactly the incidents where you need the telemetry, and a scale-down of the application fleet can never evict the component that ships the logs. We found the second one the hard way when an overnight scale-down took out the ingress replicas along with the workloads and the cluster came back in the morning without a working entry point. The pool is deliberately never interruptible and is sized by hand rather than autoscaled, because autoscaling a pool of three is more failure surface than it is worth. Anything added to that pool needs an argument, since the whole value of it is that its membership is small and stable.

Any launch expected to need more of something than the account currently allows gets its quota request filed a fortnight before the date, and the request is tracked on the launch checklist alongside the load test and the runbook. Quota increases are usually approved quickly, sometimes in minutes, and occasionally they sit with a human at the provider for days with no way to hurry them along. That variance is the whole reason for the lead time: the failure is not that a request gets refused, it is that it gets approved on the Tuesday after the Friday you needed it. We learned this during a launch where the traffic arrived, the fleet tried to scale, and the scale-up stopped at a ceiling nobody had checked, in a service where the ceiling had been fine for two years. The checklist item asks for the specific limit and the number, not for a general assurance, because half the value is in someone having worked out which limit is going to bind.

For the three busiest trading days of the year the fleet is scaled up manually the evening before and the minimum replica counts are raised, rather than being left to the autoscaler. This is not a vote of no confidence in the autoscaler, which handles ordinary daily variation perfectly well. It is that the peak on those days arrives as a step rather than a ramp, driven by a campaign that goes out at a known minute, and every autoscaler is reactive by construction, so the first minutes of a step are served by whatever was already running. Pre-warming converts a latency spike that we cannot avoid into idle capacity that we can afford for a day. The scaled-up floors come back down two days later, and there is a calendar reminder to do it because the year we forgot, the elevated floor sat there unnoticed for most of a month. Connection pools and caches are warmed as part of the same pass, since a cold cache on a freshly started replica produces the same symptom as not having the replica at all.

`tools/env_reaper.py` runs every ten minutes and scales any non-production namespace to zero once it has served no request through the auth proxy for four hours, and unconditionally at 19:30 on weekdays and for the whole weekend. Nothing is deleted, only scaled down: the namespace, its config, its volumes and its database schema all survive, so waking is cheap and nobody is afraid of the reaper. Waking happens either from the `/wake` Slack command or automatically when a request arrives at the proxy, which holds the connection while the deployment scales up and answers in about forty seconds cold. Preview environments are a special case with a hard end: they are destroyed entirely seventy-two hours after their pull request closes, because a preview whose branch is gone is never coming back. Opting out is possible and bounded, with a `reaper.skip-until` label carrying a date at most fourteen days ahead, so a long-running experiment can survive the night while a forgotten one cannot survive the fortnight. This exists because a load-test namespace running a scaled copy of the production fleet was left up after a launch and ran for six weeks before anyone noticed, at about nine and a half thousand dollars. The wake-on-request path is what made the whole thing acceptable; the earlier version required a manual restart and people simply disabled it.

A Sunday job lists unattached block volumes, snapshots with no parent volume, released load balancers and elastic addresses bound to nothing, tags anything older than fourteen days with a deletion date another fourteen days out, and posts the list to the owning team from the `owner` tag. Nothing is removed without having carried a visible deletion date for two weeks, and re-tagging an item resets the clock, which is the whole appeal-and-review mechanism. The sweep was written after we noticed we were paying for several terabytes of provisioned storage attached to nothing, most of it left behind by instances that had been replaced rather than terminated cleanly. Snapshots are the harder half, because a snapshot chain looks like a backup and deleting one feels dangerous; the job therefore never touches snapshots produced by the backup pipeline, which are identified by their own tag and managed by their own lifecycle rules. Everything else it finds was created by hand, and things created by hand are exactly what nobody remembers to clean up.

Every preview environment gets its own schema inside a single shared cluster rather than its own database instance. One instance for thirty-odd previews costs a fraction of thirty instances and, more usefully, provisions in seconds because creating a schema and running migrations is fast while creating a managed instance is a coffee break. The isolation that matters here is namespacing, not tenancy: a preview cannot see another preview's tables, and if a preview manages to saturate the shared cluster the blast radius is other previews, which is an acceptable thing to break. Connection limits are the sharp edge, and each preview's pool is capped at five so that one runaway environment cannot exhaust the cluster's connection budget for everybody. Schemas are dropped when the preview is torn down, and a weekly job drops any schema with no matching environment, because the teardown path occasionally loses a race. Nothing resembling production data ever lands there; previews are seeded from the synthetic fixture set.

Preview environments are addressed as `pr-<number>.preview.internal` under a single wildcard certificate held by the ingress, so a new environment needs no certificate issuance and no DNS record of its own. The earlier design requested a certificate per environment from the ACME provider on creation, which worked until a busy afternoon hit the issuance rate limit and every preview created for the next hour came up without TLS, and the browsers refused them in a way that looked exactly like the application being broken. A wildcard has the obvious downside that its private key covers every preview, which is acceptable precisely because previews hold no real data and live behind the company single sign-on. The certificate is renewed by one job in the platform namespace and its expiry is alerted on thirty days out, so the single point of failure is at least a watched one. Hostnames are stable for the life of a pull request, which matters because people paste them into review comments and expect them to still resolve the next morning.

Local development runs the service and its dependencies on the engineer's own machine through a compose file kept in the repository, and we have twice declined to move to remote development sandboxes. The pitch for remote is real: identical environments, no laptop-specific breakage, and heavier machines than anyone has locally. What sank it both times was that it makes development require connectivity and makes iteration require a round trip, and the daily experience of editing a file and seeing the change is the thing you least want to add latency to. It also moves a development cost onto the cloud bill, where it is paid continuously rather than once at laptop purchase. The compose file is treated as a supported artifact rather than a convenience: it is exercised by a scheduled job so that a broken one is discovered by the pipeline instead of by a new joiner on their first morning, and its dependency versions are pinned to match what production runs. Anything genuinely too heavy to run locally, which today means only the search indexer, is stubbed with a small fake.

Staging is destroyed and recreated from its Terraform and Helm definitions every Sunday at 02:00, and the run is treated as a test of the definitions rather than as maintenance of the environment. Any resource that was created by hand disappears and does not come back, which is the entire point: an environment that survives for months accumulates undeclared state, and by the time you need to rebuild it under pressure the declarations no longer describe it. Two production incidents traced back to exactly that gap, both of them a setting present in staging and absent from the repository, so the change tested fine and behaved differently on release. The rebuild takes about thirty-five minutes and finishes long before Monday, and a failure raises a ticket for the platform team rather than paging anyone. Data is reseeded from the fixture generator as part of the run. The rule that follows from all this is short: if you need something in staging to persist, put it in the repository, because Sunday does not care.

Every engineer has exactly one personal workspace for experiments, named after them, and infrastructure spun up outside it is considered undeclared. The single-workspace limit is not a resource control, it is a naming and ownership one. Before it existed, exploratory resources were created straight into shared accounts with whatever names their authors liked, and nobody could tell six weeks later whether a thing was somebody's abandoned test or a load-bearing piece of an integration nobody had documented. Attaching every experiment to a person makes that question answerable in one step: ask them. The workspace is genuinely theirs, with no review required for anything inside it, because a scratch space that needs approval is not a scratch space and people will route around it. What it does not permit is anything reachable from the public internet or anything holding customer data, and both of those are enforced by policy rather than by trust. When somebody leaves, their workspace is destroyed as part of offboarding, which has occasionally surfaced dependencies that should never have existed.

Non-production environments are seeded from a generator that fabricates accounts, shipments and invoices, and no path exists for copying a production database into any of them, anonymised or otherwise. The anonymisation argument was had properly and lost on its merits: scrubbing is never finished, since every new column is a new leak until someone remembers to add it to the scrubber, and the failure is silent because a missed field looks exactly like data that was supposed to be there. Generated data also gives us something a copy cannot, which is the ability to ask for the awkward cases on demand: an account with no invoices, a shipment stuck in an intermediate state, a customer whose name breaks naive text handling. Those are the shapes bugs live in, and a production copy is dominated by boring rows. The cost is that the generator has to be maintained alongside the schema, and it does drift, so a broken seed run blocks the pipeline rather than being skipped. Demonstration environments use the same generator with a curated, deterministic seed so that screenshots stay stable.

Scheduled jobs carry a wall-clock deadline of six hours unless they declare a longer one, and the scheduler terminates anything past it and marks the run failed rather than letting it continue. The default is not a guess about how long work takes, it is an assertion that a job running longer than that has almost certainly stopped making progress: the common causes we see are a query that lost its index and is now sequentially scanning, a paginated API loop with a cursor that never advances, and a retry storm against a dependency that is down. All three will run indefinitely and none of them will ever succeed. Declaring a longer deadline is one line in the job definition and several jobs do, most of them the quarterly reconciliation runs. A killed job posts its last progress record so that whoever looks at it can tell whether it was slow or stuck, a distinction that used to take twenty minutes of log reading to establish. Jobs are required to be safe to rerun, which is what makes killing them a cheap action rather than a decision.

The observability vendor's invoice is split by the `service` label carried on every ingested line, and `observability/chargeback.py` writes the monthly result into `log_ingest_by_service_monthly` so each team sees its own gigabytes and its own share of the bill against their tooling budget. Before that the bill was one line item called logging, owned by the platform team, which meant the people generating the volume had no signal at all and the people holding the number had no ability to change it. That arrangement survived until a service turned on debug level for a customer investigation and left it on for eleven days, taking ingest from about three hundred gigabytes a day to over four terabytes and tripling the month. Nobody was at fault in a way anybody could point at, which was the actual problem. We chose chargeback over a hard per-service quota deliberately: a quota drops lines when a service is unhealthy and noisy, which is precisely the hour you need them, whereas a bill arrives later and hurts nobody's incident. Each service gets an allocation of eight gigabytes a day and going over is allowed, visible and expected to come with a sentence explaining it. Total ingest fell roughly forty percent in the first two months without anyone mandating a single deletion; teams removed their own health-check chatter and per-row loop logging once they could see what it cost.

Everything written to standard output is a single-line JSON object carrying at minimum `ts`, `level`, `service`, `env`, `request_id` and `msg`, and the shared logging library refuses to emit anything else. Free-text lines were the norm for years and the cost of them was invisible until we tried to answer a question across services and found that every team had invented its own way of writing a duration and a customer identifier. Fixed fields mean a query written against one service works against all of them, which is the difference between an investigation taking two minutes and taking an afternoon of reading someone else's format. Message text is required to be a constant with the variable parts in fields rather than interpolated into the string, so that the same event groups together no matter which shipment it was about. The linter enforces the constant-message rule, imperfectly, and review catches the rest. Multi-line output is the one thing that genuinely breaks the pipeline, so stack traces are serialised into a single escaped field rather than printed across lines.

Raising a production service to debug level is done with `logctl debug <service> --minutes 120`, and the level reverts on its own when the timer expires. There is no way to set it permanently short of a code change that goes through review, and that asymmetry is the whole design. Debug level is genuinely useful during an investigation and genuinely harmful the rest of the time: it buries the signal you would otherwise notice, it prints argument values that were never reviewed for sensitivity, and it changes the timing of the code paths it instruments. What made a timer necessary rather than a convention is that switching it back is the step that gets skipped, since by the time the investigation is over the person doing it has moved on to fixing the thing they found. The command records who raised it and why, and posts both into the service's channel so the next person to look at odd output knows why it is odd. Two hours is the default because it is longer than most investigations and shorter than a working day.

The metrics relay drops any series whose label set includes a value it has not seen before once the series count for that metric passes fifty thousand, and it emits a rejection counter naming the offending metric so the failure is loud rather than mysterious. The guard exists because a single deploy put the customer identifier into a label on a request counter and the time-series database went from a comfortable working set to unresponsive in about twenty minutes, taking every dashboard with it, including the ones we needed to understand what was happening. Cardinality is the one resource in a metrics system that fails suddenly rather than gradually. The rule for authors is that a label value must come from a bounded set known at code-writing time, so status codes and route templates are fine while identifiers, paths with parameters interpolated, and anything derived from user input are not. When you genuinely need per-entity detail, that is what logs and traces are for, and pushing people towards those is a feature of the guard rather than a regrettable side effect.

The node agent buffers to a bounded on-disk queue of five hundred megabytes and discards the oldest entries when the collector is unreachable and the queue fills, and the application's write to standard output never blocks regardless. This is a deliberate ordering of what we are willing to lose. An outage of the logging backend must not be able to become an outage of the product, and the version that applied backpressure did exactly that once: the collector fell behind, the buffer filled, writes started blocking, and request threads piled up on a log statement in a hot path until the service stopped answering. Losing the tail of the logs during a telemetry outage is annoying and recoverable; losing the service is not. The agent exports a dropped-lines counter which is alerted on, so the loss is measured rather than assumed, and during the last collector incident we could say afterwards exactly which four minutes were incomplete. Audit records do not travel this path at all, for the obvious reason that best-effort delivery is unacceptable for them.

Redaction of sensitive values happens in the collector, on the way to the store, rather than at the call sites that produce them. Doing it in application code was the original approach and it fails for a structural reason: it requires every author of every log statement, forever, to remember, and one forgetting is enough to put a card number in a search index that many people can read. Central redaction gives one place to add a pattern when a new kind of sensitive field appears, and it applies retroactively to services nobody has touched in a year. The obvious objection is that the raw value still exists in the process and on the node briefly before the collector sees it, and that is true and accepted, because the exposure window is short and the storage is where the durable risk lives. Application authors are still expected not to log secrets deliberately; the collector is a net, not a licence. When a rule is added, we sample recent output to check what else it catches, since an over-broad pattern that redacts identifiers people need is its own kind of outage.

Distributed traces are head-sampled at one percent for ordinary requests, and any trace whose root span ends in an error or exceeds two seconds is retained in full by the tail-sampling processor in the collector. The one percent figure is not a cost target arrived at first; it came from asking how many traces we need before a latency distribution for a given endpoint is stable, which for our traffic volumes is satisfied comfortably at that rate for everything except the least-used admin endpoints. Those are handled by a per-route override rather than by raising the global rate. Sampling is decided at the edge and the decision propagates in the trace context, so a sampled request is sampled end to end and we never end up with a trace missing its middle, which was the defect of the first implementation where each service decided independently. Retention is thirty days for retained traces. The rule people forget is that a trace is not a log: it answers where the time went, not what the code was thinking, and reaching for one to answer the second question wastes an afternoon.

Direct writes to standard output outside the logging library fail the lint step in service packages, with the scripts and tooling directories exempt because a command-line tool talking to a terminal is a different thing entirely. The rule looks pedantic and its justification is narrow but real: a bare print bypasses the level filter, so it cannot be turned down when the service gets noisy, and it bypasses the structured formatter, so it lands in the store as an unparsed blob that shows up in searches as a line nobody can filter on. Both properties are invisible on a laptop, where a print is the fastest way to see something, and that is exactly why the rule has to be mechanical instead of remembered. The failure mode that made it worth enforcing was a debugging print left in a hot path that produced several lines per request, none of them attributable to anything, and which survived two releases because nobody reading the output could tell where it came from. The fix in review is always one line, so the rule costs almost nothing to comply with.

A request identifier is minted at the edge if the caller did not supply one, travels in a header through every internal call, is attached to every queued message, and is written into every log line and every audit record produced along the way. It is also returned to the caller on error responses, which is the part customers benefit from, because a support ticket that quotes one turns a vague description of a failure into a single search. The value of this is entirely in its completeness: an identifier present in eighty percent of hops is close to useless, since the missing hop is always the interesting one. That is why propagation lives in the shared client and server middleware rather than being passed around by hand, and why a service that starts a background task from a request is expected to carry the identifier into it instead of letting the chain end at the queue boundary. Asynchronous work spawned from a request keeps the original identifier and adds its own, so a fan-out is still traceable back to what caused it.

The web app has a hard byte budget per route entry, one hundred and eighty kilobytes gzipped for the initial chunk and one hundred and twenty for the shared vendor chunk, declared in `.size-limit.json` and checked on every pull request. Exceeding it fails the build and blocks the merge; it is not a warning, and it was a warning for the first three months, during which it was exceeded continuously and fixed never. The budget exists because bundle growth has no natural owner. Every individual addition is defensible and small, nobody is doing anything wrong, and the app is two hundred kilobytes heavier a year later with no decision anywhere in the history that anyone would defend on its own. What made it urgent was a date-formatting library pulled in with its full locale set, ninety kilobytes on the wire, which pushed time-to-interactive on our reference device from roughly two and a half seconds to over four; signup completion fell about four percent and stayed there for two weeks before anyone connected the two. The reference device matters: the median session is a mid-range Android phone on a mobile network, not the laptop the code was written on, so parse and execute time there is what the budget rations. Raising a number is allowed, requires the web owner's approval and a sentence in the pull request saying what the bytes bought, and has happened twice in two years.

Product imagery is delivered through a picture element offering WebP first with a JPEG source behind it, and the CDN generates both variants at three widths from the original upload. The fallback still exists although the browsers that need it are now a rounding error, because the cost of keeping it is one extra source element and one extra derivative, and the cost of getting it wrong is a page of broken image placeholders on someone's till system. Sizes are declared on every image so the browser picks a variant before layout rather than after, which was the actual win: the earlier setup served one large file to everyone and relied on CSS to scale it down, so a phone downloaded a desktop-sized photograph and then threw most of it away. Every image tag carries explicit width and height attributes, enforced by a lint rule, because the layout shift from images loading without reserved space was the single largest contributor to our cumulative shift score. Decorative images are marked as such and lazily loaded below the fold.

No third-party tag is placed in the page directly. Everything external, currently four vendors, is registered in `src/thirdparty/registry.ts` with an owner and a consent category, and a single loader injects it after the consent decision is known and after the first meaningful paint. This came out of a marketing tag that a vendor updated on their side, which began synchronously fetching a second script from a fifth domain and added a full second to first paint for every visitor, with no change on our side and nothing in our deployment history to explain it. Routing everything through one loader gives us three things we did not have: the ability to remove a vendor in one line, an inventory that is accurate because the loader is the only path, and a content security policy that can enumerate permitted origins rather than allowing anything. Scripts are loaded with the async attribute and a timeout after which the loader gives up, so a vendor having a bad day cannot hold anything of ours open. Adding a vendor requires the registry entry and a named owner.

Every route in the router configuration is a dynamic import, without exception, and the shared build lint fails on a static import of a page component. Making it the default rather than an optimisation applied where someone noticed was the important part: selective splitting produced a codebase where the four routes somebody had profiled were split and the thirty nobody had looked at were not, and the unsplit ones were disproportionately the rarely used administrative screens carrying the heaviest dependencies. Under the current setup a visitor to the shipment list downloads the shipment list, and the tariff editor's rich-text stack stays on the server until somebody opens the tariff editor. Prefetching softens the cost of the extra round trip: the router prefetches a route's chunk on link hover and on idle for the two most likely next destinations, which in practice means the chunk is usually already there when the click happens. Shared code above a small threshold is hoisted into a common chunk automatically rather than being duplicated per route.

The two typefaces are served from our own origin as WOFF2, subset to Latin and Latin Extended, preloaded in the document head and declared with a swap display so text is readable while they arrive. Hosting them ourselves rather than from the foundry's CDN removed a DNS lookup and a connection to a third origin on the critical path, and it removed a dependency whose availability we could not do anything about, which mattered on the morning that CDN was slow in one region and our pages rendered without text for several seconds. Subsetting cut the two files by about seventy percent, and the extended range is retained because customer names in our data are not confined to unaccented ASCII. Only two weights are shipped, regular and semibold; requests for a third have been declined on the grounds that the design system does not use one, and the italic variants are synthesised rather than downloaded. The font files are hashed and served with a long lifetime, so the cost is paid once per visitor per release of the typeface.

Public marketing and documentation pages are rendered on the server and hydrated afterwards, while the signed-in application is a client-rendered single page app, and the split is drawn on that line for reasons that are about audience rather than technology. A visitor arriving from a search result has no cache, no session and very little patience, and the difference between seeing content immediately and seeing a spinner while a bundle downloads shows up directly in bounce rate. A signed-in user arrives with everything already cached and stays for half an hour, so the cost of the initial load amortises away and the responsiveness of subsequent navigation matters far more. Trying to run both surfaces under one rendering strategy was attempted early and produced the worst of each: server rendering the application meant maintaining a server-side path for interactive components that only ever mattered for one screen, and client rendering the marketing pages meant search crawlers seeing an empty shell. The two share components and design tokens but not their rendering pipeline.

A synthetic performance audit runs against every preview deployment and posts its scores as a pull request comment, and it deliberately does not fail the build. Lab numbers on shared CI hardware are noisy enough that a threshold produces false failures at a rate which trains people to rerun the job until it passes, and a check people rerun until green is worse than no check because it costs time and teaches the wrong reflex. What the comment is good at is showing a direction: three consecutive pull requests each losing a couple of points is a signal worth chasing, and that pattern is visible in a comment history without anything being enforced. The scores that get taken seriously are the field measurements collected from real sessions, which are noisy in a different way but are at least measuring the thing we care about. The audit's accessibility section is the part most often acted on, since those findings are deterministic rather than timing-dependent, and several of them have been promoted into lint rules where they can be enforced honestly.

Adding a package to the web application's manifest requires an approval from someone other than the author, and the reviewer is asked to answer three questions in the pull request: who maintains it, what its licence is, and what we would do if it were abandoned tomorrow. The rule is about supply chain and maintenance burden rather than anything else. A dependency is a permanent relationship with a stranger, and the moment of adding one is the only moment anybody thinks about it; after that it is simply part of the app, upgraded automatically, until the day it stops being maintained or ships something unpleasant. We have had both, a package that changed licence between minor versions and a small utility whose maintainer handed the repository to an account that immediately published a modified release. Neither was caught by anything automatic. The questions are deliberately answerable in a couple of minutes, because a heavyweight process would just push people towards copying the code in, which trades a visible dependency for an invisible one.

The service worker precaches the application shell under a cache name that includes the release identifier, and the activate handler deletes every cache whose name does not match the current release. Getting that wrong is unusually punishing, because a service worker is the one piece of the front end that can persist a broken state on a user's device beyond your ability to fix it by deploying. We did exactly that once, shipping a worker that served a stale shell against a new API contract, and the recovery involved publishing a worker whose only job was to unregister itself and clear storage. Since then the rules are fixed: the shell is versioned, API responses are never cached by the worker, and the worker skips waiting only after the client confirms it is safe rather than on install. The registration is behind a remote switch so it can be disabled without a deploy. Offline support is limited on purpose to the shell and the last-viewed list, because a convincing offline experience over stale operational data is worse than an honest failure.

The support matrix comes from our own traffic, never from a published market-share table. `browserslist-stats.json` is regenerated on the first of each month from a query over `atlas.web_sessions_daily` covering the previous twenty-eight days, and the `browserslist` key in `package.json` reads from those figures with a half-percent threshold plus a floor of the last two versions and a hard minimum on mobile Safari. Everything downstream reads that one list, the transpilation targets, the prefix generation and the lint rule for unsupported syntax, so support is one fact rather than four opinions. Below the threshold a browser-version bucket falls out automatically, and that is where the interesting part starts, because the automatic rule is overridden by a short list of named exceptions maintained by hand. A logistics customer runs a fleet of warehouse kiosks on a pinned older Chromium; they are a fifth of a percent of sessions and a much larger share of revenue, and they stay supported until their contract renewal regardless of what the threshold says. That exception list exists because we once removed a polyfill on the market-share argument alone and took that fleet offline for a working day. So: sessions decide the default, accounts decide the exceptions, and any removal is announced to support thirty days ahead so they hear it from us rather than from a customer.

The internal admin console builds for current Chrome only, with no transpilation below native module support and no polyfills at all. It can do that because every machine that reaches it is a managed laptop with an enforced browser update policy, and the console is behind single sign-on that the fleet management already gates, so the population of clients is genuinely known rather than estimated. The saving is not really in bytes, it is in the absence of a compatibility layer to reason about: modern syntax goes in as written, new platform APIs are usable the week they ship, and nobody debugs a difference between what the source says and what the transpiler produced. The console does check the browser at startup and shows a plain instruction to open it in Chrome rather than failing in some confusing partial way, which was added after a contractor on a personal machine spent an afternoon reporting bugs that were all the same bug. Nothing customer-facing may take this approach, and the build config carries a comment saying so, because the temptation to copy it has come up twice.

The end-to-end suite runs against Chromium on every pull request, and a reduced smoke path of eleven journeys runs nightly against all three engines including WebKit and Gecko. Running everything everywhere on every change was the original design and it was abandoned inside a month: it tripled the pipeline's duration, and essentially every failure it produced was a timing difference in the test rather than a defect in the product. The nightly split keeps the signal at a cost people tolerate. The eleven journeys were chosen as the paths where an engine difference would actually be expensive, meaning sign-in, payment entry, file upload, and the two screens that use the more exotic layout features. A nightly failure opens a ticket rather than paging, and is triaged the next morning by whoever is on the front-end rotation. The genuine engine defects we have found this way in two years number four, which sounds like a poor return until you consider that two of them were on the payment screen.

Screenshot comparisons are taken in a single pinned headless Chromium at two viewport widths, and the pinned version is upgraded deliberately as its own pull request with the whole baseline set regenerated and reviewed. Capturing in more than one engine sounds more thorough and is actively counterproductive: font rasterisation and subpixel rounding differ between engines, so a multi-engine baseline is a permanent source of differences that are real, unfixable, and about nothing. One engine turns the tool into what it is for, which is noticing that a padding change moved something you were not looking at. The upgrade-as-its-own-change rule exists because an engine upgrade folded into a feature branch produces a diff of several hundred changed images with the meaningful two buried in it. Baselines live in the repository rather than in the vendor's service, which makes the review of a regenerated set an ordinary code review. Tests that need to assert behaviour rather than appearance are told to use the functional suite instead, and the boundary is policed in review.

Printed output from the shipment and invoice screens is verified manually once a quarter by generating the same three documents and looking at them, and there is no automated coverage of it at all. That is an unusual admission to write down, so here is the reasoning. Print rendering differs between browsers in ways that headless capture does not reproduce faithfully, page breaks and margin boxes especially, so an automated check would be testing the harness rather than the artefact. The volume of print usage is small but the consequences are concrete, because these pages end up in a customs file or taped to a pallet, and a page break through the middle of a barcode is a real operational failure at the other end. The quarterly cadence matches how often the underlying layouts change, which is rarely. What the check has caught, twice, is a change to the shared table component that was invisible on screen and moved the header off the printed page. The person doing it is whoever is on the front-end rotation that week, and the instructions are short enough to follow without background.

Every accommodation for mobile Safari's viewport behaviour is collected in `src/styles/ios-viewport.css` and the small hook beside it, and none of it is allowed to be scattered through component styles. The specific problems are well known: the dynamic viewport unit and the toolbar that grows and shrinks during scroll, the rubber-band overscroll on a fixed footer, and the input zoom that triggers below a certain font size. The reason they are centralised is not tidiness, it is deletability. Each one of these is a workaround for a browser behaviour that will eventually change, and a workaround scattered across forty components is one nobody will ever be confident enough to remove, so it becomes permanent regardless of whether it is still needed. Kept in one file with a comment on each block naming the behaviour and the version it was observed in, the whole set can be re-examined in an afternoon. Two blocks have already been deleted that way. New additions are expected to include a reproduction note, because the failure mode of the old scattered version was rules nobody could explain.

The tracking widget that customers embed in their own sites supports noticeably older browsers than our own application does, and it always will, because the population loading it is our customers' visitors rather than our users and we have no relationship with them at all. Several integration contracts name that obligation explicitly. The consequence is that the widget is built as a separate artefact with its own compilation target and its own dependency set, deliberately tiny and written to a conservative subset of the platform, and it shares nothing with the application build beyond design tokens. Attempts to have it share the application's component code have been rejected each time they were proposed, because the moment it shares a build it inherits the application's assumptions and the obligation quietly becomes unmeetable. The widget is also the one place where we still ship a small compatibility shim rather than requiring a native capability. Changing its baseline is a commercial conversation rather than an engineering one, and it goes through the account team.

Manual accessibility verification is done in two combinations, a screen reader on Windows with its usual companion browser and the built-in reader on macOS with Safari, because screen reader behaviour is a property of the pairing and not of either half. The same markup can announce correctly under one pairing and skip a live region entirely under another, which is not a bug in either product so much as a difference in how each interprets an ambiguous structure. Testing one pairing and assuming the other tells you very little, and that assumption was exactly how a form error summary shipped that was invisible to half the people who needed it. Automated checks run in the pipeline and catch the mechanical failures, missing labels, contrast, focus traps, and those are genuinely worth catching cheaply, but the automated tools cannot tell you whether the announced order of a dynamic update makes sense to a person. Verification happens on new flows rather than on every change, and the flows covered so far are sign-in, booking and the shipment detail view.

The public status page is hand-written HTML and a single stylesheet, served from object storage in a different account and a different region from everything else, with no framework, no build and no dependency on any internal service. That is a design constraint rather than laziness, because the status page's only job is to work during the exact conditions under which our infrastructure does not. Every layer you add is a layer that can be down when you need the page, and the page being down during an incident converts a technical problem into a credibility one, which is much harder to recover from. Updates are made by editing the file and uploading it, a procedure the on-call runbook describes in four steps and which is practised as part of incident drills so that nobody is learning it at two in the morning. The page deliberately carries no automatic health indicators; a green light driven by a check that is itself broken is worse than no light. It says what a human wrote, with a timestamp, and nothing else.

One styling system at a time, and adding a second is not a pull request. Any package that brings its own stylesheet or its own opinions about visual layout, meaning a CSS framework or a styled component kit, needs a decision record approved by the web guild and a funded plan to remove whatever it replaces, with dates. Shipping it alongside the incumbent is explicitly not an option, and that is the whole rule; the ADR is just the paperwork around it. We wrote it after living in the alternative. The application at one point carried leftovers of an old framework, a Tailwind adoption that reached about a third of the screens, and two hand-rolled grid systems, which came to roughly a hundred and forty kilobytes of largely duplicated CSS and, far worse, a specificity contest in which nobody could predict what a rule would do. Restyling the primary button took the better part of a week and still missed three places, one of them the checkout. The current system is the token set from `@aldercross/ui` composed through CSS modules, with utility classes permitted only where they are generated from those tokens. Headless component libraries are exempt because they carry behaviour and accessibility rather than appearance, on the condition that they ship no stylesheet, and that exemption is checked in review rather than assumed.

Colour, spacing, radius and type-scale values are defined once in `tokens/tokens.json` and a build step emits the CSS custom property block, the TypeScript constants and the native mobile assets from it. Nothing is transcribed by hand into a second place, and the build fails if a generated file is edited directly, which happens perhaps twice a year and is always somebody in a hurry. The rule came from a period where the palette existed in the design tool, in a stylesheet and in a mobile constants file, and the three had quietly diverged: the same named grey was three different greys, and reconciling them turned out to be a week of archaeology because nobody could establish which was correct. Generation makes the question meaningless. Adding a token is a pull request against the source file with a design reviewer, and renaming one requires a deprecation period where both names emit, because a token name is an API that other teams have written against. The generator also emits a documentation page listing every token with a swatch, which is what people actually use when picking one.

Component styles are written in `.module.css` files and referenced through the imported object, so every class name that reaches the browser is hashed and local to its component. Global selectors are permitted only in a single reset file and in the token block, both of which are on an allowlist in the build config, and a global rule anywhere else fails the lint step. This closed a category of bug that used to consume a genuinely embarrassing amount of time: a rule written for one screen matching an element on a screen the author had never opened, discovered weeks later by a customer. The hashing also makes dead style detection possible, because an unreferenced module is unreachable by construction rather than merely unused as far as anybody can tell, and we deleted several thousand lines on that basis with confidence. The cost is that styling a child component from a parent is deliberately awkward, which people complain about, and the intended answer is that the child should expose a variant rather than the parent reaching in.

The shared component package publishes a minor release every second Tuesday whether or not much has landed, and consuming applications upgrade on their own schedule from there. Publishing on merge was the earlier model and it produced a version number nobody could reason about, dozens of releases a month, so consumers pinned an old one and stayed there, which is the outcome a fast release cadence is supposed to prevent.
