A predictable train means an application team can plan an upgrade, and it means breaking changes accumulate into a boundary that can be described in one changelog rather than being scattered across thirty patches. Anything that has to reach consumers sooner goes out as a patch off the previous tag, and in two years that has happened four times, all of them accessibility or security fixes. Breaking changes wait for a major, which happens roughly twice a year and comes with a codemod, because a migration guide that asks people to hand-edit hundreds of call sites simply does not get followed.

The dark theme is a second block of custom property values applied by an attribute on the root element, and no component contains a conditional for which theme is active. That constraint is the design. The first attempt threaded a theme value through the component tree and had components choose colours from it, which meant every new component was a fresh opportunity to forget the dark case, and dark mode was permanently about ninety percent finished with a rotating cast of missing screens. Moving the whole decision to the custom property layer means a component that uses tokens is themed correctly without its author having thought about themes at all, and a component that hard-codes a colour is visibly broken in review rather than subtly wrong later. The theme attribute is set before first paint by a tiny inline script reading the stored preference, since applying it after hydration produces a flash of the wrong theme that people report as a bug every single time. Images and illustrations that cannot be tokenised carry a paired asset instead.

Icons are authored as individual SVG files, compiled into one sprite sheet at build time, and referenced by symbol name through a small component. They are not loaded individually and they are not pasted inline into components. Individual requests were the original approach and produced dozens of tiny fetches on first render, each with its own overhead and none of them cacheable as a unit. Pasting markup inline solved that and created a worse problem, which was that the same icon existed in slightly different forms in a dozen places, so a change to the stroke weight was a search-and-replace exercise that never quite finished. The sprite gives one artefact, one cache entry and one definition per icon. The component enforces an accessible name or an explicit decorative marking, which is the second reason it exists, because a bare icon with no label is invisible to a screen reader and that was consistently our most common accessibility finding. Adding an icon means adding a file and nothing else; the build discovers it.

The style attribute is allowed for values that genuinely cannot be known at authoring time, a computed position for a floating element, a progress bar width, a chart dimension measured from the container, and for nothing else. Everything static belongs in a stylesheet. The distinction is not aesthetic. Inline styles win almost every specificity contest, which means a component that sets one cannot be adjusted by the page it sits on without an override that everybody agrees is ugly, and they are invisible to the tooling that finds unused styles or checks contrast. Once a few components carried inline styling for convenience, the fastest way to make anything look right became adding another inline style on top, and the stylesheet stopped describing the application. Review is where this is caught, and the question asked is simply whether the value could have been known when the file was written; if it could, it goes in the module. Animation is the awkward edge, and the convention there is that the values interpolate but the properties involved are declared in CSS.

A `stylelint` rule fails the build on any literal colour value in component styles, hex, rgb or named, and directs the author to the token that matches or, if none does, to the process for adding one. The allowlist is short: the reset file, the token definitions themselves, and two legacy screens carrying a documented exemption with a ticket. Before the rule, the codebase contained over four hundred distinct colour literals, most of them a shade or two away from a token that already existed, and the practical consequence was that a palette change was impossible to do completely. Nobody added those literals carelessly, either; each one was somebody matching a mockup at a moment when finding the right token was slower than typing the value, which is exactly the kind of small friction a mechanical check is good at fixing. The rule's error message naming the nearest token was what made it tolerable, and adding that message cut the rate of exemption requests to almost nothing. Gradients and shadows are covered by the same rule for the same reason.

There is one grid, it lives in the design system package, and page layouts compose it rather than declaring their own column arithmetic. Historically each screen worked out its own widths and gutters, which looked fine individually and meant that two pages side by side in a screenshot never quite lined up, and a change to the page margin was a change to every file that had encoded it. Centralising it also settled an argument that used to recur, namely what a full-width section means when the viewport is very wide, because the answer is now a property of the grid rather than a judgement made independently on each page. Components are expected to fill the space they are given and never to set their own outer width, which is the rule people break most often and the one review looks for first. Breakpoints belong to the grid too, so a component reasoning about the viewport directly is a signal that something is being solved at the wrong level. Exceptions exist for the marketing pages, which are laid out by hand for visual effect.

Browser errors are sampled in the client before anything is sent, in `apps/web/src/observability/errors.ts`: five percent of sessions by default, one hundred percent of sessions that have entered checkout or payment, a hard cap of twenty events per session, and a fingerprint dedupe on message plus top frame with exponential backoff so a repeated failure reports once rather than every time. The decision is per session rather than per event, and that detail is the one people miss. Per-event sampling was the first implementation and it was worthless for debugging: you received a scattering of unrelated fragments and could never reconstruct what a single user had actually done. Hashing the session identifier means a sampled-in session reports its whole sequence, so the trail leading to the error survives. What forced the change was a release with a render loop that emitted roughly nine million events in forty minutes, burned the monthly quota inside the first hour, and got the whole organisation rate-limited by the vendor, so a genuine payment defect found that same afternoon never appeared in the tool at all. The second reason is just as decisive: most raw volume is cross-origin noise from extensions, reported as an opaque message with no usable stack, which we cannot act on and would be paying to store. Sampling rates are config, not code; changing one needs no deploy.

The reporting hook inspects the originating script URL on each event and discards anything whose origin is not ours or one of the four registered third parties, with browser extension protocols denied outright. The list lives beside the third-party registry so adding a vendor updates both. What this filters is not noise in the statistical sense but events that are not about our code: a price-comparison extension rewriting the DOM, an enterprise security agent injecting a shim, an ad blocker removing an element a handler expected. Every one of those produces a stack whose frames belong to somebody else, and no amount of investigation on our side can lead anywhere. Keeping them was actively harmful rather than merely wasteful, because the top of the error list by count was consistently a message with no stack at all, and new joiners spent their first triage rotation trying to chase it. Events with no attributable origin, which is what a cross-origin failure looks like without the right response header, are counted in a single aggregate metric so we can tell whether that population is changing, but they are not stored individually.

The build uploads source maps to the error tracker as a release artefact and then deletes them from the deployed bundle directory, so stack traces resolve to real file and line numbers in the tool while the maps themselves are never served to the public. The `//# sourceMappingURL` comment is stripped in the production build for the same reason. Publishing them makes the browser devtools experience nicer for anyone poking at the site and hands over a readable copy of the entire front end, including comments and internal endpoint names, which we would rather not do for free. The upload is a build step rather than a manual one because it has to happen for every release without exception: a missing map does not fail anything visibly, it just means that in three weeks, when a rare error finally has enough occurrences to be worth investigating, its stack is a column offset into a minified line. Maps are retained for ninety days matching event retention, and the upload is keyed by the same release identifier the runtime reports.

The release string reported by the client is the seven-character commit SHA, injected at build time, and it is the same value that appears in the deployment record and the container image tag. Using the semantic version was the earlier convention and it broke the one workflow the field exists for, which is answering whether an error started with a particular change. A version number covers many commits and is applied at tag time rather than at build time, so the mapping from a version to a diff is a lookup with judgement in it, whereas a SHA is the diff. The tracker's first-seen and last-seen release fields then become directly actionable: a new issue whose first release is a known SHA gives you the change list in one command. This also makes a regression that reappears legible, since the same issue showing a gap in releases and then returning tells you the fix was reverted or a branch was rebased over it, which has happened twice. Deploys record the SHA and the deploying user, and the error tool links back to that record.

Rejections that reach the global handler are tagged distinctly from thrown errors rather than being folded in with them, and they are triaged with a different default assumption. A thrown error is usually a defect in the code that threw. An unhandled rejection is usually a missing await or a promise chain whose failure branch was never written, which means the interesting location is not where the rejection surfaced but where the promise was created, and the stack you get points at the former. Separating the two stopped the triage rotation from applying the wrong mental model to half the queue. There is a second reason, which is that a rejection carrying a non-error value produces a useless report, so the handler wraps anything that is not an error object and records the original value as context. The habit that came out of this is that a fire-and-forget call must have an explicit failure handler even if that handler only records, since the alternative is an operation that silently does not happen and a report nobody can locate.

Field performance measurements are gathered from ten percent of page views, chosen by a stable hash so the same visitor is consistently in or out, and sent as a single beacon on page hide rather than as separate events. Ten percent was chosen by working backwards from what we need statistically, which is a stable seventy-fifth percentile per route per day. The busy routes reach that comfortably; the two lowest-traffic screens do not, and rather than raising the global rate we accept a weekly figure for those. Collecting from everybody was the first version and produced an enormous volume of measurements that were used to compute exactly the same percentiles to a precision nobody could act on. Sending on page hide rather than on load matters more than the rate does, because the layout shift and interaction metrics keep accumulating for the whole visit and a beacon sent at load captures a fraction of the truth. The measurements are segmented by connection type and device class, since an aggregate over both hides the population the numbers are supposed to be about.

The front-end team looks at its error rate once a week in the standing sync, and the review has one rule: the top issue by affected-user count gets an owner before the meeting ends, or an explicit written decision that it is acceptable. Ranking by affected users rather than by event count was the change that made the meeting useful, because event count is dominated by whichever bug fires in a loop and that bug is often trivial, while an issue hitting a few hundred distinct people once each is almost always something worth fixing. The explicit acceptance option is deliberate. Some errors are genuinely not worth fixing, and without a way to say so the list grows a permanent layer of sediment that everybody scrolls past, which is how a list stops being read at all. Accepted issues are muted with a reason and a date to reconsider. Nothing here pages anyone; the escalation path for a front-end failure serious enough to page runs through the same incident process as everything else, triggered by the availability signals rather than by this review.

A failed request while the browser reports itself offline, or one that fails during page unload, is recorded as a connectivity event and never as an application error. Those two categories were once a large fraction of the reported volume and none of it was actionable, because a request that fails when the network is gone is the correct behaviour of a system working as designed. Worse, they moved with the weather rather than with our releases, so the error rate had a daily rhythm driven by commuters on trains, and any attempt to alert on the rate had to be tuned so loosely that it would not have caught anything real. The connectivity counter is still worth having, since a sudden jump in it that is not explained by time of day usually means a certificate or a CDN problem rather than a mass outbreak of bad reception. What the user sees is unaffected either way: the interface shows an offline state and retries when connectivity returns, which is a product behaviour rather than a reporting one.

Issues are organised into projects by the surface they occur on, the customer web application, the embedded widget, the admin console, rather than by which team owns the code involved. Team ownership changes, sometimes twice a year, and every reorganisation under the old arrangement meant migrating issue history or losing it, which made the historical view useless exactly when a long-running intermittent bug needed one. A surface is a stable fact about where the failure happened. Routing to the right people is handled separately by ownership rules on the code path, which can be updated in an afternoon without touching anything historical. The other benefit was unexpected and turned out to be the more valuable one: grouping by surface makes it obvious when a single defect is hitting several surfaces at once, which is the signature of a shared package problem and used to take days to notice because each team saw only their own slice and each concluded independently that it was something local.

Every branch that used to ask which browser this is now asks whether the thing it needs exists. `src/lib/capabilities.ts` answers those questions in one place, exporting boolean checks built on `'IntersectionObserver' in window`, `CSS.supports()` and similar probes, evaluated once at start-up. Reading `navigator.userAgent` in the application is a lint failure, with two allowlisted files: the server-side bot classifier and the download page that picks a desktop installer. What forced this was a version regex in the old `utils/browser.ts` that had been written assuming a two-digit major version. When Chrome's major went to three digits the parse produced a number small enough that our comparison concluded the browser was ancient, and the payment button was replaced by an upgrade notice for a large share of traffic on a Tuesday morning. It lasted six hours and was found by support tickets rather than by an alarm, because from the server's side nothing was failing. The deeper reason is that the agent string has been deliberately misleading for decades, since every engine claims to be several others, so parsing it is guesswork that ages badly. Polyfills are pulled in by dynamic import only when a check fails, which means current browsers download none of them, and the rule for new code is to test the capability you actually need rather than the browser you believe has it.

Components that need to lay themselves out differently in a narrow space now query their own container instead of receiving a size hint from whatever renders them. The old arrangement passed a variant down as a property, which worked and quietly encoded the parent's knowledge of the child's internals: the parent had to know that this card behaves differently below some width, and every new placement of that card was another place to get the hint wrong. The bugs it produced were all the same shape, a component used in a new context looking correct in review at desktop width and wrong on a phone, because the hint had not been passed. Moving the decision into the component makes it a property of the component rather than of its placement, and it makes a component genuinely reusable in a sidebar without anybody thinking about it. The migration was done component by component as each was next touched, rather than as a sweep, and a handful of older screens still pass the property. Nothing depends on both mechanisms at once, which was the one rule during the transition.

The analytics pipeline classifies traffic as automated using a maintained device and agent database, refreshed monthly as part of the pipeline's dependency update, applied server side in the ingestion job rather than in the browser. This is the one place a user agent string is still parsed on purpose, and it is a good fit for the job for a reason worth stating: the goal is not to decide what the client can do, it is to label what the client claims to be, and for crawlers and scripted traffic the claim is usually accurate because most of them identify themselves honestly. The classification feeds session counts, conversion rates and the browser share figures, and getting it wrong in the ignorable direction inflates every number in the funnel. Before the database was introduced we used a hand-maintained list of substrings that was six months out of date and was overcounting sessions by a noticeable margin, which made a marketing campaign look better than it was. Unmatched agents are labelled unknown rather than assumed human, and the unknown share is monitored because a jump in it usually means the database needs a refresh.

Application start-up runs inside a single guarded entry that catches anything thrown before the first render and replaces the blank page with a plain apology, a reload control and the request identifier. Without it, a failure during boot produces a white screen, which from the user's side is indistinguishable from the site being down and from our side is nearly invisible, since the reporting client is often one of the things that had not initialised yet. The fallback is intentionally built from static markup embedded in the document rather than from anything the bundle provides, because a fallback that depends on the code that just failed is not a fallback. It also posts a minimal beacon directly, without the usual client, so a boot failure is at least counted. This was written after a release where a configuration value the application reads at start-up came back malformed and every visitor got a blank page for eleven minutes, with the only signal being a drop in a downstream metric that nobody was watching closely at that hour.

All reads and writes to local and session storage go through the helpers in `src/lib/storage.ts`, which swallow the quota and security exceptions and fall back to an in-memory map for the lifetime of the tab. Direct use of `window.localStorage` fails the lint step. The problem being solved is that storage access throws rather than returning null in several real situations: private browsing modes, third-party context with storage partitioning, a full quota, and enterprise policies that disable it. Those exceptions arrive from what looks like an innocuous line, frequently during module initialisation, so the failure took the whole application down rather than degrading the one feature that wanted to remember a preference. The wrapper also gives one place to namespace keys, which stopped two features quietly sharing a key name, and one place to serialise, which stopped the recurring bug of a value written as an object and read back as the string that object stringifies to. Anything that must survive a reload is written to the server instead; storage here is for convenience state only.

The duplicated float and old-syntax flex declarations that shadowed the modern layout rules were removed in a single change rather than being cleaned up gradually as files were touched. Piecemeal removal had been the plan for over a year and had progressed almost nowhere, because each individual fallback is small, nobody wants to own the risk of deleting something in a file they are visiting for another reason, and there is never a good moment. Doing it at once made the risk visible and reviewable: one change, one round of visual comparison across the whole screenshot baseline, one person watching the error rate afterwards. It also produced a stylesheet that finally reads as one thing, which matters more than the bytes saved, because the shadowed declarations were a constant source of confusion about which rule was actually in effect. The audit that justified it looked at the support data first and confirmed nothing in the current audience needed any of it. Nothing broke, which was mildly anticlimactic given how long the change had been avoided.

Keyboard handling reads `event.key` and, where physical position matters, `event.code`; `keyCode` and `which` are banned by lint and the last occurrences were removed with the shortcut rewrite. Beyond the obvious fact that the old properties are deprecated, the numeric codes were actively wrong for a product used across several countries: they describe a position on a notional keyboard, so a shortcut chosen because it sat under a finger on one layout landed somewhere unreachable on another, and a customer in a warehouse using a Nordic layout could not trigger the scan shortcut at all. Named values also make the code readable, since a comparison against a spelled-out key name needs no comment where a bare number always did. Modifier state is read from the event's boolean properties rather than tracked across key events, which removed a persistent bug where a modifier released while the window was unfocused left the application believing it was still held. Shortcuts are registered in one table so that conflicts are detectable and the help overlay can be generated from it.

Dates, times, numbers and currencies are formatted with the platform internationalisation API and its formatter objects, and the formatting library that used to do it was removed entirely. The library was not bad; it was simply carrying a large table of locale data that the browser already ships, in every bundle, for every visitor. Two other things came with the switch that mattered more than size. The platform formatter follows the user's own locale and time zone settings rather than a value we guessed, which was the source of a recurring complaint from customers whose operations straddle a time zone boundary and who kept seeing timestamps an hour off from what their own systems said. And relative time, the "three days ago" strings, is handled natively with correct pluralisation in every language we ship, where the previous approach had a hand-written English rule and awkward workarounds elsewhere. Formatter objects are constructed once and reused, because constructing one per row in a long list is measurably slow. Parsing, as opposed to formatting, is still done from the interchange format on the server.

The application checks at boot whether it is framed and, if the embedding origin is not on the short allowlist, stops and renders a message with a link to open it directly. The response header that instructs browsers to refuse framing is set as well, and the runtime check exists because headers get lost: a misconfigured proxy in front of a customer's deployment stripped it once, and the header is also the wrong tool for the case where we want to permit exactly two partner origins rather than none. The threat is the ordinary one, an invisible frame over a hostile page collecting clicks that the user believes are landing somewhere else, which is worth defending against in a product where a click can release a shipment. The allowlist is configuration rather than code so a partner can be added without a release, and both current entries are partner portals that embed the tracking view. The check runs before any credentialed request is made, which is the ordering that matters, since a session established inside a hostile frame is already the problem.

Versioning is enabled on every bucket that holds data we cannot regenerate, with a lifecycle rule expiring non-current versions after thirty days and cleaning up incomplete multipart uploads after seven. The trigger was a deployment script whose destination prefix came from an unset variable, so it uploaded a build over the top of a directory of customer documents, and the recovery consisted of a very uncomfortable afternoon and a partial reconstruction from a downstream system. Versioning turns that event into a scripted restore of the previous versions. Thirty days is a deliberate compromise: long enough that a mistake discovered at the end of a month is still recoverable, short enough that the storage overhead stays in single-digit percentages, and it is measured from when the version became non-current rather than from when it was written, which is the setting people get backwards. The multipart cleanup was added after we found several hundred gigabytes of abandoned upload parts, invisible in the console's object listing and billed all the same. Versioning is not enabled on the derived-artifact buckets, since regenerating is cheaper than storing history.

Local seed data is generated, never copied. `make seed` runs `tools/seed/build_seed.py`, which drives a deterministic generator: every random draw comes from a seed pinned at 1729 in `seed/config.toml`, so two laptops that run it against the same schema produce byte-identical rows down to the tenant UUIDs. That determinism is the point: a bug report saying tenant 0004, invoice 12 means the same record on every machine. The generator emits roughly fourteen thousand rows across sixty tables and it is built to be awkward on purpose: three tenants on different plan tiers, one stuck mid-migration with the old address shape, one with a suspended subscription and unpaid dunning history, and one deliberately hostile tenant full of unicode names, negative line items and a note field a hundred thousand characters long. The result lands in `seed/dev_snapshot.sql.gz`, about eleven megabytes, tracked with git-lfs and rebuilt by a weekly workflow that fails if the schema fingerprint in `seed/schema.lock` no longer matches head. None of it derives from production. We used to hand new engineers a scrubbed customer dump, and that stopped when one turned up in a personal cloud backup during an access review. The values were scrubbed but the company names and volumes were not, which was enough to make it a reportable question. Generating from a fixed seed removed the question entirely.

Tests build the rows they need and no others. Every model has a factory in `tests/factories/`, each test constructs exactly the objects its assertions touch, and there is no shared module-scope fixture that inserts a standing cast of customers for everyone to lean on. We ran the other way for about a year and it rotted the suite. A single `sample_org` fixture accumulated attributes because every new test needed one more field set on it, until it had a trial expiry, a suspended card, two seats and a legacy tariff, and half the suite was asserting against a state no real account had ever been in. Worse, tests started depending on each other's mutations, so reordering the file broke four of them. The rule now is that a test which needs a suspended subscription creates a suspended subscription in its own body, in the two or three lines that takes, and a reader can see the entire setup without opening another file. Factories carry only the fields required to satisfy database constraints; anything else is passed explicitly at the call site. A twice-weekly job runs the suite under a shuffled order to catch anything that quietly reintroduced cross-test coupling.

Staging carries a scrubbed copy of production, refreshed every Sunday night by the `staging-refresh` pipeline. The job restores the most recent physical backup into an isolated account, runs `tools/scrub/apply.py` against it before anything is allowed to reach the staging network, then swaps the restored cluster in behind the endpoint. Scrubbing rewrites names, email addresses and phone numbers to per-row deterministic pseudonyms, replaces payment tokens with sandbox tokens, blanks free-text notes entirely, and truncates the event tables to the trailing thirty days so the refresh finishes inside its four-hour window. The scrub runs before the network swap because of the time it did not: an early version scrubbed in place on a cluster already reachable from staging, and a background job there sent real reminder emails to about nine hundred real customers in the eleven minutes before the pass finished. Staging outbound mail is now pinned to a sink domain as a second layer. The refresh exists because performance work needs realistic table sizes and cardinalities, which no generated dataset reproduces honestly.

The demo environment does not track whatever the current development dataset happens to look like. It carries a curated tenant maintained by the solutions team, frozen between releases and versioned as its own artefact with its own changelog, refreshed only when someone has decided the story it tells needs to change. The reason is that a demo is a narrative. The account has to have a plausible history, invoices arriving in a sensible order, a support thread that reads like a real customer wrote it, and numbers on the dashboard that look like a business rather than like a test harness. Randomly assembled content cannot do that, and every attempt to make it do that turned into weeks of tuning nobody wanted to own. It also has to be stable, because sales rehearse against it and a demo that quietly changes under a rehearsed script is worse than no demo at all. Engineers can look at it and can reproduce bugs against a copy of it, but changing it requires the owning team's sign-off, and it is never used as a starting point for local work.

Wiping a local database is a two-step ritual and that is deliberate. `make db-reset` stops the local Postgres service, deletes the data directory, starts a clean instance, applies every migration in order and stops there, leaving an empty schema with no rows in it. Loading anything into that schema is a separate command you have to type yourself. We split them after enough people burned an afternoon on a bug that turned out to be their own half-applied local state, and after the opposite failure: a combined target that silently reloaded data made it impossible to test the migration path itself, which is the thing that actually breaks in production. Keeping reset schema-only means you can reset, apply the pending revision, and see exactly what a fresh production apply would do. The target refuses to run if `DATABASE_URL` points anywhere that is not localhost, a guard added the week someone ran it with a staging URL still exported in their shell from an earlier debugging session. A reset takes about forty seconds, most of it migrations.

Customer data does not leave the production account, and that is a boundary rather than a preference. There is no path by which a live table, a backup, or an export of either can be copied onto a laptop, into a scratch project, or into a vendor tool, and the network and identity controls are arranged so that the easy thing is also the allowed thing: production credentials are short-lived and only mint inside the production perimeter, and the object store holding backups denies reads to any principal outside it. When someone genuinely needs to look at real records to understand a defect, they do it through a read-only session inside that perimeter, with the query logged and attributed to them. The rule came out of a long argument that ended when we accepted the plain reading of our own customer contracts: we promise that data stays in one place under one set of controls, and every convenient exception erodes that promise without being written down anywhere a customer could see it. The practical effect on engineering is that nobody debugs against real rows on their own machine, and every workflow has to be designed knowing that.

Binary test assets live in object storage, not in git. The PDFs the invoice renderer is compared against, sample bank statement uploads, the reference PNGs the visual diff suite uses, and the fixed WAV files the transcription adapter is tested with are all pulled from the `halyard-fixtures` bucket by `tools/fixtures/sync.py`, which reads `fixtures.lock`, downloads by content hash into `.cache/fixtures/` and verifies each digest. The lock file is what gets reviewed and committed; the payload never is. We moved after the repository crossed two gigabytes and a fresh clone on a hotel connection took eleven minutes, most of it fetching successive revisions of a hundred-and-forty-megabyte sample statement that only ever mattered in its current form. Rewriting history was not on the table, so the old blobs are still down there and clones are shallow by default in CI. The sync step is idempotent and runs from the same setup target as everything else, so nobody has to remember it, and a missing digest fails loudly with the bucket path rather than as a confusing file-not-found deep inside a test.

The local search index is treated as derived state and is rebuilt from the database on demand. `bin/dev reindex` truncates the local OpenSearch indices and streams every row through the same indexer the production consumer uses, which takes about ninety seconds against a normal working dataset. Nothing else writes to the local index and no snapshot of it exists anywhere, on purpose. Keeping it derived means the indexer is exercised constantly instead of only in production, and mapping changes get caught locally: change an analyser, rebuild, and if the document builder disagrees with the mapping the rebuild fails immediately rather than silently producing an index nobody can query correctly. It also removes a whole category of confusing local state, where search results reflect rows deleted three days ago. The one cost is that the rebuild is not incremental, so anyone working on relevance runs it repeatedly; `REINDEX_TENANTS` takes a comma-separated list to narrow the pass to a single tenant and brings it down to a few seconds.

Every export that leaves the support tooling passes through one anonymisation library, and nothing is allowed to implement its own pass. Support engineers frequently need to hand an attachment or a record set to an engineer, and for a while each surface did that differently: one redacted email addresses but not the reply-to headers, another masked card fingerprints but left the billing address intact, and a third had no redaction at all because it had been written as a quick internal helper and then quietly became load-bearing. Consolidating gave us one place to reason about what is sensitive, one place to update when a new field type appears, and one place to test. The library is deny-by-default, so a field it has never been told about is dropped rather than passed through, which means adding a column to a table cannot silently widen what an export reveals. Getting a new field allowed requires a small declaration and a reviewer from the data protection rota. The friction is real and intentional, because the failure it prevents is invisible until someone outside notices it.

The compose file in the root of the repository is unsupported and carries a header saying so. The supported way to bring the stack up is `bin/dev up`, and we made that switch for three reasons that all came from measurement rather than taste. First, speed: with the application source bind-mounted into a Linux VM on macOS, the integration suite took eleven and a half minutes against roughly two minutes running the same tests natively against the same services, and file watching was unreliable enough that people restarted containers instead of trusting reload. Second, drift: the compose topology was a hand-maintained guess at production and it went stale silently, most memorably by pinning Postgres 14.6 for eight months after production had moved to 16, which cost an engineer a full day chasing a generated-column behaviour that only existed on their laptop. Third, blast radius of the abstraction: when something failed inside a container, debugging meant learning the container's networking before you could get to the actual bug, and that tax fell hardest on the people with the least context. We keep the file because two contributors on Windows still rely on it and CI images are built from adjacent definitions, but nothing in `docs/` references it, and a check in the docs workflow fails if that changes.

Language runtimes and CLI tools are pinned in `.mise.toml`, which lists the Python, Node and Go versions along with `terraform`, `just` and the protobuf compiler. Activating the directory installs exactly those versions and shims them onto the path, so two people in the same directory run the same binaries whether or not they installed anything themselves. Before this, the version of Node someone happened to have was a genuine source of pull requests: a lockfile regenerated under a different major would reorder and re-resolve half the tree, and reviewers could not see the real change underneath the noise. The pinned versions are the same ones the CI images are built from, and a check compares the two on every run so they cannot drift apart quietly. Upgrading a pinned version is an ordinary pull request with the CI image change in the same commit, which makes the upgrade reviewable and, more importantly, revertable in one step. Anything not in the file is fair game to install however you like; the pinned set is deliberately small and covers only what affects build output.

Postgres, Redis and the message broker run as ordinary background services on the developer's own machine, installed through the platform package manager and managed by `bin/dev services`. Postgres listens on 5433 rather than the default so it cannot collide with an unrelated install someone already had, Redis on 6380 for the same reason, and both are configured from checked-in files under `dev/services/` so settings that matter, like `max_connections` and the logging of statements slower than two hundred milliseconds, are the same for everyone. Data directories live under `~/.local/share/aldercross/` and survive reboots, which matters more than it sounds: keeping a working dataset across a week of debugging is the difference between chasing a bug and rebuilding an environment. Startup from cold is around three seconds and attaching `psql` needs no wrapper, so the tooling everyone already knows works directly. The services are deliberately single-node and unreplicated; nothing about production topology is reproduced here, and anything that depends on replication behaviour is tested in the shared integration environment instead.

Integration tests in CI run inside containers, and that is not in tension with how anyone works locally. The pipeline needs an environment it can construct from nothing, identically, on a fresh runner, thousands of times a week, and throw away without leaving residue; a container image built from a pinned digest does that better than anything else available. The runner starts the service images the job declares, waits on their health checks, runs the suite against them, and destroys everything at the end, so a poisoned state cannot leak into the next build. That is the property CI actually needs, and it is a different property from the one a developer's machine needs, which is fast feedback on an incremental change against state they can inspect and keep. Conflating those two requirements is what produces setups that satisfy neither. The images are built from the same base as production images so library versions match, and the job publishes the resolved digests into the build log, which is what people check first when a test passes locally and fails in the pipeline.

There is a devcontainer definition in `.devcontainer/`, and it exists for exactly one audience: the two contributors who work on Windows and anyone who needs a throwaway environment for a security review of an unfamiliar branch. It is not the default and it is not what the onboarding path installs. Keeping it narrow is the point. A second fully supported environment doubles the surface anyone maintaining developer tooling has to keep working, and in practice the second one is always the one that is broken when someone reaches for it, because it is exercised weekly rather than hourly. Scoping it to a named audience means we know who to ask when it breaks and we know the cost of it lapsing. The definition is checked by a scheduled build that boots it and runs the unit suite, so at least the basic path stays honest, and the readme in that directory says plainly that anything beyond running tests is untested territory. Anyone using it who hits something broken files it like a normal bug rather than working around it silently.

Production images are built from a distroless base with no shell, no package manager and a non-root user. The build is a multi-stage Dockerfile: the first stage installs build dependencies and compiles wheels, the final stage copies only the virtual environment and the application tree onto the runtime base, which brought the published image from about nine hundred megabytes down to a hundred and ninety and cut the vulnerability count reported by the scanner by most of its length, because most of those findings were in utilities we never invoked. The absence of a shell is the part people notice first, since you cannot exec in and poke around. That was a deliberate trade: debugging happens through logs, metrics and a sidecar started explicitly for the purpose, which is slower on the rare occasion and safer every other day, because a compromised process has nothing to pivot with. Images are pinned by digest in the deployment manifests, never by tag, after a rebuilt upstream tag once changed the OpenSSL version under a service without any change on our side.

The dev runner starts services in a declared order with real readiness checks between the stages, rather than starting everything at once and hoping. The order is written in `dev/processes.yaml`: the datastore layer first, then the migration step, then the broker, then the API, then the worker fleet, then the web dev server. Each stage has a readiness probe with a fifteen-second budget, and the runner refuses to start the next stage until the current one answers. The rule came from a stream of confusing first-run failures where the API booted before migrations finished and crash-looped against a table that did not exist yet, which reads to a newcomer as a broken repository rather than a race. Failures now name the stage that did not come up and print the last twenty lines of its log inline, which is the single change that reduced setup questions the most. Restarting one process without restarting the tree is `bin/dev restart <name>`, and the runner tears everything down in reverse order on exit so nothing is left holding a port.

Local traffic goes through one shared reverse proxy that terminates TLS for every service, so everything is reached over https on a real hostname instead of a plain port. Certificates come from a locally trusted authority installed once during setup, and the hostnames follow the same pattern the production ones do, which matters because a surprising amount of behaviour is hostname and scheme sensitive: cookie attributes marked secure, strict same-site rules, the redirect the identity provider will accept, the service worker registration, and the mixed-content rules the browser applies. Testing any of that against an insecure loopback port means testing a different code path from the one users get, and we found that out through a login bug that only appeared in production because the cookie was rejected there and quietly accepted locally. Running one proxy rather than per-service certificates keeps the trust store clean and means adding a service is a two-line configuration entry rather than a certificate ceremony.

We spent most of a quarter trying to run the platform on a local Kubernetes cluster with a live-sync tool in front of it, and then we stopped and deleted the configuration. The pitch was parity with production, and it was a real pitch: the manifests are the deployment contract and being able to exercise them on a laptop would have caught a class of mistakes that currently surface in the shared environment. What killed it was the cost per iteration. A code change took the better part of a minute to reach a running pod even on a good day, the cluster ate enough memory that a browser and an editor alongside it made the machine unpleasant, and roughly a third of the team hit a networking or storage problem that needed someone else's afternoon to fix. Parity turned out to be partial anyway, since the identity, secret and load balancer layers were all substituted with local stand-ins, so the failures it caught were not the failures we actually have. We kept one useful piece from the experiment, a manifest validation step that runs in the pipeline, and dropped the rest.

Environment variable names follow a fixed shape and `tools/env_lint.py` fails the build when they do not. Upper snake case throughout. A service prefix comes first, matching the service directory, so `LEDGER_`, `GATEWAY_`, `HARBORLANE_`; anything shared across services carries `PLATFORM_`. No environment ever appears in a name, so there is no `PROD_DB_URL`, because the value differs per environment and the name must not. The suffix carries the type and this is the part that is enforced hardest: durations end in `_SECONDS`, `_MS` or `_DAYS` and the unit in the name is the unit of the value; booleans end in `_ENABLED` and accept only `true` or `false`; endpoints end in `_URL` and must include a scheme; counts end in `_MAX` or `_LIMIT`; and anything secret ends in `_TOKEN`, `_SECRET`, `_PASSWORD` or `_KEY`. Two incidents wrote those rules. A bare `TIMEOUT=30` meant seconds in the gateway and milliseconds in the ledger client, and a retry loop that should have waited half a minute hammered a recovering dependency thirty milliseconds apart until it fell over again. Separately, a variable called `DB_CREDS` was printed in full at boot because the log redactor matches on the secret suffixes and had nothing to match on. New names are declared in `config/env.schema.yaml`, and the linter checks the declaration and the code reference agree.

Secrets are fetched at process start from the secret store and handed to the process by the launcher; they are never written into an image layer, a manifest, or a build argument. The entrypoint exchanges the workload identity token for a short-lived lease, reads the paths listed in the deployment's `secrets:` block, and execs the application with those values in its environment, so the running process sees ordinary variables while nothing durable on disk ever held them. Leases last one hour and renew in the background; a renewal failure kills the process rather than letting it run on a value the store has since revoked. This replaced a period when a handful of values lived in the deployment repository, encrypted at rest but decryptable by anyone who could read the repository, which turned out to be most of engineering. The rotation story is the real win: rotating a database password used to mean finding every copy of it, and now it means writing one new version and rolling the deployments that read it. Nothing about how the values are spelled changes here; only where they come from.

Every setting a service reads must be declared before the code can read it. The declaration lives with the service and lists the setting, its type, whether it is required, a default where one is allowed, and a one-line description of what it does; reading anything undeclared raises at import time rather than returning nothing at the moment it is first needed. That ordering is the whole benefit. An undeclared setting used to fail at whatever hour the first request happened to reach the branch that read it, usually as a confusing downstream error rather than a missing configuration message. The declarations also generate the reference page in the internal handbook, so the documentation cannot lag behind the code by construction, and reviewers see a configuration surface change as an explicit diff rather than as an incidental line inside a function. Removing a setting follows the same route in reverse: delete the reads, ship, then delete the declaration, so a rollback never lands on a process that will refuse to boot.

A required setting has no default and a missing one stops the process before it accepts traffic. The loader collects every required setting that is absent, prints all of them together with the declaration file and line where each is defined, and exits non-zero rather than failing on the first one, because discovering four missing values across four deploy attempts is a bad afternoon. The temptation this policy resists is the harmless-looking fallback. We shipped a service where the cache endpoint quietly defaulted to localhost, and in production it happily connected to nothing, ran every request against the origin, and stayed green on every health check while p99 latency tripled. Nobody had made a decision; a default made it for us and hid it. Optional settings still exist, and they are genuinely optional in the sense that the service is correct without them, which is a much smaller set than people expect. The health endpoint reports the configuration fingerprint the process booted with, so an operator can tell whether a pod is running the values they think it is.

Feature toggles do not live in the environment. Anything that gates behaviour for a subset of users, or that anyone might want to flip during an incident, is declared in the flag service and read through the flag client; the environment is for values that identify and connect a process, such as endpoints, pool sizes, credentials and the deployment identity. The split follows from what each mechanism can do. Changing an environment variable requires a deploy of every replica, takes minutes, cannot be scoped to a tenant and is invisible to anyone not reading deployment manifests. A flag flips in seconds, targets a cohort, records who flipped it and when, and can be reverted by someone with no deploy access at three in the morning. Mixing them produced the worst version of both: a rollout gate that was an environment variable meant a partial rollout required a separate deployment per cohort, and a connection string that had drifted into the flag service meant a database endpoint could be edited from a web console by anyone with the link.

The local `.env` file is generated and the first line of it says so. `bin/dev env` reads your identity token, pulls the development values you are entitled to from the secret store, merges them with the non-secret defaults in `dev/env.defaults`, and writes the file with mode 600. Hand-editing it works until the next regeneration overwrites your change, which is exactly the behaviour we want: a value you need permanently belongs in the defaults file where everyone gets it, and a value you need for ten minutes belongs in your shell. Before this, the file was passed around as an attachment, and its contents diverged so far from reality that new engineers were debugging settings that had been dead for a year, including a queue endpoint pointing at a broker that had been decommissioned. The generator also prunes: any variable present in the file but absent from the schema is removed with a note, which is how stale entries stop accumulating. The file is in `.gitignore` and a pre-commit hook rejects it if someone forces the issue.

Configuration is read once at startup and never re-read while the process runs, so changing a value means rolling the deployment. Hot reload was tried and removed. The reason is that a long-running process which re-reads configuration has two states nobody tracks: what it booted with and what it currently believes, and during a partial rollout of a configuration change you can have replicas in both, which is the exact scenario where a debugging session goes wrong. It also makes every value a mutable global as far as the code is concerned, which quietly forbids caching a derived setting anywhere, and derived settings are common. The cost of the rule is that a configuration change takes a rolling restart, roughly ninety seconds across the fleet, which is acceptable because genuinely urgent behaviour changes belong in the flag system and that path is unaffected. Consumers of a setting can therefore treat it as a constant, and the loader freezes the parsed structure so an accidental write raises rather than diverging one replica from the rest.

A given setting may be defined in exactly one layer, and the loader raises on a duplicate rather than resolving it. There is a precedence order on paper, with the process environment above the deployment manifest above the checked-in defaults, but relying on that order in practice is what we stopped doing. The incident was a pool size defined both in the manifest and in a base configuration file; someone reduced the file value during a database incident, nothing changed because the manifest still won, and the next twenty minutes were spent looking at the wrong layer. Failing loudly turns that into a startup error naming both locations, which is a thirty-second fix instead of a twenty-minute misdiagnosis. The rule has a real cost, since sharing a base value across services now needs an explicit include rather than a silent override, and one team's deployment took two passes to untangle when it landed. It has held anyway, because a configuration value you can find by searching once is worth the extra explicitness.

Database connections are configured with a single URL rather than a set of separate host, port, user, password and database fields. One value means one thing to get wrong, one thing to rotate, and one thing to copy into a debugging session, and the same string works unchanged with `psql`, the migration tool and the application driver, which removes an entire genre of mistake where the application and the migration runner were pointed at different databases. Discrete fields also invite partial overrides, and we had one: an override that set the host for a read replica but inherited the writer's database name from the base configuration, which sent an analytics job to the wrong catalogue on the right server for two days before anyone noticed the numbers. Options that genuinely vary per deployment, such as the SSL mode and the application name, ride in the query string of the same URL. The parsed result is logged at boot with the password component replaced, so operators can confirm which endpoint a process actually reached without exposing the credential.

The suite talks to a real Postgres on your machine, at the same major version production runs, and there is no in-memory substitute and no mocked repository layer for anything that issues SQL. We ran SQLite underneath the ORM for about a year because it was fast and needed no setup, and we stopped after the third bug that existed only because the two engines disagree. The expensive one was a partial unique index on active subscriptions: SQLite accepted the definition and never enforced the predicate the way Postgres does, so a duplicate-prevention test passed on every laptop while production accepted two active subscriptions for the same account and double-billed eleven customers. The same class of divergence covers `ON CONFLICT` with a partial index target, `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`, timestamp arithmetic across a daylight saving boundary, row locking semantics, and how each engine casts an empty string. None of those are exotic; all of them are load-bearing here. The cost is paid down by making the real thing cheap: `tests/conftest.py` builds a template database once, each of the eight `pytest-xdist` workers clones it with `CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE`, and every test runs inside a transaction that is rolled back at teardown. Cold start is about six seconds and a warm run of the unit tier is under ninety.

The test process cannot open a socket to anything outside the machine. A guard installed in `tests/conftest.py` patches the socket constructor and raises with the destination host and the test name whenever an address outside the allowed set is dialled; the allowed set is loopback and the unix socket paths for the local services. Anything reaching further has to be stubbed explicitly at the boundary. This came from a suite that was quietly hitting a vendor sandbox, which meant our green build depended on somebody else's uptime, and it went red at midnight for two days running while the vendor did maintenance. It also meant a test could accidentally create real records: one did, repeatedly, in a sandbox that shared a rate limit with production traffic. The error message is the important part. A blocked call names the host and points at the recorded-response helper, so the fix is usually one line rather than an investigation. Turning the guard off for a single test requires a marker, and the markers are reviewed like any other exception.

Parallel test workers do not share a namespace. Each worker gets its own schema, named from the worker id, created at session start and dropped at the end, with the search path set so the code under test never has to know which one it is in. We arrived here after chasing intermittent failures that only appeared above four workers and only in CI, all of them the same shape: two tests truncating the same table, or one advancing a sequence another asserted on. Per-worker isolation makes those impossible rather than rare, which matters because a rare failure gets retried and forgotten instead of fixed. The tradeoff is memory and catalogue bloat with many workers, so the count is capped and the runner refuses to start more workers than the configured connection budget divided by the per-worker pool size, which was the other way this used to fail, by exhausting connections and producing an error that looked like a code bug. Teardown is best-effort with a startup sweep that drops orphaned schemas older than a day, since killed runs leave them behind.

CI does not build the test schema by replaying migrations. The pipeline restores `ci/schema.sql`, a plain dump of the head schema regenerated by a nightly job and committed, and then asserts that applying the migration chain from empty produces a schema identical to it, failing with a diff when it does not. Replaying two hundred and forty revisions took four and a half minutes at the front of every job, on every job, for a result that is the same every time. Restoring the dump takes eleven seconds. The equality check is what keeps the shortcut honest, and it has caught real problems twice: a revision edited in place after merge, and a hand-applied fix on a shared environment that had never been captured as a revision at all. The migration path itself is still exercised, in a dedicated job that runs the full chain against a copy of the previous release's schema, which is closer to what production actually does than replaying from empty ever was.

Nothing in the codebase calls the system clock directly. Time comes from a single clock object injected into the services that need it, and tests swap in a fixed or scriptable implementation. A lint rule rejects direct calls to the standard library's now functions outside that one module. This started as a flakiness problem and turned into a correctness one. The flaky version was a subscription test that failed for anyone running the suite in the last second of a month; the correctness version was a proration calculation that had never been exercised across a daylight saving change because nobody could write the test, and it was wrong by an hour in one direction for half the year. With an injectable clock you can write the awkward cases directly: the end of February, the second Sunday in March, a leap second boundary, and a renewal that falls on a day the target month does not have. It also removes sleeps from tests. Anything that used to sleep waiting for a scheduled action now advances the clock and asserts, which took a chunk of wall time out of the suite as a side effect.

Redis is faked in the unit tier with an in-process double, and that is a deliberate contrast with how the relational store is handled. The reasoning is about what the dependency is being asked to do. Our Redis usage is a small, boring surface: get, set with an expiry, increment, and a sorted set for the leaderboard, with no scripting, no cluster-specific behaviour and no transactional semantics we depend on. A double covering that surface is a couple of hundred lines and cannot meaningfully diverge from the real thing for the operations we use. It buys a suite that needs no running Redis and tests that can assert on expiry behaviour by advancing the clock rather than waiting. Where the double stops being trustworthy is eviction, connection loss and the cluster's key distribution, so there is a small integration tier that runs against a real instance in CI and covers exactly those, currently eleven tests. The rule of thumb we settled on: fake a dependency when its contract fits on a page, and use the real one when the contract is the entire manual.

A test that fails on the trunk without a corresponding code change gets quarantined within one working day. The pipeline records every failure into a small table keyed by test id, and a test that has failed and then passed on the same commit twice within a week is flagged automatically. Quarantine means the test moves to a marked group that still runs and still reports, but does not block merges; the owning team gets an issue with the failure history attached and two weeks to fix or delete it, and a quarantined test that ages past that window is deleted outright. Both halves matter. Leaving flakes in the blocking set trains people to hit retry, and once retrying is normal a real regression gets retried too, which is exactly what happened the afternoon a genuine race in the payment callback handler was retried three times and merged. Deleting them without a window instead throws away coverage, because roughly a third of the flakes we investigated turned out to be real bugs with bad timing rather than bad tests.

A factory called with no arguments must produce an object that would be accepted by the application's own validation, not merely one the database will store. That sounds obvious and it was not what we had. Factories had drifted into producing minimal rows with empty strings where a name belonged and a plan reference pointing at a tier that had been retired, because each one had been written to satisfy the constraints in force on the day it was added. The consequence was a slow leak of tests asserting behaviour against objects the system could never actually be in, and at least one bug fixed twice because the reproduction was built from an impossible customer. The check is enforced by a test that walks every registered factory, builds one instance with defaults, and runs it through the same validators the API applies to inbound payloads. Overrides are still free to build invalid states deliberately, which is how validation itself gets tested; the requirement is only about what you get when you ask for nothing in particular.

The browser-driven end-to-end suite does not run on pull requests. It runs on the release branch, on a schedule twice a day, and on demand from a chat command. There are forty-one of those tests and they take nineteen minutes against a deployed environment, and when they were part of the pull request gate the median wait to merge went past half an hour and the failure signal was mostly noise: a slow environment, a third-party script, an animation that had not settled. What replaced them at the pull request layer is a wider band of API-level tests against a real database plus component tests for the front end, which cover most of the same ground in seconds and fail with a stack trace instead of a screenshot. The end-to-end tier keeps the jobs no other layer can do, namely the handful of paths that cross the browser, the API and the payment provider's hosted page in one flow. A failure there blocks the release and pages the release owner, which is the level of seriousness those tests deserve when they are not crying wolf.

Day one is a clone and one command. A new engineer runs `git clone` on the monorepo and then `./bin/bootstrap`, which is idempotent and safe to re-run: it installs the toolchain manager and the pinned versions, installs the system packages it needs through the platform package manager, starts the local services, generates the local environment file from the secret store using the SSO session that was set up during account provisioning, applies migrations, loads the development dataset, builds the front end once, and finishes by running `make verify` and printing a short checklist of what now works and the command that proves each item. Target is a green test run inside ninety minutes of sitting down, and the last four hires came in at fifty-five minutes, two hours, forty minutes and an hour and ten. The standing rule is fix the script, not the laptop: when bootstrap fails, the buddy's job is to patch `bin/bootstrap` and land it that day, not to work around it in a shell and move on, and roughly every third hire produces such a patch. `docs/onboarding.md` is generated from the script's step annotations, so the written instructions cannot drift from what actually runs. This replaced a forty-step wiki page where the honest average was three days and about a third of the steps were stale.

Laptops arrive already enrolled in device management with full-disk encryption on, the screen lock at 5 minutes, and the endpoint agent installed, and repository access is not granted until the enrolment check reports green. IT ships the machine to arrive two days before the start date and the enrolment happens on first boot with the person's own credentials. The ordering is what changed after a review found two contractors who had been working for weeks on unmanaged personal machines because access had been granted on their first morning and enrolment was chased afterwards, which meant nobody was chasing it at all. Tying the grant to the check makes it self-enforcing: the identity provider will not add anyone to the `eng-all` group until the device inventory has a compliant machine registered to them. The practical cost is that a delayed courier delays a start, so the checklist now has an escalation path and a pool of 3 pre-enrolled spare machines in each office. Nothing about this touches how the repository itself is set up; it is the gate that comes first.

Nobody gets read access to production data in their first month, and that is not a comment on trust. It is a consequence of two things: the access is auditable and every grant has to be justifiable to an auditor by role rather than by convenience, and a person who has been here three weeks does not yet know which queries are dangerous on a live replica. The first month is deliberately arranged so that it is not needed. The development dataset covers the shapes a newcomer will meet, the shared integration environment has realistic volumes, and anything that genuinely requires looking at a real record goes through someone on the team who has the grant, which doubles as a teaching moment about why the request was necessary. At the end of the month the manager requests the grant explicitly and it is time-boxed and renewed rather than permanent. Two people have told us the constraint was the single best thing about their first weeks, because it forced them to understand the system rather than to poke at its output.

By tradition the first pull request anyone opens here fixes documentation. It is not assigned and it is not a task on a checklist; it is simply what people do, and it works because a newcomer is the only person in the building who can see which sentences are wrong. Everyone else has compiled around the gaps. The change is usually small, a stale command or a step that assumes a tool you no longer need, and its real function is to walk the whole path end to end while the stakes are nothing: branch, commit, open, get review comments, respond to them, watch the checks, merge, see it deploy. Doing that once on a change that cannot break anything makes the second pull request, which can, much less fraught. It also sets the expectation early that documentation is part of the codebase rather than someone else's problem, and it gives the buddy an easy, low-pressure review to do properly, modelling the tone of review the team wants rather than the terse version people default to when they are busy.

Every new engineer is assigned a named buddy before their start date, and the buddy's calendar is blocked for a third of their time in week one. The buddy is not the manager and is deliberately someone who joined within the last year, because they still remember which parts were confusing and have not yet forgotten what they had to guess. The commitment is concrete rather than an open invitation: a scheduled half hour each morning of the first week, then twice weekly for a month, plus first call on anything that blocks. Open-door offers had failed repeatedly for the obvious reason, which is that a person three days into a job will not interrupt someone who looks busy, so they sit stuck for two hours instead of asking a two-minute question. Naming the buddy also gives the rest of the team a clear signal about who is handling things, which stops the pattern where a newcomer gets three contradictory explanations of the same subsystem in one afternoon. Buddies rotate and nobody does two in a row.

All nine services, the front end, the shared libraries, the infrastructure definitions and the internal handbook live in one repository. There is one issue tracker view over it, one continuous integration configuration, and one place to search. The decision was made after a period with 11 repositories, where a change touching the API and the client meant two pull requests merged in an order nobody could enforce, and where a shared library update took a version bump, a publish, and then five dependent bumps that people forgot to do. Cross-cutting changes are now one atomic commit, and renaming a field across producer and consumer is a single reviewable diff. The costs are real: the pipeline needs path filtering so a front-end change does not run the ledger suite, the ownership rules in `CODEOWNERS` have to be maintained carefully, and checkouts are large enough that CI clones shallow. We judged those costs to be mechanical and solvable, whereas coordinating merges across repositories is a human problem that reappears every week.

Git access uses short-lived certificates issued by the identity provider, not long-lived keys pasted into a profile page. Running `bin/dev auth` opens the browser, completes the SSO flow with the hardware key already registered for that person, and writes a certificate valid for sixteen hours into the agent; the git host trusts the certificate authority rather than a list of individual public keys. This closed a real gap. Deprovisioning used to mean removing someone from the organisation and hoping their key was not also registered on a personal account with access to a mirror, and during one offboarding we found exactly that, a key still valid three weeks after the last day. With certificates, access ends when the identity session ends, with no list to reconcile. The daily cost is one browser prompt each morning, which people tolerate because the alternative is remembering which of three keys is on which machine. Automation uses separate scoped credentials with their own rotation and never reuses a person's identity.

Documentation about a service lives in that service's directory and is reviewed in the same pull request as the code it describes. The handbook site is generated from those files nightly, so nothing is authored in the wiki any more and the wiki itself is frozen and read-only, kept only for historical decisions we have not yet migrated. The rule exists because a document that is not next to the code will not be updated by the person changing the code, and every attempt at a documentation review ritual failed within a quarter. Proximity plus review is the only mechanism that survived. Code owners for a directory own its documentation, which means a reviewer can reasonably block on a missing update the same way they would block on a missing test, and that turned out to be the behavioural change that mattered rather than any tooling. A weekly job lists pages untouched for a year alongside the change volume in their directory, which is a decent proxy for finding the ones that are quietly lying.

Contractors work against a fork with a narrowed subset of the tree, synced by a mirroring job that excludes the billing service, the fraud rules, the customer data pipeline and the infrastructure definitions. Their pull requests land on the fork and are pulled across by an employee after review. This is not about suspicion; it is about what the contracts we sign with customers say we control, and about limiting the number of people who can reach the systems that move money. It also forced a genuine improvement, because building the exclusion list surfaced how much unrelated code imported directly from the billing package for trivial helpers, and untangling that made the boundary real rather than notional. The friction is honest: a contractor who needs a change inside the excluded set pairs with an employee who makes it, which is slower and occasionally frustrating. We accepted that in exchange for an access story that can be explained in a sentence during a customer security review.

We keep a second payment processor wired up, contracted, and carrying live traffic, and switching between them is a runbook, not a project. The primary is Northgate and the secondary is Verity, and roughly 2% of authorisations are routed to Verity at all times, chosen by a stable hash of the customer id so a given account always lands on the same processor. That trickle is the entire point: credentials stay valid, webhook signatures stay verified, the reconciliation importer keeps parsing their settlement format, and the tax fields keep matching, so on the day it matters the path has been exercised that morning rather than eighteen months ago. The reason we pay for that is a six-hour Northgate outage that landed on the twenty-eighth, our heaviest renewal day, during which about four thousand renewals failed and eleven hundred subscriptions lapsed into dunning that we then had to unwind by hand. Failing over took five hours, almost all of it discovering that nobody had ever completed Verity's merchant onboarding. The contractual remedy was a credit worth a rounding error against the revenue we did not collect, which settled the argument about whether a second processor was worth its integration cost. Flipping is one flag, `PAYMENTS_PRIMARY_PSP`, documented in `docs/runbooks/psp-failover.md`, and we drill it once a quarter by holding the flipped state for a full working day.

Card numbers never reach our servers. The payment form is composed of fields hosted by the processor and embedded in an iframe, so the entry happens in their origin, and what comes back to us is a token. Our own JavaScript cannot read those fields and our backend never sees a pan, which is what keeps the compliance scope to the self-assessment questionnaire that applies to redirect and iframe integrations rather than the full audited assessment, a difference measured in months of work every year. The trade is real and worth naming: the fields are harder to style, the layout shifts a little on load, and one browser update broke autofill inside the frame for a fortnight with nothing we could do but wait. We accepted all of that because the alternative puts card data inside our logs, our crash reports, our error tracker and our database backups, and every one of those has been the origin of somebody's breach notification. Anywhere a support agent needs to identify a card, they get the last 4 digits and the fingerprint the processor returns, which is enough for every workflow we actually have.

A declined renewal enters a fixed dunning schedule rather than being retried whenever something notices it. Attempts go out on day 1, day 3, day 7 and day 14, each paired with an email, and the subscription is suspended after the fourth failure with a grace period of seven days before any data is touched. The schedule is stored per subscription in `dunning_attempts` so the state survives restarts and can be inspected during a support conversation. It is fixed rather than adaptive because adaptive retrying is how you get blocked: issuers treat rapid repeated attempts on a declined card as suspicious, and our authorisation rate dropped noticeably during a period when a background job retried failures every hour. Soft declines from insufficient funds are the ones worth retrying at all, so the schedule is skipped entirely for hard declines like a closed account, which go straight to the customer email and the suspension countdown. Recovery on the current schedule sits around 41% of failed renewals, which is what the timing was tuned against.

Every processor webhook is signature-verified before it is parsed, and the handler is idempotent on the event id.
