The verification uses the shared secret from the secret store with a constant-time comparison, and any request that fails it is dropped with a 400 and counted on a metric that alerts if the rate goes above a handful per hour, because a sustained failure means either a rotated secret or somebody probing. Idempotency is enforced by inserting the event id into `processed_webhook_events` inside the same transaction as the effect; a duplicate hits the unique constraint and the handler returns 200 without doing the work twice. Both properties came from the same bad week. The processor retried a batch of events after a timeout on our side, and a payment-succeeded event applied twice credited an account twice, which took three days to notice and a manual reconciliation to fix. Handlers also do the smallest possible work synchronously, writing the event and enqueuing follow-up, because the processor's delivery timeout is short and a slow handler turns into a retry storm that makes the original problem worse.

Refunds are issued through our own refund service and never from the processor's dashboard, and the dashboard accounts everyone uses have the refund permission removed so the rule is not a matter of discipline. The reason is that a refund is four things happening together: money moving, a credit note existing, the revenue recognition entry reversing, and the customer being told. The dashboard does exactly one of those. For a while we had a support workflow that used it for urgent cases, and the month-end close began failing because refunded amounts appeared in the processor's settlement file with no matching entry on our side, which took a finance analyst two days to reconcile every month until we stopped. The service does all four in one operation, writes an audit record naming the agent and the reason code, and enforces the policy limits, including the ceiling above which a second approver is required. The only remaining path into the dashboard is read-only investigation, and the processor's own support team knows not to action refunds on our behalf when asked.

Every night a job pulls the previous day's settlement file from the processor and matches it line by line against our own ledger entries, and anything unmatched in either direction lands in an exceptions queue that a named person clears each morning. The job writes to `settlement_reconciliation` with the settlement id, our transaction id and a status, and it alerts if the unmatched count exceeds 20 or the total absolute difference exceeds fifty pounds. Matching on the day rather than at month end is the change that mattered. A discrepancy is a solvable puzzle when the transaction is a day old and the customer interaction is still in support history; the same discrepancy at month end is archaeology, and we spent one close going through six weeks of records to find a currency rounding difference on refunds of odd amounts. The most common exceptions are genuinely boring, chargeback fees we did not book and a small class of authorisations that expire without capture, and both are now handled automatically because the queue made them visible enough to count.

The exchange rate applied to an invoice is captured when the invoice is issued and stored on the invoice itself, and nothing downstream recalculates it. Rates are pulled once a day at 05:00 UTC from the reference feed into `fx_rates` keyed by currency pair and date, and the invoice records the rate, the date and the source it used. This exists because a credit note that used today's rate against an invoice raised last month produced a residual balance of a few pence on thousands of accounts, and those pennies blocked automatic closure of the accounts, which generated support tickets far out of proportion to the amounts. Storing the rate makes an invoice self-contained: a customer disputing a figure eighteen months later can be shown exactly what was applied and why, and the total on the paper always adds up. The rule extends to refunds, which reverse at the original rate even when that means the amount returned differs from the current market value, which is what our terms say and what the customer expects.

Invoice numbering still lives in the old billing service, and it will keep living there until someone works out how to move a legally significant sequence without breaking it. Everything else migrated years ago, but the number on a customer invoice must be unique, gapless and monotonic per legal entity, and tax authorities in two of our markets treat a gap as something you have to explain. The old service issues those numbers from a single row it locks per entity, which is unfashionable and correct, and the new service calls it and stores what it gets back. Attempts to replace it with a distributed scheme foundered on the gapless requirement, because every design that scales introduces the possibility of a reserved-but-unused number, which is precisely the thing not allowed. The pragmatic consequence is that the old service cannot be turned off, so it gets patched and kept in support, and its deployment is included in the release train even though the rest of it has been dead code for a long time. Anyone proposing to retire it starts by solving numbering.

When a chargeback notification arrives, a job assembles the evidence package automatically and files it, and a human only reviews the ones the rules flag as ambiguous. The package pulls the authorisation record with its address and security code results, the login and device history around the transaction, the delivery or activation evidence, the terms accepted at signup with their version and timestamp, and the support correspondence, then renders it into the format the processor expects. Doing it by hand took an agent about forty minutes per case and, more damagingly, missed the deadline often enough that we lost disputes by default rather than on the merits. Automation moved the win rate from just under a third to a little over half, and most of that gain came from filing at all rather than from filing better. Cases with no delivery evidence or with a prior dispute from the same account still go to a person, since those are the ones where a judgement call about whether to fight is worth making, and fighting a dispute you will lose costs the fee twice.

We find out that a vendor is down from our own probes, not from their status page. `tools/vendor_probe/` runs as a small scheduled workload in two regions outside our main network, and every 60 seconds it performs one cheap but genuinely functional call per vendor: a zero-amount authorisation against the payment sandbox, a message accepted and discarded by the mail provider's test endpoint, a token exchange against the identity provider, a one-object read from the object store. Each result writes `vendor_probe_success` and `vendor_probe_latency_ms` tagged with vendor and region. The page fires on three consecutive failures observed from both regions, which is the condition that separates a vendor problem from our own egress problem, and the alert body names the customer-facing symptom rather than the vendor, so the first responder reads 'password resets will not send' instead of a company name they may not recognise. Running from outside our own network is the part people underestimate: probes inside the same egress path go quiet for exactly the same reasons production traffic does, and then you learn nothing. The whole thing was built after our mail provider was degraded for fifty minutes while their status page stayed green and the first report came from a customer on Twitter. Status pages are still ingested, but only as annotations on the dashboard.

Vendor status page notifications go to one low-traffic channel that nobody is expected to watch in real time, and none of them page anyone. Every provider we depend on offers a subscription, and subscribing to all of them was briefly a policy until we counted the traffic: mostly scheduled maintenance for regions we do not use, components we do not touch, and post-hoc confirmations that arrive after the fact. Routing that into an on-call path taught people to dismiss the notifications without reading them, which is the worst possible outcome for a signal you might one day need. In its own channel the material is genuinely useful for context during an incident and for the write-up afterwards, especially the timeline a provider eventually publishes, which is usually the only authoritative account of what happened on their side. Two people skim it in the morning as part of the operational review. The standing agreement is that nothing in that channel is treated as authoritative for whether a vendor is currently working for us.

Every outbound call to a third party goes through `platform/http/client.py`, and constructing a bare session elsewhere fails the lint step. The wrapper sets a connect timeout of 2 seconds and a read timeout the caller must pass explicitly with no default, retries only idempotent methods with jittered backoff capped at three attempts, attaches the request id so a vendor call can be traced back to the user request that caused it, and emits duration and status metrics tagged by vendor. Requiring an explicit read timeout is the rule that earned its keep: the incident that prompted all of this was a vendor whose responses slowed to ninety seconds without failing, and our workers, having no read timeout at all, held their connections until the pool was exhausted and the whole service stopped serving unrelated traffic. Being slow is a far more common vendor failure than being down, and the default library behaviour of waiting forever turns their degradation into our outage. The wrapper also refuses to follow redirects across a host boundary, after one integration quietly started redirecting to a different domain.

There is one file, `platform/vendors.yaml`, listing every external service we depend on at runtime, and a service that talks to something not in it will not pass review. Each entry carries the vendor, what it is used for, the owning team, the internal criticality tier, whether customer data is transmitted, the contract reference and the sandbox endpoint. It exists because we could not answer a simple question during a security review, which was how many third parties touch customer data, and the exercise of answering it took two engineers most of a week and found four integrations nobody had a current owner for, including one still authenticating with a key issued to somebody who had left. The registry is now the input to several things that used to be separate spreadsheets, including the annual review and the risk register, and it is checked by a job that flags any entry whose owning team no longer exists. It deliberately says nothing about health or availability; it is an inventory, and keeping it purely an inventory is what has kept it accurate.

Calls to a failing dependency get cut off rather than queued. The breaker trips when the error rate over a rolling window exceeds 50% with a minimum of twenty requests in the window, stays open for thirty seconds, then admits a single probe request before closing. While it is open the caller gets an immediate typed failure and decides what to do, and the decision differs by call site, which is the part that matters: the recommendation service degrades to a static list, the address validator lets the address through unvalidated with a flag on the record, and the payment path refuses outright rather than pretending. The behaviour was written after a slow vendor turned into a full outage for us, when every worker was blocked waiting on it and requests that never touched the vendor at all could not be served. A breaker converts a dependency failure into a bounded, visible degradation. Trips are logged with the dependency name and duration, and a breaker that has opened more than five times in a day raises a ticket for the owning team even if nobody noticed at the time.

Customer reports land in the same incident queue as automated alerts, with the same severity scale and the same acknowledgement clock. Support raises them with one button in the helpdesk and it creates a real incident record rather than a ticket that someone might escalate later. The change came out of a review that measured the gap between the first customer report of a problem and the first engineering acknowledgement, and the median was 50 minutes, almost all of it spent inside support deciding whether the thing was worth escalating. That decision was being made by whoever happened to pick up the conversation, without the context to make it. Now 3 reports of the same symptom within 15 minutes escalate automatically, and a single report of anything touching payments or authentication escalates immediately. The volume of false escalations went up, which we expected and accepted, and the cost of each one is a two-minute look by the on-call engineer. Support reports remain the fastest detector for a whole class of problems that no monitor watches, especially anything visual or specific to one browser.

An outage caused by a supplier still gets a written review, and the review does not stop at establishing that it was their fault. That framing is useless to a customer, who experienced our product not working, and it is useless to us, because the only actionable material is on our side of the boundary. So the questions are ours: how long before we knew, how long before customers were told, did the failure stay contained to the feature that depended on the vendor or did it spread, was there a degraded mode we could have entered and did anyone consider it, and was the runbook correct. Those reviews have produced almost all our resilience work, including the degraded modes on several paths and the decision to keep a warm alternative for one dependency. They also produce the vendor conversation, which is far more effective with a timeline and a measured impact attached than with a complaint. The one thing we do not do is action items that amount to asking the vendor to be better, because we cannot verify those and they quietly never close.

A scripted browser runs the full signup and checkout flow against production every 60 seconds from 3 locations, using a dedicated test account and a card in the processor's test mode. It loads the marketing page, signs in, adds a plan, completes payment, confirms the receipt page renders the right amount, then cancels and cleans up after itself. Two consecutive failures from 2 locations page the on-call engineer. This catches things no unit test can: a content delivery cache serving a stale bundle, an expired certificate on a subdomain only the checkout uses, a third-party script blocking render, and a misapplied configuration that broke the plan selector for new visitors only. It is deliberately end-to-end and deliberately in production, because every one of those failures was invisible in the staging environment. The cost is a small amount of junk data, which the cleanup step and a nightly sweeper handle, and the discipline of keeping the script current, which falls on the team that owns the checkout page and is enforced by the check going red when they change the flow.

Claiming service credits from a supplier is finance's job, not engineering's. When an incident involved a vendor, the review names the vendor and the duration and finance takes it from there, reading the agreement, filing the claim within the notification window, and chasing it. This was engineering's job for exactly one claim, which we missed because the contract required notice within 30 days and everyone assumed somebody else was handling it while they were busy with the actual remediation. Handing it over also improved the negotiating position, because finance is already in a renewal conversation with the same account manager and a documented outage is leverage there in a way that an engineer's email never was. What engineering owes is the timeline and the impact measurement, produced as part of the review we would have written anyway, in a form that can be attached to a claim. Nobody is asked to quantify a business impact in currency, which is finance's work and which engineering consistently got wrong in both directions.

Before anyone creates an account with a new tool, they open a request in `procurement/requests/` describing what it does, what data it will hold and who will own it. Two questions decide the route. If the tool will hold customer data or connect to anything of ours by API or OAuth, it goes through the security review, which means a questionnaire, a signed data processing agreement, and mandatory single sign-on before the first real record enters it, with no exceptions for pilots. If it costs more than 200 a month or commits us beyond a year, it also needs the budget owner. Everything else, the small single-seat utilities, is self-serve, but still gets a row in `vendors.yaml` with an owner and a renewal date, because unregistered is the state we are actually trying to eliminate. Free tiers count as signups, since the data leaves the building whether or not money changes hands, and that clause is there because the incident that produced this policy was free: a monitoring integration set up on someone's personal account with a production API key, still live and still ingesting eight months after they left. Renewals surface in the finance review thirty days out, which is also how we found three overlapping diagram subscriptions bought by three teams in the same quarter.

Any application that holds company or customer data authenticates through our identity provider, and local passwords are disabled on it. Integration is SAML or OIDC, group membership drives roles so access follows the org chart rather than a per-tool invitation list, and SCIM provisioning is required wherever the vendor supports it. The reason is deprovisioning. Without a central identity, removing someone means visiting each console in turn and trusting a list that is out of date the moment it is written, and we proved that during an offboarding where an account in a project tracker stayed active for six weeks and still had access to a private roadmap. With SSO, ending the session ends everything at once. It also gives one place to require the hardware key and one audit log of who signed in where. Where a vendor charges extra for the feature, we pay it, having decided that arguing about that particular line item costs more than the fee. Where a vendor cannot do it at all, the tool is limited to material we would be relaxed about seeing in public.

Once a quarter every vendor console with more than 5 users gets an access review. The owner receives a generated list of who has access at what role, and has 10 working days to confirm each line or mark it for removal; anything not confirmed is removed automatically, which is the detail that makes the exercise work rather than turning into a rubber stamp. The pull is automated where a vendor has a usable API and manual where it does not, and the manual ones are the reason the list of tools we are willing to adopt keeps shrinking. Reviews consistently remove around a tenth of grants, mostly people who changed team and kept an access they no longer use, plus a steady trickle of shared accounts that someone created for a one-off and never deleted. The findings feed back into the tooling decisions: any vendor whose review has to be done by hand twice in a row gets flagged, since the recurring cost of that is larger than the licence.

Offboarding runs `ops/offboard.py` with the person's identity, and the script does the whole sequence: suspends the identity, revokes active sessions and tokens, transfers ownership of documents and calendar resources, removes them from the code host, rotates any shared credential their group had access to, and files tickets for the handful of vendors with no API. It runs within the hour on a planned departure and immediately on an unplanned one, and the output is a report attached to the ticket so the completion is evidence rather than an assertion. The checklist it replaced was a page in the handbook with seventeen items, and the last three audits found the same pattern: the first ten were always done and the tail was hit and miss, because by item eleven the person running it had been interrupted twice. A script does not get interrupted. Adding a vendor to the sequence is part of the procurement flow, so the offboarding path is built at the same time as the account, and a vendor that cannot be automated at all is a mark against adopting it.

Every cloud resource carries an owner tag and a service tag, and untagged resources are reported daily and deleted after 14 days. The point is not tidiness, it is that a monthly bill without attribution is an argument nobody can win: everyone believes their share is small, and the total goes up anyway. With tags the report goes to each team as their own number with a month-on-month change and the top three movers named, which turns a company-wide problem into eight tractable ones. Doing that found a forgotten staging cluster costing more than the production database it was a copy of, an over-provisioned log retention setting, and a set of orphaned volumes from instances long since terminated. The enforcement is at creation time in the infrastructure module rather than by policing afterwards, so an untagged resource generally cannot be created through the sanctioned path at all, and the daily report exists to catch the things made by hand during an incident. None of this covers subscription software, which is billed and tracked separately.

Any commitment longer than twelve months has to arrive with a written exit plan before it is signed. The plan is short and answers three things: how we get our data out and in what format, what it would take to move to a named alternative, and how long that would take with the people we actually have. It is not a promise to leave; it is a check that leaving is possible, which is a very different thing from a slide that says the data is exportable. The habit came from a search vendor whose export produced a proprietary archive that only their own product could read, discovered during the renewal conversation rather than before it, which turned a negotiation into a formality. Writing the plan takes an afternoon and has twice changed the decision outright, once towards a slightly worse product with a straightforward export path. It is revisited at renewal, because the honest answer drifts as more of the product grows around the tool, and a plan that was two weeks of work at signing can quietly become two quarters.

Every data processing agreement we have signed is recorded with its counterparty, the categories of data it covers, the subprocessors it names, the transfer mechanism, and the date it expires or auto-renews. The register is generated from the same source as the vendor list so the two cannot disagree, and it is what gets handed over when a customer's legal team asks, which happens in most enterprise deals and used to consume a fortnight of someone's time assembling documents from three inboxes. Expiry tracking is the part that surprises people: agreements referencing a legal mechanism that has since been invalidated do not announce themselves, and we had four still pointing at a framework that had been struck down. Now anything within 90 days of expiry, or naming a mechanism flagged as obsolete, appears on the compliance review. The register also records the vendor's own subprocessor notification address, since the obligation to pass those notices on to our customers only works if somebody is receiving them.

Evaluating a tool happens in a sandbox tenant with generated data, never against production traffic or real customer records. Whoever is running the trial gets a copy of the development dataset and, where the tool needs a live feed, a mirrored stream with identifiers replaced. This exists because a trial is the moment when the normal controls are weakest: nobody has signed anything, the account was created in a minute, and the person evaluating is trying to answer whether it works rather than what it holds. We pointed a log analysis product at real logs during a trial once, and when the trial ended a month later the vendor still held a copy of everything we had sent, which was not covered by any agreement and took a formal deletion request to resolve. Sandboxing also gives a better evaluation, because a synthetic dataset can be made to contain the awkward cases deliberately rather than whatever happened to occur that week. If a tool can only be judged against real data, that itself becomes part of the review, and the trial waits for the agreement.

We buy rather than build unless the vendor cost passes roughly two engineers a year, and even then the bar for building is that the thing is close to our core. The heuristic exists because engineering time is systematically undercounted in these arguments: the build estimate covers writing it and never covers operating it, upgrading it, being paged for it at three in the morning, or the six months where the person who wrote it is the only one who can change it. Counting a fully loaded engineer against a licence fee makes most of these decisions obvious in the buy direction, and it has stopped at least three home-grown replacements for products that cost less than a month of the work proposed. It has also gone the other way once, for the routing component that sits on every request, where the vendor pricing scaled with traffic in a way that crossed the line within a year and where the behaviour was specific enough to us that a general product fitted badly. The rule is a prompt for an honest estimate, not a formula.

Transactional mail moved off Postmile onto Sendhaven in March, and the trigger was a reputation failure we had no control over and no visibility into. We were on Postmile's shared sending pool, and when a co-tenant on those addresses was blocklisted, our delivery rate to one of the large mailbox providers fell to about 62% for two days. Nothing on our side had changed and nothing in our dashboards showed it, because Postmile reported those messages as delivered when they had been accepted by the receiving edge and then quietly binned. What we saw was a jump in support contacts about password resets that never arrived, and it took most of a day to work out that our own metrics were measuring the wrong event. Sendhaven gives us dedicated addresses that no one else sends from, so our reputation is the consequence of our own behaviour, and they expose per-message engagement events on a stream rather than a webhook 20 minutes behind. Warming took 3 weeks at a ramped volume before the cutover completed. Marketing sends stayed on Postmile deliberately, since the two categories should never share reputation. The transport is selected by `EMAIL_TRANSPORT` and every send is recorded in `mail_delivery_events` with the provider that carried it, so the comparison is still available.

A hard bounce or a spam complaint adds the address to `mail_suppressions` immediately, and every send checks that table before it is handed to the provider. Suppression is permanent for hard bounces, ninety days for repeated soft bounces, and permanent with a flag for complaints so support can see why a customer says they get nothing. Relying on the provider's own suppression list was the earlier arrangement and it failed in a specific way: the list lives in their account, it is not visible in our support tooling, and an agent looking at a customer who reports missing email had no way to see that the address had been suppressed six weeks earlier for bouncing. They would resend, it would silently do nothing, and the conversation would go around again. Holding the list ourselves also means it survives a provider change, which matters more than it used to. Removing a suppression is possible but requires an agent action with a reason recorded, because the usual cause of a hard bounce is a typo in the address and the correct fix is to change the address rather than to keep trying the broken one.

Bulk sends are scheduled outside the invoice run window, which is 02:00 to 05:00 UTC on the first four days of the month. The scheduler refuses to accept a campaign inside that window and the marketing tool's send times are constrained to match. The reason is a queue collision rather than anything about email itself: campaign sends and invoice notifications shared a worker pool, a large campaign filled it for forty minutes, and invoice emails for that month's run were delayed behind it, arriving after several customers had already been charged and before they had been told why. Splitting the pools was the first fix and separating the windows was the second, because even with separate pools the shared rate limit at the provider produced the same shape of problem at a smaller scale. The rule is enforced by configuration rather than by convention, since campaign timing is chosen by people who have no reason to know about the billing calendar, and expecting them to remember it was the version that failed.

Every message we send carries a plain text alternative generated from the same template source, and the renderer fails the build if a template produces an empty one. This is not nostalgia. Filters weigh a missing text part, some corporate gateways strip HTML entirely before delivery, and screen readers handle the text part more predictably. We learned the corporate gateway part expensively: an enterprise customer's security appliance was converting our messages to text, and because the text part was an unhelpful line telling the reader to view the message in a proper client, several hundred of their staff received exactly that and nothing else, including the invitations that were supposed to onboard them. The generator produces something readable rather than a stripped tag soup, keeping the heading structure as underlined lines and rendering links as visible URLs after the anchor text, and the template tests assert the important values appear in both parts. That assertion has caught real bugs where an amount or a date was rendered only in the visual layout.

A password reset link is valid for 30 minutes and can be used once. The token is a random value stored as a hash in `password_reset_tokens` with the issue time and a used flag, and it is invalidated when the password changes, when another reset is requested, or when the session that requested it signs out. Short and single-use is the answer to a set of unglamorous realities: reset emails sit in mailboxes forever, mailboxes get shared or breached long after the fact, and corporate link scanners fetch every URL in an incoming message, which will consume a single-use token before the human ever clicks it. That last one is why the link consumes the token on submission of the new password rather than on the first GET, a change we made after an enterprise rollout where every reset arrived pre-expired. Requesting a reset for an address we do not know returns the same response and the same timing as one we do, because the alternative is an account enumeration oracle, and we treat that as part of the same feature rather than a separate hardening task.

The published DMARC policy is now reject, reached deliberately after six months at none and two at quarantine while we read the aggregate reports. The reports were the whole exercise. They showed four legitimate senders nobody had inventoried, including a recruiting tool, a survey product used by one team, and a decade-old script on a machine in the office that sent a weekly report, all of which would have been silently dropped had we jumped straight to enforcement. Publishing reject is what stops a plausible invoice email arriving from our domain, and we care about that specifically because we send invoices and our customers pay them. The move to enforcement is also what forced every sender through the alignment work, which is the durable outcome: anything sending on our behalf signs with a key we control on a subdomain, and adding a new sender means adding a record, which is a small step someone has to take rather than something that just happens. Aggregate reports are still ingested weekly and reviewed by the platform team.

All outbound message content is rendered by one internal template service that owns the layout, the localisation and the brand, and callers pass a template key and a payload rather than any markup. The service validates the payload against the template's declared schema and refuses to render on a mismatch, which turns a broken email into a failed job with a clear error instead of a message that goes out with an empty amount in it. That failure had happened twice before the schema check existed. Consolidation started when a brand refresh required touching 17 separate templates spread across four services, three of which had their own subtly different footer and one of which was still using the previous logo eleven months later. Templates now live in one repository directory with a preview server, and non-engineers can see a rendered example of every message with sample data. Localisation is part of the same move: the language is chosen from the recipient's stored preference at render time, in one place, rather than by each caller passing a locale it may or may not have.

Nothing sends an email inside a request. The handler writes an outbox row in the same transaction as the state change that justifies the message, and a relay picks it up and hands it to the provider. This gets us two properties we could not get any other way. The message cannot be sent for something that was rolled back, which used to happen on the signup path whenever a later validation failed after the welcome email had already gone out, leaving people with a welcome to an account that did not exist. And the request does not wait on the provider, which is what turned a provider slowdown into user-visible latency on registration and checkout, the two pages where latency costs the most. The relay retries with backoff and gives up after several attempts into a dead letter table someone looks at each morning. The pattern also makes the send testable without any network at all, since a test asserts the outbox row exists rather than mocking a client, which removed a long tail of brittle assertions.

Inbound mail is not our problem to run. Anything arriving at the support address, the security address or the reply-to on notifications lands in a hosted helpdesk that owns parsing, threading, spam filtering and attachment scanning, and our systems interact with it through its API rather than with mailboxes. We ran our own inbound pipeline briefly and it was a bad trade. Receiving mail well means handling every malformed encoding anyone has ever produced, matching replies to threads when clients mangle the headers, deciding what to do with automatic out-of-office responses, and scanning attachments, none of which is our business and all of which produces a steady drip of one-off bugs. The one integration we kept is a small consumer that turns a support conversation into an incident record when an agent tags it, which is the only place the two systems need to agree on anything. Replies to notification addresses used to vanish into an unmonitored mailbox, which is the specific failure this arrangement was set up to end.

Dependency bumps arrive as automated pull requests grouped by ecosystem once a week, and what happens next depends on one list. Anything named in `deps/critical.yaml` gets a manual evaluation; everything else auto-merges when CI is green. The list currently holds the payment SDK, the identity client, the database driver, the HTTP library and the serialisation library, chosen because a silent behaviour change in any of them costs money or leaks data. The evaluation is four steps and takes about an hour. Read the changelog for behaviour changes rather than API changes, which is where the danger lives, and write down what you found. Diff the resolved lock file, because a patch bump of one package routinely drags in a minor of three others. Run the contract suite against the vendor's sandbox, not against our recorded fixtures, since recorded responses cannot show you a changed default. Then deploy to a single canary pod for 24 hours with error rate and latency compared against the fleet. The outcome is a short note in `docs/dependency-notes/` naming the version and what was checked, which makes the next upgrade cheaper. This exists because a patch bump of the payment SDK changed its internal retry default from none to three, and we double-charged 340 customers before anyone connected the two. We pin exact versions, never ranges, and upgrades never ride inside a feature branch.

Advisories are patched on a clock that starts when the advisory is published, not when someone notices it. Critical severity with a known exploitation path is a same-day deploy and the on-call engineer owns it; critical without one is 3 days; high is 14 days; medium rides the normal weekly batch; low is recorded and left. The scanner runs against the lock files on every build and daily against what is actually deployed, which is the check that matters, because a fixed lock file in the trunk tells you nothing about the version running in a service that has not shipped for a month. Deadlines are visible on a board with the owning team named, and a breach escalates to the engineering leads rather than sitting in a report nobody opens. The clock came out of an audit finding that our mean time to patch a high severity issue was fifty-one days, and the reason was not disagreement about urgency but the absence of any owner: the advisory arrived in a shared inbox and every recipient assumed the same thing about who was handling it.

The lock file is the source of truth for what gets installed, and CI fails if resolving the manifest would produce a different one. Installs everywhere use the frozen mode that refuses to update anything, so a build cannot quietly resolve a newer version than the one that was reviewed. Before that, we had a build that succeeded on Friday and failed on Monday with no commits in between, which took an afternoon to explain and turned out to be a transitive dependency publishing a release over the weekend. The same mechanism protects the reproducibility of an old build: checking out a tag from a year ago and installing gives the tree that shipped, which matters when reproducing a customer's reported behaviour on a version they are still running. The cost is that adding a dependency requires regenerating and committing the lock, and merge conflicts in a large lock file are unpleasant, so they are resolved by regenerating rather than by hand editing, and a check verifies the committed file matches a clean resolve.

One library sits vendored in `third_party/tariffcalc/` with its own directory of tests we wrote ourselves. It is a small tariff calculation package we depend on heavily, published by a maintainer who ships breaking changes in patch releases and has twice republished the same version number with different content. Vendoring it was a last resort after the second time a rebuild produced different totals with no change on our side, and we chose it over forking publicly because the code is a few hundred lines and we did not want to maintain a fork's release process. The directory carries a readme with the upstream version, the date it was taken and the two local modifications, and a scheduled job compares upstream against our copy monthly and opens an issue when they diverge so the decision to update is made deliberately. This is deliberately rare, and the bar is a library that is small enough to own and has actually burned us more than once; vendoring anything large trades a supply chain problem for a maintenance problem that is worse.

Application code does not import a vendor SDK directly. Each integration has a thin adapter in `integrations/` exposing our own types and our own error taxonomy, and the SDK is imported inside that module and nowhere else, which a lint rule enforces. The wrapper is intentionally boring and adds nothing clever, because its value is entirely in the boundary. Swapping the mail provider touched one adapter and a configuration value rather than forty call sites, and the same shape made it possible to run two payment processors behind one interface. It also gives one place to apply timeouts, metrics and the request id, and one place to translate a vendor's fifteen exception classes into the four outcomes our callers actually branch on. The rule was written after a first attempt to change a provider stalled for a quarter, because the SDK's objects had leaked into service signatures and even into a serialised job payload, which meant the migration required draining a queue of messages containing the vendor's own types.

A framework major version is planned as a piece of work with an owner, a branch strategy and a scheduled window, not attempted as a pull request that someone picks up between other things. The trigger to start is the upstream end-of-life date minus one quarter, tracked on the platform roadmap so it never arrives as a surprise. What makes majors different is that the work is not the code change; it is the sequencing. Deprecation warnings get cleared on the current version first so the actual upgrade diff contains only what genuinely changed, dependent libraries are checked for compatibility before anything starts, and the rollout goes service by service with the shared libraries supporting both versions in between. We learned that from an attempted upgrade that lived on a branch for 11 weeks, was rebased 40 times, and was eventually abandoned because the trunk had moved too far underneath it. The current approach ships small compatible steps on the trunk with a flag choosing behaviour, which is slower to start and much faster to finish.

A dependency that nothing imports gets deleted in the same week it is noticed. A weekly job builds the import graph, compares it against the declared dependencies, and opens a pull request removing anything unreferenced, which a human reviews because the analysis cannot see plugin registration or anything loaded by name at runtime. Most weeks it finds nothing and some weeks it finds three. The motivation is not disk space. Every declared dependency is something the scanner reports on, something that constrains resolution when other packages are upgraded, and something a person evaluating an advisory has to reason about, and the effort of deciding that an unused library's vulnerability does not affect us is spent every single time it appears. We had a package that produced four advisories over a year and had not been imported since a rewrite two years earlier, and each one cost somebody half an hour. Removing it cost five minutes once. Test-only and build-only dependencies are declared in their own groups so they are never shipped in the runtime image.

Licences are checked automatically before a dependency can land. The pipeline resolves the tree, maps every package to its declared licence, and fails the build on anything outside the allowed set, which covers the permissive licences and the weak copyleft ones we have decided are compatible with how we ship. Strong copyleft is blocked outright and anything unrecognised or missing a declaration fails as unknown rather than passing quietly, because an absent licence field is the case most likely to be a real problem. Exceptions go through legal and are recorded in the allowlist with the reason and the reviewer's name attached, which keeps the list from becoming a place where things get added to make a build go green. The check exists because a customer's procurement questionnaire asked for a complete licence inventory and producing it by hand took two people three days, and the second time it was asked we wanted the answer to be a generated file. It runs on every build rather than periodically, since catching a licence problem before merge is trivial and catching it after release is a conversation with lawyers.

Internal packages are published to one private index and consumed by version like anything else, never by a path reference or a git URL. There are 6 of them, covering the shared HTTP conventions, the domain types, the telemetry setup, the test helpers, the client for the identity service and the migration tooling. Each publishes on merge to the trunk with a version derived from a conventional commit prefix, and the release notes are generated from the commit messages. Path references were how it worked in the earliest days of the monorepo, and they made every consumer track the shared library's head, so a breaking change in the telemetry package broke four services at once with no window in which to react. Versioning gives each consumer its own upgrade moment. The index is also where the vendored artefacts and the internal build of one native extension live, so a build needs exactly one registry credential, which simplifies the CI configuration and, more usefully, means an outage of the public registry does not stop a deploy of something already cached here.

Every upload lands in the `hlane-uploads-quarantine` bucket first and is not addressable by anyone until a scanner has cleared it. The create call returns 202 with an object id in state `pending_scan`, and the media service refuses to sign a read URL for an object in any state other than `clean`. Scanner workers pull from the `uploads.scan` queue, stream the object into a sidecar running ClamAV with signature updates every four hours, and separately sniff the leading bytes with libmagic instead of trusting the declared content type or the file extension. That mismatch is the whole reason this exists: someone uploaded a file called `invoice.pdf` that was a Windows executable, the old path believed the `Content-Type` the browser sent, and the object sat in the customer-facing attachments bucket for nine days until a support engineer's own antivirus flagged it on download. A clean verdict copies the object to the serving bucket under its content hash and deletes the quarantine copy. An infected verdict moves it to `hlane-uploads-infected`, which no role but security can read, writes a row to `upload_scan_verdicts`, and emails the security channel with the account id rather than paging, because one hit is a customer's problem and a cluster of them is ours. A scan that has not finished within ninety seconds fails closed and the object stays quarantined.

The twenty-five megabyte cap on a single upload is enforced by the gateway through `client_max_body_size`, not by the application. The application still checks, because defence in depth is cheap, but by the time a request reaches a worker the body has already been buffered and the memory has already been spent, so a check there only tells you about a resource you have finished consuming. We found this out when a script with a retry loop pushed the same four hundred megabyte file at us eleven times in a minute and took three workers out of rotation while they read bodies they were going to reject. The gateway answers 413 as soon as the declared length exceeds the limit and drops the connection if a chunked body runs past it mid-stream. The limit is per plan tier, expressed as an annotation on the route rather than a hard-coded constant, so raising it for one enterprise account is a config change and not a deploy. Anything genuinely larger goes through the multipart path instead, which is a different route with a different limit and different accounting.

The browser never sends file bytes to our API. The client asks for an upload ticket, gets back a presigned POST with a five minute expiry and a policy that pins the key prefix, the maximum size and the account id, and then talks directly to the object store. Our servers see two small JSON requests and no payload at all. Before this the file went through the API so that we could attach it to a record in the same transaction, which sounded tidy and meant every large upload occupied a request worker for the duration of a customer's home broadband upstream — a twenty megabyte file from a bad connection could hold a worker for four minutes. Throughput on the API tier improved immediately and the p99 on unrelated endpoints stopped tracking the upload volume. The cost is that the object exists before the database row does, which is why the client has to call back to finalise, and why anything never finalised is treated as garbage rather than as data.

Thumbnails and the other three derivative sizes are produced by the `media-derive` worker pool, which runs on its own nodes with a memory limit of two gigabytes per process and a hard wall clock of forty-five seconds per job. They are not produced inline and they are not produced on first read. Decoding untrusted image data is the single most expensive and most crash-prone thing this system does — a malformed progressive JPEG can make the decoder allocate wildly, and when that shared a process with anything else it took the whole thing down with it. Isolating it means a decoder that dies kills one job, the job is retried twice, and after that the object is marked `derive_failed` and the original is served as-is with the browser doing the scaling. The derived objects are written under a `/d/` prefix keyed by the original's hash plus the size name, so they are trivially regenerable and are excluded from every backup we take.

The key an object gets in the bucket is the SHA-256 of its bytes, split into two leading directory levels, with no extension. The name the customer gave the file is kept in the `attachments` table as a display attribute and is used only in the `Content-Disposition` header when the file is handed back. Original filenames as keys gave us three distinct headaches at once: two customers uploading `report.pdf` in the same folder, keys containing characters that behave differently in a URL than in a shell script, and a support tool that reconstructed a path by concatenation and walked out of the prefix it was supposed to be confined to. Content addressing also deduplicates for free, which matters more than expected because the same onboarding PDF gets uploaded by nearly every account. The database keeps a reference count, and nothing is deleted from the bucket until the last row pointing at that hash is gone.

Objects that exist in the bucket with no row referencing them are garbage, and a nightly sweeper deletes any that are older than a day. They accumulate because the upload is a two-step dance: the bytes arrive first, the record that gives them meaning arrives second, and anything can happen in between — the tab is closed, the phone loses signal, the finalise call is rejected because the parent record was deleted while the file was in flight. None of that is an error worth surfacing to anyone, but the bytes still cost money and still count against the account. The sweeper compares the bucket listing against the reference table, refuses to run at all if the listing looks implausibly short, and logs a count rather than a list. The age threshold exists so that an upload genuinely in progress is never mistaken for abandoned, and it has been raised once already after a customer with a very slow link had a legitimate transfer collected.

Anything over one hundred megabytes has to use the multipart path, and the ticket endpoint refuses a single-shot presign above that size rather than issuing one that will fail later. Parts are sixteen megabytes, which is a compromise between the part count ceiling and the amount of work lost when a part fails. The reason for the hard floor rather than a suggestion is that a single-shot PUT of a large file has no resume: a transfer that dies at ninety-five percent starts again from nothing, and for the customers moving archive bundles over office links that was a twenty minute loss every time it happened, several times a day. With parts, only the failed part is retried, and the client can walk away and come back within the assembly window. The upload id is recorded so support can tell the difference between a transfer that is still going and one that stopped, which used to be pure guesswork.

Avatars and any image attached to a public-facing profile are decoded and written back out fresh rather than stored as received. The point is the metadata block. Phone cameras embed precise coordinates, a device serial and often the owner's name, and none of that is visible in the picture, so nobody uploading a photo of themselves has any reason to think they are publishing where they live. A journalist using the product pointed this out to us politely, having extracted a colleague's home neighbourhood from an avatar in about a minute, and the fix shipped that week. Re-encoding drops every ancillary chunk, normalises the colour profile so the image looks the same in every browser, and applies the orientation rather than leaving it as a tag that half of our surfaces honoured and half did not. The visible quality loss is real but small, and it is confined to profile imagery — files a customer uploads as documents are stored byte for byte, because there the exact original is the thing they are paying us to keep.

The in-flight state of an upload — parts completed, bytes received, last heartbeat — lives in Redis under a key with a twelve hour TTL, and never touches the primary database. It was in Postgres originally and it was the single hottest write path we had, because a client uploading a large file updates that row every few seconds and every one of those updates is a dead tuple by the next one. During one busy afternoon the table's bloat was bad enough that autovacuum could not keep up and the planner started choosing a sequential scan on it, which had nothing to do with uploads and slowed everything sharing that connection pool. Progress is disposable by nature: if Redis loses it, the client restarts the transfer, which is annoying but correct. The rule that came out of it is that anything a client rewrites on a timer belongs in a store that expects to be rewritten on a timer. Only the terminal outcome, success with a final key or a definitive failure, is written to `attachments`, and that is exactly one row per upload.

The `atlas-exports` bucket carries a lifecycle rule that deletes every object under the `generated/` prefix fourteen days after creation, and the rule is the enforcement mechanism rather than a cleanup job we run ourselves. Two things drove it. The first was the bill: exports are the cheapest thing in the world to create and nobody ever goes back and deletes one, so the prefix grew by roughly forty gigabytes a week and was the third largest line on the storage invoice within a year, entirely composed of CSVs that had been downloaded once on the day they were made. The second was worse. An export contains a flattened copy of whatever the requester could see, and its download link had been pasted into a shared document; the underlying permission was revoked months later and the object was still sitting there, still fetchable by anyone holding the link, because nothing about revoking access to live data touches a snapshot of it. Expiry bounds that window to a fortnight without anyone having to remember. We put it in the bucket rather than in a cron job on purpose — a cron job runs on a host that can be down, needs credentials to delete, and silently stops; the lifecycle rule is evaluated by the storage service itself and cannot drift from what the configuration says. Users are told the fourteen days in the UI and in the notification email, and a re-run costs them one click.

Objects under the `events/` prefix move to the infrequent access class after thirty days and to archive after ninety, and they are never deleted. The access pattern is what makes this work: analytics reads yesterday constantly, last month occasionally, and last year only when a regulator or a very determined finance question turns up. Paying hot storage rates for four years of data that gets touched twice a year was the mistake we were making, and the transition rules cut that prefix's monthly cost by about sixty percent without changing a line of code. The one trap is the minimum storage duration — an object moved to archive and then deleted a week later is billed as though it stayed for the full term, so anything with a genuine expiry must never be tiered first. Restoring from archive takes hours rather than seconds, which is fine for the questions this data actually answers, but it means no interactive dashboard is ever allowed to read from that prefix directly.

Every bucket we create has a rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads after seven days, and it is in the module default so nobody has to think about it. Abandoned parts are invisible: they do not appear in a normal object listing, no tool most engineers use will show them, and they are billed at full rate for as long as they exist. We discovered a hundred and ninety gigabytes of them in the media bucket while trying to work out why the storage line was larger than the sum of everything we could see, some of it more than two years old, all of it from a client library that gave up mid-transfer without cleaning up. Seven days is longer than any legitimate transfer we support and short enough that the residue never accumulates. The same rule is why the storage dashboard now graphs the size reported by the inventory report rather than the sum of the objects we can list, because those two numbers disagreeing is exactly the signal we missed the first time.

Bucket lifecycle configuration is owned by the `storage/buckets` Terraform module and a drift check runs against it every night. Nobody edits a rule in the provider console, and the accounts we care about have the console permission for it removed outright. This is not process for its own sake: a lifecycle rule is a scheduled, silent, irreversible delete, and a change to one produces no visible effect until days later when the objects it was going to keep are gone. Somebody widening a prefix pattern by hand at four in the afternoon is the kind of change that no review would have caught anyway if it lived only in a web form. In the module it gets the same treatment as anything else — a plan output showing the exact before and after, a reviewer, and a commit that says why. The drift check exists because provider defaults have changed under us twice, and finding out from a nightly diff is much better than finding out from a customer.

The bucket holding database backups is configured in compliance mode with a retention period, which means neither an engineer nor the root credentials can remove an object before its term is up. It has no expiry rule of any kind, and that asymmetry is deliberate. Everywhere else the risk we are managing is accumulation, so things are set up to remove themselves. Here the risk is the opposite one: an attacker who has taken an administrative credential and wants the recovery path gone before anyone notices, or an automation with a wildcard that is broader than its author believed. Both of those look exactly like a legitimate delete at the moment they happen. Retention that the account itself cannot override is the only control that survives an adversary holding the account. The cost of keeping everything for the full term is real and it is budgeted for, and the trade was settled on the basis that we would rather pay for storage we do not need than discover the backups were tidied away by the same event we needed them for.

Public access block is switched on at the account level, not per bucket, so a bucket policy or an object ACL granting anonymous read is rejected at write time rather than quietly taking effect. There is one carve-out, the static assets bucket behind the CDN, and it lives in a separate account precisely so the block can stay absolute in the account holding customer data. Per-bucket settings were what we had before, and the failure mode was exactly what you would expect: a new bucket created quickly during an incident, defaults not applied because it was made by hand, and a prefix of diagnostic dumps readable by the internet for a fortnight before a scanner told us. Nothing sensitive was in it, which was luck rather than design. An account-level block cannot be forgotten during a hurried Tuesday, and the audit question becomes one setting to check instead of a list that grows every time somebody needs somewhere to put something.

Server access logs for the customer-data buckets are delivered to `kestrel-audit-access` in the logging account, which no application role can write to and only two people can read interactively. Logging a bucket into itself is the obvious shortcut and it is wrong twice over: the log deliveries generate their own log entries, which grows without bound, and anyone who can write objects into the bucket being audited can also write into its audit trail. Separating the accounts means the record of who read what survives a compromise of the thing being read. Delivery is best effort and can lag by hours, so they are an investigative record and never an alerting source. The logs are the only way we can answer the question that always comes after a leaked credential, which is not whether the key worked but exactly which objects it touched, and they are the reason we could tell one customer with certainty that a stolen token had listed a prefix and downloaded nothing from it.

Replication of the media bucket into the secondary region was turned off after a review of what it was actually buying us. The premise had been regional durability, but the objects in there are customer uploads whose originals sit on the customers' own machines, and the recovery plan for the region disappearing has never involved serving media in the first hour — it involves the application coming back with attachments temporarily unavailable. What replication cost was not just the second copy but the egress on every write, forever, for a bucket whose whole purpose is to accumulate. The databases still replicate, because they hold state that exists nowhere else and cannot be reconstructed from anything. That is the distinction we settled on: replicate what only we have, accept the loss on what can be asked for again. Anyone proposing to turn it back on has to say which recovery scenario it changes and how long that scenario is allowed to take.

The Terraform module refuses to create a bucket without `owner` and `cost_code` tags, and a policy in the account denies `s3:CreateBucket` outright when they are absent, so the console route is closed too. Before that we had a spreadsheet of buckets whose owner was a guess, several of which nobody was prepared to say could be deleted, and one that turned out to be feeding a report the finance team ran every quarter and had never mentioned to anyone. Untagged storage is not merely an accounting inconvenience — it is storage that cannot be cleaned up, because nobody will delete something they cannot attribute. The tags flow into the cost report so a team sees its own storage line without asking, and the monthly review has a name attached to every row that grew. When somebody leaves, their buckets show up in a query rather than becoming folklore, and the handover conversation happens while they are still here to have it.

Customer-uploaded files are served from `hlane-usercontent.net`, a separate registrable domain that we own but that shares nothing with `harborlane.com`. Not a subdomain — a different site as far as the browser's origin rules are concerned. The reason is that any file a stranger can upload and another user can open is, in effect, code we are hosting, and the same-origin policy is the only boundary that reliably contains it. We learned this the direct way. A support attachment was an SVG with an inline script block; SVG is served as an image but rendered as a document when you navigate to it, the script ran with the app's origin, and it read the session cookie of the agent who clicked the link. Nothing was exfiltrated because our egress rules stopped the fetch, which was luck. Moving the content to its own domain means the worst case is a script running in an origin that has no cookies, no local storage, no tokens, and nothing worth stealing. The separate domain is also cookieless by construction: it is not in the session cookie's `Domain` scope, so a request for a file never carries credentials in the first place, which incidentally makes it cacheable at the edge. Access control is done with signed URLs instead of cookies. A subdomain was proposed and rejected because cookies scoped to the parent domain would follow it there.

A read URL for a private object is signed for fifteen minutes and is bound to the object key, so it is neither long-lived nor reusable for anything else. The number is a compromise nobody loves: long enough that a user can start a large download and finish it, short enough that a link pasted into a chat is dead before most people click it. The alternative we ran for a year was a permanent obscure URL, on the theory that an unguessable key is effectively private, and the failure mode was completely predictable in hindsight — those links end up in email threads, in support tickets, in browser history on shared machines, and in one case in a screenshot on a public forum. Unguessable is not the same as revocable. Signing also gives us a place to hang the audit record, because the signature is issued by our service after a permission check and that issuance is logged with the account and the object. The client re-requests a signature when one expires, which is a round trip nobody notices.

An SVG that arrives as an image attachment is converted to a raster image and the original vector file is discarded. Customers occasionally complain that their logo looks soft when scaled up, and that complaint is the price of the decision. SVG is not really an image format, it is a document format that happens to describe pictures, and it can contain scripts, external references that fetch on render, and entity declarations that have historically been a reliable way to make a parser read files it should not. Every one of those is a live capability rather than a theoretical one. The conversion runs in a sandboxed renderer with network access removed and a memory cap, because the converter itself is parsing the hostile input and is not automatically trustworthy either. Vector output is still available in the one place it genuinely matters, the branding settings for enterprise accounts, and there it goes through a much stricter allowlist of permitted elements and is reviewed by a human before it goes live anywhere a customer's users can see it.

The CDN distribution in front of media is configured to forward no cookies and only three headers to the origin, and to key the cache on the path and the signature parameters alone. Forwarding cookies to an origin that ignores them is not harmless: it makes the cache key vary per user, which turns a shared cache into a per-visitor cache, and our hit rate on that distribution was under twenty percent for months before anyone worked out why. Stripping them took it above ninety. The security benefit is a side effect but a welcome one, since a header that never reaches the origin cannot be misinterpreted by it. The forwarded set is pinned in the distribution's Terraform resource so that adding one is a reviewed change rather than a console toggle. Anything genuinely user-specific is expressed in the signed URL rather than in a header, which keeps the cache key honest — two users with permission to the same object get the same bytes from the same cache entry, and a user without permission never gets a signature at all.

Anything outside a short allowlist of types goes back with `Content-Disposition: attachment` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, so the browser saves it rather than displaying it. Images, PDFs and plain text render inline; everything else downloads. This came out of a support thread rather than a security review. A customer uploaded an HTML file exported from a spreadsheet tool, another user clicked it expecting a download, and got a page that looked like it belonged to us, complete with a form. Nobody was attacked, but the shape of the problem was obvious once we had seen it. Forcing the download also settles a much duller argument about file types the browser half-supports, where the behaviour differs by browser and by version, and a support answer that begins with the words depends on your browser is an answer nobody can act on. The stored type is the one the scanner determined, not the one the uploader claimed.

The media domain's certificate is issued through its own ACME account with its own key, and the renewal job runs from a different pipeline than the one that renews the application certificates. Neither can request a certificate for the other's names. This was a small change with an outsized reason behind it: a single ACME account credential that can name every domain we own is a credential whose compromise is total, and the blast radius is worth splitting even when the operational cost is a second cron entry and a second alert. It also means a renewal failure is isolated. There was a Sunday where a validation record went missing and the renewal loop failed for two days without anyone noticing; because the accounts were separate, the outage that eventually happened was media not loading, not the entire product being unreachable. The alert on days-to-expiry fires at twenty-one days for both, and it now names which of the two is at risk.

Several enterprise customers have asked to have attachments served from a hostname in their own zone, so that links look like they come from them rather than from us. We said no, and the answer has held through three renewal cycles. Serving their content from their name means issuing and renewing certificates for domains we do not control, on a validation record they have to keep in place, and every one of those becomes an outage we get paged for and cannot fix ourselves. It also quietly transfers a security property: the isolation we get from keeping user content off the application's origin only works if the content domain is not also the customer's own application domain, and for exactly the customers who want this, it usually is. The compromise we offered instead is a branded landing page on the shared content host, which satisfied the actual request in most cases, since what people wanted was for a link not to look like it came from an unrelated third party.

Public assets — the ones a customer has explicitly marked shareable — can be embedded from anywhere, and we do not check the referrer or attempt to stop it. This gets raised roughly once a year as a bandwidth concern, and the arithmetic has never supported doing anything about it. The traffic in question is a rounding error against the video the marketing site serves, and the mechanism people reach for is unreliable in both directions: referrer headers are stripped by privacy settings and by plenty of legitimate clients, so blocking on them breaks real embeds, and any determined re-hoster simply copies the file once and serves it themselves. Where abuse is actually possible is the private path, and that is controlled by signatures with a short life rather than by guessing at who is asking. If a single asset ever did become expensive enough to matter, the answer would be a per-object cap, not a referrer rule.

Requests to `/files/{id}` on the application host still work and answer with a 302 to a freshly signed location. That route was supposed to be temporary and has now outlived two of the people who agreed it would be. It exists because links to attachments were embedded in emails we sent for years, in customer wiki pages, and in at least one integration a partner built against a URL shape we never documented, and every one of those breaks the day the route goes away. The redirect costs a request to our tier per download, which is measurable but small, and it is instrumented so we can see the rate. It has fallen by about eighty percent over three years, mostly as old email ages out. The agreed removal trigger is a rate below a hundred requests a day sustained for a month, at which point the route starts answering with a page explaining where the file moved rather than disappearing silently.

An export request does not return a file. It returns 202 with an export id, the work is enqueued, and the requester is notified when the object is ready. Anything the estimator thinks will exceed five thousand rows goes down that path automatically; below that the response is inline because a small export finishing in a second is a better experience than an email. The reason for the split is that a synchronous export is a request whose duration is set by the customer's data volume, and there is no timeout you can pick that is right for both a fifty row export and a two million row one. Ours were dying at the gateway's sixty second ceiling, which was bad enough, but the real damage was what happened next: the client retried, the retry started the same query again, and by the third attempt one account had four copies of the same enormous scan running against the primary while holding four request workers hostage. That afternoon is why the rule exists. The asynchronous path also gets us the things a long request cannot have — the job is idempotent on the export id so a retry attaches to the existing run rather than starting a new one, progress is observable, a failure can be retried without the customer sitting there, and the work runs on a pool sized for it rather than on the tier that also has to answer the login endpoint. Status is polled at `GET /exports/{id}`.

The row source for an export is a named cursor on the reporting replica, fetched two thousand rows at a time and written straight through to the output stream. Nothing accumulates a full result set in memory. The naive version built a list of dictionaries and then serialised it, which was fine on the fixtures it was written against and allocated several gigabytes on real accounts, and the process that died taking a job with it usually took the two other jobs on the same worker as well. Fetching in batches keeps the memory profile flat regardless of how much data the account has, so the only thing that scales with size is the time. The replica choice is about not putting a query that walks a year of history onto the same instance that serves interactive traffic; the export is allowed to be slow and is not allowed to be disruptive. Cursors do hold a transaction open on the replica, which is why the fetch loop is not permitted to do anything else while it runs.

Our CSV output starts with a byte order mark, and this is a decision that gets questioned by every engineer who encounters it for the first time. It is there because Excel on Windows opens a Unicode file without one as though it were the legacy code page, and the result is mangled accents in every customer name. That is not an edge case for us, it is the majority of how these files are actually opened. Purists point out that the mark is meaningless for a byte-oriented encoding and that it breaks naive parsers which do not strip it. Both true, and we still ship it, because the population that opens these files in a spreadsheet is enormous and the population that pipes them into a hand-written parser is small and technical enough to cope. Line endings are carriage return and line feed for the same reason. The JSON output has neither, since nothing reading it has this problem, and the two formats being inconsistent with each other is the honest consequence of serving two different audiences.

The export API refuses a filter set that would produce more than one million rows and tells the caller to narrow the range, rather than producing a truncated file. The cap is checked with an estimate before the work starts and again as a hard stop while writing. Truncation was the old behaviour and it was the worst of the options: a file that looks complete, has no marker saying it is not, and gets loaded into somebody's warehouse as though it were the whole picture. One customer reconciled against a silently clipped export for two quarters. The number itself is arbitrary in the sense that it is not a technical limit — it is roughly where the resulting file stops being something a human or a spreadsheet can do anything with, and beyond it the honest answer is that the customer wants a data feed rather than an export, which is a different product with a different price. The error names the row count it estimated so the caller can work out how much to narrow by.

Scheduled exports that used to be configured per customer by our support team now live in the reporting product as a saved report with a delivery schedule, and the bespoke ones were migrated over a quarter. The old arrangement had accumulated a couple of hundred hand-made schedules, each one a row somebody had inserted, several referencing columns that no longer existed, at least one still mailing a former employee. Nobody owned them and nobody could say which mattered. Moving them into a product surface means the customer owns their own schedule, can see it, can change it, and can turn it off without opening a ticket, and it means a column being renamed breaks a report the customer can see rather than a job that quietly fails at three in the morning. Support kept the ability to create one on a customer's behalf, because the people asking for these are often the least technical users we have, but it creates the same object through the same interface rather than a special one.

The link in the notification email points at our application, not at storage, and following it requires being logged in as a user who still has permission to the data in the export. The signature is redeemed once; a second click gets a fresh one if you are still entitled to it and an error if you are not. Emailing a direct storage link was the first implementation and it took about a week for someone to point out what it meant: an export is a flattened snapshot of everything the requester could see, the email may be forwarded, the mailbox may be shared with an assistant, and none of those people were ever checked against a permission. Routing the download through the application also means the access is recorded against a user, which is the first thing anyone asks for when a customer wants to know who took a copy of their contact list. The cost is that the person clicking has to log in, which generates a small but steady trickle of confused support tickets, and we consider that acceptable.

PDF output is produced by a headless Chromium in a dedicated container with no network egress and a one gigabyte memory cap, restarted after every hundred documents. It does not share a process, a pool or a node with anything else. Browsers are heavy, leaky and occasionally decide to take a very long time over a single page, and every one of those properties is fine in isolation and unacceptable when it is sitting next to work that has to finish predictably. The restart interval is empirical: memory use climbs steadily regardless of what we do, and recycling on a count is simpler and more reliable than trying to find the leak in something that large.
