Egress is removed because the templates are ours but the data in them is not, and a rendering engine that will happily fetch a remote image is a rendering engine that can be pointed somewhere by a customer-supplied string. Fonts are baked into the image for the same reason and because a missing font produces a document that is wrong in a way nobody notices until a customer prints it.

Every export format has a version, requested as `format_version` and defaulting to the oldest still supported rather than to the newest. Columns are only ever appended within a version, never removed, renamed or reordered. This is unglamorous and it is the single thing that has saved us the most support pain in this area, because the people consuming these files have written scripts that index by position, load them into a warehouse table with a fixed schema, or have a spreadsheet with formulas pointing at column K. Any of those breaks silently, and it breaks on their side, so we find out weeks later through a confused ticket about numbers not matching. A new version is announced, both are served in parallel for two release cycles, and usage of the old one is graphed so we can see who has not moved. Defaulting to the old version rather than the current one is the part people argue with, and it is correct: a caller who did not ask for a change should not receive one.

An export job gets three attempts with a growing delay, and after the third it is marked failed, the requester is told, and it stops. It is not parked in a dead letter queue for somebody to look at later. The distinction that matters here is who is waiting: for internal work, silently retrying until an engineer notices is often the right call, but a person asked for this file and is refreshing a page, and the cruel version of this system is one where they wait a day to find out nothing was coming. Most failures are also not transient — a filter that produces a pathological query, a record with a value the serialiser cannot represent, a permission revoked between request and run — and no number of retries fixes any of those. The failure message is deliberately vague to the customer and precise in the log, which is a compromise we revisit occasionally when support cannot tell from the customer-facing text which of half a dozen causes they are looking at.

Each account has a byte allowance from its plan, stored on the account row as `storage_quota_bytes`, and a running total in `account_storage_usage` that is adjusted in the same transaction that creates or deletes an attachment record. The check happens when an upload ticket is requested, not when the bytes land: the presign endpoint adds the declared size to the current total and refuses with 413 and a machine-readable `quota_exceeded` code if that would cross the limit. Checking at the end is useless, because by then you have already paid to store the thing you are about to reject. At eighty percent the account owner gets one email and a banner in the product, and neither repeats more than once a week. Enterprise plans are configured to warn and record an overage rather than block, because cutting off a customer mid-quarter over storage is a commercial decision and not an engineering one, and the flag for that is on the plan rather than sprinkled through the code. The counter drifts — a delete that fails after the row is gone, a job that writes objects directly, a restore that reinstates rows — so `tools/reconcile_usage.py` runs nightly against the bucket inventory report and rewrites totals that differ by more than one percent, logging every correction. It exists because one account ran six times over its allowance on a counter stuck since a failed bulk delete.

All customer objects live in one bucket under an `a/{account_id}/` prefix rather than in a bucket each. A bucket per tenant is superficially attractive — clean separation, per-tenant policies, a metric per customer for free — and it runs into a hard account limit measured in the low thousands, which is a number we would have hit during a growth year rather than at some comfortable distance. Provisioning would also have moved onto the signup path, meaning a new customer cannot finish registering when the storage control plane is having a bad day. Prefixes have no such ceiling and cost nothing to create. What we gave up is per-bucket accounting, which is why usage has to be tracked by us rather than read off an invoice, and per-bucket policy, which is replaced by the signing service refusing to sign a key outside the caller's own prefix. That last check is the only thing keeping tenants apart, so it has its own tests and its own review requirement.

The storage service writes a daily inventory of every object in the customer bucket as Parquet under `inventory/`, and the analytics cluster reads it directly. Before this, any question that began with how much is in there was answered by a script that listed the bucket, which took most of a day for a prefix of that size, cost a fortune in list requests, and returned a number that was already out of date. The inventory is produced by the provider from metadata it already has, so it is close to free and complete in a way a paginated listing never is. It carries the key, size, storage class, last modified time and encryption status, which is enough to answer nearly everything we ask: where the cost is concentrated, what has not been touched in a year, whether anything is unencrypted. It is a day stale by construction, so it is never used for anything a customer sees in real time, only for analysis and for the reconciliation jobs that run overnight anyway.

The usage screen in the product reads `mv_account_usage_hourly`, refreshed on the hour, and says so on the page with the timestamp of the last refresh. It does not query live. Rendering that screen used to run a set of aggregates over the attachment and event tables per page load, which was fine for a small account and took eleven seconds for our largest, and because it was on the billing settings page it was hit hardest at exactly the moment someone was already annoyed about a number. A materialised view makes it a single indexed read. The interesting part was the product decision that followed: showing a slightly stale figure turned out to be uncontroversial once the page said when it was from, whereas an honest live number that took ten seconds to appear generated tickets claiming the page was broken. Refresh is concurrent so the view stays readable while it runs, and a failed refresh alerts rather than leaving yesterday's numbers up silently.

Files attached to a support conversation are deleted ninety days after that conversation is closed, and the customer is told so in the attachment tooltip and in the terms. The transcript stays; only the binaries go, replaced by a tombstone showing the filename and who uploaded it, so the history still reads coherently. Support attachments are the single most sensitive pile of data we hold and the one with the least deliberate governance around it — customers send screenshots containing other customers' details, exported spreadsheets, occasionally an entire database dump because someone asked them to attach the logs. Keeping that forever is a liability that grows every day and buys nothing, since a closed conversation from last year is reopened roughly never and the file is almost never the reason. The purge runs weekly rather than continuously so that a wrong retention setting is caught by the dry-run diff before it removes anything, and it refuses to run if the count it is about to delete is more than three times the trailing average.

The demo accounts sales uses are destroyed and recreated from a seed script at the start of every week. Nothing in them is preserved, and everyone who touches them knows it. They rot otherwise, and they rot in a particularly embarrassing direction: a rep tries something during a call, leaves a half-finished record behind, the next rep opens the same account in front of a different prospect and finds a customer called test test with a negative balance. Rebuilding weekly also keeps the seed script honest, because a script that is only run when someone needs a fresh environment is a script that has been broken for a month by the time you need it. It exercises the signup path, the invitation flow and the sample data importer every Monday morning, and it has caught real regressions in all three before a customer did. Anyone who wants to keep something they built in a demo account has to save it somewhere else, and the tooling makes that a single export.

The storage line on an invoice is computed from the bytes held at the moment the billing period closes, not the average over the month and not the highest point it reached. Everyone agrees this is not the most accurate possible measure, and it was chosen because it is the one a customer can verify. A peak figure means the bill reflects a number the customer never sees anywhere in the product and cannot reproduce; an average means explaining a weighted calculation in a support reply. The closing figure is on their usage screen, and if they delete a large amount of data before the period ends the reduction is visible on the next invoice, which is exactly the behaviour people expect and the behaviour that stops the argument. It does mean someone could in principle upload an enormous amount, use it, and delete it before the close, and we have decided we do not care, because the transfer and request charges are metered separately and that pattern has never actually appeared.

An account whose prefix passes one terabyte is migrated to a dedicated bucket, with the location recorded on the account row so the signing service knows where to look. This is a handful of customers and is handled as a planned piece of work rather than automatically. The trigger is not really size, it is the operational awkwardness that arrives with it: at that scale the customer starts asking for their own encryption key, their data in a particular region, a separate lifecycle policy, and an answer to what happens if they leave, and every one of those is a bucket-level setting that cannot be expressed on a prefix. Doing it before they ask is much cheaper than doing it under commercial pressure, because the migration itself is a copy that takes days and has to run while they are actively writing. The indirection through the account row was added at the same time and applies to everyone, so the shared bucket is just the default value rather than a special case in the code.

When a trial ends without converting, the account is locked immediately and its data is moved to an archive prefix thirty days later, where it stays for a further six months before being deleted for good. The number that mattered in that sequence was the thirty days, and it came from sales rather than engineering: a meaningful share of trials convert after the trial has technically expired, often because the person evaluating went on holiday, and deleting their work makes that conversation impossible. Restoring from the archive tier is slow and manual, which is acceptable for something that happens a few times a month and is always accompanied by a human on both sides. The locked state is the important part technically, because it stops all writes and all API access while leaving the data intact, and it took two attempts to get right — the first version left background jobs running for locked accounts, which meant expired trials were still generating webhooks nobody was reading.

A service's runbook is a markdown file in that service's own repository under `docs/runbooks/`, and the alert that would send you to it carries a `runbook_url` annotation pointing at that path at the deployed commit. It is not in the wiki, and the wiki page that used to hold it now redirects. The argument for this is entirely about drift. A runbook in a separate system is edited by whoever last got paged and is never touched by the change that invalidates it, so it decays silently and you find out at the worst possible moment. In the repository it sits in the same diff as the code, it shows up in review when the behaviour it describes changes, and `CODEOWNERS` puts it in front of the same people. The night that settled the argument, the on-call engineer followed a wiki page that told them to run a script which had been deleted eight months earlier in a refactor nobody thought to cross-reference, and spent forty minutes reconstructing what it used to do while the queue backed up. Two mechanical rules keep it honest: `make alerts-check` fails the build if any alert rule has a `runbook_url` that does not resolve to a file in the tree, and the pull request template asks whether the runbook needs updating whenever a path under `alerts/` or `deploy/` is touched. Resolving the link at the deployed commit means the page you read describes the version actually running.

Incident write-ups all go into a single repository, one directory per incident, regardless of which service was involved. This is the opposite of where our operational documentation lives, and the reason is that the audience is different. A runbook is read by someone working on one thing and needs to be near that thing. A write-up is read by someone looking for patterns — has this failure mode happened before, did we already decide something about this, what did we learn the last time a dependency behaved this way — and that reading is only possible if they are all in one place, in one format, searchable together. Scattering them across service repositories was the original arrangement and it meant an incident spanning three services either got written up three times or once in an arbitrary place nobody would think to look. The single collection also makes the quarterly review possible, where someone reads a season of them end to end and reports what keeps recurring, which is a piece of work that simply cannot be done against a scattered set.

Any runbook instruction that is a sequence of commands has been replaced by a single `make` target in the same repository, and the prose now says which target to run and what to expect from it. `make drain-consumer`, `make replay-dlq`, `make rotate-worker` and a dozen others exist because a numbered list of six commands to be typed at half past three in the morning is a defect list waiting to happen — one of them gets skipped, one gets run against the wrong environment because the export from step two was in a different terminal, one has a flag that has changed since it was written. The targets print what they are about to do and require confirmation for anything destructive. What remains as prose is the part that genuinely needs judgement: how to decide which of the three targets applies, what the symptom looks like when you have chosen wrong, and when to escalate rather than proceeding. The split has held up well, and the honest test of a runbook now is whether the parts left in English are the parts a script could not have decided.

Both the Prometheus rule files and the Grafana dashboard JSON are rendered from `monitoring/signals.yaml` by a generator, and neither output is edited by hand — the pipeline regenerates and fails if the committed artefacts differ. Maintaining them separately meant the query in the alert and the query on the panel diverged constantly, usually by a label filter, so the graph you opened from the alert showed a subtly different thing than the alert was firing on. Chasing that discrepancy has wasted more time than any actual outage in the last year. One source also makes bulk changes possible: when the metric prefix changed during the collector migration, it was one edit and a regeneration rather than a hundred and forty dashboard panels edited in a web interface. The generated files are committed rather than produced at deploy time so that a diff shows exactly which alerts a change moves, which is the review most people actually want to do.

Every service repository's `README.md` has the same five sections in the same order: what it does in two sentences, how to run it locally, how to run its tests, what it talks to, and who owns it. A lint step checks the headings exist and fails the build if one is missing. The uniformity is the whole value. Someone dropping into an unfamiliar service under time pressure should not have to read a wall of prose to find out whether it has a local development story, and the ownership line is the first thing anyone looks for when a service they have never heard of is implicated in an incident. Before the template, READMEs ranged from a single line to a small book, and the small books were worse, because they were three years out of date in ways that were not obvious. The rule that keeps it short is that anything beyond those five sections belongs in a file under the documentation directory with a link from the fourth section, not in the README itself.

The wiki still exists and nobody can edit it any more. Everything that had a live home elsewhere was moved, and what remains is the sediment: old proposals, meeting notes, design discussions that record how the company thought about something at the time. That material has real value and no maintainer, which is exactly the combination that makes freezing the right answer. An editable page with no owner invites someone to make a small correction, which makes it look current, which makes the next reader trust it. Read-only with a banner saying when it was last touched tells the reader what they are holding. Search still indexes it and results are marked as archived so nobody arrives without the context. Deleting it was proposed and rejected on the grounds that the questions it answers — why was this built this way, who objected at the time, what were the alternatives — are asked often enough to be worth keeping, and are answered nowhere else.

The note the outgoing on-call leaves for the incoming one is a comment on a recurring ticket rather than a document anywhere else. It is deliberately ephemeral. The content is things like a customer who will probably write in again, a job that has been retried twice and is being watched, a dependency whose provider has an open status page entry — all of it true for a few days and misleading after that. Putting it anywhere durable creates a document that reads like guidance and is actually a snapshot of somebody's Tuesday. The tracker gives it a timestamp, an author, a thread if the incoming person has questions, and no pretence of permanence. Anything from a handover that turns out to matter beyond the shift gets promoted deliberately: a ticket if it is work, an update to the operational documentation if it is a lasting behaviour change. The test people use is whether they would want to read it again in a month, and for nearly everything in a handover the answer is no.

The glossary of business terms — what exactly a consignment is, how it differs from a shipment, what we mean by settled versus reconciled — is maintained by product, not by engineering, and lives in the product documentation rather than in any code repository. Engineering kept it briefly and it was a mess, because engineers documented the terms as the code uses them, which is not the same thing and is sometimes flatly wrong where the code has a legacy name that nobody outside the file understands. When the two disagree, the glossary wins and the code is the thing that has drifted. What we did keep on our side is a rule that a new concept entering the model has to have a glossary entry before it can be used as a type or a table name, because half the naming arguments in review turn out to be two people using the same word for different things, and looking it up settles the argument faster than discussing it does.

A pull request that only touches files under the runbook directory needs one approval and is exempt from the two-reviewer rule that applies to the deploy and payments paths, and the `CODEOWNERS` entry for those paths is scoped so it does not pull in the infrastructure group. This is a deliberate lowering of a bar. The failure mode we had was not bad runbook edits, it was engineers finishing an incident at two in the morning, knowing precisely what the page should have said, and not writing it down because filing a change that needs two people to wake up and read it is a thing you do tomorrow, and tomorrow the detail has gone. Making the correction cheap at the moment the knowledge exists is worth more than the review would have caught. The one exception is a runbook step that grants access or touches production data, which still needs the second pair of eyes, and those are marked in the file so the check knows which is which.

The OpenAPI description is generated from the server, never written. The route decorators and the request and response models are the source of truth, `make openapi` renders them to `docs/openapi.json`, and a pipeline step regenerates it and fails the build if the committed file differs by so much as a description string. That failure is a one-line fix — regenerate and commit — but it is what guarantees the artefact and the code cannot part ways. The documentation site builds from that file, so the reference a customer reads is a rendering of the running code rather than someone's recollection of it. On top of that, the examples in the spec are executed: `tests/contract/test_examples.py` walks every documented request example, sends it at the service running in the test environment, and asserts the response validates against the documented schema for that status code. An example that no longer works is a failing test rather than a support ticket. All of this came out of a bad stretch with a hand-maintained specification. A field was dropped from a response and the document kept describing it for four months; two customers had generated clients that treated it as required, and untangling whose data was wrong took longer than the change did. Prose that cannot be generated lives beside the spec, is reviewed by hand, and is kept deliberately small.

The changelog for the public interface is written by a person, in prose, and is not derived from commits or from a diff of the schema. Every attempt to automate it produced something technically accurate and useless: a generated list tells a reader that a field appeared and cannot tell them whether they need to do anything, which is the only question they have. A human entry says what changed, who is affected, whether action is required and by when, and it groups three related commits into one sentence because they are one change from outside. The rule is that anything visible to an integrator gets an entry, and the author is whoever made the change rather than a nominated writer, because the context needed to write two good sentences evaporates within a week of shipping. Reviewers are asked to read the entry as though they were a customer with an integration they have not touched in a year, which catches most of the entries that are really release notes for ourselves.

The four client libraries we publish are produced by a nightly job that runs the generator against the published description and opens a pull request when the output differs. Nobody writes client code by hand any more. The libraries used to be maintained separately by whoever cared about that language, which meant they were at four different levels of completeness, and the Ruby one lagged the interface by roughly a release and a half on average. Generated output is boring in a good way: every endpoint exists, the types match, and the diff in the pull request is a readable summary of what changed. What is not generated is the hand-written layer on top — retries, pagination helpers, the auth flow — which lives in a directory the generator does not touch and is the only part with its own tests. Release is still a human decision, because a generated change can be technically correct and a breaking change for anyone who upgrades without reading.

The documentation site is compiled to static files by a pipeline job and served from a bucket behind the CDN, with no application server anywhere in the path. It ran on a small dynamic service until an incident where the database was unreachable, the documentation went down with it, and the runbook link in our own status update pointed at a page that would not load. Documentation is the thing people reach for when everything else is broken, so it has to have the fewest possible dependencies, and a bucket with a CDN in front of it fails at roughly the same time as the internet. The build takes about ninety seconds and deploys on merge, which is fast enough that nobody has asked for a preview environment beyond the artefact the pipeline attaches. Nothing on the site reads from our own systems at request time, and a proposal to add a live status banner was declined on exactly that basis. Search is the only part that used to need a server, and moving it to a prebuilt index removed the last one.

Every machine-readable error string the interface can return is registered in `error_catalogue.yaml` with a stable code, a customer-facing sentence and a longer explanation, and the service refuses to start if it can raise a code that is not in the file. Support owns the wording. Engineering owns the codes. That split exists because the sentence a customer sees after a failed request is the single most-read piece of documentation we produce and it was being written in passing by whoever added the branch, in a rush, in engineering vocabulary. A code with no entry used to be common and produced tickets that support could do nothing with except escalate. Now the catalogue is published as part of the reference, the codes are guaranteed stable so integrators can branch on them, and rewording an unclear message is a change support can make and ship without an engineer, which they do a few times a month.

The narrative guides — as distinct from the generated reference — can be edited by anyone in support or solutions, and their changes need review from the documentation group rather than from engineering. Routing every wording fix through an engineering queue was the previous arrangement and it worked exactly as badly as you would expect: the people who read customer confusion all day, who know precisely which paragraph makes everyone ask the same question, had to file a request and wait behind feature work. Most of what they want to change is a sentence. Opening that up doubled the rate of small improvements and has not produced a single technically wrong statement, partly because the reference material they would be most likely to get wrong is generated and not editable at all. Anything that would change described behaviour rather than describe it better still goes to the owning team, and the review guidance says that is the line.

The endpoint reference and the how-to material are built and navigated as two separate things, cross-linked but never interleaved. They were one site originally, organised by topic, with reference sections sitting inside tutorials, and it satisfied nobody. Someone integrating for the first time wants a narrative that starts at the beginning and does not stop to enumerate every optional parameter. Someone who has been running against us for two years wants a dense list they can search, and finds the narrative infuriating. Merging them produced pages that were too long for the first reader and too chatty for the second. The split also matches how the two are maintained, since one is generated on every change and the other is written occasionally by hand, and mixing generated and hand-written content in a single page turned out to be a persistent source of confusion about which parts anyone was allowed to edit.

Search on the documentation site is a prebuilt Lucene-style index shipped as a static asset and queried in the browser, replacing the hosted widget we used before. Three things drove it. The crawler behind the hosted service indexed on its own schedule, so a freshly published page was unfindable for up to a day, and during an incident that gap is the entire useful lifetime of the page. It also sent every query a customer typed to a third party, which came up in a security review and had no good answer. And the crawler could not see anything behind our staging authentication, so the preview of a documentation change could never be searched. The index is built by the same job that builds the site and adds about four hundred kilobytes to the initial load, which is paid once and cached. Ranking is worse than the hosted product's, noticeably so for vague queries, and we took that trade knowingly.

We no longer publish a collection for the popular request client. Every endpoint page carries a copy-and-paste shell example instead. The collection had been maintained by hand, was perpetually a version behind, and the mismatch was worse than having nothing because a tool that fails silently against a stale definition sends an integrator hunting through their own code for a bug that is ours. Shell examples are also universal in a way a vendor format is not: they work for someone on a locked-down machine, they paste into a support ticket where an engineer can run them unchanged, and they can be read by a person who has never installed the tool in question. The complaint we get is from people who liked being able to import everything at once and click around, which is a real loss for exploration, and the answer offered is that the description document can be imported by that client directly and is always current because nobody maintains it by hand.

Documentation changes ship in the same pull request as the change that makes them necessary. There is no follow-up ticket option any more. The pipeline runs `tools/docs_impact.py`, which looks at the changed paths and, if anything under `api/handlers/`, `config/settings/` or `deploy/` was touched without a corresponding change under `docs/`, requires the author to add a `no-docs-needed` label with a one-line reason that lands in the pull request body. It is not a blocker you cannot get past — it is a question you have to answer in writing, which turns out to be enough. The follow-up ticket was the previous policy and we killed it after an audit: of forty-one tickets opened that year with the docs-follow-up label, eleven had been closed, and of the eleven, four were closed as no longer relevant because the feature had changed again in the meantime. The tickets were not a plan, they were a way of feeling better about not doing it. The other half of the argument is that the documentation is never as cheap to write as it is at the moment you finish the work, when you still remember which parameter combination is the confusing one and why the obvious approach does not work. A week later that is gone and you are reconstructing your own change from the diff. The rule costs perhaps ten minutes per pull request and it removed an entire category of stale page from the site.

A pull request whose diff touches nothing outside `docs/` and the site configuration runs a reduced pipeline: the documentation build, the link check and the spell check, and none of the service test suites. It takes about two minutes instead of fourteen. The path filter is evaluated against the merge result rather than the branch tip, so a pull request that adds a documentation change on top of code changes does not sneak through the short pipeline — that was the first version and it was wrong for exactly two days before someone noticed. The saving is not really about compute, it is about the behaviour a slow pipeline produces on trivial changes. When fixing a wrong sentence costs a quarter of an hour of waiting and a context switch, people stop fixing wrong sentences, and the documentation degrades one uncorrected paragraph at a time. Making the smallest useful contribution fast is the whole point.

The template has a field asking how this change is undone, and reviewers are told to treat an empty one as an unfinished pull request. Most of the time the honest answer is a single word — revert — and writing it takes no effort. The value is entirely in the cases where the author starts typing and discovers there is no good answer, because the change writes to a new column that the old code will not populate, or it consumes from a queue in a format the previous version cannot read, or it is a migration that cannot be reversed once traffic has touched it. Every one of those is a change that needs to be split or sequenced differently, and the cheapest moment to find that out is before it is written rather than during the incident where somebody wants it gone. Asking the question in the template rather than in review also puts it in front of the person who knows the answer, instead of relying on a reviewer to think of it.

Images used by a documentation page are committed under `docs/assets/` beside the page that references them, and the build fails on a reference to anything outside the tree. Half the diagrams and screenshots used to be hotlinked from a shared drive or an issue tracker attachment, which meant they disappeared when a folder was reorganised, they were invisible to anyone reading the source, and one of them turned out to have been shared with the whole company by accident rather than deliberately. There is a size check at two hundred kilobytes per file, which is generous for a screenshot and forces anyone committing something enormous to think about whether it needs to be a picture at all. Binary files in git are not free and people are right to be wary, but a documentation repository accumulates a few megabytes a year of them, which is nothing against the cost of a page whose illustration is a broken image icon.

The note that goes into the engineering channel on every deploy is generated from the titles of the pull requests in the range, grouped by the leading conventional-commit type and linked to the diff. Nobody writes it. This is the reason pull request titles are linted for the type prefix and rejected if they are the branch name, which reads as bureaucratic until you see the output of a week where the rule was not enforced and half the entries said fix. The generated note is not documentation and does not pretend to be — it is a lookup table for the question people actually ask during an incident, which is what went out in the last hour and which of those touched the thing that is now on fire. Nobody is expected to read it top to bottom, and it is deliberately kept to one message per deploy rather than one per merge. Anything needing explanation gets written somewhere a human will read it deliberately rather than being squeezed into a title, and the generator deliberately does not try to be clever about that.

Every screenshot in the documentation is captured at the same viewport width, in the light theme, with the same demo account, and with the browser chrome cropped out. It sounds fussy and it is the difference between a page that reads as a document and one that reads as a scrapbook. Mixed widths mean the reader cannot tell whether two images show the same screen at different times or two different screens; mixed themes make people wonder whether they are in the wrong mode; and a real account in the background of one image is how a customer name once ended up in a public guide. The demo account is also the reason the numbers in the images are plausible rather than being someone's local fixtures with rude test data in them. The convention is written down in the contributing guide with the exact settings, and the review expectation is that an image which does not match gets retaken rather than being waved through as close enough.

A change under `docs/` that only touches prose, does not add or remove a code block, and is under twenty changed lines can be merged by its author with no approval at all, enforced by a ruleset condition rather than by trust. The bar for review should be proportional to what a bad change can do, and the worst outcome here is a sentence that is briefly less clear and gets fixed by the next person. The previous arrangement had every documentation change waiting in the same queue as production code, and the observable effect was that people stopped opening pull requests for small corrections — they would mention the error in a channel, someone would say good catch, and nothing would happen. Removing the review step took the median time to correct a reported error from days to under an hour. Anything touching a command, a code sample or a configuration key falls outside the exemption, because those are the parts a reader will paste without thinking.

The convention for a commit body is that it explains the reason for the change and not its contents. The diff already says what happened, in more detail and with more accuracy than any summary of it, so a message restating the diff is a message that costs time to write and gives nothing back. What the diff cannot tell you is why the obvious simpler version does not work, which alternative was tried first, or which incident this is a response to. That is the material somebody wants when they run blame on a strange-looking line two years later, and it is almost always the material that has been left out. The guidance people find most useful is to write the paragraph you would want to read if you found this line and could not work out why anyone would do that. Reviewers are asked to push back on a body that could have been generated from the diff, which happens rarely enough now that it is a mild embarrassment rather than a routine comment.

The translated versions of the documentation are updated a release behind the English source, and each translated page carries a banner naming the version it corresponds to with a link to the current original. Trying to keep them in step was the first plan and it failed in the worst way — the translation queue became a merge blocker, so people either waited or shipped with a machine-translated placeholder that stayed in place for months and said something subtly wrong in a language none of us could check. A deliberate, visible lag is more honest than a pretence of parity. It also means the translators work from text that has settled, rather than from a paragraph that will be rewritten twice more before release, which was a real and reasonable complaint from the agency. Anything security-relevant or anything describing a destructive action is exempt and blocks release until it is translated, because those are the pages where being a version behind is not a cosmetic problem.

Architecture diagrams are text that a build step turns into pictures. The sources are `.d2` files under `docs/architecture/`, rendered to SVG by `make diagrams` in the documentation pipeline, and a pre-commit hook rejects any PNG or JPEG added under that directory so the drawn version cannot creep back in. The service-to-service edges are not written by hand at all: a generator reads the `depends_on` lists out of every repository's `service.yaml` and emits the graph, so a dependency that exists in the manifests appears on the picture and one that does not cannot be drawn. A hand-drawn diagram is a claim about the system made once, by one person, on the day they made it, and nothing afterwards ever contradicts it. The one that finally made the case showed a queue between two services that had been removed fourteen months earlier; a new engineer debugging a delivery problem spent most of a day looking for a consumer that did not exist, because the picture in the onboarding pack was more confident than the code. Generated sources also review properly — a diff on a text file shows exactly which edge moved, where a replaced image shows nothing at all — and they merge without anyone hunting for whoever has the editable original. The hand-drawn exception is anything speculative, which is not architecture documentation and does not live here.

The timeline picture in an incident write-up is drawn by whoever writes it, by hand, in whatever tool they like, and pasted in as an image. Nobody has to justify the choice. What that picture shows is a specific sequence on a specific afternoon — this retried while that was still draining, and the alert only fired after the third one — and there is no source of truth anywhere that could generate it, because it is an account of one particular ordering rather than a description of a structure. It is also finished the day it is written and never edited again, which removes the strongest argument for keeping things in a text format that diffs well. Asking people to express a one-off narrative in a diagram language would mean fewer diagrams, and in write-ups the picture is often the part that makes the sequence click for a reader who was not there. The one convention is that the image is committed alongside the write-up rather than linked from somewhere it can vanish.

Screen designs live in the design tool and that is deliberately not treated the same way as our system documentation. The file is the artefact designers work in, it holds the component states, the spacing, the behaviour annotations, and every attempt to mirror any of that into the repository has produced a second copy that disagrees with the first within a sprint. Engineers link to a frame rather than transcribing it. What we did have to fix was permanence: links used to point at a page that kept moving, so the convention now is a link to a named, versioned frame, and a screenshot of the agreed state is attached to the ticket so the record of what was actually built survives the file being reorganised. The boundary that matters is between what a design describes and what the code does. Once shipped, the code is the truth about behaviour, and a design file that no longer matches production is a historical document rather than a specification.

We keep one system context diagram and one container-level diagram per bounded area, and nothing below that. The component and code levels were tried for two quarters and abandoned. At that depth the picture changes with almost every merge, so either it is wrong most of the time or maintaining it becomes a tax on ordinary work, and neither is worth it when the code itself answers the same question more precisely and is guaranteed current. The levels we kept answer things the code cannot: which systems exist, who owns each one, what talks to what across a team boundary, and where the trust boundaries sit. Those change a few times a year. People asking for more depth are usually asking a question about one service, and the answer to that is its own repository rather than a picture of it. The rule of thumb written into the contributing guide is that a diagram is worth maintaining when the thing it describes changes more slowly than the diagram can be updated, and every level below container fails that test for us.

Every diagram embedded in a documentation page needs an alternative description, and the site build fails on an image element without one. The check has been in place since an accessibility audit, and the interesting part is that it improved the pages for everyone rather than only for readers using a screen reader. A useful alternative text is a sentence saying what the picture is meant to show, and being forced to write it exposes the diagrams that do not have a point — several were replaced with a paragraph once their author tried to summarise them and found the summary was shorter and clearer than the picture. The requirement is a description of the meaning rather than a transcription of the boxes, and the guidance gives examples of both so people stop writing lists of node names. Purely decorative images are permitted an empty attribute, and there is almost nothing in our documentation that qualifies.

A proposal document can contain a photograph of a whiteboard, and reviewers are asked not to comment on the format. Proposals are short-lived by design: they exist to get a decision, they are either accepted or they are not, and once the work is underway the proposal is a historical record rather than a description of anything. Demanding a polished picture in a document whose whole purpose is to be argued with adds an hour of work to the least valuable stage and, more importantly, discourages people from writing the proposal at all, which is the outcome we care about avoiding. The one rule is that a photograph never survives into the permanent documentation, so when a proposal is accepted, the parts of it that describe how the system now works have to be rewritten in the maintained form before the work is called finished. Keeping the two stages separate lets the early one be as scrappy as it needs to be.

The renderer runs from an image pinned by digest in `docs/Makefile`, and upgrading it is a deliberate pull request with the regenerated output attached. Layout engines are not deterministic across versions — a minor release nudges edge routing or changes a default font, and the result is that every diagram in the repository produces a diff the next time anyone runs the build, on a branch that has nothing to do with diagrams. That churn is not just noise, it hides the one diagram that genuinely changed. Pinning also means the pictures rendered on a laptop match the ones the pipeline produces, which stopped a recurring argument about whose output was correct. Nothing else in the documentation build is pinned this tightly, and the difference is that everything else produces text output whose diff means what it appears to mean. The upgrade pull request is reviewed by looking at the rendered images rather than the sources, since the point of it is to see what moved, and it happens perhaps twice a year.

Every node on a system diagram carries the name of the team that owns it, and a node with no owner is not allowed to be added. This started as a cosmetic suggestion and turned into one of the more useful conventions we have, because the ownership label is the thing people actually need from these pictures. Nobody opens an architecture diagram to admire the topology; they open it because something is broken or because they need to change something and want to know who to talk to first. Requiring the label also surfaces the awkward cases, which are the point. Twice now, adding a box has produced a genuinely difficult conversation about who owns a piece of infrastructure that everybody depends on and nobody had claimed, and both times that conversation was overdue and would not have happened otherwise. An unowned node in a proposal is fine and is expected to be resolved before the work lands.

A diagram source file sits in the same directory as the page that embeds it, not in a shared `diagrams/` folder at the top of the repository. We started with the shared folder because it felt tidier and it collected orphans within months — pictures nobody could match to a page, several near-duplicates of the same graph made by different people who could not tell what the existing ones showed, and a build that rendered eleven images for the four the site actually used. Colocation makes the relationship obvious to anyone reading the tree, makes deletion safe because moving a page takes its assets with it, and means a review diff shows the page change and the picture change side by side. The one genuinely shared diagram, the whole-system context, lives at the root of the architecture directory and is the exception that people cite when they want to make another one, which is why the guide says there is exactly one.

The onboarding pages are executable. Any fenced block tagged `verify` is extracted by `tools/docs_exec.py` and run top to bottom in a clean container by a scheduled job every Sunday night, in the same order a reader would run them, with no cached state and no credentials beyond the ones a new joiner is issued. A non-zero exit anywhere fails the run, opens a ticket against the page's owner with the failing block and the output, and posts the summary into the documentation channel. Roughly one run in five fails, which is the number that justifies the whole thing. On top of the executed blocks, every page carries a `verified_on` line in its front matter, the build warns when it is more than ninety days old, and a human reading the page end to end and confirming it still makes sense is what resets it — the job can prove a command still works and cannot tell you that step four now happens automatically and should be deleted. What prompted this was three people starting in the same week and losing most of a day each to a page that told them to set an environment variable which had been removed in a config refactor; the error it produced was unrelated and unhelpful, and each of them debugged it independently before anyone thought to ask. The rule that came out of it is that a documented instruction nobody executes is a claim nobody has checked.

Every page in the onboarding set names a single person as its owner, not a team and not a group alias. This was argued about, because naming an individual creates an obvious problem when they leave, and the counter-argument won on the evidence: pages owned by a team were owned by nobody. A question raised against a group alias sat until someone felt guilty enough to pick it up, which was usually never, whereas a question addressed to a person gets answered or explicitly handed on. Departures are handled by a check that fails the build when an owner is no longer in the directory, which forces a reassignment as part of the leaving process rather than leaving an orphan behind. The owner is not expected to write the page or to be the expert on everything in it; the responsibility is narrower and more realistic, which is to make sure a reported problem with the page results in either a fix or a decision to delete it.

Every new engineer is assigned a buddy from a different team than their own for their first few weeks, with a standing short call every morning that they can cancel whenever they stop needing it. The different-team part is the deliberate bit: their own team will teach them the work, and the buddy exists for the questions people are reluctant to ask a colleague they are trying to impress. What that call catches is the material no document can hold — which channel a particular kind of question actually gets answered in, who to ask about the thing that is nominally owned by a team that no longer exists, and whether the anxious feeling about a piece of code is a misunderstanding or a well-known piece of ugliness everyone shares. Written guidance is better than folklore for anything that can be written down, and a large part of what makes an organisation navigable in the first month genuinely cannot be, which is the gap the buddy fills.

A new starter gets a ticket created from the `onboarding-week-one` template with a subtask for each administrative item — payroll forms, badge, laptop encryption enrolment, the security training module, the introduction to the team's rituals — each with an assignee who is not the new person. It used to be a page with checkboxes, which had the failure mode that a page cannot chase anybody. Items that depended on someone else silently stalled, and the new joiner had no way of telling whether waiting was expected. As tickets they show up in the assignee's queue, they age visibly, and the manager can see what is outstanding without asking. Nothing technical is tracked here at all, deliberately, since that material has its own home and its own owner. The template is edited a few times a year, most often to remove a step that has been automated away, and the removal is done at the moment the automation lands rather than being noticed later by the next person to use it.

All the access a new engineer needs is requested in a single ticket derived from a role profile, approved once by their manager, and granted by a script that reads the profile and applies the group memberships. Nine separate requests to nine owners was the old way, and the effect was that people arrived, discovered a missing permission at the moment they needed it, and asked in a channel, which produced grants that were quick, undocumented and usually broader than necessary. Batching them makes the access review meaningful too, because a role profile is a list somebody can look at and challenge, where a scatter of individually approved exceptions is not. The profiles are deliberately minimal and it is expected that a few extra grants will be needed in the first month; those go through the normal request path with a reason, and any grant that turns up in three consecutive months of exceptions gets folded into the profile.

The internal documentation site collects no per-user analytics. The tracking script was removed and the access logs are aggregated to a daily count per path with no identifier attached, retained for thirty days. Two reasons, in order of weight. The first is that a record of exactly which pages an individual employee read and when is a surveillance dataset that we would then have to protect, justify and eventually hand over in some situation nobody has anticipated, and there is no use for it that comes close to that cost. The second is that the metric was misleading anyway: the most-read pages are the ones people cannot remember, which is a sign of a bad page rather than a good one, and we caught ourselves briefly treating traffic as a quality signal. The aggregate counts survive because they answer one narrow, useful question, which is whether a page anybody links to still exists, and that question needs no names attached.

Every page on the documentation site has an edit link in the footer pointing at the exact source file in the repository, generated by the site build from the page's path so it cannot go stale. It is the single highest-return thing we have added to the site. The distance between noticing a mistake and being able to fix it is what determines whether the fix happens, and before the link that distance was: work out which repository the site is built from, find the file among several hundred, hope the directory structure matches the navigation, which it does not. Most people gave up somewhere in the middle. The link opens the file directly in the web editor, so a one-word correction is three clicks and a pull request. The same footer shows when the file was last changed and by whom, pulled from the commit history at build time. A meaningful share of documentation contributions now come from people outside engineering, which never happened before, and the review load that produced has been trivial.

The recorded walkthroughs were retired and the remaining ones are marked as archived with a warning that they show an older version of the product. Video looked attractive because it is quick to produce and shows a workflow the way it actually feels, and it turned out to be the most perishable format we have. A written step that has changed can be corrected in a sentence by anyone who notices; a recorded one requires re-recording the whole segment, so nobody does, and the video keeps confidently showing a screen that no longer exists. Video is also unsearchable, cannot be skimmed by someone who needs one detail, and cannot be copied from by someone who needs to type a command. The one place recording survived is culture and orientation material, which does not go out of date at the same rate and which nobody needs to search, and even there the practical instructions were pulled out into a written page beside it.

There is one onboarding path per role rather than one per team, so every backend engineer reads the same material regardless of which group they joined, with a short team-specific appendix on top. Per-team guides were what grew naturally and the duplication was substantial — the same explanation of the deployment pipeline written five times, in five states of accuracy, and a new joiner's experience depending on which team happened to have someone conscientious that year. Consolidating meant an argument about whose version was right, which was uncomfortable and worth having, since three of the five were describing behaviour that had changed. The appendix is deliberately capped at a short page and reviewers push back when it grows, because anything long enough to matter is usually something every team needs and belongs in the shared path, where far more people will notice when it goes wrong.
